title: UCSF, Notre Dame or Emory: which winter research field fits you?
excerpt: Pharmaceutical chemistry with UCSF's Jason Sello, foreign policy with Notre Dame's Sebastian Rosato, or math and economics with Emory's David McMillon: how to match a broad interest to the right winter field.
content:
Three professors, from UCSF, Notre Dame and Emory, are teaching the 2026 Winter Online Research Program. That doesn't mean their students get the same experience. A student drawn to biology and medicine, one who wants to dig into international conflict and foreign policy, and one who wants to take math and engineering into economic and social problems can't all be doing the same research.

Good research takes more than picking a famous professor. The first question is how a student's interests line up with a professor's field. Here is what each of the three studies, and the kind of student each field tends to suit.

![A student seen from behind at a desk with a DNA model and lab glassware on one side, a globe and flags in the middle, and a laptop showing charts on the other](/editorial/224418816555-01.jpg "Illustration: the three winter research paths, from life sciences to international relations to quantitative social science")

## Life sciences, chemistry and pharmacy: Jason Sello, UCSF

Jason Sello is a professor of pharmaceutical chemistry at the UCSF School of Pharmacy. His research covers the discovery, design and synthesis of bioactive molecules, and the mechanisms by which drugs act.

"I'm interested in medicine" is not yet a research topic. To get there, a student has to narrow the scope to something concrete: how a particular disease develops, how a specific molecule behaves in a living system, or how a drug candidate is designed. This direction works well for students who want to bring chemical questions to what they already know about biology.

A good fit if you:

- are considering a major in the life sciences, chemistry or pharmacy
- want to know how drugs work or what drives a disease
- enjoy tracking down scientific evidence and analyzing data

## International relations, political science and foreign policy: Sebastian Rosato, Notre Dame

Sebastian Rosato, a professor of political science at Notre Dame, studies international relations theory, great-power competition and foreign policy. With the international relations scholar John Mearsheimer, he co-wrote *How States Think: The Rationality of Foreign Policy*, a book that examines how states reach their foreign-policy decisions.

Plenty of students follow world affairs, but an opinion is not research. Instead of stopping at "this country made the wrong choice," students in this field use theory and case studies to work out how a state judged its rival's intentions, and why it chose conflict or cooperation.

It suits students who want to turn an international conflict they first met in the news into a research question that can be tested, not just argued.

A good fit if you:

- are considering international relations, political science or history
- care about conflict and cooperation between states, and about foreign policy
- want to apply theory to real-world cases

## Math, engineering, economics and public policy: David McMillon, Emory

David McMillon, of Emory's economics department, earned master's degrees in applied and interdisciplinary mathematics and in industrial and operations engineering before completing a PhD in public policy at the University of Chicago. Today he researches the economics of education, economic inequality and intergenerational mobility.

What sets this path apart is that it cuts across the usual divide between STEM and the social sciences. The quantitative habits of math and engineering become tools for studying social problems, such as how differences in educational opportunity affect a person's economic opportunities.

For students who want to carry their STEM skills into research on economics, education and social policy, this is an especially interesting direction.

A good fit if you:

- are considering math, engineering, economics or public policy
- want to analyze social problems with numbers and data
- want to extend your STEM strengths into social-science questions

## No topic yet? Start with what you're curious about

You don't need a finished paper topic before the program starts. Begin by listing the subjects you enjoy, the topics you keep reading about on your own, and the questions from class you wanted to take further. Then, in meetings with the professor, you narrow that down to a question you can actually investigate within ten class days. The examples in each field above show what that narrowing looks like.

The full path from interest to paper looks like this:

1. A field of interest
2. A problem you're curious about
3. A question research can answer
4. A design for the data and methods
5. A draft, revised with feedback
6. A final research paper in English

You don't need prior research experience. You do need to be ready to revise your writing again and again in response to feedback, and to give the research real focus over the winter break.

![Overhead view of a wooden desk with a question-mark sketch and travel photos on the left, a printed draft, a marked-up draft with a pen, and a bound final paper on the right](/editorial/224418816555-06.jpg "Illustration: from a first question to a marked-up draft to a finished paper")

## The 2026 winter program at a glance

- **Dates:** December 19–30, 2026, with no class on December 24 and 25
- **Format:** live online classes, capped at five students
- **Who can join:** high school and college students
- **Language:** taught in English, with the paper written in English
- **Mentoring:** 10 hours with the professor and 31 hours of TA support

Still deciding between the life sciences, foreign policy and economics? Share your grade, the major you're considering, your favorite subjects and any research you've done, and CRI admissions will suggest the fields open to you and walk you through the schedule. Full program details are on the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter) page.
author: CRI Editorial

title: The 2026 Winter Online Research Program: ten days from question to finished paper
excerpt: Professors from UCSF, Notre Dame and Emory lead this December's live online program. See who teaches, how ten class days turn a question into an English paper, and who it suits.
content:
Ten class days, one research question, one finished paper. From December 19 to 30, 2026, CRI's Winter Online Research Program meets live online with professors from UCSF, Notre Dame and Emory. Students begin with their own interests, sharpen them into a research question with their professor, and work toward a complete research paper in English, revised through feedback from the professor and a TA.

## A ketamine project and a Harvard admission

A past CRI student who researched with Professor Jason Sello of UCSF, one of this winter's faculty, was admitted to Harvard. The project looked at ketamine's uses as an anesthetic and an antidepressant, then asked whether the drug might also treat irritability in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Working from the way ketamine blocks NMDA receptors, the student explored its potential for drug repurposing. Starting from a broad interest, the student narrowed it to a specific question and, with feedback from the professor and TA, finished an English research paper. Read the full story on the [Student Success](/success/harvard-admit-ketamine-drug-repurposing-research) page.

No single experience decides a college admission; colleges weigh academics, activities, essays and more together. What research can do is show a student's academic direction in concrete terms, especially when the student can explain why the topic mattered to them, what they investigated, and which conclusions they changed after feedback. Other CRI students from 2025 also received offers from Harvard, Princeton, Stanford, Penn, Duke, Johns Hopkins, Columbia and the University of Chicago, among others.

## This winter's faculty

This year's program brings together three professors with very different academic backgrounds.

### Life sciences and pharmacy: Jason Sello, UCSF

Jason Sello is a professor of pharmaceutical chemistry at the UCSF School of Pharmacy. His research covers the discovery, design and synthesis of bioactive molecules, and how drugs produce their effects. Students drawn to biology, chemistry or pharmacy can use his course to turn a general interest in medicine into precise questions about molecules, drugs and disease mechanisms.

### International relations and foreign policy: Sebastian Rosato, Notre Dame

Sebastian Rosato is a professor of political science at the University of Notre Dame who studies international relations theory. With John Mearsheimer, he co-wrote *How States Think: The Rationality of Foreign Policy*, an analysis of how states make foreign-policy judgments. In his course, students move past personal opinions about international conflicts. Using theory and case studies, they analyze how states read one another's intentions, and why they end up in conflict or cooperation.

### Economics and quantitative social science: David McMillon, Emory

David McMillon is a professor of economics at Emory University whose research covers the economics of education, economic inequality and intergenerational mobility. He holds master's degrees in applied and interdisciplinary mathematics and in industrial and operations engineering from the University of Michigan, and a PhD in public policy from the University of Chicago. His course suits students who want to bring mathematical or engineering thinking to problems in education, economics and social policy.

![Portrait photos of three professors side by side](/editorial/224416201552-02.jpg "From left: Jason Sello (UCSF), Sebastian Rosato (Notre Dame) and David McMillon (Emory)")

## Ten class days, from question to paper

Professors do not hand out topics for students to follow. Each student starts from an interest of their own and works through four stages with the professor, drafting and revising along the way:

1. Discuss interests and settle on a research question and its scope.
2. Choose the sources and data, and design the analytical methods, that will answer that question.
3. Write a draft in English and revise it using feedback from the professor and TA.
4. Strengthen the argument and evidence, and complete the final research paper in English.

Each class day runs four to five hours, and students need extra time outside class to read, write and revise. The program is built for students who want to stay with one question all the way to the end, not for those looking to sample a short hands-on activity.

![A December 2026 calendar with December 19 to 23 and 26 to 30 highlighted as class days and December 24 and 25 marked as no class](/editorial/224416201552-05.jpg "The ten class days of the 2026 winter program, with a break on December 24 and 25")

## New to research? Start with a question

Students do not need a finished research topic before the program begins. They can start from a field they care about or a question they want to explore, and shape a direction in meetings with their professor.

![A three-panel still life: a molecular model and lab glassware, a globe over a world map, and bar charts beside a calculator](/editorial/224416201552-04.jpg "This winter's three fields: life sciences and pharmacy, international relations, and economics")

Just as important as prior experience are a few habits: the patience to stay with a question, the follow-through to act on feedback, and a readiness to read, write and revise in English. The program is a poor fit, though, for a student who wants quick, ready-made answers or mainly hopes to add one more short activity to their record.

## Dates and details

| Item | Details |
|---|---|
| Dates | December 19–30, 2026 |
| No class | December 24 and 25 |
| Format | Live online classes in small groups |
| Open to | High school and university students |
| Language | English, for both classes and the paper |
| Goal | A finished research paper in English by December 30 |
| Recommendation letter | Written by the professor for students who earn a B+ or higher; taking part alone does not earn one |

The work continues after the final class. Once the paper is finished, CRI supports students through submission to an academic journal, at no additional cost.

## What past winter courses looked like

CRI's 2025 winter program also ran online, on Zoom, in small groups. Students were placed with a professor based on the intended major and research interests they described in their application, and each group met its professor for an orientation about two weeks before classes began to talk through ideas and set a research direction. That year's faculty, with examples of paper topics from their earlier CRI groups:

- **William Burke-White, University of Pennsylvania** (international politics and law): how international law applies to the war in Ukraine; conflicts between climate change and human rights
- **Brian Stoltz, Caltech** (organic synthesis and drug discovery): structural analysis of natural anticancer compounds; the environmental impact of chemical synthesis, from a green-chemistry perspective
- **Aziz Aboobaker, University of Oxford** (genetics and stem cells): genes involved in regeneration and aging; the mechanisms that regulate stem-cell differentiation
- **Haifeng Xu, University of Chicago** (AI and data science): fairness and accountability in AI; privacy-preserving data analysis

## Finding the right fit

If you have done research with CRI before, tell the admissions team about that project and what you want to explore this winter. If you are new to CRI, share your grade, intended major and any research experience, and the team will explain which fields and class formats fit and how the schedule works. The point of that first conversation is to check, together, whether a student is ready to research and finish a paper in English over a short winter break. Applications for the 2026 cohort are accepted in two rounds, and current dates and details are on the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter) page.
author: CRI Editorial

title: What is CRI? How student research grows into projects, competitions and startups
excerpt: At CRI, a student and a professor turn an interest into a research question and see it through to a finished paper. Here is why that paper is a process rather than the goal, and how it can lead to a competition, a service or a startup.
content:
Most people who come across CRI think of it as a student research program. That's fair: nearly everything it does begins with research, as a student and a university professor shape a question and work it through to a finished paper. The paper, though, is rarely meant to be the last step.

CRI's best-known program, the Seoul Research Program (SRP), works this way: students meet professors who guide them through their papers. It grew out of a wish to give students in Korea the kind of deep research experience that the Research Science Institute (RSI) at MIT offers in the United States.

The larger aim is for students to research something they genuinely love, then take the results further. The next step might be a published paper, a competition entry, a service the student builds or, if the idea has real promise, a startup. That's why "research program" never quite covers it. One student's love of basketball shows what that can look like.

## It started with a love of basketball

One student CRI worked with recently was a devoted basketball fan who could also code a little. There was no grand plan. This wasn't someone who arrived saying "I want to do AI research" or "I want to write a paper and enter competitions."

So CRI tried connecting basketball and code: what if AI could predict who wins a game?

![Illustration of a student in a gray hoodie taking notes at a desk beside a basketball and a laptop showing charts](/editorial/224388364206-01.jpg "Illustration: the starting point was nothing more than basketball and a little coding.")

That question became the research. The student collected game data, weighed which variables to use, and built machine-learning models to predict wins and losses. Comparing the models' performance and analyzing the results shaped the work into a study, then a finished paper, which was published in a journal.

In the past, the program might have ended there. Instead, the finished paper raised a new question: what if real people could use this algorithm? So the student built a website, and the website raised another question: does any company actually need this? The student and CRI are now working out whether it could be offered as a B2B service to sports businesses and companies that work with data.

One interest carried this student from basketball to AI research, then to a paper, a website and a possible business. That kind of path is much closer to what CRI is meant to be.

## Why research comes first

Why start with research at all? Going straight to building a service or entering a competition might seem faster.

Many projects with students have taught CRI that building something well means first understanding a field deeply, and caring about it. You need to know:

- what the real problems are
- which methods people already use
- where those methods fall short
- whether your own idea actually matters

Research is one of the best ways to find out. That's why, at CRI, **a paper is a process, not the goal**. Students don't do research just to produce a paper. As they work, they come to understand the field far more deeply, and from inside it they begin to see what to do next. It's also why CRI calls its approach research-based education.

## Not every student needs a startup

Some students, like the basketball fan, take their work all the way to a business idea. No one has to. What makes sense after research depends on what the student discovers along the way:

- **Enjoy the academic side?** Develop the paper further and take it to a journal or a conference.
- **Found a strong idea in the research?** Enter a competition with it.
- **Have an idea that can be built?** Create a program or a website.
- **Care about a social issue?** A project or campaign may be the better fit.

That's also why there is no single program for every student, and no path designed in advance and sold as a package. What should follow the research differs from student to student. The point is not to fix an impressive outcome at the start, but to take one step at a time until the next one comes naturally into view.

## "I don't know what to research" is a fine place to start

In consultations, CRI hears one line again and again: "I know what I'm interested in, but I don't have a research topic." Nothing about that is unusual. Very few students arrive with a specific research question in hand.

A student might love basketball or movies, follow the stock market, or keep reading about environmental problems. That is enough to begin. The real work, done together, is finding a question inside that interest.

For a basketball fan, that doesn't mean gathering facts about basketball. It means turning the interest into questions that can be tested, such as "Which data actually influence the outcome of a game?" or "How well can AI predict the result?" That is the moment an interest becomes research.

![Illustration of three students in conversation around a table with a laptop, a tablet and notebooks](/editorial/224388364206-04.jpg "Illustration: turning a broad interest into a question that can be tested.")

## The professor's job isn't to hand out answers

CRI runs its programs with professors from a range of universities. Institutions and careers matter, of course, but in practice what counts most is the role a professor plays in a student's research.

Good research never comes together in a single pass. A question that is too broad has to be narrowed. A method that doesn't fit has to be redesigned. Thin evidence means more digging, and a flawed argument means rewriting.

The professor isn't there to produce the right answer for the student, but to keep holding the work to a clear standard throughout that process. That's why feedback and revision are so central to the programs. From the student's side it can be tedious, even hard. But working through it is what makes the research the student's own.

![Illustration of a mentor gesturing toward a laptop as a student in glasses studies the screen, with sketches pinned to the wall behind them](/editorial/224388364206-03.jpg "Illustration: rounds of feedback and revision turn a project into the student's own work.")

## Why the paper isn't the end

This is the question CRI keeps coming back to. A student spends months on research and completes a paper. Is that really the right place to stop?

Along the way, the student may have built a dataset or an algorithm, or come up with a new idea. If any of it can be put to use, building something with it is far more rewarding. Research worth putting before outside reviewers can go to a competition or a conference. An idea with commercial promise invites harder questions: who the customer is, and whether people would have a real reason to pay for it.

So CRI no longer offers only research programs. It is also building the tracks students need for the next step: competitions, projects, website building and startups. These tracks are less separate products than stages of one connected process.

![Illustration of a student talking with two mentors at a table beneath a whiteboard that maps Idea, Research, Build, Test and B2B](/editorial/224388364206-05.jpg "Illustration: a paper can be one stage of a longer path, from idea and research to building, testing and a business.")

## So what is CRI?

Asked to describe itself in one sentence, CRI puts it this way: **an educational organization that develops a student's interest into research, then carries that research into real projects and challenges.**

For one student, the next step is publishing the paper; for another, a competition; for a third, a website or a product. Where there is real potential, it may even be a startup.

No one can know at the outset how far a student will go, and it's better not to decide in advance. The experience CRI wants to create is simple: dig a little deeper into something you love, turn it into a question, research it yourself, and carry what you find into the next step. Interest into research, and research into reality: that is the path it builds, together with its students.

If you have an interest but no question yet, that is exactly where this work begins. You can [explore the research programs](/research) to see the formats and cohorts currently open.
author: CRI Editorial

title: How much of a research paper can a high school student finish in 10 days?
excerpt: Follow one Seoul Research Program student from a broad interest in music and the brain to a full draft, a research poster, and a revised manuscript for the professor.
content:
Can a student really write a research paper in 10 days? It's one of the questions families ask most often in Seoul Research Program consultations, and a fair one. Choosing a topic and reading the relevant literature sounds like a lot of work on its own, so a whole paper in that time can be hard to picture.

Here is what actually happens. Students don't stop at picking a topic and sketching an outline. Over 10 days they sharpen a research question, analyze prior studies, and write the substance of each part of the paper themselves: the central argument, the methods, the limitations, and directions for future work. By the end of the program, a draft with the paper's full structure and main content is largely in place. They then spend about a week revising with specific feedback from a TA before submitting the finished manuscript to their professor.

One student, who arrived interested in music and neurological disease, shows how that plays out.

## A broad interest, narrowed down

The student came in curious about music, music therapy, and neurological disorders, but without a research question. "How does music affect the brain?" is an interesting topic. It is also far too broad for a single paper.

With feedback from the professor and a TA, the student stopped treating music as one undifferentiated stimulus and began looking at its individual elements: rhythm, timbre, and tonality. Reading the literature then suggested that each element might connect to a different biological pathway, such as neuroplasticity, gene regulation, or changes in brainwave activity.

That led to a much sharper question:

**How do the individual acoustic elements of music affect the biological mechanisms associated with Alzheimer's disease?**

A loose curiosity had become a question that spelled out what to analyze and which relationships to examine.

![Illustration of a student and a mentor seated at a table, the mentor pointing to printed notes beside a laptop showing a brain graphic and sound waveforms](/editorial/224362791165-03.jpg "Illustration: refining a research question with feedback from a mentor.")

## From reading papers to building an argument

With the question set, the student searched the academic literature and broke down each study's aims, methods, main findings, and limitations. Preparing presentations along the way meant putting complex research into the student's own words.

The next step went beyond summary. The student grouped scattered findings by theme (rhythm and neuroplasticity, timbre and brainwave changes, music and gene regulation) and compared how the themes related to one another.

Out of that sorting came the student's own analytical framework, a chain that runs **from an individual musical element, to a biological pathway, to an Alzheimer's-related change**. As material from many papers was rebuilt around a single question, the core logic of the paper's main body began to take shape.

## Planning how the question could be tested

Organizing existing research was not the end point. To show how the question could lead to an actual study, the student worked out how individual elements of music might be measured and compared.

That meant considering frequency analysis to separate the acoustic features of a piece of music, and methods for tracking brainwave changes over time. The student also weighed factors that could affect the results, including differences in people's musical experience and the gap between animal studies and human studies.

As a result, the project moved past the familiar claim that music might help with Alzheimer's. It asked which musical features might act through which biological pathways, and how that could be tested in future research.

## What was finished by day 10

In the final days of the program, everything was pulled into the shape of a paper, with the research question at the center. The draft also weighed the limitations of existing studies and where future research should go. Rather than listing only the evidence that favored the argument, the student set out what the research still cannot answer.

By the last day, the student had far more than a topic and a table of contents:

- a focused research question on musical elements and Alzheimer's-related mechanisms
- background and a literature review organized around that question
- an analytical framework linking musical elements, biological pathways, and Alzheimer's-related changes
- proposed ways to measure those elements, and the factors that could skew results
- a section on limitations and future research
- a full manuscript draft that carries the argument from start to finish
- a research poster presenting the question, background, core analysis, limitations, future directions, and conclusion as a single structure

![Illustration of a student reading a printed draft at a desk in front of a large illustrated research poster](/editorial/224362791165-04.jpg "Illustration: pulling the draft and poster together in the final days.")

## The week after: revising with a TA

The writing didn't end when the 10 days did. Over roughly a week, guided by TA feedback, the student tightened the logic between paragraphs, added prior studies where the evidence was thin, and cleaned up academic phrasing and citation format.

This stage wasn't about producing new material from scratch. It turned a complete draft into a clearer, more persuasive manuscript. CRI's TAs gave specific guidance so that the student could test and revise their own claims and evidence.

Once the revisions were done, the final manuscript went to the supervising professor. The program, in other words, doesn't end with 10 days of class. It continues until the student's draft becomes a finished paper.

![Illustration of a student and a mentor reviewing a printed manuscript together at a table, with a research poster on an easel behind them](/editorial/224362791165-05.jpg "Illustration: a week of TA feedback turns the draft into a final manuscript.")

## Why 10 days was enough

The speed didn't come from cramming the writing into fewer days. Setting the question, searching the literature, analyzing prior studies, building the core argument, and drafting the manuscript were each tied to daily assignments, one leading directly into the next.

Each person had a clear role:

| Who | What they did |
| --- | --- |
| Professor | Checked the direction of the research and whether the question was well framed |
| TA | Tracked the student's progress and pointed out exactly what to strengthen at the next step |
| Student | Worked the feedback in every day and built the research up stage by stage |

The work moved fast not because anyone wrote the paper for the student, but because systematic guidance made sure the student carried out every stage of the research, without skipping a step.

## So, can a paper be finished in 10 days?

The draft, yes. This student started with a wide interest in music and neurological disease and left the program with a full manuscript draft, built on a clear question and analytical framework, plus a research poster. The finished paper took about one more week: after revisions based on feedback, it went to the professor.

The point of the Seoul Research Program isn't a quick paper produced for form's sake. Its aim is for students to go through the whole process themselves: turning an interest into an academic question, finding the evidence, and completing a logically argued piece of research. To see how the program's courses, faculty, and TA support are organized, start with the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Is a longer research program better? 10 intensive days vs. 10 weeks online
excerpt: Weeks on a calendar matter less than hours with a mentor. See how the Seoul Research Program's 50 in-person hours over ten days compare with a typical ten-week online program.
content:
When families compare research programs, one question comes up again and again: "It's a research paper. Won't a longer program produce a better one?" Ten weeks sounds more serious than ten days. Yet the idea behind a hackathon points the other way: a few days of complete focus can accomplish more than months of stop-and-start effort. The Seoul Research Program (SRP) is built on that idea.

## Ten weeks online vs. ten days in Seoul

A common online format pairs a student with a mentor for about an hour a week over ten weeks. Across the whole program, that typically comes to about 10 to 15 hours of guidance, spread over two and a half months.

SRP compresses the work instead of stretching it. For ten days in Seoul, students set their other commitments aside and concentrate on a single paper: 30 hours of instruction with their professor and 20 hours with TAs from master's and doctoral programs at leading universities. That is 50 hours in all, three to four times the total mentoring in a typical ten-week online program, and all of it in person.

A college credit hour is a useful yardstick. One credit represents about 15 to 16 hours of class time, so a three-credit course comes to roughly 45 to 48 hours. Students routinely ask the professor of a single three-credit course for a graduate school recommendation, even when they shared that class with as many as 100 classmates. SRP's 50 hours go to a class that averages five or six students.

|  | Typical 10-week online program | Seoul Research Program |
|---|---|---|
| Length | 10 weeks | 10 days |
| Format | Video calls, about 1 hour a week | In person in Seoul |
| Total mentoring time | About 10–15 hours | 50 hours: 30 with the professor, 20 with TAs |
| When a student gets stuck | The question waits for next week's call | Worked through with the professor on the spot |
| Basis for a recommendation letter | Roughly 10–15 hours of contact | About 50 hours of direct observation |

## A tighter feedback loop

Weekly video calls work like a stop-and-go commute. A student who hits a problem between meetings has to wait until the next session, and the project sits idle in the meantime.

Ten days in the same room are closer to an open highway. When a draft stalls, the student can take it straight to the professor, talk it through and correct course right away. That continuous cycle of writing, questioning and revising is what gives an intensive program both its speed and its depth.

## Teaching research is its own skill

Writing a strong paper and teaching a high school student to write one are two different abilities. A student with no research background needs a mentor who can build academic thinking from the ground up, which takes teaching insight on top of subject expertise.

That is the standard SRP sets for its faculty. Every professor is named publicly, and each is an experienced university teacher who has mentored many students. Rather than setting the direction and working out the analysis on a student's behalf, they ask pointed questions that make students reason through the research themselves, and they hold high school students to a demanding standard. Research questions start from the students' own interests and take their final shape in discussion with the professor.

## A paper students can explain and defend

A research paper on a college application invites questions. Why this topic? How did you analyze the data? Why did you control for that particular variable? The paper is only worth as much as the student's ability to answer.

Fifty hours of working through the reasoning with a professor and TAs is what makes those answers the student's own. Students come away understanding why they chose their topic and how they handled their data, well enough to explain and defend the work with confidence, even when a demanding interviewer presses them on the details.

## A letter grounded in 50 hours of observation

The same hours shape the recommendation letter. US admissions officers read tens of thousands of letters every year, and a line like "this student is diligent and bright" carries little weight on its own. What stands out is specific evidence.

After ten days of working alongside a student, an SRP professor can supply exactly that: where the research ran into a limit and how the student got past it, and what insight the student found in the data on their own. It is a letter written from direct observation of how the student thinks and grows.

## Support after the ten days

The work does not stop when the manuscript is finished. CRI continues to support each paper through journal submission and the publication process, with no fixed cap on mentoring hours. In the 2026 program, journal submission costs are included, so families do not face separate charges at that stage.

## Measured in hours, not weeks

A first research paper is shaped by the hours a student spends thinking alongside an expert, not by how many weeks the program spans. Ten weeks can look more substantial, but what a student takes away depends on how deeply they worked and how well they understand their own research by the end. The goal is a student who can sit across from a skeptical interviewer and explain their research clearly because they built it.

To see how the ten days are organized and who teaches, explore the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Building wearable health sensors with Northwestern professor Nabil Alshurafa
excerpt: How Northwestern's Nabil Alshurafa guides students to build ECG, PPG and motion-sensor prototypes, turn their own questions into hypotheses, and defend a research poster in ten days.
content:
Plenty of students headed for pre-med, computer science, or bioengineering can point to a health-monitoring app they built after a summer coding class. Far fewer have assembled a sensor, fought its signal noise, and watched it read a live heartbeat. That second kind of work is the focus of Northwestern University professor Nabil Alshurafa's track in CRI's Seoul Research Program: ten days of building wearable health sensors, collecting real physiological data, and turning students' own questions into a group research paper.

## Why the course starts with hardware

Applications from aspiring doctors and engineers tend to look alike. Students memorize disease mechanisms for biology class, then use the coding they already know to build a generic health app for a research report. Many sense the limits of that work: an app that only runs on a screen rarely comes close to preventing a real illness.

What top US universities and medical schools look for, in CRI's view, is intellectual vitality: students who connect the body's signals and behavior to hardware sensors, think through a system that could predict disease, and ask their own questions. The course is built to develop exactly that habit of mind.

## Who teaches it

Nabil Alshurafa earned his bachelor's, master's, and PhD at UCLA, studying computer science and artificial intelligence. He is a tenured associate professor at Northwestern, with appointments in Preventive Medicine at the Feinberg School of Medicine and in Computer Science and Electrical and Computer Engineering at the McCormick School of Engineering. He is also a Senior Member of the IEEE.

- **Wearables.** He has won several million dollars in research funding from the National Institutes of Health and leads large projects funded by the NIH and the National Science Foundation as principal investigator. He builds devices such as FaceBit, a smart face mask, and NeckSense, a necklace that tracks eating habits.
- **Behavior prediction.** His HABits Lab develops AI-based systems that use wearable sensor data to measure and predict behaviors such as stress, overeating, and poor posture.
- **Publications.** His research has appeared in leading journals and conferences, including *npj Digital Medicine*, ACM IMWUT, and IEEE BSN.

His students' track record speaks to his mentoring. The HABits Lab takes questions from undergraduates and interns as seriously as those from graduate students and develops them into papers and working devices. Students he has mentored have gone on to Northwestern's Feinberg School of Medicine, been recruited by the US National Security Agency, and founded healthcare startups of their own. Students who worry that their coding or questions are too basic will find a professor who knows how far a rough idea can go.

## Ten days as a junior researcher

For the length of the course, students work as the newest members of the lab. They build hardware prototypes and study how physiological data such as ECG (electrocardiography), PPG (photoplethysmography, which uses light to track blood flow), and stress-related signals arise in the body and how sensors capture them. Signal noise and hardware constraints can be frustrating at first. A few days in, the sensor system students assembled themselves is reading live biological data.

The larger aim is to understand mobile health (mHealth) as a system in which hardware, biological signals, and human behavior connect.

| Stage | What students do |
| --- | --- |
| Days 2–3 | Learn how wearable health sensors (ECG, PPG, motion) work and design their own hardware prototypes |
| Days 4–5 | Track physiological markers of stress, cardiovascular health, and metabolic health, and build a framework for turning them into sensor-based interventions |
| Day 7 | Analyze the collected data, connect it to patterns of behavior, and draw out meaningful health insights |
| Day 10 | Present and defend an academic poster of the group paper |

From there the course turns to preventive medicine: how could this data lead to preventive solutions for metabolic and cardiovascular disease? Students wear smartwatches and other devices to gather their own data and explore how stress, posture, caffeine, and exercise show up in their biosignals. Core topics include:

- Measuring stress, posture, sleep, and eating with wearable sensors, including heart rate variability (HRV) and galvanic skin response (GSR)
- Visualizing and statistically analyzing the data
- Designing machine-learning algorithms that predict behavior
- Team-based research design, experiments, paper writing, and poster presentation

Students also learn the basics of scientific writing and of institutional review boards (IRBs), design experiments with human participants, and practice handling medical and health data.

![Professor Alshurafa sits with three students in front of a projected slide listing study design, skeletal tracking, and an inertial measurement unit sensor](/editorial/224155738463-03.jpg "One student team's methods combined an IMU sensor with skeletal tracking.")

## From a hunch to a hypothesis

In a school science club, the topic is usually assigned, and it is usually the safe one. Here, research begins when students put their own questions on the table:

- How could everyday devices like smartphones or earbuds be repurposed as preventive health monitors?
- How do particular behavior patterns interact with the biological data that predict disease?
- How do environmental stressors such as heat waves or poor air quality affect the signals a wearable records?

After brainstorming, one question centered on mHealth systems becomes the team's research topic. Professor Alshurafa does not simply mark ideas right or wrong; he answers with a sharper question, something like: *To test that hypothesis, would ECG or a motion sensor give you better data? If signal noise creeps in, what does that do to the reliability of the whole system?* Working through follow-ups like these is how a vague curiosity becomes a hypothesis with solid engineering logic behind it.

## What students leave with

Teams build their sensors, analyze the data they collect, and draft and revise with close feedback until they have a finished group research paper with every member's name on it. The course produces four outputs:

1. **A group research paper.** Students write it with guidance from Professor Alshurafa and TAs from leading universities, and CRI supports each paper through submission to a journal or conference indexed in Scopus or CPCI.
2. **Research integrity.** Universities increasingly screen student research for plagiarism and AI ghostwriting, so CRI keeps similarity scores at or below 15% and verifies the data.
3. **An academic research poster.** Students learn to present complex technical work at a glance, the same skill 2025 students relied on at IEEE EMBS.
4. **A recommendation letter grounded in observation.** Over roughly 50 hours of class, Professor Alshurafa watches students assemble sensors and analyze data. Students who prove themselves can earn a letter that speaks to their individual abilities, contributions, and enthusiasm.

## Poster day and what can follow

On Day 10, the paper becomes an academic poster. Students explain, in English, the sensor they designed, the data they collected, and the logic of their proposed interventions to Professor Alshurafa and other experts, then field their questions. It is the kind of defense graduate students go through, and strong preparation for college interviews.

The work does not have to end there:

- **Conferences.** Students who commit fully to the program are given the opportunity to take part in an IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBS) conference.
- **Competitions.** The hypotheses and prototypes can grow into entries for ISEF or the Conrad Challenge.
- **Internships.** A small number of students who show exceptional potential may be offered internships at healthcare startups or companies Professor Alshurafa is involved with.

In 2025, student teams from this class presented posters at IEEE EMBS BSN 2025, the International Conference on Body Sensor Networks. Their projects included:

- **Exercise and academic stress.** A comparison of running, meditation, and phone use as stress relief, measured with HRV and GSR, which found running the most effective.
- **TurtleTrack.** A neck-worn IMU device that detects poor posture and gives real-time feedback.
- **Caffeine and focus.** A study of how caffeine affects high school students' concentration, tracking HRV, heart rate, and GSR before and after caffeine intake.

Read the teams' story, and that of a student who built a runner's-knee rehabilitation wearable with Professor Alshurafa, on our [Student Success](/success) page.

![Two students stand at their research poster in a crowded conference hall while attendees look on](/editorial/224262412735-05.jpg "Seoul Research Program 2025 students presenting at an IEEE EMBS conference poster session.")

## Who the course suits

The 2026 track ran in person in Seoul from July 7 to 17, with Professor Alshurafa teaching on site for all ten days. It is designed for students interested in biology, medicine, biomedical engineering, electrical engineering, bioinformatics, or preventive medicine, and it suits those drawn to AI, psychology, and the life sciences as well. Basic coding knowledge is recommended. Groups are kept small so every student gets close mentoring and real time with the hardware.

Whatever their intended major, students practice defining a research problem, designing an experiment, and reasoning from data, and they gain a practical understanding of digital health technology. The project can also become part of their research portfolio for college applications.

Professor Alshurafa's course is one of the faculty-led tracks in CRI's summer research programs, where small groups work directly with visiting professors from leading universities. To see how the summer cohorts run and which tracks are open, explore the [Seoul and Global Research Programs](/research/summer-camp).

title: From morphine to medicine: organic synthesis and drug design with Caltech's Brian Stoltz
excerpt: What Caltech chemist Brian Stoltz teaches in Seoul: stereochemistry, reaction mechanisms and synthesis design, built around students' own questions and a final poster defense.
content:
Morphine is one of medicine's essential painkillers. Attach two acetyl groups, among the most ordinary building blocks in organic chemistry, and it becomes diacetylmorphine: heroin. The small change lets the molecule cross the blood–brain barrier far faster, turning a hospital analgesic into one of the world's most notorious drugs. How can one simple step in a flask change what a molecule does to the entire nervous system?

Questions like that drive the organic chemistry track Caltech professor **Brian Stoltz** teaches in CRI's Seoul Research Program. The 2026 track ran in person in Seoul for ten days in July. It is aimed at students heading toward chemistry, materials science, pre-med or pre-pharmacy, especially those who have memorized functional groups and enantiomers for AP Chemistry and wondered what any of it is for.

## Why go past the AP textbook

School chemistry often means titrations with a known outcome and lab reports on the same topics everyone else picks. Selective US colleges and medical and pharmacy programs want more than correct answers. They look for what admissions officers call intellectual vitality: the habit of asking your own questions.

Organic chemistry is a good place to build that habit, because it asks what high school chemistry rarely does: how molecules react, and how to make new ones. Most medicines, from cancer drugs and antibiotics to everyday painkillers, are designed and made this way. So are plastics, polymers and functional fibers, and organic reactions explain even the aroma of coffee and chocolate.

## Meet Brian Stoltz

Stoltz earned his PhD in organic chemistry at Yale University, then did postdoctoral research at Harvard University in the group of E. J. Corey, winner of the 1990 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, working on the synthesis of complex natural products. He opened his own laboratory at Caltech in 2000 and is a professor of chemistry there.

His group is known for cracking long-standing problems and for developing new methods:

- **2-Quinuclidonium tetrafluoroborate**, a molecule chemists had tried and failed to make for decades.
- **Jorunnamycin A and cyanthiwigin F**, rare natural products otherwise obtained from marine organisms and directly relevant to anticancer and antibiotic drug discovery. The lab has also synthesized **cylindrocyclophane**.
- **Metal-catalyzed allylic alkylation**: his lab developed new, enantioselective versions of this reaction that are now standard tools in research labs worldwide.

The American Chemical Society gave him the Elias J. Corey Award in 2009, named for his postdoctoral mentor, and the ACS Award for Creative Work in Synthetic Organic Chemistry in 2018; in Japan he received the Mukaiyama Award. He is editor-in-chief of the journal *Tetrahedron*, an associate editor of the *Beilstein Journal of Organic Chemistry*, and has consulted for drug companies including Novartis and Vertex.

For a high school student, the most important credential may be his teaching. In 2017 he received Caltech's Richard P. Feynman Prize for Excellence in Teaching, and the scientists he has trained include UCLA chemist Neil Garg. A longtime member of CRI's faculty, he has also given invited lectures at universities around the world, including Seoul National University.

![Brian Stoltz, holding a drink, chats with a group of students at an evening gathering](/editorial/224021442427-03.jpg "Stoltz talks with students at a 2025 Seoul Research Program gathering.")

## What the course covers

The course, **Organic Chemistry: Structure, Reactivity, and Synthesis**, centers on catalysis, stereochemistry, and materials and pharmaceutical chemistry. It runs as a research seminar, not a lecture series. Instead of tidy summary handouts, students read real research literature at the depth Caltech undergraduates work with. Terms like stereochemistry and reaction mechanism can feel overwhelming at first; within a few days, students start decoding complex molecular structures on their own.

The organizing theme is *Environment as Chemical Systems*: how interactions between molecules govern larger systems, from materials and energy to pharmaceuticals and the biological environment inside the body. The 2026 syllabus built toward that in stages:

| Day | Focus |
| --- | --- |
| Day 2 | Stereochemistry and molecular information, central to drug development and biological systems |
| Days 4–6 | Redox chemistry in organic reactions, and arrow-pushing to reason through mechanisms |
| Day 9 | Advanced synthesis design: planning multistep routes to complex structures |
| Day 10 | Academic poster session and defense |

Once the principles are in place, the course turns to application. Students ask how pharmaceutical synthesis can generate less waste (green chemistry) and trace why a particular molecule works well as a drug. The point is to think like a molecular architect, someone who uses chemistry to treat disease and build new materials, rather than to memorize reactions.

![Brian Stoltz reaches up to write on a whiteboard in a bright classroom](/editorial/224154651312-02.jpg "Stoltz works through a problem at the whiteboard during his Seoul class.")

## From a student's question to a research hypothesis

In most school projects, the teacher sets the frame and students pick the safest topic with a known answer. Stoltz's class starts with the questions students bring. Sample questions from the course include:

- How does the molecular structure of a synthetic polymer affect how it breaks down in the environment?
- How can catalyst systems make complex organic syntheses more efficient?
- What factors decide whether green chemistry approaches are actually adopted in pharmaceutical synthesis?

After brainstorming, a question the team cares about becomes its research topic. Stoltz does not mark ideas right or wrong; he answers with sharper questions. As students work through the literature and argue out their answers, a loose curiosity becomes a focused, well-reasoned hypothesis.

Students then analyze an organic chemistry system using the published literature, draft their paper, and revise it with Stoltz's close feedback until the logic holds. The result is a **group research paper** with each student's name on it, grounded in a question they asked themselves.

## The poster and the defense

On Day 10, each group turns its paper into an academic research poster and presents it at a semi-public poster session. Nobody reads from a script. Students explain their hypothesis and conclusions in English to Stoltz and invited guests, then field pointed questions and defend their reasoning. It is the same kind of defense Caltech undergraduates and graduate students face, and good preparation for college and medical school interviews.

Ten days of close work also means Stoltz learns how each student thinks. Those who distinguish themselves may earn a recommendation letter from him that speaks to their own work and potential. Tracks are small, averaging five or six students in 2026, so that kind of mentoring is realistic.

The poster is not the finish line. CRI keeps working with students on the manuscript after the program and supports it through submission to a journal.

## What students have researched with Stoltz

Past student topics in Stoltz's classes at CRI show how far a question can travel from the textbook:

- **Carbon capture meets emissions control (SCR-CESAR-1):** combining CO₂ capture with the amine solvent CESAR-1 and selective catalytic reduction (SCR) of nitrogen oxides, to cut greenhouse-gas emissions while optimizing catalyst performance. Building on a group project on amine-based carbon capture, this became one student's single-author paper in the SRP Extension; the story is on our [Student Success](/success/carbon-capture-group-paper-to-solo-author) page.
- **Centratherolide A:** how this natural product's α-methylene-γ-lactone ring reacts with proteins such as TOP3B to cause cytotoxicity, and whether it could become a cancer drug or another therapy.
- **Penidaleodiolide A:** analyzing the structure of this complex natural product, designing a retrosynthesis to make it in the lab, and weighing its potential as a neuroactive compound for treating epilepsy.
- **Penicillin and β-lactams:** a winter class project on how penicillin's structure produces its antibiotic activity, how resistance develops, how penicillin is made, and how structural changes alter potency.

![Brian Stoltz stands with arms crossed among about ten students striking playful poses in front of a classroom whiteboard](/editorial/224021442427-07.jpg "Stoltz with his 2025 Seoul Research Program class.")

Stoltz's [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter) course is built as a progression of projects. At the introductory level, students trace the impact of one historically important molecule, such as how antibiotics lengthened human lives. Intermediate projects plan a synthesis of a complex molecule, and advanced projects attempt graduate-level route design through retrosynthesis, working backward from the target. Students aiming for chemistry or life science majors write papers intended for high school or undergraduate journals. In the 2025 Winter Online Research Program, five students divided a single penicillin review among themselves, each taking one part of the molecule's story.

## Who the course suits

- **Future science and engineering majors** in chemistry, life sciences, materials engineering or environmental science.
- **Pre-med, pre-pharmacy and life science students**, since organic chemistry sits at the center of drug development.
- **Students who love asking why** a reaction happens, or whether a new substance could be made.
- **Students outside chemistry** who want practice in creative problem solving: organic chemistry is less about memorizing than about designing a new way through a problem.

Stoltz teaches this track in the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp), where visiting faculty from US and UK universities work with small groups in person in Seoul. Current details and the application are on the program page.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Studying how memory forms and fails with Harvard professor Samuel Kunes
excerpt: How Harvard's Samuel Kunes guides students from classic memory research to their own hypotheses, a group paper on memory and Alzheimer's disease, and a Day 10 poster defense.
content:
Students headed for pre-med or the life sciences know the feeling: the school lab experiment already has its answer in the textbook, and the report looks like everyone else's. Sooner or later they ask, *couldn't I dig into something I actually want to know?* Harvard professor Samuel Kunes's track in CRI's Seoul Research Program starts from that question. Over ten days, students read the research literature on memory, sharpen their own questions into hypotheses, and write a group paper on how memory forms and how it fails in disease.

## Beyond the high school textbook

Admissions officers at top US universities and medical schools have read about cell structure and mitochondria in countless applications. What they hope to find is intellectual vitality: the drive to ask a question with no ready answer and keep pursuing it with academic rigor.

A Harvard professor does not fly to Seoul to reteach high school biology. From the first class, students set the high school label aside and are treated like the newest junior researchers in Professor Kunes's lab.

## Who teaches it

Samuel Kunes is a professor in Harvard University's Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, where he studies neuroscience and the formation of memory. He earned a bachelor's degree in chemistry at the University of Oregon and a PhD in genetics at MIT in 1988.

His lab uses the fruit fly, *Drosophila*, to study how neural circuits relate to behavior. He has paid particular attention to Hedgehog signaling, the development of the visual system, and how visual experience is stored as memory in the brain. His work has identified molecular pathways central to long-term memory, and he has published widely in leading journals. Key papers include:

- A 2006 paper in *Cell* on synaptic protein synthesis and the memory-related RISC pathway
- A 2004 paper in *PNAS* on how neural connections form

At Harvard he has long taught core courses on brain development and plasticity (MCB 129), developmental neurobiology, and the structure and function of the nervous system. He is also committed to research education for younger students and co-founded BioResearch Academy, a program that gives high school students experience in advanced biology research under a Harvard professor's guidance.

## Memory as a living system

His course, Molecular Biology of Memory & Neurological Disease, examines memory, learning, and brain dysfunction through the lens of molecular and cellular biology. Memory and learning are treated not as isolated functions but as dynamic brain systems, shaped by molecular processes, neuronal circuits, and input from experience and the environment. Students trace these systems from genes and synapses up to neural networks, learn how they encode experience and regulate behavior, and follow the same concepts to the disease mechanisms behind memory disorders such as Alzheimer's.

The course moves through three stages:

- **Real papers, not summaries.** Students work from David Sweatt's *Mechanisms of Memory*, a textbook Harvard students themselves find demanding, and from classic papers in neuroscience. Dense academic English and terms such as long-term potentiation (LTP) can feel overwhelming at first, but within a few days, decoding a difficult text on their own starts to feel rewarding.
- **Memory at the molecular level.** How does your brain remember a YouTube video you watched yesterday? "The brain stores it" is not an answer here. Students dig into how synapses make proteins and change their structure in response to a visual stimulus, the process known as synaptic plasticity.
- **Tracking down what goes wrong.** Once students understand how a healthy brain learns, the course turns to disease. Rather than memorizing Alzheimer's as the illness that erases memories, they trace where, at the molecular level, a finely tuned system starts to break down. It is biology as detective work.

Lectures draw on Professor Kunes's own research, and through lectures and seminars each team settles on a research question. Midway through the course, the team writes a group paper grounded in a literature review; at the end, it condenses that paper into an academic poster for the final poster session.

## From a hunch to a hypothesis

School assignments and science clubs tend to steer students toward the safest topic, one with a known answer, inside a framework the teacher sets. Here, the real work begins when students put their own questions on the table, however odd or half-formed:

- Does pulling all-nighters during exams actually damage synaptic connections?
- Could the short bursts of stimulation from a smartphone interfere with how teenagers encode memories?
- Does stress lead to dementia faster in people who carry certain genes?

What a team genuinely wants to know, not a topic someone assigned, becomes its research question.

Professor Kunes does not grade these ideas as right or wrong. He answers with sharper questions, along the lines of: *Interesting. To test that hypothesis, which model organism would work better, fruit flies or zebrafish? And if synthesis of a particular protein were blocked at that step, what would go wrong across the whole system?* Answering and debating follow-ups like these is how a blunt curiosity becomes a well-reasoned research hypothesis.

This is not a school report stitched together from websites. Teams back their hypotheses with evidence from Sweatt's textbook and the neuroscience papers they read earlier, and they revise in real time as Professor Kunes points out gaps in their logic. After ten days of intense discussion, they have a complete draft of a research paper in English with their names on it, ready for the revision stage.

## Sample project topics

Examples of group papers students might write:

| Topic | What the team does |
| --- | --- |
| Gene expression during memory training in flies | Reviews published studies on how learning experiences in fruit flies activate specific memory-related genes, then proposes a new hypothesis |
| Neuroplasticity and the environment | Uses the literature and case studies to explore how light, sound, temperature, and other external stimuli affect synaptic connectivity and neuronal reorganization |
| Blocking protein synthesis | Designs, from existing animal-model studies, an investigation of how memory changes when protein synthesis is blocked by drugs or genetic manipulation |
| A fruit fly model of memory loss | Designs a hypothetical experiment that introduces gene variants linked to Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease into *Drosophila* to model memory loss, and predicts the results |

Whether a team synthesizes published studies or designs a hypothetical experiment, each project takes students through the full arc of a study, from research design to presentation.

## What students leave with

Ideas and debate alone can read as just another summer-camp story, so the course is built to produce three results that others can verify.

### A paper prepared for publication

The work continues after the ten days in Seoul, with about a month of revision under exacting feedback from experts. Research-ethics standards are strict: before moving to the publication stage, a paper must score 15% or below for plagiarism and AI-generated-content similarity, a university-level check. Papers that clear that bar receive support for publication in internationally recognized journals for high school and undergraduate researchers. Unlike a certificate of completion, a published paper is a permanent academic record that appears under the student's name on Google Scholar.

### A poster defense on Day 10

On the final day, each team turns its paper into an academic poster and presents it at a showcase. There is no memorized script: students explain their hypothesis and conclusions in English to Professor Kunes and invited guests, then defend their reasoning against pointed questions. It is an early taste of the defense graduate students face, and something students can speak about with confidence in US college interviews.

![Cartoon illustration of a poster session: a student in a school blazer points to a poster titled "Mechanisms of Stress and Memory Consolidation in Drosophila" while a man holding a notepad asks how she accounted for confounding factors in the stress induction protocol](/editorial/224258737607-03.jpg "Illustration: a Day 10 poster defense, where students present their findings and answer questions from the professor and guests.")

### A recommendation letter, for those who earn it

Ten days of constant back-and-forth show Professor Kunes each student's academic passion, insight, and persistence. Letters are not handed out for attendance; only students who fully demonstrate intellectual vitality can expect a distinctive letter that tells their own story.

## Who the course suits

The course is an especially good fit for students who:

- Have a deep interest in biology, neuroscience, or genetics
- Want to take on the challenge of writing a research paper
- Plan to study the life sciences at universities such as Harvard or MIT
- Want substantive research experience to bring to US college applications

In 2026 the track was offered as a ten-day, in-person intensive in Seoul, with a small, selective group so that every student could be mentored closely by Professor Kunes. Stories from past CRI students, including their admissions and competition results, are collected on our [Student Success](/success) page.

Professor Kunes's course is one of several faculty-led tracks in CRI's summer research programs, where small groups work directly with visiting professors from leading universities. To see how the summer cohorts are structured and which tracks are open, explore the [Seoul and Global Research Programs](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Ivy Day 2026: Yale applications rise 9.4% as SAT and ACT requirements return
excerpt: Yale's applicant pool grew 9.4% and Penn required test scores for the first time since 2020. Here is what the Class of 2030 results say about standing out when top scores are the baseline.
content:
On Ivy Day, the evening of March 26, 2026 (U.S. time), all eight Ivy League universities released regular decision results for the Class of 2030, the students entering college in fall 2026. Some of the news was good: students from the previous summer's Seoul Research Program let us know they had been admitted to schools including Harvard, Columbia and Penn, and you can read more CRI student stories on the [Student Success](/success) page. For many families, though, the night brought results far harsher than they had expected, and the first official numbers helped explain why.

## Yale's second-largest applicant pool

Yale was the first to publish official figures. According to [YaleNews](https://news.yale.edu/2026/03/26/yale-admits-2328-applicants-class-2030), applications rose 9.4% over the previous year, producing the second-largest applicant pool in the college's history. From those tens of thousands of applicants, Yale admitted 2,328 students to the Class of 2030, a total that includes those admitted early.

The squeeze was felt close to home. At leading international schools in Korea, one top student after another, some with perfect GPAs, was turned down. Flawless numbers are no longer enough on their own. So what changed?

## Required testing is back

The biggest reason this cycle felt so unforgiving was the return of required SAT and ACT scores. On March 26, [The Daily Pennsylvanian](https://www.thedp.com/article/2026/03/penn-regular-decision-2026-results-class-of-2030), the University of Pennsylvania's student newspaper, reported that more than 61,000 students had applied to Penn in its first admissions cycle since 2020 to require standardized test scores. With that change, Penn joined Harvard, Brown, Dartmouth and a growing list of highly selective universities that now require applicants to submit scores.

The effect is simple, and it is harsh. When everyone submits scores, the whole pool looks stronger on paper. Admissions officers now face tens of thousands of files with the same profile: an SAT above 1550 and a perfect GPA. Academic ability that can be proven with numbers has stopped being an advantage. It is the baseline, the thing every serious applicant is expected to bring.

## The academic spike is what stands out

If thousands of applicants look identical on paper, what separates them? The answer admissions experts keep returning to is the **academic spike**: sharp, demonstrated depth in one field.

Ivy League readers are, in effect, asking one question: could this student arrive on campus and contribute to a research lab right away? Answering yes takes more than excellent coursework. It takes an interest developed into real, graduate-level research and written up as a paper.

A school club or a routine class report rarely holds an admissions reader's attention. What does is research that is genuinely the student's own, especially work that outside experts have already evaluated, through competitions such as the GENIUS Olympiad or USACO, or through an academic journal's review process.

## Who guides the research matters

Few high school students can produce a paper at that level on their own, or with the help of a typical tutoring academy. Who supervised the work, and how rigorously, shapes both the quality of the paper and how much an admissions reader trusts it. That trust is harder to earn than it used to be: as AI writing tools improve, readers have grown more skeptical of student research papers in general.

This is the gap CRI's Seoul Research Program is designed to close:

- **Faculty who teach in person.** Professors and working researchers from institutions such as Harvard, MIT, Caltech and NASA guide students face to face.
- **A research story that fits the major.** The aim is not one paper in isolation. The paper becomes the culmination of a longer academic story tied to the student's intended major, one that shows why a topic has held their attention since Grade 9.

The point is not to collect another credential. It is to work alongside leading scholars at the edge of a field and turn real academic curiosity into the clearest evidence a student can offer.

## What the Class of 2030 results suggest

A generic summer camp or a familiar list of activities will struggle to carry an application through a cycle this competitive. The students selective universities are looking for ask their own questions and do the work to answer them.

If you want to build that kind of research with a faculty mentor, the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) brings visiting professors from US and UK universities to Seoul, where they guide small groups of students through writing their own research paper in English.
author: CRI Editorial

title: What RSI at MIT looks for: independent research, not just perfect scores
excerpt: RSI admits roughly 80 students a year, free of charge. Here is how the program works, what the application asks for, and why independent research is the real bar.
content:
Every March, roughly 80 high school students from around the world learn that they have a place at the Research Science Institute (RSI), the summer research program hosted at MIT. It costs participants nothing, and fewer than 2.5% of applicants get in. Top test scores are common in that pool, so they are not what decides it. What sets admitted students apart is evidence that they can already do research on their own.

## How RSI works

RSI is organized by the Center for Excellence in Education (CEE), and its structure is simple. The program opens with a week of concentrated STEM classes taught by professors. The next five weeks are a research internship: each student carries out an individual project with guidance from a mentor who is a working scientist or researcher. At the end, every student writes up the results as a research paper and presents the work at the RSI Symposium.

## How selective it is

By CEE's count, RSI draws more than 3,000 applications a year, and only a sliver of them succeed.

| RSI at a glance | Figure |
|---|---|
| Applications from the US each year | More than 2,500 |
| Applications from other countries each year | 600 |
| Acceptance rate | Under 2.5% |
| Students admitted each year | Roughly 80 |
| Cost to participants | Free |

CEE has also tracked where RSI alumni went on to study. Across the cohorts from 1984 to 2024, a third enrolled at Harvard and nearly a quarter at MIT.

| University | Share of RSI alumni, 1984–2024 |
|---|---|
| Harvard | 33% |
| MIT | 23% |
| Stanford | 12% |
| Yale | 5% |
| Princeton | 4% |
| Caltech | 3% |
| Duke | 2% |
| Other universities | 18% |

## What the application asks for

On paper, the RSI application looks like many others. The details can change from one cycle to the next, but for 2026, CEE asked for:

- **Essays** answering the application's questions, which should lay out the applicant's goals in science, technology, engineering or math.
- **Two recommendations** from math or science teachers, or from a research supervisor, who know the applicant and their academic record. Students who have spent four weeks or more on a research project at a university or in a lab are asked to get a letter from that supervisor. No more than three letters are accepted.
- **An official high school transcript.**
- **Every national standardized test score**, including the PSAT, SAT, ACT and AP exams. Students who plan to apply are strongly encouraged to take the PSAT.

Look closely at the recommendation rule. It assumes that some applicants will already have spent a month or more on real research, and it wants to hear from the person who supervised them.

## The real bar: independent research

Among applicants at this level, near-perfect PSAT or SAT scores and a flawless GPA are the baseline. The published requirements alone will not get a student in. What RSI actually selects for is the ability to do independent research.

That follows from what the program is. RSI does not teach students how to do research from scratch. It is a proving ground: students who arrive already prepared spend five weeks on real projects in working labs, alongside established scientists. So by the time they apply, strong candidates usually have research they led themselves, and a well-developed paper that documents it. No rule lists a paper as a requirement, but in practice it comes close to being one.

## Why strong Korean students still fall short

Korean high school students win medals at international olympiads, yet many of them struggle to get into programs like RSI. CRI sees a structural reason: Korean high schools offer almost no opportunity to do university-level research and write a proper paper.

Many families respond by looking for outside research mentoring, and this is where the choice of mentor matters. Much of what is available is led by instructors with master's degrees or by a small number of PhDs. They may well be excellent researchers, but CRI sees two limits:

- **Breadth.** A mentor whose training has centered on one narrow specialty may struggle to take a high school student's inventive, often interdisciplinary idea and develop it from several angles to suit that student.
- **Supervision experience.** Working as a researcher in a lab is not the same as leading someone else's first research project from start to finish and teaching them to write the paper.

Weak guidance tends to produce a paper that exists mainly to fill a résumé line: ghostwritten, or too thin to hold up. That kind of work will not get past the people who read RSI applications, whose job is to find the most capable young researchers in the world.

## What a strong first research experience looks like

For students writing their first paper, or looking for their first serious research experience, the starting point shapes everything that follows. Two things make the difference:

- **Learning the whole process.** The goal is not just to end up with a paper. It is to see how a raw idea becomes an academic research question, how that question is tested and checked, and how the results become a finished paper.
- **Working directly with professors.** Faculty whose expertise spans more than one discipline can take a student's idea and develop it to international standards, and they act as the student's research mentor themselves.

The shift that RSI rewards is the move from being a student who is very good at math and science to being a researcher. Students who have made that leap are the ones who stand out, first at RSI and later with college admissions officers, who look for the same kind of genuine research record.

Two other guides on the [CRI blog](/blog) pick up these threads. *How to evaluate a summer research program* explains what "working with a professor" should really mean, and *Regeneron ISEF: what 2025 finalists researched, and how Korean students compared* looks at the world's largest high school science fair.

If you are looking for that first step, the [Seoul Research Program (SRP)](/research/summer-camp) places students in small groups with visiting professors, who guide each project from the first idea to a finished paper.
author: CRI Editorial

title: UC fall 2026 applications hit a record, but international interest has stalled
excerpt: UC drew a record 251,907 applicants for fall 2026, a rise driven mostly by transfers. Here are the campus-by-campus numbers, the international slowdown, and what two admitted students say set them apart.
content:
The University of California received applications from 251,907 prospective undergraduates for fall 2026, the most it has ever recorded. Look closer, though, and the growth came mostly from transfer students. First-year applications barely moved, and international first-year applications dipped slightly, a year after jumping 8%.
