UC released these preliminary counts while many students were still waiting on decisions from the most selective US universities and liberal arts colleges. Here is what the numbers show, which campuses drew the most competition, and what two admitted CRI students say set their applications apart.

## The systemwide numbers

The University of California's preliminary fall 2026 application tables show these totals (changes are from fall 2025):

- **Total applicants:** 251,907 (up 0.8%)
- **First-year applicants:** 205,431 (up 0.1%)
- **International first-year applicants:** 32,070 (down 0.1%)
- **Transfer applicants:** 46,476 (up 3%)

Overall, the year-to-year shifts are small. The record total owes most of its rise to transfer applications, and of the 46,476 transfer applicants, 38,264 applied from California community colleges.

## Campus by campus

Five campuses again drew more than 100,000 applications each: UC Berkeley, UC Irvine, UCLA, UC San Diego and UC Santa Barbara. UC Davis, which crossed the 100,000 mark last year, held its place above it.

| Campus | All applications | First-year | International first-year | International share of first-year | Transfer |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **UC systemwide** | 251,907 | 205,431 | 32,070 | 16% | 46,476 |
| Berkeley | 159,344 | 133,128 | 25,220 | 19% | 26,216 |
| Davis | 122,271 | 104,850 | 21,024 | 20% | 17,421 |
| Irvine | 153,025 | 125,987 | 21,908 | 17% | 27,038 |
| Los Angeles | 177,317 | 146,672 | 24,718 | 17% | 30,645 |
| Merced | 54,900 | 48,499 | 5,340 | 11% | 6,401 |
| Riverside | 87,048 | 72,295 | 6,254 | 9% | 14,753 |
| San Diego | 168,066 | 141,752 | 25,480 | 18% | 26,314 |
| Santa Barbara | 127,369 | 108,503 | 19,026 | 18% | 18,866 |
| Santa Cruz | 92,333 | 78,832 | 6,490 | 8% | 13,501 |

*The systemwide row counts each student once. Most students apply to several campuses, so the campus figures add up to far more than the total.*

## International applications level off

International first-year applications fell 0.1%. Set against last year's 8% surge, that points to a clear plateau in international demand for UC. At the most popular campuses, the international share of applicants is almost exactly where it was a year ago.

The wider picture is starker. Common App's mid-February update, covering applications through February 1, 2026, showed international applicants down 9% overall, including a 9% drop from Asia and a 16% drop from Africa. Projections from NAFSA and JBI point the same way, with international enrollment in the US expected to fall in 2025–26 after several years of growth.

Taken together, the data suggests that fewer international students are entering US higher education overall, and US universities are working hard to attract and keep the ones they have. International students matter to a university's finances, and they are central to the diversity of its campus. Wendy Wolford, Cornell's vice provost for international affairs, has voiced concern about government policies aimed at international students, asking how the US can recruit the best and brightest if more of them come to feel the country is ambivalent about having them.

Two companion pieces on the [CRI blog](/blog) go deeper: one on UC's record fall 2025 enrollment and what its 18% cap on nonresident students means for international applicants, and a breakdown of UCLA and UC Berkeley admit rates by major.

## Where the competition is fiercest

**UCLA** drew more applications than any other UC campus. It received 24,718 international first-year applications for fall 2026, up 518 from last year, and the international share of its first-year pool rose from 16.7% to 17%. UCLA admitted international students at a rate of around 6% for fall 2025. That rate is unlikely to move much this year, so expect the competition to stay intense.

**UC Berkeley** received 25,220 international first-year applications. Getting in is as hard as it is at UCLA, and the bar is expected to be higher still in popular majors such as public health, computer science and business.

**UC San Diego** drew 141,752 first-year applicants, second only to UCLA. Its 25,480 international first-year applicants were the most at any UC campus this year.

## What admitted students say made the difference

CRI alumni admitted to these highly competitive campuses point to the same two things that made them stand out: in-depth academic research experience and a detailed recommendation letter from a professor. Here is how two of them describe it.

> "I wanted to build a stronger background in materials chemistry, so through CRI I did research with Professor Anish Tuteja at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor. The experience gave me a systematic grounding in literature searches and academic writing, and I completed my first research paper. Most of all, I earned a strong recommendation letter from the professor. I was admitted to UC Berkeley, and that in-depth research experience was the secret weapon in my application."
> — Former CRI student, admitted to UC Berkeley chemistry

> "I worked my project experience, and what I achieved through it, into my essays. One paragraph of my UK personal statement was entirely about CRI, and one of the four essays I submitted to the UCs focused on my CRI experience as well. Those experiences, together with a strong recommendation letter from Professor Brian Stoltz, are how I was admitted to several world-renowned universities at once."
> — Former CRI student, admitted to UC Berkeley and Imperial College London

Neither student leaned on template phrases. Each told a specific story of growth drawn from real work: the details of actual academic inquiry, the concrete stages of a research project, and a genuine working relationship with a professor. That is how they made their individuality clear and won over the admissions officers reading their files.

The close faculty guidance these students describe is what the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) is built around: small groups of students work with visiting professors from US and UK universities on a real research project and write it up as a paper in English.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Why assembled portfolios fall flat, and what a connected research story looks like
excerpt: An app from one academy and a paper from another rarely add up to a story. Learn why admissions officers see through patchwork portfolios, and how one research question can tie it all together.
content:
"We've worked out the essay plan with our consultant down to the last detail. The app is being built at one academy, and the paper is being written at another." It's a structural problem that frustrates families aiming for the most selective US colleges, and even the admissions consultants who work with them. A consultant can draw up an excellent master plan, but no consulting firm can house everything needed to carry it out.

## When the pieces don't fit

The usual workaround is to shuttle students from a paper-writing academy to a coding academy, or to hand pieces of the portfolio to freelancers the family has never met. The results can be painful. A student's essay might set out a real conviction, say, building an AI model to tackle environmental pollution. Meanwhile the app attached to the application, turned out by a freelancer or a tutor, has nothing to do with that idea. It's an empty shell.

Admissions officers notice. A portfolio stitched together with money and no connecting context, what CRI calls an "assembled" or Frankenstein portfolio, is easy to spot, and it tends to be set aside quickly. The trouble isn't any single activity. It's that farming out each piece to a different vendor cuts the student's story into fragments.

The alternative is to grow every piece from one root, a line of research the student genuinely owns, so the parts add up to a single, authentic story.

## Coherence starts with the research question

A connected story needs a real starting point, and that means the research topic. The idea that a high school student will arrive with a perfect topic already worked out is a fantasy. Research programs for high school students tend to respond with one of two extremes. Some hand students a ready-made list of topics to pick from. Others leave students to find a topic on their own, starting from a blank page.

CRI's Seoul Research Program does neither. It treats the professor's expertise as the student's compass, in three stages:

1. **Absorb the field.** Students first learn from the professor, building an academic perspective that reaches well beyond the high school curriculum.
2. **Connect it to a spark.** They then combine that new knowledge with a small interest of their own. One student paired a professor's expertise in AI with a love of math and basketball, and the result was a model that predicts the outcomes of basketball games.
3. **Sharpen it into a topic.** Through in-depth consultations and one-on-one conversations, a vague idea is refined into a research topic that belongs to that student alone.

Because the topic is the student's own, everything that grows from it later shares the same origin.

## Depth depends on the right mentor

Many of the most interesting topics cross disciplines, which raises a second problem. Hand AI-based protein analysis to a tutor trained in biology, or sports statistics to a coding instructor, and the result is usually shallow and predictable. Academic fields run deeper and narrower than most people expect. Even professors in the same department can't always follow one another's work.

That's why CRI keeps working to bring in faculty from Ivy League and other leading universities, along with dedicated TAs. However unusual a student's combination of interests, the aim is a pinpoint match: a scholar and a mentor whose specialty fits that exact subfield.

## A process families can follow

Families who pay for an expensive overseas program often worry that their child will be left to drift on the far side of a Zoom call. At CRI, each student works closely with a bilingual TA from a top university, who helps the student communicate with the professor and keeps their morale steady. Parents also receive reports directly, covering their child's research progress and the feedback they've received, so they can see how the student is developing through the work.

Just as important, the finished paper isn't meant to sit in a drawer as a PDF. CRI's TAs and tech mentors can work as one team with the family's admissions consultant to extend the paper into a working website, a startup, or an entry in a major competition. Families don't have to commit to all of it up front: when each project ends, CRI reviews the results and suggests a next step, and the family decides whether to take it.

![Illustration of a mentor pointing at a monitor labeled AI Basketball Prediction while a student in a hoodie works at the keyboard, with a tablet showing a business plan and a printed weekly report on the desk](/editorial/224213626208-04.jpg "Illustration: a mentor and a student turn a research model into a working product.")

## Five papers that kept going

Admissions officers respond to authentic impact. Here are five cases in which a CRI research paper went further, grouped by the kind of evidence each one produced.

### Recognition from experts

"I was mentored by a professor" is a thin line on its own. Top US universities look for signs that experts in academia and industry actually treated the student as a colleague.

- **Co-author with an Ivy League professor.** On the strength of a Seoul Research Program paper, a student was named co-author alongside their professor on a blog post published on the University of Pennsylvania's official website. In effect, an Ivy League professor put their own name beside the student's work to vouch for the student's ability. The student was later admitted to Stanford University.
- **An internship earned through research.** Impressed by a student's research ability and work ethic, the professor who supervised the paper brought the student on as an intern at the law firm the professor heads. Experience that grows out of an academic relationship produces a far richer recommendation letter than an internship bought through an agency.

### From paper to product

A student who writes that a problem needs solving and a student who builds a solution and launches it are in very different positions.

- **A business model with MIT Sloan.** Under close guidance from a professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, a student turned the idea behind their paper into a business model, moving past a mock startup toward pitching it to investors in the US. That kind of entrepreneurship gives a leadership essay real substance.
- **A live basketball-prediction website.** After writing a paper that combined AI and basketball, a student worked with CRI's in-house tech team to launch a public website that predicts basketball games. As product owner, the student turned the model from their own paper into a working service with real users.

### Competition results

In a crowded field of credentials, a major competition award carries weight because it has been judged independently.

- **KSEF gold and a place at ISEF.** Starting from a paper whose framework took shape in the Seoul Research Program, a student developed the work closely with a dedicated competition TA. The student won a gold medal at the Korea Science and Engineering Fair (KSEF) and advanced to the International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF) as one of Korea's national representatives, without a separate competition-prep academy.

## One thread from start to finish

None of these students assembled a portfolio from parts. Each outcome grew out of research the student already owned, and that is why it reads as genuine. A student's ideas and time are too valuable to scatter across unrelated vendors. The stronger story runs from a single paper all the way to its impact beyond the classroom.

Every path above began with a research paper. If you'd like to start one of your own, the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) brings visiting professors from US and UK universities to Seoul to guide small groups from a first question to a finished paper, the starting point for whatever comes next.
author: CRI Editorial

title: When should students start research? The case for ninth grade
excerpt: Why ninth grade is the right time to start research, what younger students should do first, and how one student turned math and basketball into an AI prediction website.
content:
One question comes up in almost every conversation I have with parents: "When should my child start research? Is earlier better?"

Since research is what I do, many parents probably expect me to say "as early as possible." But my answer is always clear: **I think ninth grade is the best time to start.**

I would actually talk a family out of research that starts before then, or research a student has no interest in and is pushed into only to add a line to a résumé for selective colleges. Both the student and the parents burn out quickly. Worse, the student can lose interest in learning itself.

So why ninth grade? And what is research for in the first place?

## Before ninth grade: build interests through projects

Doing research properly takes two things: a clear interest and a foundation of basic knowledge. That's why, through eighth grade, I'd rather students not fixate on writing a formal paper. Their time is better spent on hands-on, project-based activities such as coding or simple experiments.

These are years for exploring. Students should build things, get stuck, try again, and slowly work out what they enjoy and which fields pull them in. Demand paper-level research at this age and you usually get a patchwork of other people's writing, stitched together by a student who never really understood the material.

![Illustration of two teenagers at facing desks: a younger boy wires a small robot beside his laptop while an older student studies a draft paper on screen, pen in hand](/editorial/224212317233-02.jpg "Illustration: hands-on projects come first; research follows once a real interest takes shape.")

## Around ninth grade: real interests and critical thinking

Young children's interests change almost daily. Around ninth grade, students begin to know what they like and what genuinely fascinates them.

They also start to think critically. Instead of simply accepting what they're told, they ask, "Why is that?" or "I see it differently." That shift matters, because research is more than gathering information. You listen to what a range of experts have said, add your own opinion and perspective on top, and then put the work out into the world. Ninth grade is roughly when students reach the intellectual maturity to do that naturally rather than by force.

## Not a credential, but a reason to enjoy learning

Take coding. Imagine learning it purely as complicated syntax and mathematical theory, drilled from the front of a classroom. Most students would be bored.

I went to university in Korea, and I suspect this kind of rote, lecture-driven learning is why preparing for Korean college admissions can feel so joyless. Whatever fun there is has to come from the competition to raise your grades.

Now picture the same student building a game they've always wanted to make. Somewhere between getting a character to move and getting the score to count, they hit a wall, and suddenly they're up all night searching YouTube and digging through books to solve it. Knowledge earned that way is never forgotten, and it grows into deeper interest.

Research works the same way. It takes the dry material from school subjects like math, science and history and applies it to a field the student truly loves, going deep. It isn't homework done under duress. It's the surest way for students to motivate themselves and grow more curious about their studies.

People often imagine a research paper as something grand, the work of scientists in white coats laboring for years. It doesn't have to be. All research really needs is this: **listen to what a range of experts have to say, add your own logically argued view, and share it with the world.** That is how research papers began, and it's how students should approach them.

## Math, basketball and an AI prediction site

One student shows what this looks like in practice. Math and basketball were this student's passions, and anything outside them was a hard sell. So instead of a predictable topic chosen for admissions, we decided to dig into what the student actually cared about, starting with one small suggestion: "Why not analyze the basketball games you love, using math?"

That suggestion went a long way:

- **Exploring the topic:** The student analyzed basketball data mathematically, from player statistics to the flow of each game.
- **Writing the paper:** Going a step further, the student used AI to build a model that predicts which team will win, and wrote a paper based on it.
- **Launching a service:** The research didn't stay on the page. The student built a real website so people could see the analysis for themselves.
- **Still going:** Today the student is gathering users and their feedback, less a high schooler with a project than the person running a live service.

## A first step toward solving the world's problems

As this student's story shows, genuine research isn't something squeezed out at a desk. It's the process of carrying your own interests out into the world and turning them into something real. Students who have done that grow into people who find problems and solve them on their own, in college and long after. It's also exactly what top universities are looking for.

So watch, quietly, for what your child loves. Then talk together about how that interest could go deeper. That conversation is the best possible start to research.

When a student reaches ninth grade with an interest worth pursuing, the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) is a natural next step: students work in small groups with visiting professors from US and UK universities to shape a question and carry it through to a finished paper.
author: CRI Editorial

title: How the Seoul Research Program selects students, and what reviewers look for
excerpt: Application, interview, decision: how SRP chooses students, why faculty are matched by problem rather than major, and what to do if your topic is too big or missing.
content:
Students interested in the Seoul Research Program (SRP) tend to ask the same three questions. What if there's no professor in my intended major? Will lower grades count against me? Can I apply without a research topic? They're fair questions, and they usually rest on the same assumption: that you have to be flawless from the moment you apply.

SRP looks at applicants differently. Students don't just pitch ideas here; they work with a professor to take a real paper all the way to completion. So every decision turns on one question: will this student see the paper through? Reviewers answer it by looking at **direction, feasibility and commitment**.

## Three stages: application, interview, decision

Selection happens in three steps:

1. **Application.** Your written application is reviewed first.
2. **Interview, by invitation.** Only students who pass that review are invited to interview, online or in person.
3. **Final decision.** Admission is decided after the interview.

Each stage asks something different of you. Your application has to be persuasive enough to earn an interview. The interview has to leave reviewers convinced that you will finish.

## Why follow-through outweighs credentials

Writing a research paper takes more than being smart. Every project reaches a point where it stalls, and the students who finish are the ones who keep pushing instead of giving up. That is why SRP weighs how likely a student is to finish more heavily than their current credentials.

## "There's no professor in my major"

CRI hears this one constantly. "I want to study economics. Can I still do SRP if there's no economics professor?" "I'm interested in the environment. What if nobody teaches environmental science?"

The key point is that research today doesn't divide neatly along department lines. Most of it is interdisciplinary, so what matters is the problem you want to solve and the method you use to solve it, not the title of your major.

Take Professor Haifeng Xu of the University of Chicago, who researches agentic AI. A student might reasonably assume an AI professor only suits future computer science majors. Look closely at his work, though, and you find AI used as a tool to tackle economic problems: markets, decision-making, resource allocation. So a future economics major can be a strong match, as long as they are clear that they want to solve economic problems with AI methods.

![Illustration of three students at a library table with laptops and economics textbooks, one pointing to a whiteboard titled "Interdisciplinary Problem Map: AI & Economics"](/editorial/224205568424-02.jpg "Illustration: one problem, several fields. Agentic AI connects to resource allocation, market mechanisms and economic modeling.")

This is why CRI encourages students to start with a consultation. Choosing a professor by department name is an easy way to get confused. In a consultation, the faculty match is built around the problem you want to solve.

## "Will lower grades count against me?"

To be candid, strong grades can help. But SRP is not a contest ranked by scores. Because every student has to finish a paper, whether an applicant will follow through carries real weight.

One anonymous case makes the point. When this student applied, their profile looked like this:

- Rising 11th grader
- SAT score in the 1300s
- GPA of 3.3
- An unaccredited international school outside the Seoul area

Grades were not this student's strength, and they were admitted anyway. They knew exactly what they wanted to study and why, and above all they showed a strong determination to finish what they started. Later, the student was admitted to the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC).

The lesson is simple. SRP isn't looking for the "perfect" student; it's looking for the one who will finish.

## "Do I need a research topic before I apply?"

Many students picture the ideal applicant as someone who arrives with an impressive, fully formed topic. In practice, two other situations are far more common.

### The topic is too big

Some topics can't become a paper as they stand:

- The data it needs is realistically out of reach.
- The scope is too large to finish in a year or two.
- The idea is exciting, but there is no way to test it.

In these cases, SRP keeps the core idea, narrows the scope, switches to data and methods that are actually available, and redesigns the project into something that can become a paper.

### There's no topic at all

Other students say, "I don't have a topic, but I really like this field." SRP doesn't send them away to come back with one. Instead, student and professor build it together, moving from interest to question, from question to method, and from method to the structure of a paper.

What matters is not whether your topic is finished, but whether you are ready to see that process through.

## What to show in your application

Put simply, your application should show three things.

**1. Direction: what you're curious about.** "I like AI" isn't enough. Aim for one sentence that says what you want to solve with AI.

**2. Feasibility: whether your approach could work.** You don't need a perfect plan, but it helps to be able to say something like "I think I could use this kind of data or source material" or "I'd like to approach this through analysis, simulation or a literature review."

**3. Commitment: whether you'll finish.** Every paper stalls at some point. Reviewers want to know you won't give up when yours does.

## Where a consultation helps

Most applicants who stall hit one of three sticking points: there seems to be no professor in their major, their grades feel borderline, or their topic is too big or missing entirely.

A consultation works through those first:

- Turning your interests into a research question
- Designing a faculty match around your problem and method rather than the name of your major
- Mapping out a plan you can realistically carry to the finish

For many students, that conversation becomes the first step in designing the paper itself.

## The short version

SRP is looking for students who will finish their paper. Whatever your major, grades or topic, what counts is a clear direction and the will to see the work through. To see how the program runs, explore the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp), and when you're ready, the [admissions page](/admissions) walks through each step of applying.
author: CRI Editorial

title: How to evaluate a summer research program: what “working with a professor” should mean
excerpt: Programs that sound identical can be built very differently. Learn how faculty titles, meeting hours and fine print reveal how much a professor is really involved.
content:
"There are so many programs now. I honestly can't tell which ones are the real thing." Parents often say some version of this in their first conversation with CRI, and it's a fair reaction. A few years ago, programs that let students do research directly with a professor at a university abroad were rare. Today, phrases like "mentored by top-university faculty" and "one-on-one research with a professor" turn up on one program page after another.

More choice is a good thing. But programs that use the same phrases can differ widely in price, and the gap most likely reflects how a program is built rather than whose name is on it. When a working professor sets aside real time, takes responsibility for a student's research design and keeps giving feedback, that costs something. When the professor's name is on the brochure but their actual involvement is thin, the costs are bound to differ. So the useful question isn't the price. It's what "working with a professor" should concretely mean.

## What the title "professor" tells you

"You'll work with a professor" covers more ground than most families realize. Universities use a range of academic titles, among them:

- Tenured Professor
- Tenure-track Assistant Professor
- Adjunct Professor
- Research Fellow
- Postdoctoral Researcher

All of them are serious researchers, but their roles, authority and responsibilities inside the university differ. A tenured professor typically runs an independent lab, supervises graduate and doctoral students, and makes decisions about research direction and personnel. Postdoctoral researchers and research fellows, by contrast, carry out research on contracts. Their work can be excellent, yet their formal authority and responsibilities within the university are limited.

That difference goes well beyond a line on a business card. It affects:

- how deeply the person can mentor a student,
- how much responsibility they can take for the direction of the research, and
- what standing they have to write a recommendation letter, and how much weight that letter carries.

So when a program says students work "with a professor," check the exact title. The point isn't to rank researchers. It's to understand how the program is structured.

## How involved is the professor, really?

Once you know the title, look at the depth of involvement. Plenty of programs describe themselves as "one-on-one research," but what happens inside varies a great deal:

- How many meetings does the professor attend over the whole program?
- Is the professor directly involved in designing the study and setting its direction?
- Does the professor give feedback on drafts personally?
- Or does a TA handle most of the day-to-day mentoring?

A professor's name can sit front and center while the real arrangement is a few meetings with the professor and TAs doing most of the mentoring. In other programs, the professor is involved from the research-design stage, works through repeated rounds of interim feedback and revision, and stays responsible until the work is finished.

That difference is about more than hours on a schedule. It shapes how deep the research goes, how far the student's thinking stretches, and how polished the final work turns out. Who takes part matters, but just as important is how deeply that person actually takes part.

## Why structure shows up in the price

Differences in title and involvement lead naturally to differences in cost. When a working professor commits real time and takes responsibility from research design through the finished product, that time and responsibility have a price. Expert time is priced this way in other settings too: an outside lecture by a tenured professor commands a very different fee from one by a research fellow.

If the professor's role is limited and the program actually runs on TAs, it can be priced differently as well. That isn't a question of expensive versus cheap. It's a question of structure. Two programs that both advertise "faculty mentoring" can turn out to be entirely different depending on:

- the professor's actual share of the mentoring time,
- how often the professor gives feedback directly,
- how much of the research design the professor is responsible for, and
- who actually writes the recommendation letter.

That's why comparing programs on price alone can mislead you. The better question is not "How much is it?" but "How is it built?"

## Reading the fine print

Similar wording can hide different arrangements, so it pays to read a program description line by line. A few examples:

- **A university's name in large type**, with "independent program," "not affiliated" or "external organization" in small print further down.
- **"10 sessions,"** which tells you little until you know whether a session lasts 30 minutes or two hours.
- **"One-on-one,"** where the actual arrangement is two or three meetings with the professor and a program run mostly by TAs.

None of this wording is necessarily wrong. It simply needs interpreting. Research isn't a one-off event; it is a process in which time and depth build up. A single line in small print, or one choice of phrase, can reveal a real difference in structure, and that difference can change how deep the results go.

## Warning signs to watch for

As research programs have multiplied, so have cases like these:

- programs that promise a published paper, then keep adding costs afterward;
- programs that emphasize a professor's involvement while graduate students do the actual teaching;
- projects bent to fit the mentor's specialty until the student's own interest disappears.

The more common the word "research" becomes, the more it matters to tell genuine mentoring apart from programs that only borrow the label.

## Questions to ask before you choose

Rather than going by names and slogans, look at the specifics. These questions aren't meant to attack any program. They are a way to understand how it works:

1. Is the professor currently listed as faculty on the university's official website?
2. What is their exact title: tenured, tenure-track, adjunct, postdoc or something else?
3. What is the program's official relationship with the university, if any?
4. How many direct meetings with the professor are there, and how long does each one last?
5. How many hours of mentoring are there in total, and what share of them come from the professor?
6. At which stages of the research design and the final paper is the professor involved?
7. If a recommendation letter is offered, who actually writes it?
8. Beyond the names, how is responsibility actually divided?

Research is more than a class. At its core, it is about how deeply one researcher guides a student's thinking. With more options than ever, the criteria need to be sharper too, and the details are worth reading slowly.

The same questions apply to CRI. In the Seoul Research Program, visiting professors from US and UK universities teach small groups of up to about ten students, and the standard schedule includes 30 hours with the professor and 20 hours with a TA. You can see how CRI's summer programs are organized on the [Seoul and Global Research Programs page](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Reading cities and power through design with RISD's Ijlal Muzaffar
excerpt: RISD architectural historian Ijlal Muzaffar's Seoul Research Program course treats buildings and cities as design systems, from Rajasthan's stepwells to the boulevards of Paris.
content:
Is there a link between the radiating boulevards of Paris and the machinery of surveillance and control? What can the stepwells of Rajasthan teach a world running short of water? Questions like these drive "Possible Modernities: Design Systems, Architecture, and Environmental Futures," a ten-day course Ijlal Muzaffar of the Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) designed for CRI's 2026 Seoul Research Program, traveling to Seoul to teach it in person.

The course starts from a simple premise: design is about more than beauty. Buildings and cities carry political, economic, and environmental choices. Who holds power over urban space, how inequality gets built into it, and how it can respond to a changing climate are no longer questions for specialists alone. They are part of what every future designer needs to understand.

![Students sit on a sunny campus lawn beneath a "Lawn Party" banner, with brick buildings behind them](/editorial/224171113832-01.jpg "Campus life at RISD in Providence, Rhode Island, where Muzaffar teaches")

## An architectural historian who reads design as a system

Muzaffar is a professor of modern architectural history at RISD, where he also heads the Department of Theory and History of Art and Design. Educated at MIT, he approaches architecture and design as systems and examines how people, power, and the environment interact within them. His work traces the institutions and currents of power that shape urban space, and the ways those forces take physical form in buildings and city plans.

His research centers on colonial architecture, sustainability, social justice, and cultural identity as expressed through design. This is history with present-day stakes. His analysis carries into contemporary urban design and environmental policy, and his lectures and writing are cited in urban policy and environmental studies as well as in design journals.

## Inside the ten-day course

Muzaffar uses the idea of the "design system" to analyze architecture and urban form from the ancient world to the present. The course is organized around five threads:

1. **Designing with environment and materials.** The sustainable building strategies of ancient civilizations, and how materials circulated in ways suited to the local climate.
2. **Infrastructure and power.** What the water systems, transportation networks, and methods of organizing labor in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Rome mean for urban design today.
3. **Non-Western modernities.** The many forms of modernity found along the Silk Road, in Buddhist architecture, and in the cities of Latin America.
4. **Design and inequality.** Making visible the power structures embedded in housing, zoning, and public space.
5. **From history to the future.** Drawing on past design solutions to devise creative responses to today's sustainability problems.

Every day includes team research, as students build an analysis of a single historical design case. On the final day, they turn that work into a research poster and present it to Muzaffar and their classmates.

![Muzaffar points toward a projected black-and-white photograph labeled "Charlotte Perriand in chaise-longue, 1929"](/editorial/224171113832-06.jpg "Muzaffar lecturing on the history of modern design")

## From a research question to a poster and paper

Typical projects fall into areas such as these, each shown with an example of the kind of question students pursue:

| Research area | Example question |
|---|---|
| Traditional building systems as a response to the climate crisis | What can the underground stepwells of Rajasthan, India, offer a world facing water shortages? |
| Power and urban design | How does the radial boulevard system of Paris relate to structures of surveillance and control? |
| Sustainable materials, past and present | Could traditional mud-brick construction help reduce carbon emissions? |
| Network-based design systems | How did the circulation of knowledge and goods among Silk Road cities shape urban planning? |

The work goes beyond simple observation. Students turn their analysis into visual diagrams and system maps built from real urban data. With feedback from Muzaffar, they then develop it into a finished academic poster and paper.

## Who the course suits

The course is an especially good fit for:

- Students who want to tackle social problems through cities, architecture, and design
- Students drawn to interdisciplinary thinking that crosses the arts, humanities, and social sciences
- International-school high school students considering a major in architecture or design
- Students who hope to contribute to urban policy, environmental design, or design for social justice

Participants come away with more than architectural knowledge. They build design thinking grounded in historical insight, along with a polished piece of research that reflects their own point of view. Because the class meets in person in Seoul, feedback from the professor is close and intensive, and the finished poster and paper give students a substantial project to feature in their college application portfolio.

Muzaffar's course was part of CRI's Seoul Research Program, where visiting professors teach small groups in person. To see the faculty and courses planned for upcoming cohorts, visit the [Seoul and Global Research Programs page](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Testing finance theory on real market data with Cambridge's Michael Ashby
excerpt: In his course for the 2026 Seoul Research Program, Cambridge economist Michael Ashby has students test asset pricing, ESG, and behavioral finance ideas on real market data, then write and present a team research paper.
content:
When the Federal Reserve announces a rate hike, do financial stocks and tech stocks react the same way? Do companies with high ESG scores actually earn better returns over the long run? Questions like these drive the empirical finance course Cambridge economist Michael Ashby designed for CRI's 2026 Seoul Research Program. Students learn the theory, work with real market data, and find out in a team research paper whether the theory holds.

## Who teaches it

Michael Ashby teaches economics at the University of Cambridge, where he is also a deputy director of admissions at one of the university's colleges. Because he helps select and advise students as well as teach them, he is an unusually well-placed mentor for high school students who hope to study at a selective university.

His research sits where financial markets meet econometrics. He analyzes asset markets, measures risk, evaluates policy, and uses causal inference to study the questions behind real financial decisions. A central thread is measuring and forecasting uncertainty in the financial system, work with practical uses for policy institutions, investment firms, and academic researchers.

At Cambridge, his teaching centers on financial econometrics and empirical asset pricing. He is known for moving students past theory toward an understanding of how real markets and real data behave. The Seoul Research Program extends that teaching to students in Asia.

## What the course covers

Empirical finance puts every theory to one test: does it survive contact with the data? Professor Ashby's course builds toward that test in four stages.

1. **Core concepts.** Students learn the structure of financial markets, the theory of market efficiency, and the main asset pricing models, including the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) and multifactor models.
2. **Quantitative tools.** Using regression and panel data analysis, students learn to study asset prices, risk, and investor behavior, practicing on real financial datasets along the way.
3. **ESG, climate risk, and behavioral finance.** The course examines how environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors and climate risk affect asset prices, and it tests the influence of investor psychology and other behavioral factors with data.
4. **The research project.** Each team chooses a topic and writes one paper built on its own empirical analysis. The work moves from a first draft through analysis and feedback to a poster and a final presentation.

Professor Ashby leads the entire course in person in Seoul. Alongside the daily lectures, he gives students detailed feedback and close mentoring.

![A hand holds a smartphone showing a candlestick price chart in front of a laptop displaying stock charts](/editorial/224170054306-03.jpg "Market price data is the raw material students learn to analyze.")

## Sample research topics

Team papers grow out of questions like these:

| Research area | Example question |
| --- | --- |
| Climate risk and asset prices | How did share prices in particular industries move after a carbon tax was announced? |
| ESG scores and stock returns | Do companies with high ESG scores really earn higher long-term returns? |
| Policy announcements and market reactions | How did Federal Reserve rate-hike announcements affect financial stocks compared with technology stocks? |
| Behavioral finance | How does investor overconfidence drive stock market volatility? |
| Sustainable investing strategies | How do ESG ETFs perform against conventional ETFs? |

Every one of these topics rests on empirical analysis of real financial data, so the papers call for university-level structure and analytical depth. At the end of the course, teams present their findings on posters in the style of an academic poster session and receive final feedback from Professor Ashby.

## Who the course suits

The Seoul Research Program is built so that students preparing for selective US universities can complete a research paper under a professor's guidance. Professor Ashby's course is open to any high school student interested in economics, finance, data analysis, or policy analysis, and it is an especially good fit for students who:

- want to connect financial theory with how real markets behave
- are drawn to current topics such as ESG, behavioral economics, and financial crises
- want to learn quantitative analysis or data-driven writing
- plan to study economics or finance, or are still exploring the field

## What students take away

Rather than simply passing on theory, the course has students handle real data, analyze a problem, and reach insights of their own. By the end, they have:

- **Analytical skills** built on real financial data
- **Firsthand experience of the full research cycle**, from planning and analysis to writing and presenting
- **Rigorous, finished research**, completed with feedback from a Cambridge professor
- **A co-authored research paper and a poster** they can draw on in college applications

This is research, not a camp or a workshop: students complete a real study alongside a professor from a leading university, and the work can outlast the summer. Some Seoul Research Program alumni have kept collaborating with their professors after starting college, building research portfolios of their own.

Professor Ashby's course was one of the faculty-led tracks in the 2026 Seoul Research Program, where small groups work directly with visiting professors from US and UK universities. To see how the summer cohorts run and which tracks are open now, explore the [Seoul and Global Research Programs](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Climate research with NASA satellite data, guided by Columbia's George Tselioudis
excerpt: How NASA climate scientist and Columbia professor George Tselioudis teaches students to analyze satellite cloud data, build a simple climate model, and write a group research paper.
content:
What happens to temperature and rainfall under different greenhouse gas emission scenarios, or if renewable energy spreads faster? In George Tselioudis's course in CRI's Seoul Research Program, students don't just read about questions like these. They work with real NASA satellite observations of clouds and radiation, build a simple climate model of their own, run greenhouse gas scenarios through it, and write up what they find as a group research paper.

## Who teaches it

George Tselioudis is a senior research scientist at the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) and a professor in Columbia University's Department of Applied Physics and Applied Mathematics. He leads a team that combines observations with climate model simulations to study clouds, radiation, changes in precipitation, and radiative feedbacks.

Satellite data analysis and climate modeling are his specialties. He has used the GISS coupled atmosphere-ocean model to simulate and analyze long-term climate change, and he has been active in international climate research, serving as an author of the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). In 2004 the American Geophysical Union recognized his work with the **Charles S. Falkenberg Award**.

![George Tselioudis gestures as he speaks, set against the columns of a Columbia University library building and the university's crown logo](/editorial/224165437067-01.jpg "George Tselioudis, NASA GISS senior research scientist and Columbia University professor")

## What the course covers

The course moves from atmospheric physics to the satellite data researchers use to study it, and then to models students build themselves:

- **Cloud and radiation physics.** Professor Tselioudis's lectures cover the basics of cloud particles and atmospheric radiative processes, and how they shape the climate system.
- **Reading satellite data.** Students analyze actual NASA satellite observations of cloud and radiation properties in the atmosphere, and learn how to use that data to evaluate climate models.
- **Designing a climate model.** As a hands-on exercise, students build a simple climate model, feed it human-driven greenhouse gas scenarios, and predict how temperature or precipitation might change.
- **Lectures paired with workshops.** Every class combines theory with small-group data analysis. Each day includes a live session in which the professor explains the concepts, followed by an assignment analyzing real data.
- **A group research paper.** Teams choose a research topic, carry out the data analysis and simulations, and write up their results as an academic paper. They then present the draft and revise it.

## From first lecture to symposium

The course unfolds in three stages, each building on the last:

| Stage | What students do |
| --- | --- |
| Foundations | Introductory lectures on the underlying theory |
| Workshops | Small-group sessions analyzing real satellite data |
| Team research | Group projects that develop into the final research paper |

It ends with a symposium-style session where students present the posters and papers they created together. By then they have learned the core concepts, worked with real data, and built a research paper one step at a time.

## What students research

Students pursue research individually or in small groups, starting from their own interests. Once the theory is in place, a team might use NASA satellite data to investigate climate anomalies such as extreme heat or shifts in rainfall, or build a project that forecasts regional weather patterns. Others design climate policy scenarios and model the future climate under assumptions such as changes in greenhouse gas emissions or a faster expansion of renewable energy.

Along the way, students build practical research skills such as statistical analysis and scientific writing, and their results become the starting point for lively discussion of climate issues.

Climate work in the Seoul Research Program can also reach readers outside the classroom. In another class, one student co-authored a climate policy piece with their professor that was published on the official blog of the University of Pennsylvania's Kleinman Center for Energy Policy. That student's story is on our [Student Success](/success/climate-finance-paper-penn-law-stanford-admit) page.

## Who the course suits

The course is a strong fit for students interested in environmental science, physics, data science, or policy. It is designed mainly for high school students in Grade 9 and above, and participants are selected for genuine intellectual curiosity and commitment.

Classes are in person, and students are mentored directly by faculty from leading universities such as MIT, Harvard, and Caltech. During the program's short, intensive research period, they experience the research process firsthand, learning to plan a study, analyze data, and write a paper, and they finish with a completed research paper written under the professor's guidance.

Professor Tselioudis's course is one of the faculty-led tracks in the Seoul Research Program, which is built so that students preparing for selective US universities can complete a research paper with a professor. To see how the summer cohorts run and which tracks are open, explore the [Seoul and Global Research Programs](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: How research experience shows up on the Common App
excerpt: What to enter in each Common App Activities field for a research project, how program records shape a professor's letter, and what Publications sections ask about your contribution.
content:
If everyone does research now, why do the results look so different? Read enough applications to selective universities and many files begin to blur together: strong grades, a long list of extracurriculars, service, maybe an internship. On the surface, nobody looks short of anything.

Admissions officers don't read by counting, though. What matters more than the number of activities is where an experience is recorded in the application and how it is read in context. Two students can both list "research" and be read very differently: for one, it registers as just another extracurricular; for the other, as real research experience.

The gap rarely comes from how impressive the result sounds. It comes from how the research was carried out, who supervised it, and how deeply the student engaged. So before treating research as a nice thing to have, it pays to understand where it fits in an application: the Activities section, recommendation letters, and Publications sections.

## The Activities section: what goes in each field

Many students and parents assume that simply having done research helps. On the application, how you describe it counts for far more than the fact that you did it.

The Common App asks applicants to list activities in order of importance and fill in several fields for each. The first is the activity type, and a student who did research through a CRI program can choose **Research**. The fields that follow are where the real work begins.

| Common App field | Limit | What to enter for a research project |
|---|---|---|
| Activity type | Drop-down menu | Research |
| Position/Leadership description | 50 characters | The role you actually held, not "Participant" |
| Organization Name | 100 characters | The institution where the research took place (CRI), not the program name |
| Description | 150 characters | The topic, the method, your role and what you produced |
| Participation grade levels | Check boxes | The grade or grades in which you did the work |
| Timing of participation | Check boxes | "During school break" for a summer or winter program |

### Position: name your real role

The position line can show where you stood within the research. For example:

- Research Team Member
- Research Team Leader
- First Author (where it applies)

When more than one is true, you can combine them, as in "Research Team Leader, First Author of the Paper."

### Description: 150 characters of actual research

This is the field students agonize over. It should describe the research itself, not the fact that you joined a program. Try to cover four things:

1. What the research was about
2. How you analyzed the data or ran the experiments
3. What your role was
4. What you produced at the end

CRI research follows a set arc under faculty supervision: choose a topic, form a hypothesis, design a method, and turn the results into a finished paper. That arc is what you can fit into 150 characters. The reader no longer sees "attended a program over break." They see a student who pursued one question over a sustained period, did the research, and wrote up and submitted the results.

The difference between two research experiences, then, doesn't come from a program's name. It comes from what you can put in each box. CRI designs its research so that when it ends, students have more than a story they might tell someday: they have experience they can transfer directly onto the application.

## Recommendation letters: written from records, not memory

If the Activities section shows what a student did, the recommendation letter shows how someone who watched the work judges it. Of everything an admissions officer reads, it is also the one document written by a third party rather than the student.

CRI structures its programs so that letters don't rest on a professor's memory alone. While the research is under way, professors and TAs record their assessment of each student at every stage, both in class and throughout the project. The record begins with attendance and basic participation, then follows a set of predefined questions:

- What questions did the student raise when choosing a research topic?
- How did they understand and act on feedback?
- How did they respond when the research stalled?
- What role did they take on within the team?
- How did they grow and change while completing the paper?

These notes aren't pieced together after the fact to support a letter. They work more like a running record of how the student thinks and behaves as a researcher.

So when a student later asks for a letter, the professor isn't writing from a vague impression. They can draw on specific moments and decisions preserved in the record. The letter that results centers on what the student actually did and decided during the research, rather than on abstract descriptions of character. The project and role summarized in Activities come back into focus, this time through someone else's eyes.

This is why research carries weight in an application: the activity entry, the letter, and any later evidence of academic work connect into one continuous account instead of standing apart.

For how to make the request itself, see our separate guide to asking a professor for a recommendation letter on the [CRI blog](/blog).

## Publications sections: where the work itself can be checked

Activities and letters explain what research a student did. Some applications go a step further and ask for material that lets readers examine the results directly. The clearest example is the Publications or Pre-prints section found in graduate school applications and in some applications to the most selective undergraduate programs.

This section isn't simply an invitation to list any paper you have. The questions it asks are specific:

- What is the paper's title?
- Which journal or scholarly platform was it submitted to?
- Is it peer-reviewed, or a pre-print?
- Is there a DOI or another link where it can be read?
- Most important of all: what did you contribute?

It is less a place to show off results than a place to explain your contribution. Two real application forms show what this looks like. One asks for the title, the authors, a DOI, the venue, and whether the paper is peer-reviewed, non-peer-reviewed or unpublished, followed by a description of your contribution, contact details for a professor who can confirm it, and an uploaded copy. Another gives each paper a date, the journal and article title, a DOI or full web address, and 200 characters for your contribution, and asks sole authors to say so.

For students who completed a paper through CRI, this section is more than a box to fill. The topic and role summarized in Activities return here in more concrete form, and the Contribution field is where you spell out:

- how you framed the research question
- which analyses or experiments you carried out yourself
- what you did in interpreting the data and writing the paper

Not every applicant needs a paper just because the section exists. But if you have a paper or other research output, the application will try to confirm that experience far more directly than Activities or letters can. That is why many forms ask for the supervising professor's name and contact details: the point is less to prove that a paper exists than to check that the research was genuinely supervised and verified.

At CRI, the whole research process runs under a professor's supervision, and both the research record and each student's contribution are clearly documented. When a section like this appears, students don't need to dress anything up. They can simply report the facts as they are.

## Three sections, one story

In the end, what sets one research experience apart from another isn't simply whether there is a paper. It is how the same work is:

- **summarized** in the Activities section
- **vouched for** in a recommendation letter
- **checked** in a Publications section

When all three tell the same story, research becomes the most persuasive academic narrative in the application.

If you are planning research with applications in mind, [CRI's research programs](/research) take students from a faculty-guided question to a finished paper, keeping a clear record of each student's role along the way.
author: CRI Editorial

title: From storyboard to premiere: directing a short film with USC's James Savoca
excerpt: Each student develops, shoots, and edits a three- to five-minute film, then screens it at a class premiere for notes from Savoca, whose feature Sleepwalk was selected for SXSW.
content:
Most filmmakers remember the first time their own work played on a screen in front of an audience. Few get that moment in high school. James Savoca's summer directing course with CRI builds toward it: students take a film of their own from first idea to finished cut, then watch it play for the class and hear what a working director thinks.

## An independent filmmaker who teaches at USC

Savoca is a directing professor at the University of Southern California's School of Cinematic Arts, with more than 20 years of experience directing films and writing plays. He began off-Broadway in New York and went on to build a reputation in American independent film with features such as *Sleepwalk*, which was selected for SXSW, and *Around June*. His films have also found wider audiences on Amazon Prime and Showtime.

At USC he has taught a range of directing courses, among them Production I, Directing Techniques, and Acting for Film & Television, and he designed a creative curriculum of his own, Lateral Thinking for Filmmaking. He has also taught directing and storytelling in Saudi Arabia, China, and San Francisco, and brings that international experience to the classroom as both a teacher and a filmmaker.

## Three stages, one short film

The course treats directing as both an art and a craft, and it pushes each student to tell a story from their own point of view. It unfolds in three stages.

1. **A workshop on the essentials.** The course opens with intensive lectures and hands-on practice in the core elements of directing: story structure, visual language, scene composition, and directing actors. Students break down scenes from existing films and try short shooting exercises, learning each element by using it.
2. **A personal short, developed step by step.** Each student builds a concept for a three- to five-minute short film around an idea of their own, then develops it into a storyboard, a shooting plan, and a strategy for directing the actors. In one-on-one feedback sessions, Savoca works through the story's structure, its thematic depth, and how the film will be directed.
3. **Shooting, editing, and a premiere.** Later in the course, students shoot their films and move into post-production. Finished cuts are screened at an in-class premiere, where Savoca and classmates give each film detailed feedback. Students finish with a polished piece for their portfolio.

![Professor Savoca, in a patterned white shirt and blue cap, stands in a classroom with three people who each hold up a handwritten note](/editorial/224164063133-03.jpg "Savoca with members of the program after class")

## What students have made

Students in the course have taken creative, real-world questions and turned them into films and written research. Two projects show the range:

- ***Moving Pictures, Moving Forward*** is a video essay on how the way people watch films has changed with technology. It looks at where traditional theaters, streaming, and VR content meet, and it reframes cinema around the audience's experience.
- ***Lights, Camera, Algorithm*** is a research video on how adopting AI in filmmaking affects budgets, creative work, and diversity. Using *The Eternaut* and Staircase Studio as case studies, it extends the analysis to the wider film industry.

Other students have tried short narrative films, experimental films, and interview documentaries. Some have entered their work in international youth film festivals, and others have used it in their portfolios for college applications.

![Professor Savoca gives a thumbs-up beside four members of the program in front of a gray tiled wall](/editorial/224164063133-02.jpg "Savoca with members of the summer program")

## Who the course suits

Savoca's course is a strong fit for students who:

- Are drawn to storytelling, film, or video directing
- Want training in turning ideas into images
- Are preparing to apply to universities known for film and media arts, such as USC, NYU, and UCLA
- Want to complete a portfolio piece shaped by a working director's feedback

Students go through the whole filmmaking process, from planning and directing to shooting and editing. They come away with a deeper understanding of film language and a finished film. The larger question the course asks is not how to make a video, but how to show the world the story you want to tell.

Savoca taught this course as part of CRI's summer research program, where students work directly with faculty from leading universities. To see how the summer cohorts are structured and which tracks are open, explore the [Seoul and Global Research Programs](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Designing global institutions with Penn law professor William Burke-White
excerpt: How do you keep one veto from undercutting UN sanctions? In William Burke-White's course, student teams design a new treaty or international organization to tackle a global problem, from climate change to the control of AI.
content:
How do you keep one veto from undercutting UN sanctions? What legal design would draw private money into climate projects? Students in William Burke-White's course take on questions like these, and in team projects they approach them the way institution builders do: by designing the organization or treaty that could address the problem.

Burke-White, a professor of law at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, has spent his career where international law meets foreign policy, both in academia and in government. He is one of the faculty mentors for CRI's 2026 Seoul Research Program.

## A law professor who has worked inside foreign policy

Burke-White graduated from Harvard University, earned a master's degree in international relations at the University of Cambridge, and received his J.D. from Harvard Law School. Since then he has stayed active in international human rights and in efforts to reform international organizations.

![William Burke-White, in a blue blazer and open-collared white shirt, stands outside a brick and stone building next to a small garden](/editorial/224162761170-02.jpg "William Burke-White teaches international law at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School.")

His work has never been confined to the classroom. During the Obama administration he served on the State Department's Policy Planning Staff, where he advised on international law, took a direct part in shaping US foreign policy, and led strategy work related to the United Nations and the International Criminal Court (ICC). That experience shapes his teaching, which goes past theory to show how diplomacy and international politics actually play out.

His research moves across international law, human rights law, global governance, and foreign policy. Three themes run through it: how international institutions should be designed and reformed, how international law can be enforced more effectively, and how emerging powers take part in the international order.

## A course built around designing institutions

Burke-White's course is about designing international institutions to solve global problems, and it is project based. Instead of stopping at a theoretical understanding of world affairs, students work through the practical steps of building an institution and proposing policy. The course draws on law, international politics, economics, and development studies, and it asks students to think like the architects of international institutions and like diplomatic strategists.

It runs in three parts.

### 1. Core concepts and case studies

The opening sessions lay the groundwork: the history and main types of international institutions, including the UN, the WTO, the IMF, and the ICC. Through real cases, students examine how each one was designed and where it has succeeded or failed. Burke-White adds stories from his own time on the Policy Planning Staff, a view of what these institutions can and cannot do that students will not find in a textbook.

### 2. Team projects on global issues

Each team then picks a global problem, such as climate change, refugees, international human rights, global health crises, or the regulation of technology and international control of artificial intelligence. The team's task is to design a new international organization or treaty to address that problem, working in four stages:

1. Define the problem.
2. Analyze the institutions that already exist.
3. Design a mechanism that could solve it.
4. Plan how the new institution would be put into practice.

One-on-one feedback from Burke-White and a midpoint presentation move each design, step by step, toward a finished policy proposal.

### 3. Policy report and final presentation

At the end of the course, each team presents its design as a formal policy report and an academic poster. Burke-White gives feedback against a demanding standard: reasoning and structure sound enough to be adopted on the international stage. In the process, students get hands-on practice with the formats of real diplomatic documents and communication.

## What students have written

Students who have taken Burke-White's course with CRI have produced strong papers on real problems in international law and global governance, and a number of them have gone on to publish in international journals or compete in global research competitions. A sample of their topics:

- **Reforming UN Security Council sanctions (K.).** How rivalry among the permanent members and abuse of the veto weaken international sanctions, with proposed institutional reforms to bring sanctions back under multilateral coordination.
- **US–China rivalry and international organizations (C.).** The structural instability that China's rise and its conflict with the United States create for international organizations, including paralysis at the Security Council, with a comparison of possible remedies.
- **Climate agreements and non-state actors (S.).** The role of city governments, NGOs, and other non-state actors in implementing the Paris Agreement, using the C40 Cities network to set out practical policy mechanisms.
- **Public–private cooperation in climate finance.** How public finance can lower the risks of private investment, with a legal design that brings in new international investment law and the concept of Climate Clubs.
- **Why states comply with UN sanctions (Y.).** The legal, diplomatic, and political factors that decide compliance, drawn from the cases of Libya, North Korea, and Iraq, and an argument for structural reform.
- **Enforcing the rulings of regional human rights courts (M.).** A comparison of successful systems in Europe and the Americas with the challenges facing Asia, and practical strategies for strengthening regional human rights institutions.
- **Cooperation between the UN General Assembly and the Security Council (S.).** A fresh look at the General Assembly's role in keeping the peace and responding to crises, with concrete proposals for cooperation, including a Joint Crisis Council.
- **International governance of GMOs (K.).** A comparison of how the United States, Kenya, and India regulate genetically modified organisms, and a look at how legal harmonization could pull fragmented global rules together.

Each student began from a question of their own and built research that reflects how international politics and institutional design work in practice. Work like this can become a stepping stone to further study and to a career in global affairs.

## Who the course is for

The goal is not to absorb theory but to build the ability to design and propose institutional solutions to real international problems. The course is a particularly good fit for students who:

- are considering careers in international organizations such as the UN, the ICC, or the WTO, or in diplomacy
- want to go deep on international politics, international law, international human rights, or climate policy
- want to build policy thinking and structural problem-solving skills together
- are curious about how institutions are designed, and how their decisions are enforced, in real diplomacy

Students come away able to analyze a problem closely and work out legal and institutional solutions. They also leave with a substantial piece of self-directed work to show when they apply to university programs in international relations, law, or public policy.

For students who like to define an international problem for themselves and then work out how to solve it, Burke-White's class offers an intellectual challenge that crosses the line between scholarship and practice. Courses like his run in the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp), where visiting faculty from US and UK universities work with small groups of students in person.
author: CRI Editorial

title: From campaign ads to hotel linens: game theory research with UChicago's Ryan Fang
excerpt: Inside Ryan Fang's decision-making course, and four student papers that used game theory to model hotel incentives, campaign media, upcycled art and North Korean deterrence.
content:
How should a hotel persuade guests to skip a fresh set of sheets? Should a candidate spend campaign money on cable and radio, or on posts built to be clicked and shared? What could make deterrence fail on the Korean Peninsula? Students have taken on each of these questions in research sessions with Professor Ryan Fang of the University of Chicago, turning everyday puzzles and front-page issues into formal game-theory models.

## An economist who models decisions

Fang is an economist whose teaching centers on game theory and information economics, fields that study how people, companies and governments choose when the outcome depends on what others do and on what each side knows. His own work uses mathematical modeling to study market behavior and strategic decision-making.

In practice, that means describing a real situation in terms of its players, their options and what each stands to gain, then solving the model to see which strategies hold up. The same method runs through his course and through the student papers described below.

![Ryan Fang, wearing glasses and a black T-shirt, gestures as he speaks in front of wooden bookshelves](/editorial/224161617621-01.jpg "Ryan Fang of the University of Chicago guides students through research in economics and game theory.")

## Inside the course

Fang's course for the 2026 Seoul Research Program is about decision-making in the real world. It covers the mathematical, data-driven tools needed to analyze problems in markets, business and technology, and public policy. Students study topics such as auction theory and market design, then put them to work in team projects built on cases and datasets that Fang supplies. A team might design an auction mechanism, for example, or analyze a social system that has to balance fairness against efficiency.

The syllabus mixes lectures, seminars, problem-based learning and group discussion, and students connect the theory to hands-on data-analysis projects. The work is demanding, asking for advanced mathematical reasoning and practical problem-solving at once, and the course is research-driven throughout.

## Four student papers

Students who have done research with Fang chose their own topics, each one linking rigorous theory to a real-world problem, and wrote full research papers. Classes were driven by discussion, and Fang gave close, detailed feedback as each analysis took shape. Some of that work has gone on to appear in international journals. Four papers show the range.

### Hotel housekeeping as an incentive problem

In *To Change Linen or Go Green*, Y. examined hotel housekeeping strategy through the lens of information economics. The paper looks at how a hotel designs incentives that steer guests' choices, locates the balance point between what the service costs and what guests believe it is worth, and proposes a model that weighs sustainability and economic viability together. The story of how Y. built that model is on our [Student Success](/success/hotel-linen-screening-economics-paper-nyu-early-decision) page.

### Clicks versus cable in a political race

J. and L. used game theory to model how campaigns divide their resources between traditional media and social media in *Campaign Media Strategy: Clicks and Reposts vs Cable and Radio*. Modeling the contest between rival candidates, they solved for a **mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium**, a stable outcome in which each candidate keeps their choices unpredictable and neither can do better by changing course. From there they worked out the strategic value of each platform and how each candidate should respond to the other.

### Upcycled art and what buyers will pay

C. and W. asked how the idea of upcycling affects what consumers are willing to pay for art. Their paper, *How does this increase Pricing and Consumers' Willingness to Pay in the Art Market?*, approaches the question through **signaling theory** and **screening models**, two ways of analyzing markets in which buyers and sellers hold different information. The paper develops pricing strategies aimed at consumers who place value on environmental benefits, and identifies the conditions under which an artist's expected utility is maximized.

### Deterrence on the Korean Peninsula

K. turned to regional security in *Structural Vulnerabilities and Deterrence Failure: A Game Theory Analysis of Potential North Korean Invasion*. The paper analyzes North Korea's military provocations and the threats they pose to Northeast Asia, discusses why deterrence is so difficult to sustain, and weighs possible policy responses. K. structured the strategic interaction among the United States, South Korea and North Korea as a multiplayer game, which made for a particularly sophisticated study.

Taken together, the papers show students doing more than absorbing theory. They took complicated real-world problems and modeled them, and Fang's guidance gave them a genuine research experience.

## Who the course suits

The course is open to any student interested in mathematics, computer science, economics or data science. It is especially rewarding for students who want to understand how financial markets, public systems or the technology industry are structured, and for anyone who wants to work through a complex problem using real data.

Students come away with stronger mathematical reasoning and data-driven decision-making skills, along with the ability to present their problem-solving in academic form. Completing a research project with Fang can also strengthen a student's US college applications and help clarify a future path in research.

Fang's course is part of the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp), where small groups of students work in person with visiting professors from US and UK universities. If one of these questions sounds like something you would want to model yourself, that page explains how the summer programs work.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Startup thinking, MIT-style: entrepreneurship research with Kit Hickey
