excerpt: MIT Sloan's Kit Hickey, co-founder of Ministry of Supply, guides student teams through the 24-step Disciplined Entrepreneurship framework, from customer segments to a final pitch.
content:
Kit Hickey teaches entrepreneurship from experience. While studying at MIT, she co-founded Ministry of Supply, a technology-driven fashion startup whose shirts, made with NASA technology, wick away sweat and help regulate temperature. Today she teaches at the MIT Sloan School of Management, and in CRI's Seoul Research Program she walks student teams through the same step-by-step process founders use to turn an idea into a company.

## A founder in the classroom

Hickey ran Ministry of Supply successfully for several years. The shirts drew wide attention, and the company is still actively in business in the US. That experience shapes how she teaches. Her classes focus on the strategies and ways of thinking that founders actually need, organized around **Disciplined Entrepreneurship**, a 24-step framework developed at MIT. Step by step, it shows how a startup idea grows into a business and what it takes for that business to succeed in the market.

For Hickey, a startup is never just "a good idea." It is a system in which market analysis, customer understanding, fundraising, team building, and execution all depend on one another. Her course is designed so that students work through each stage of that system in order, practicing entrepreneurial thinking rather than just reading about it.

Her teaching style is warm and approachable, so students feel free to float ideas and form teams to explore the whole journey of launching a venture. Many students have said afterward that, for the first time, starting a company felt personal to them.

## What the course covers

The course, **"Innovation, Entrepreneurship, and Management: A Comprehensive Guide to Venture Creation,"** puts the 24-step Disciplined Entrepreneurship model, MIT's signature approach to entrepreneurship education, into practice. It centers on six topics:

- Market segmentation and customer analysis
- Product development and minimum viable product (MVP) design
- Building a business model
- Fundraising strategy and attracting investment
- Team building and organizational design
- Entrepreneurial storytelling and pitch strategy

Each day combines lectures and workshops on the core concepts, and a team project lets students apply them. Teams go well beyond proposing a business idea: they carry out market research, customer interviews, product design, and revenue-model analysis themselves. By the end, each team has written a report in the form of a research paper and designed a poster that presents its findings. The posters are shared at a poster session on the program's final day.

## From customer research to a research paper

In the team projects, a startup idea becomes the subject of research. Each team defines a real or hypothetical business opportunity, segments potential customers to pin down the problem worth solving, and designs a product and business model to fit. Customer research and market validation show students how the theory holds up once it meets real conditions.

![Students work on laptops at desks in a bright classroom](/editorial/224159932106-03.jpg "Students at work during the Seoul Research Program.")

Projects can also step back to study how the startup world works. In the 2025 Seoul Research Program, one team studied how venture-backed startups exit, in a paper titled **"From IPO to M&A: Analyzing the Strategic Shift in VC Exit Dynamics."** Working from ten years of data on the US IPO market, the students traced how it had changed and used correlations with a range of economic indicators to explain the rise of SPACs and M&A as exit routes. They also examined how founders use IPOs and M&A as strategies, connecting those choices to investment flexibility and market uncertainty.

Projects like this teach students to read real trends in the startup world and build strategy from data, approaching entrepreneurship and management as an academic subject. The finished poster is also a practical result: students can add it to their college application portfolio as a record of their research.

## Beyond the summer

For some students, the summer course is only the beginning. In the SRP Extension, a continuation track after the Seoul Research Program, Hickey helps students develop an idea from the summer into a business model, working through market research, customer segmentation, revenue design, and a pitch deck.

In summer 2025, one of her students, J., completed a paper with her called **"The Power of Mismatch: How Incongruous Pairings Drive Ad Effectiveness,"** which examined how mismatched pairings can make advertising more effective. The logical reasoning and data analysis he practiced in that research led him to a new question: could the same way of thinking work in sports, a field he loves? The result was a statistics app for amateur basketball leagues, launched first in Korea, which he has developed further in the Extension with an eye on the US market. His story is on our [Student Success](/success/research-paper-to-sports-data-startup) page.

## Who the course is for

Any student interested in entrepreneurship, business strategy, economics, data analysis, or marketing can take on this course. No prior startup experience is needed. In fact, teams that mix students from different backgrounds are a key part of the learning.

The course trains students not only to come up with an idea but to shape it, systematically, into a business that could actually run. Along the way they build logical reasoning, empirical analysis, teamwork, and communication skills. For students who have long been curious about startups, it is a valuable chance to test that curiosity alongside an MIT faculty member who has built a company herself.

Professor Hickey's course runs in the Seoul Research Program, CRI's in-person summer program where visiting professors from leading universities teach small groups. To see how the summer cohorts are structured and which courses are open, visit the [Seoul and Global Research Programs](/research/summer-camp) page.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Do professors really mentor every student? How CRI chooses its faculty
excerpt: Graduate students often get just an hour or two of advising a week. Here is how CRI selects its faculty and fixes four points where professors must step into each student's research.
content:
"Will the professor really work with each student?" Many parents and students ask CRI exactly this, and it is a fair question. Anyone familiar with university research knows that professors are stretched thin, that labs are full of graduate students, and that "mentoring" means something different in every program. So rather than sidestep the question, let's start with it.

## The doubt is well founded

The data bears this out. A 2024 research-environment survey by the student council at KAIST, one of Korea's leading research universities, found that professors spend only about one to two hours a week, on average, directly advising each graduate student. One-on-one time is especially scarce:

| Weekly one-on-one time with an advisor | Share of respondents |
| --- | --- |
| No individual meetings | 15.6% |
| Under 15 minutes | 25.4% |
| 15 to 30 minutes | 23.1% |
| 30 to 45 minutes | 17.1% |
| 45 to 60 minutes | 8.5% |
| An hour or more | 9.6% |

*Source: KAIST student council, 2024 Research Environment Survey (all respondents).*

Group meetings add some time, with the most common answers falling between 30 minutes and an hour and a half a week, but 12.8% of respondents said they had no group meetings at all. Asked whether their advisor devotes enough time to advising them, about half (50.2%) agreed, and 23.4% disagreed.

None of this means professors are careless. Quite the opposite. They are juggling research, teaching, administration, peer review and conference work at the same time, and the system simply leaves little room to give each student enough attention. That leads many families to a sensible follow-up: if this is how much guidance graduate students get, can research by high school or undergraduate students really work? Asking that isn't cynicism. It's realism.

## CRI starts from that reality

CRI doesn't wave the question away. It designed its programs with this data as the starting assumption.

The way CRI sees it, the problem isn't a professor's enthusiasm. It's the structure that decides where a professor's time actually goes. So instead of telling families that "the professor will do their best," CRI first builds a structure in which the professor's involvement isn't optional.

## What faculty mentoring means in the Seoul Research Program

In CRI's Seoul Research Program (SRP), faculty mentoring isn't a matter of attitude or good intentions. It is a designed system, with clear roles, clear responsibilities and fixed points at which the professor steps in. Three principles define it.

### 1. The professor leads the research, not just the lectures

At CRI, a professor is not simply someone who gives lectures. The professor acts as the research lead, or principal investigator (PI): shaping the direction of the project with the students and helping turn a student's curiosity into a genuine academic research question.

TAs play a supporting role, but the core feedback and the key judgment calls belong to the professor. That division of roles is set from the very beginning. For more on how this works day to day, two companion pieces on the [CRI blog](/blog) hear from SRP professors about how they teach and profile the TA mentors who work alongside them.

### 2. Faculty checkpoints are built into the program

Faculty mentoring at CRI does not work on a "we'll take a look when there's time" basis. The program formally schedules four stages at which the professor must be involved:

1. **Setting the research question**
2. **Feedback on the interim report**
3. **Reviewing the structure and content of the final paper**
4. **Completing the final outputs, the paper and the poster**

Because these checkpoints are written into the program itself, faculty involvement doesn't depend on goodwill or favors.

### 3. Only faculty who will put their name on the work

A letter of recommendation isn't something just any professor can write. It is only possible when the professor can honestly say, "I supervised this student myself."

That is why CRI does not work with professors who would have no real basis for saying they mentored a student, or who can't make the time. CRI selects its faculty for accountability, not name recognition.

## Why the faculty roster stays stable

SRP's faculty doesn't turn over wholesale from one year to the next. Instead, CRI:

- works long-term with professors who have met its standards,
- refines the program structure with them based on their actual mentoring experience, and
- keeps partnerships in which faculty can take responsibility for student research all the way to the end.

That stability isn't the product of personal connections. It is what happens when a program is designed around standards.

## What the structure changes for students

The difference shows up in the results:

- Stronger, more fully developed student-led papers
- Posters accepted at academic conferences
- Recommendation letters with specific detail
- Opportunities for follow-up research and research assistant (RA) positions

In admissions, what matters is less what you did than how well you can explain it. CRI's faculty mentoring structure is what makes that explanation possible.

## The right question to ask

"Will the professor really work with each student?" is exactly the question families should ask. CRI answers it with structure rather than promises. It doesn't invite every professor, and it doesn't accept every student, and that is why the results are different.

To see how professors and students work together in practice, explore the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: How language is learned and taught: a research course with Oxford's Victoria Murphy
excerpt: Does learning in more than one language make students more flexible thinkers? In a course led by the head of Oxford's Department of Education, teams investigate questions like this through interviews, surveys, and a literature review.
content:
Why does the same teaching method work in one classroom and fall flat in the next? Can a lesson be designed to build systematic thinking rather than rote memorization? Questions like these drive "Language, Learning, and Teaching Across Educational Systems," the course Oxford's Victoria Murphy leads in CRI's 2026 Seoul Research Program. Students study how children acquire language and how schools teach it, then investigate a question of their own in a small team research project.

## Who teaches it

Victoria Murphy heads the Department of Education at the University of Oxford and is an internationally recognized expert in applied linguistics and language acquisition. Much of her research concerns children who speak English as a second language: how their language develops, and how vocabulary growth relates to the development of literacy. In interdisciplinary work on bilingual children, she has also investigated how learning a foreign language early in life affects literacy in a child's first language.

![Portrait of a smiling woman with shoulder-length wavy blonde hair, photographed outdoors against green foliage](/editorial/224154324111-02.jpg "Professor Victoria Murphy, head of Oxford's Department of Education")

She has written two books and published widely in academic journals, and she has served as chair of NALDIC, the National Association for Language Development in the Curriculum, a UK association for language education in multilingual classrooms. In Seoul, she shares her latest research on language learning and teaching, along with her practical experience in the field.

## What the course covers

The course examines language learning and teaching across different education systems, drawing on the fields of education, linguistics, and psychology. It works on three levels:

- **Acquisition:** the theory of how children acquire language
- **Teaching:** approaches to teaching in multicultural and multilingual classrooms
- **Policy:** how education policy connects to what happens in actual classes

Built on Professor Murphy's research on language development, multilingual settings, and educational contexts, the course also brings in educational psychology and teacher education, and asks how a commitment to equity and inquiry-based learning can become everyday classroom practice. The aim is for students to understand how language, literacy, and knowledge take shape and keep developing in schools.

Theory and practice stay closely linked. Lectures and seminars introduce the concepts, while case analyses and team projects put them to work. Students might dissect a case from a multilingual classroom, for example, or debate how education policy shapes day-to-day teaching.

![A teacher leans over a table of smiling young children writing with pencils in a primary school classroom](/editorial/224154324111-01.jpg "The course looks at how children acquire language and how it is taught in real classrooms.")

## From research question to paper and poster

The core of the course is a small research project carried out in teams. Under Professor Murphy's guidance, each team frames a research question based on real classroom cases and investigates it through interviews, surveys, and a review of the literature. One team might interview teachers and students about a school's bilingual program; another might survey learners in different learning environments to compare their cognitive abilities. Gathering and analyzing that data teaches students the methods of education research firsthand and gives them practice approaching real-world problems scientifically.

Questions that frame the course's research include:

- How does multilingual education affect cognitive flexibility?
- How does the learning environment affect problem-solving?
- Why does the same teaching method produce different results in different classrooms?
- How can the design of instruction build systematic thinking rather than rote memorization?

Each team finishes with two pieces of work:

- **A research paper** setting out the theoretical background, methods, results, and discussion
- **A research poster** that presents the paper visually, shown at a poster session at the end of the program

The timeline is short, but students design and carry out a complete study from beginning to end, building communication and critical-thinking skills as they work together.

## Who the course suits

The course is a natural fit for students interested in language education, linguistics, education, child development, or psychology. A background in those subjects is not required: anyone open to interdisciplinary research can get a great deal out of it. It will especially appeal to students who are curious about how languages are learned and taught, or who care about solving problems they see in schools.

## What students take away

Students see where theory meets practice from a researcher's point of view. Questions they have wondered about at school or in after-school academies become subjects of formal inquiry, explored with data. That process sharpens both problem-solving and research skills.

The work can also go further. Strong projects can be developed into papers for journal submission or conference presentation, and the finished paper and poster give students concrete material for college essays and portfolios. Down the line, the results and the working relationship with an Oxford professor can lay the groundwork for a recommendation letter from Professor Murphy.

Professor Murphy's course is one of the faculty-led tracks in CRI's Seoul Research Program, where small groups work directly with visiting professors from US and UK universities. To see how the summer programs run and which courses are open, explore the [Seoul and Global Research Programs](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Designing experiments on anxiety, stress and the mind with Oxford's Robin Murphy
excerpt: How Oxford psychologist Robin A. Murphy's course combines learning theory, AI modeling and hands-on experiments on anxiety, negative thinking and stress, from design to statistics.
content:
Show one group of volunteers a short frightening video and another group an ordinary one, then time how quickly everyone responds on a simple task. If the anxious group is slower, what has fear done to working memory or processing speed? Questions like this sit at the center of Oxford psychologist Robin A. Murphy's course in CRI's 2026 Seoul Research Program. Students plan an experiment, collect the data, run the statistics and write up what they found.

## An Oxford researcher of learning and emotion

Robin A. Murphy is a professor in the University of Oxford's Department of Experimental Psychology. He studies how the brain learns, approaching the question through associative learning theory and neurophysiology. Since joining Oxford in 2009 he has focused on associative learning and computational psychopathology, and he has published more than 80 papers.

His lab examines learning, memory and emotional behavior in both human and animal models. A central thread is the link between brain function and mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety disorders and schizophrenia. That work is helping researchers understand how the brain functions and informing the development of treatments.

![Robin Murphy, smiling, in a dark suit and tie, seated in front of shelves of books](/editorial/224153489252-01.jpg "Robin A. Murphy, Department of Experimental Psychology, University of Oxford")

## Psychology, neuroscience and AI in one course

The course, **Behavioural and Cognitive Neuroscience for Human Psychopathology**, is an advanced program that brings together experimental psychology, neurobiology and AI modeling. Students use AI techniques such as neural network models and reinforcement learning to analyze the brain mechanisms behind human learning, decision-making and emotional disorders.

It starts with the foundations: associative learning, how the brain computes prediction errors, and the neural mechanisms of decision-making. Students then carry those theories into clinical territory, using computer models to explore depression, anxiety disorders and schizophrenia. Brain imaging (fMRI) and behavioral data help characterize the neural networks involved in cognitive and emotional disorders, so theoretical modeling and clinical application are studied side by side.

The course draws on current research methods in psychology, cognitive neuroscience and AI, yet no programming background is required. It is structured to take students step by step from theory to hands-on practice.

## Designing an experiment of your own

At the heart of the course is a small research project. Each student chooses a topic and works through the full cycle: designing an experiment, collecting data, analyzing it statistically and writing up the results as a paper. In the experimental-design sessions, for instance, students receive real experimental data, learn techniques such as t-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA), turn their results into graphs, and present them as a report, a poster and a paper. Along the way they learn how research in cognitive and behavioral neuroscience actually unfolds.

Three sample designs show the kinds of studies students can build:

- **Anxiety and cognitive performance.** Participants in the experimental group watch a short frightening video to induce anxiety, then complete a simple reaction-time task. A control group watches an ordinary video and completes the same task. Comparing the two groups' reaction times with a t-test or a similar method shows whether anxiety affects working memory or processing speed.
- **Negative thinking and cognition.** A computer-based cognitive-control task, such as the Stroop test or a memory task, is paired with a smartphone diary (experience sampling) to study how cognitive performance relates to repetitive negative thinking. Students might present emotionally negative and neutral words and measure differences in recall or response patterns, or compare attention-task performance between people prone to negative thinking and a general group. Correlation or multivariate analysis then shows how cognitive function relates to psychiatric symptoms.
- **Social support and stress.** Participants are exposed to a set level of stress, then divided into a group that receives support and a group that does not. Measures of psychological state, along with physiological signals such as heart rate, reveal how the two groups' stress responses differ. ANOVA helps pin down under which conditions, and for whom, social support eases stress.

## From raw data to a paper

Whatever the topic, the workflow is the same. Students plan an experiment that fits their question, gather data from participants and analyze it in SPSS or Python. They organize the results into graphs and tables, then write a report structured like a research paper. In practice, that has meant analyzing raw data with t-tests and ANOVA, visualizing the findings, and handing in the final work as a report or poster.

Finished projects are then submitted for publication in a journal for high school researchers. Professor Murphy has guided this kind of work before: K., an international-school student in Jeju who worked with him in winter 2024, published a study in the *International Journal of High School Research* on how the sight of tears shapes the way people judge someone's control over their own outcomes. That story is on our [Student Success](/success/oxford-psychology-tears-experiment-published-ijhsr) page.

## Who the course suits

The course is designed for high school and university students interested in psychology, neuroscience, cognitive science or AI. It is a genuine challenge for students who want to investigate the relationship between mental health and brain function scientifically, and for those drawn to experimental design and computer modeling.

In 2026 it was offered through the Seoul Research Program as a ten-day, in-person intensive. The group was kept small and selective, and every participant carried out research under Professor Murphy's direct guidance. Students finish with a completed research paper, and those selected as outstanding researchers can also receive a recommendation letter from him.

Research at this depth is more than another assignment. It gives students firsthand experience that school curricula rarely offer, a foundation for college applications and later academic work, and a clearer sense of whether psychology, neuroscience or AI is the right path.

The Seoul Research Program is built around this kind of small-group work with a visiting professor. To see how the summer programs are structured and which tracks are open now, explore the [Seoul and Global Research Programs](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: UC tops 300,000 students: what the 18% nonresident cap means for international applicants
excerpt: UC enrolled a record 301,093 students in fall 2025 as its nonresident share fell to 15.6%. See what drove the growth, campus by campus, and where that leaves international applicants.
content:
The University of California enrolled 301,093 students in fall 2025, the largest student body in its history. UC San Diego set a campus record of its own, with more than 45,000 students. Behind the headline, though, UC is steadily shifting its undergraduate seats toward California residents, and that matters to anyone applying from outside California.

The UCSD Guardian, UC San Diego's student newspaper, reported the record on January 12, 2026, in "UC Fall 2025 enrollment numbers reach record high." The figures below come from that report and from the UC Office of the President's own release. Here is what drove the growth, where the students went, and what it all means for international applicants.

## Fall 2025 at a glance

| Measure | Fall 2025 |
| --- | --- |
| Total UC enrollment | 301,093, up about 0.6% from the year before |
| California-resident undergraduates | More than 200,000, a 10th straight year of growth |
| Nonresident share of undergraduates, systemwide | 15.6% (campus limit: 18%) |
| New international undergraduates | 7,292, up 21% |
| Largest campus | UCLA, more than 47,000 students |

## Why enrollment keeps rising

Much of UC's growth is a matter of policy. In 2022, the university signed a compact with the state of California, promising to enroll a steadily growing number of California residents each year through 2026.

The fall 2025 count shows that promise at work. Total enrollment rose about 0.6% over the previous year to pass 300,000, and the number of California-resident undergraduates climbed above 200,000, its tenth consecutive year of growth.

![The domed California State Capitol building framed by palm trees and pines under a cloudy sky](/editorial/224153238498-03.jpg "The California State Capitol in Sacramento. UC's 2022 compact with the state committed it to enrolling more California residents each year.")

## Campus by campus

UCLA remains UC's largest campus, with more than 47,000 students, followed by UC Berkeley at about 46,000 and UC San Diego at more than 45,000.

UC Riverside stood out. It welcomed 8,297 new first-year and transfer students combined, the sharpest year-over-year increase of any campus. With enrollment up at most campuses, the system as a whole keeps getting bigger.

## The 18% cap on nonresident students

The other half of the story is who fills those seats. To make room for more Californians, UC has been managing the share of nonresident students, a category that covers both out-of-state and international students.

UC limits nonresidents to no more than 18% of undergraduates at each campus, and some campuses have been admitting fewer of them to bring their numbers in line with that limit. Across the system, the nonresident share of undergraduates fell to 15.6% in 2025. That has widened opportunities for California students and, by comparison, made the competition stiffer for international students.

## Growing on a tight budget

UC is expanding at a financially difficult moment. Recent cuts to federal research funding and rising operating costs have squeezed its budget. It has kept adding students anyway, thanks to long-range planning and cooperation from the state.

UC San Diego is a good example. It aims to add more than 10,000 students by 2040, reaching a total of 56,000, and it is building out campus infrastructure and student housing to match. Plans like these are an encouraging sign that UC is preparing for the future.

## What this means for international applicants

Because UC gives priority to California residents, the international share of its student body will stay limited. That does not mean the door is closed. In fall 2025, 7,292 new international undergraduates enrolled at UC, 21% more than the year before.

UC is also test-blind, meaning it does not use SAT or ACT scores in admission decisions. With test scores off the table, the rest of the application carries the weight: grades, a challenging course load, essays and extracurricular activities. International school students need to show their own strengths in each of these.

The competition is intense, but students who prepare the right way can still expect good results. For the next chapter of the story, our breakdown of UC's fall 2026 application data, including international first-year applications at UCLA, UC Berkeley and UC San Diego, is on the [CRI blog](/blog).

For students looking for an extracurricular with real academic depth, research is one path. In the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp), small groups work with visiting professors from US and UK universities on a genuine research question and write up their findings as a research paper in English. It is the kind of work students can draw on later in their activities list and essays.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Anastasia Romanou of Columbia and NASA on modeling as a basic skill for the future
excerpt: How NASA climate scientist Anastasia Romanou teaches students to turn real phenomena into math, what impressed her about CRI students, and what makes a good recommendation letter.
content:
Why does this phenomenon look the way it does? And what do we have to simplify before we can understand it? Anastasia Romanou's course at CRI starts from those two questions every time, whether the subject is engineering, climate science, or economics. A climate modeler at NASA and a faculty member at Columbia University, she treats mathematical modeling not as a specialist's technique but as a basic way of making sense of a complicated world.

> "We have already entered an era in which data and algorithms drive society as a whole. Tools such as numerical modeling and machine learning no longer belong to one particular major; they are used in almost every field. Students interested in this area should actively look for learning opportunities outside the classroom, too. Hands-on experience with the actual tools will help them enormously as they grow."
> — Anastasia Romanou, Columbia University and NASA GISS

## A career spent modeling the climate

Romanou studied at the University of Athens in Greece and earned her PhD at Florida State University. Today she is an adjunct associate professor of applied physics and applied mathematics at Columbia University and a physical research scientist at the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS), where she uses mathematical models to study problems as complex as climate change and ocean circulation.

Her research interests include:

- **Ocean circulation**, in particular the meridional overturning circulation: how it varies, how stable it is, and its tipping points
- **How the Earth system responds to changing emissions**, including the heat and carbon the ocean takes up and whether climate change can be reversed
- **Air-sea interactions and extreme events**, including gas exchange across the air-sea interface and extreme variability in the Earth system
- **Ocean and coupled ocean-atmosphere models**, from general circulation models to full Earth system models
- **Planetary modeling**, adapting Earth system models to other planets in our solar system and to exoplanets

She is a former member of a research group on the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), has been an invited speaker at scientific meetings including those of the American Geophysical Union (AGU), and contributed to the decadal survey report on Earth science and applications from space. Her teaching covers applied mathematics and machine learning, numerical computation and statistical analysis, and the models used in engineering practice and the social sciences.

![Anastasia Romanou stands beside a wall-mounted NASA logo above the words Goddard Institute for Space Studies](/editorial/224153208455-01.jpg "Anastasia Romanou at the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies, where she is a physical research scientist")

## A class about how to see a problem

Romanou's course is less about methods for solving problems than about how to look at them in the first place. Students use data to bring order to complex phenomena, then use mathematical models to expose the structure inside them, one layer at a time. She calls this process an exercise in "thinking about reality exactly as it is."

Her research is a large part of why the approach carries weight: for someone who models the climate and the oceans for a living, modeling is simply how you understand a complex system. In her view, it isn't reserved for students who have chosen a particular major; it is a strength every student will need for the many choices and judgments ahead of them.

The CRI course is built around that idea. Instead of grinding through textbook exercises, students translate real phenomena into the language of mathematics and carry the calculation through to the end on a computer. Getting the right answer quickly is not the point. Being able to explain why you reasoned the way you did is. As she often tells students in class:

> "Mathematics and artificial intelligence are extremely powerful tools. But it is always people who decide how to use them."
> — Anastasia Romanou

## What stood out about her CRI students

What impressed Romanou most about the Korean students she met at CRI was their attitude rather than their results. Whether an assignment was easy or hard, they kept thinking it through to the end instead of stopping halfway.

The teams she remembers best refused to settle for a single answer. They went back to ask whether another method might work, or whether one of their assumptions was wrong. That habit, she says, resembles the way a researcher approaches a problem.

She describes CRI students as "learners who aren't in a hurry." Even before they had covered all the theory, they framed their own questions and worked to understand the concepts behind them. An attitude like that says more about how far a student can grow over the long run than any short-term result does.

An environment like CRI's, where students learn from professors with many different backgrounds, also widens how they think. In classes that don't demand an instant answer, where questions are taken seriously, students gradually learn to think more deeply.

## Interest shows in what you choose

Romanou tells students they don't need to work so hard at looking impressive. Instead, she asks them to notice where they actually spend their time: the topic that catches their eye while they read a syllabus, the question that keeps pulling at them even when it gets difficult. Choices like these, she believes, add up to a student's direction.

Admissions officers look for something similar. How seriously a student has committed to one subject matters more than how much they know. Romanou's class is a place to build exactly that kind of experience. In it, numerical modeling and machine learning are tools for organizing your thinking, not techniques for showing off results.

The attitude and choices students reveal along the way find their way into recommendation letters, too.

> "A good recommendation letter doesn't explain the student. It simply lets who that student is come through naturally."
> — Anastasia Romanou

Professor Romanou has taught CRI students in person in Korea and was scheduled to return for the 2026 summer program. To see how the summer courses run and which faculty-led tracks are open, explore the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: From draft to DOI: how a student research paper gets published and put to use
excerpt: What happens to an SRP paper after the program ends: revision, journal selection, peer review, the standards a manuscript must meet, and how students use the finished work.
content:
When the Seoul Research Program (SRP) ends, every student team has a complete research paper, written in two weeks. It is also, in practice, a first draft. The months that follow, spent revising with a professor, choosing a journal, and answering peer reviewers, are what it takes to turn that draft into a published article with a DOI. Here is how the process works, the standards a paper has to meet along the way, and how students put the finished paper to use.

## From draft to publication

### Revising after the program

The work continues after the last class. Professors and students keep refining the manuscript through online meetings and email. The professor tightens the writing into polished academic prose and points out what the paper still needs, whether that is more literature to cite or results that should be strengthened. Students work that feedback into a final version.

### Choosing a journal

Once the paper reaches a publishable standard, the professor helps the team choose a journal. Fit matters here: the aim is the journal that best matches the topic and the findings, and professors often draw on their own expertise and professional network to find it. On the professor's recommendation, some teams submit to a journal where the professor publishes regularly, as one past SRP team did. The team then reformats the manuscript to that journal's requirements and submits it through the journal's online system.

### Peer review

After submission comes peer review. The journal's editor sends the paper to two or three experts in the field, who judge its originality, the soundness of its methods, and the significance of its results.

![Word cloud in which the words peer, review, and paper appear largest, surrounded by smaller words such as reviewers, findings, journal, and scientists](/editorial/224151678297-01.jpg "Peer review: two or three experts in the field assess each submission before the journal decides.")

Requests for revision are the norm. The students and their professor respond to the reviewers' comments and resubmit, perhaps by clarifying their interpretation of the data or adding results a reviewer asked for. Review usually takes several months. A lucky paper is accepted in the first round, but most go through one or two rounds of revision before the journal makes its final decision.

### Publication

After acceptance, the journal does its final editing and publishes the paper. Online journals usually post it fairly soon after the decision; print journals run it in a later issue. The whole journey from submission to publication typically takes about six months, though depending on the journal's standing and how fast its reviewers work, it can take as little as three or four months or more than a year. Because SRP papers are developed under close faculty guidance, they tend to move through review relatively quickly.

A published paper is assigned a DOI (Digital Object Identifier) and becomes a formal piece of scholarship that anyone, anywhere, can find and read. The students are listed as its co-authors, a rare accomplishment for high school students and one that carries forward into later study and work.

Here are the four stages at a glance:

| Stage | What happens | Typical timing |
|---|---|---|
| Revision | Professor and team refine the draft through online meetings and email | Begins when the program ends |
| Journal selection | Professor recommends a journal; team reformats and submits online | Once the paper is publishable |
| Peer review | Two or three reviewers assess the paper, usually with one or two rounds of revision | Several months |
| Publication | Journal edits and publishes; the paper receives a DOI | About six months from submission, ranging from three or four months to more than a year |

## The standards a paper has to meet

A student's first paper still has to clear the same academic bar as any other submission. SRP professors and TAs build these standards into the writing process, so students learn them by using them.

**Length.** SRP papers usually aim for about 10 to 15 pages, or 5,000 to 8,000 words. That is enough room to cover the background, methods, results, and discussion properly. Because time in the program is limited, students also learn to write tightly, cutting unnecessary exposition and keeping the argument moving logically.

**Structure.** Every paper follows the IMRaD format. Professors and TAs explain in detail what belongs in each section:

| Section | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Introduction | The research question and its background |
| Methods | The data or materials used and the procedures followed |
| Results | The main experimental or analytical findings |
| Discussion | What the findings mean, their limitations, and directions for future research |

Students also learn a citation style, such as APA, MLA, or Chicago, and use it to credit every source accurately.

**Originality.** Before publication, every paper goes through a similarity check with software such as Turnitin. A similarity score of 15% or lower is generally considered acceptable; SRP aims for under 10% wherever possible. Students practice explaining what they have learned in their own words instead of borrowing other researchers' sentences, with particular care that no run of consecutive sentences matches another text.

**Research ethics.** Students learn the ethical rules of academic publishing: cite every source, never fabricate or falsify data, and be transparent about each co-author's contribution. For research involving people or animals, they are introduced to ethics review through an institutional review board (IRB), and they learn to weigh safety and privacy. Most high school research relies on published literature or public datasets, so serious ethical problems are uncommon, but building sound research habits is a goal in its own right.

Only papers that meet these standards make it into a journal, and close faculty guidance is how SRP students get there. For more on the writing itself, CRI's seven-part paper-writing guide and its explainers on journal rankings and on what makes a journal internationally recognized are on the [CRI blog](/blog).

## How students use the finished paper

A paper produced in a short, intensive program goes on to serve a student in several ways.

**College applications.** The paper is a strong point in an application, and the research behind it gives students real material for personal statements and essays. One participant said the program played a big part in their admission:

> "Thanks to this program, I was able to build research experience that fit my major, and it became the center of my essay."
> — SRP participant

Students who do outstanding work may also receive a recommendation letter from their professor. SRP gives students about 50 hours with faculty and TAs, so the letter can be detailed and grounded in direct observation, which leaves a strong impression on admissions officers.

> "I received a recommendation letter from my professor, and the direction I wanted to take became clear."
> — SRP participant, admitted to Stanford

Together, the paper and the letter show admissions readers concrete evidence of academic drive and research ability.

**Research internships.** A co-authored journal paper from high school is a real advantage when applying for research internships at universities or research institutes. A student applying to a lab in their mentor's field can walk through the research and share the paper, showing both understanding and commitment. The same holds in college, when students apply for faculty mentoring programs or undergraduate research positions. A student who has written a paper already understands the research cycle of literature review, study design, data analysis, and writing, and can settle into a new lab quickly.

**Conferences and competitions.** SRP papers can be entered in student research competitions, from science fairs in Korea and abroad to paper contests for high school students. Humanities and social science papers can also go to student journals such as *The Concord Review*. CRI sometimes supports SRP graduates in presenting at international conferences as well. In Professor Nabil Alshurafa's course, top students have had the chance to present posters at conferences of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBS).

**What comes next.** Students can develop their topic into a more advanced research project or use it as a foundation for studying a related major in depth at university. They can also keep in touch with their teammates and go on supporting one another's studies and careers. Most of all, defining a problem, solving it, and writing it up changes how students think. Whatever field they study next, they are better prepared to ask their own questions and chase the answers.

## Staying with a question

Holding on to a research question and reasoning it through to a finished paper is a real challenge for a high school student. That challenge is also where the depth of thinking and the lasting interest in a field come from. If you want to keep asking why a question matters and then answer it in a paper of your own, the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) page explains how the program works and how to apply.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Inside the Seoul Research Program: how small teams spend ten days with a professor
excerpt: How SRP's ten days unfold: small teams, 30 faculty and 20 TA hours, a week of research design, a week of writing, and a final poster showcase.
content:
The Seoul Research Program (SRP) doesn't begin with "Let's try this." It begins with a harder question: "Could this become a paper?" Ten days later, every team stands beside a research poster, answering questions from professors and guests about a study that started as a loose interest. Here is how the program gets them there.

## One question per team

SRP is an in-person summer program in Seoul, taught by professors who travel from US and UK universities such as Harvard, Caltech, MIT, Columbia, UChicago, and Oxford. Courses range from neuroscience and chemistry to climate modeling, economics, law, education, psychology, film, and architecture.

A class takes up to about 10 students, who split into teams of three to five, and each team pursues a single research question. Teams are built around the interests students describe when they apply. The final question is settled in class: students bring rough ideas, and the professor weighs each for value and feasibility and helps set a direction. A student who can't settle on a topic can choose from a few options the professor suggests. From there, the team spends the rest of the ten days on that one problem.

Master's and PhD students from leading universities serve as TAs, helping with background research, experiments, and writing. Between small teams and close guidance from the professor and TAs, first-time researchers learn methods quickly. In one past cohort, a team with no prior research experience completed its study and, on the professor's recommendation, submitted the paper to a journal in its field.

## How the program is designed

SRP research is dry-lab work, built from data, published studies, and models rather than wet-lab biology or chemistry experiments. Most projects center on data analysis, literature review, or economic and social modeling. The reasoning is practical. A high school student who spends months in a wet lab rarely generates original biological or chemical data beyond assisting a graduate student, but a well-framed analytical project is one students can control and back up on their own.

A few principles shape everything else:

- **Interest becomes an academic question.** Conversations with the professor turn a vague curiosity into something researchable.
- **The question gets a paper-scale design.** The work follows the logic of an academic study, not an essay or a report.
- **Faculty give feedback, not answers.** The professor acts as an advisor rather than a lecturer: a research partner who follows each team's work, tests its thinking, and pushes the question further.
- **The output is research, not an activity log.** Each student finishes with a paper that shows how they think, which gives the professor clear evidence for evaluating them.

Because professors watch students reason, take feedback, and grow over ten days, a later recommendation letter can rest on direct observation. CRI picks faculty for their mentoring experience and depth of supervision rather than name recognition, and it measures success by whether students can explain their own research process, not only by where they are admitted.

## A day at SRP

The program runs for ten class days on a campus in Seoul, and the schedule is tight on purpose. Students spend more than 50 hours with faculty and TAs, more contact time than a typical three-credit university course: about 30 hours of faculty lectures and seminars and about 20 hours of TA sessions and group work. Before the program begins, students join an online pre-meeting, and the first class day opens with an orientation.

| Time | Session | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 9:00 a.m.–12:00 p.m. | Faculty session | Core concepts in the field, analysis of prior research, research methods, and discussion that sets each team's direction |
| 1:00–3:00 p.m. | TA session | Hands-on work: literature searches, data collection, methodology design, and structuring the paper |
| Late afternoon and evening | Team time | Teams meet on their own to push the project forward, with faculty and TAs checking in with feedback |

Every class is face to face, so a session can shift with the questions students raise and how well they are following, instead of delivering fixed content one way. CRI considers that in-person exchange the most important part of teaching research.

![Three students working together at a desk with a laptop in a classroom](/editorial/224154644260-10.jpg "A team at work in an SRP classroom")

One day off, usually on the weekend after the first week, gives students time to rest or catch up, with no classes or official activities.

## Week one: foundations and research design

The first five days build the background a topic needs and the plan for studying it. Professors teach core concepts, theory, and recent research. In a psychology course, that might mean principles of behavioral and cognitive neuroscience and academic perspectives on mental health; in an applied computer engineering course, hands-on basics of sensor technology and biosignal processing. That grounding helps students sharpen their questions.

The research starts right away. On Days 1 and 2, teams brainstorm to choose and narrow a subtopic, then read prior studies to refine a hypothesis or research question, while TAs teach literature searching, reference management, and basic statistics. Teams also design their methods: what data to collect and analyze, and how to structure an experiment or survey. An engineering team might design and test a sensor prototype; a social science team might draft a questionnaire or interview guide.

![Students standing around a desk as a teammate works on a laptop in an SRP classroom](/editorial/224154644260-11.jpg "Teammates confer around a laptop at SRP")

At the end of the week, each team brings a draft research plan to a checkpoint. The professor reviews the ideas and materials so far and says what to pursue and what to shore up, so the study has a solid frame before writing begins. That weekend, students and faculty get together for a program dinner, where students compare progress and talk with professors about more than coursework.

## Week two: from results to a full draft

In the second week, the plan becomes a paper. Teams finish collecting data or run their analyses, then write section by section. Around Days 6 and 7, they analyze early results and focus on the Methods and Results sections. The professor rotates among the teams every day, reviewing drafts and giving feedback on the spot, so each paper improves through daily rounds of revision. TAs cover formatting and citation style, the details first-time authors tend to miss.

Around Day 8, each team completes a full draft and meets one-on-one with the professor to discuss the logic of the argument, the interpretation of results, and the conclusions. Over Days 8 and 9, students tighten the writing and run any further experiments or analyses the feedback calls for, until the final manuscript is done.

## The poster showcase

Week two also includes poster design and presentation practice, so students learn to summarize findings visually and present them. Each team distills its paper into a single poster (title, background, methods, results, conclusions and implications) with charts and images. Faculty and TAs advise on what to emphasize and how to lay it out, and rehearsals bring feedback on delivery, timing, and handling likely questions.

The final day is the Research Poster Showcase. Posters go up in a classroom or hall, teams take turns presenting, and students from other teams, professors, and a few invited guests circulate to listen and ask questions. Faculty give their overall feedback, and the program closes by celebrating the finished work. The work doesn't stop there: after the program, CRI supports each manuscript through journal submission.

## Who SRP suits, and who it doesn't

SRP is selective, and it isn't for everyone. It tends to suit students who:

- have plenty of activities but struggle to explain how they connect to an intended major
- attend international schools and want to show deeper engagement with a field than participation-based activities allow
- learn better in person than online, and think best by asking questions and debating
- are ready to dig into an interest, form their own questions, and explain them in writing and in conversation
- value the depth of their thinking over the result itself
- want a lasting piece of work to show for the program, not just a short-term experience

It may not be the right fit for students who want a fast, visible credential, who expect an instant answer to "What will I get out of this?", or who want set answers handed to them.

What students take home is a research poster and a paper. In CRI's view, college admissions reward not so much what a student did as how deeply they can explain it, and ten days of SRP work carries naturally into essays, interviews, and recommendation letters. SRP doesn't promise outcomes. What it does is build a research environment designed to lead to them.

## Eligibility and selection

SRP is open to students in Grades 9–12 and to first- and second-year college students preparing to transfer. Selection starts with a written application covering academic background and interests, followed by an individual interview. The interview is less a test than a conversation about what a student is curious about and whether they are ready for the research process. Admitted students are notified individually, and professor assignments and preparation follow.

Past SRP projects have ranged from a literature review on the CO₂ absorption limits of amine-based solvent systems to a study of how cognitive biases and heuristics affect consumer behavior. More of that work appears on the [Student Success](/success) page.

If you have a question you'd like to test against real data and real feedback, the [Seoul Research Program page](/research/summer-camp) has the current program details and how to apply.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Meet the 2026 Seoul Research Program faculty, part 2: humanities and social sciences
excerpt: Seven professors from MIT, Penn, UChicago, Cambridge, Oxford, RISD, and USC: what each research course covers, sample questions, and the students it suits.
content:
What system-level obstacles do sustainability startups run into? How do international organizations respond when climate change becomes a security threat? Can a film turn a tangled environmental and social problem into a story that moves an audience? Questions like these drive the humanities and social sciences courses of the 2026 Seoul Research Program.

Each course is built around student research, not lectures. Students choose a question, investigate it with a professor's guidance, and finish with an academic poster presented to the professor and classmates; most courses add a written research paper. Part 1 of this series covered the STEM faculty. Here are the seven professors in the humanities and social sciences, with what each course covers, sample research questions, and who it suits.

## At a glance

| Professor | University | Course focus |
|---|---|---|
| Kit Hickey | MIT Sloan School of Management | Entrepreneurship and venture creation |
| William Burke-White | University of Pennsylvania | International law and global governance |
| Ryan Fang | University of Chicago | Economic modeling and game theory |
| Michael Ashby | University of Cambridge | Empirical and sustainable finance |
| Victoria Murphy | University of Oxford | Language learning and teaching |
| Ijlal Muzaffar | Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) | Architectural history and environmental design |
| James Savoca | USC School of Cinematic Arts | Filmmaking, screenwriting, and new media |

## Kit Hickey (MIT Sloan): building a venture step by step

Kit Hickey teaches entrepreneurship at the MIT Sloan School of Management. Her course, *Innovation, Entrepreneurship, and Management: A Comprehensive Guide to Venture Creation*, is built on MIT's well-known 24-step entrepreneurship framework and treats a startup as a system, from the first idea to a business model and growth strategy.

Teams take a real or hypothetical venture through market research, customer discovery, prototype planning, and financial strategy, working out market segments, customer personas, and a competitive strategy along the way. Under Hickey's guidance they write interim reports on their business plan, then finish with a venture-analysis paper and a poster, presented the way founders pitch to investors. Teams that want to go further can also build a mock investor pitch or a full business plan.

Sample research questions:

- What system-level challenges do startups tackling sustainability face?
- How can founders test a startup idea with limited resources?

No startup experience is needed; the course starts from the basic concepts. It suits students interested in business, economics, or entrepreneurship who like to speak up and work in teams, including humanities and social science students who want a hands-on look at the business world.

## William Burke-White (Penn): international law across borders

William Burke-White, a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania, looks at how states use international law to govern problems that cross borders, from climate change and pandemics to trade and security. Students learn how treaties and customary international law take shape, what bodies such as the UN and the WTO do, and how disputes are settled.

Much of the class runs on participatory formats such as mock international conferences and mock trials. Teams then run case studies, analyze the relevant legal provisions, and present a research paper and poster. Projects range from international legal responses to climate change to proposals for reforming the UN Security Council.

Sample research questions from the 2026 syllabus:

- How does international law shape international environmental disputes?
- How do international organizations respond to climate-related security threats?

No legal background is required, only an interest in current affairs and a willingness to debate. The course fits students drawn to international relations, law, or political science, including future lawyers and diplomats.

## Ryan Fang (UChicago): modeling strategic decisions

Ryan Fang of the University of Chicago teaches strategic decision-making through microeconomics and game theory. Students learn to reduce the interactions among markets, firms, consumers, and governments to economic models, using rational choice theory, equilibrium analysis, and optimization.

The class then becomes a research workshop: each team picks an economic problem, writes a model-based paper, and presents and discusses its model at a poster session. One team might analyze how firms respond to environmental policy; another might model how irrational consumers move a market.

Sample research questions:

- How do economic incentives affect cooperation over shared resources?
- How do behavioral biases shift market equilibrium?

Calculus and basic economics help, but a high school economics course is enough, since Fang builds the core concepts from scratch. The course suits students of economics, business, or political economy who enjoy quantitative work, strategy games, and puzzles.

## Michael Ashby (Cambridge): testing finance on real data

Michael Ashby, who teaches economics at the University of Cambridge, leads *Empirical Finance: Capital Markets, Investment, and Asset Pricing*. Students learn portfolio theory, the capital asset pricing model (CAPM), and the efficient market hypothesis, then test them against real financial data; the course also covers ESG investing, green finance, and climate risk.

In the second half, teams form a hypothesis and test it with econometric models. A project might be an event study of share prices around a climate policy announcement, an analysis of what drives green-bond yields, or a multiple regression on how ESG scores relate to firm value.

Sample research questions:

- How are environmental risk factors reflected in asset prices?
- How does investor irrationality affect market efficiency?

Basic math and some probability and statistics are required. Over the course, students build skills in processing data with programming, statistical inference, and economic interpretation. The course suits students interested in finance and data analysis, from future fund managers and analysts to anyone curious about the economics of climate change.

## Victoria Murphy (Oxford): how language is learned and taught

Victoria Murphy, head of the Department of Education at the University of Oxford and a specialist in applied linguistics, teaches *Language, Learning, and Teaching Across Educational Systems*. The course asks how children learn language and how teachers teach it, covering multilingual development in multicultural classrooms, how teaching changes over a teacher's career, and how language-education policy reaches the classroom. Teams build research projects grounded in the literature. They can add interviews, surveys, or analysis of existing data, then present a research paper and poster at a small, conference-style session.

Sample research questions:

- How does the learning environment affect students' ability to solve complex problems?
- How does multilingual education affect cognitive flexibility?

No prior study of psychology or linguistics is needed. The course suits students interested in education, linguistics, psychology, or child development, including future teachers and education-policy specialists.

## Ijlal Muzaffar (RISD): design history and environmental futures

Ijlal Muzaffar, an architectural historian at the Rhode Island School of Design, teaches *Possible Modernities: Design Systems, Architecture, and Environmental Futures*. Rather than treating architectural history as a record of the past, the course reads architecture and design within the environmental, material, and social systems that shaped them.

Students study Mesopotamian irrigation, water management in medieval cities, and industrial-age building materials to see how designers worked within limits of climate and resources. Teams mine a historical case for lessons in sustainable design, comparing, say, the urban infrastructure of ancient Rome and China, or tracing architectural styles along the Silk Road. They present their findings on a poster, with design drawings, at a closing exhibition.

Sample research questions:

- How did modern urban planning affect environmental sustainability?
- What can traditional architecture in non-Western societies teach contemporary design?

No background in architectural history is needed, since Muzaffar supplies the context. Because the course looks at modern architecture well beyond the West, it also rewards students interested in cultural history and aesthetics. It suits students of architecture, design, and history, including future art school and architecture applicants who want theory and history alongside studio work.

## James Savoca (USC): film as a system

James Savoca teaches at USC's School of Cinematic Arts and specializes in storytelling and screenwriting. His 2026 course on next-generation filmmaking, covering screenwriting, the screen, and the future of new media, treats contemporary film as a system: how screenplay, image, sound, and editing combine to create meaning, and how those choices reflect their social and cultural context. Small groups write a research paper on a film topic and present a poster. They can also add creative work, such as a short screenplay or a storyboard, as long as it grows out of their research.

Sample research questions from the syllabus:

- How can film turn complex environmental and social systems into emotionally compelling stories?
- How do the constraints of low-budget filmmaking shape creative decisions?

Production or screenwriting experience helps but is not required. The course suits students who want to study the narrative and direction of films such as Bong Joon-ho's *Parasite* or Park Chan-wook's *Oldboy* as a scholar would, and future film, creative writing, and media students building a portfolio.

## Research the way universities do it

In all seven courses, students pick a topic, investigate it, and see it through to finished work, guided by faculty from MIT, the University of Pennsylvania, the University of Chicago, the University of Cambridge, the University of Oxford, RISD, and USC. The courses are taught in person in Seoul during the summer, in small groups. To see how the program is structured, explore the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Meet the 2026 Seoul Research Program faculty, part 1: seven STEM professors
excerpt: Seven STEM professors from Harvard, Oxford, Northwestern, Caltech, Columbia and UChicago: what each course covers, who it suits, and what to know before you start.
content:
Can a wearable sensor catch the early signs of a health problem? Why can two events that start from similar conditions end so differently? How does the brain make sense of uncertain information from its surroundings? Questions like these run through the STEM courses of CRI's 2026 Seoul Research Program.

The 2026 lineup included fourteen professors. This first part of a two-part series covers the seven who teach science, technology, engineering and math: who they are, what each course covers, who it suits, sample research questions, and the fields each one opens up.

## What the courses have in common

None of these courses is a lecture series. Each is built around student research and runs more like a university seminar than a class: students read the literature, tackle a question in teams, and finish with a research paper and an academic poster. What differs is the preparation each professor expects, from high school biology to first-year university math.

| Professor | University | Focus | Background expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| Samuel Kunes | Harvard University | Memory and brain plasticity | High school biology |
| Robin Murphy | University of Oxford | Neuroscience of mental health | No psychology needed; suits quantitative, logical thinkers |
| Nabil Alshurafa | Northwestern University | Wearable sensors and mobile health | High school biology; coding or electronics a plus |
| Brian Stoltz | Caltech | Organic chemistry and synthesis | Interest in chemistry and lab work |
| George Tselioudis | Columbia University | Observing Earth by satellite | Required: basic linear algebra, calculus and differential equations |
| Anastasia Romanou | Columbia University | Numerical modeling | Required: first-year university linear algebra, calculus and differential equations |
| Haifeng Xu | University of Chicago | Algorithms and agentic AI | Recommended: math fundamentals and basic programming, such as Python |

## Samuel Kunes, Harvard: the biology of memory

Samuel Kunes, a professor of molecular and cellular biology at Harvard University, teaches how memories form and how the brain changes with experience, seen through molecular biology. His course treats the brain as one biological system, following learning and memory from genes and synapses to neural circuits and on to diseases such as Alzheimer's. It runs as a research seminar: students read the literature themselves and debate it.

High school biology is enough to take part. The course suits students drawn to neuroscience who are considering brain science or medicine, especially those who would rather do research than sit through lectures, and anyone curious how events inside a cell connect to behavior.

Research questions in the course include:

- How do interactions between genes and environment affect memory decline?
- How does stress in a learning environment affect brain development?

Teams finish with a paper and poster, an early look at biomedical research for students headed toward neuroscience, medicine or the life sciences.

## Robin Murphy, Oxford: the neuroscience of mental health

Robin Murphy, a professor of experimental psychology at the University of Oxford, teaches **Behavioural and Cognitive Neuroscience for Human Psychopathology**. The course treats brain and mind as a system that adapts to its environment, combining experimental psychology, neurobiology and computational models. Students examine how learning, prediction errors and decision-making shape behavior, and how breakdowns in those systems can surface as depression, anxiety or schizophrenia. Each team then analyzes a psychiatric topic through a neuroscientific model.

No prior psychology is required. The course fits students interested in psychology, brain science or psychiatry who like bringing mathematical and logical reasoning to human behavior. Because it also covers modeling brain function on a computer, students drawn to cognitive science or AI will find plenty to work with.

Sample questions:

- How does the brain process uncertain information from its environment?
- How do different cognitive systems respond to stress?

Students design an experiment, analyze the data, and write up a paper and poster. The work points toward clinical psychology, neuroscience and cognitive science, and later toward mental health or AI-driven brain research.

## Nabil Alshurafa, Northwestern: wearable sensors and mobile health

Nabil Alshurafa, a Northwestern University professor whose work spans medicine and engineering, teaches **Behavioral Medicine and Bioengineering in Mobile Health**. His subject is mobile health, or mHealth: systems that use biosignals and lifestyle data from wearable sensors to monitor health and prevent disease. The course runs in two phases. Students first design and build sensors that measure signals such as heart rate, activity and stress, then analyze the data they collected for insights into preventive medicine.

It is a strong match for students aiming at biomedical engineering, computer science or pre-med who pair high school biology with a liking for coding or electronics. The work is hands-on and project-driven, so it rewards students who enjoy building devices and solving problems creatively, and those curious about health startups and digital health.

Questions from the syllabus:

- How do environmental factors such as air pollution affect the body's signals?
- How could a wearable device detect early signs of a health problem?

Teams form a hypothesis, build a sensor system, collect and analyze data, and produce a paper and poster, gaining hands-on research experience that connects directly to biomedical engineering, digital health and preventive medicine. Some students have taken that work further: four teams from his 2025 class had abstracts accepted as posters at IEEE BSN, the International Conference on Body Sensor Networks. Their story is on our [Student Success](/success/srp-teams-wearable-health-ieee-bsn-2025) page.

## Brian Stoltz, Caltech: organic chemistry at work

Brian Stoltz, a professor of chemistry at Caltech, teaches **Organic Chemistry: Structure, Reactivity, and Synthesis**. Students learn the field's core ideas, such as molecular structure and reaction mechanisms, and apply them to real chemical systems: the roles organic molecules play in materials, energy and medicine, and how catalysis and stereochemistry can make synthesis cleaner and more efficient. Alongside the lectures, each group chooses a system to research, such as polymer degradation or green chemistry, then writes a paper and presents a poster.

The course fits students interested in chemistry, biotechnology or materials engineering, especially those drawn to polymers, medicinal chemistry or the lab. Its steady move from theory to application helps future pre-med students and would-be drug developers see the bigger picture, and its treatment of green chemistry speaks to students who want to tackle environmental problems.

Example topics:

- How does a synthetic polymer's structure affect how it breaks down in the environment?
- How can catalysts make organic synthesis more efficient and less wasteful?

Groups work through a literature review and experimental design in search of creative answers, such as a greener chemical process. It is groundwork for university lab research and for careers in pharmaceuticals and advanced materials.

## George Tselioudis, Columbia: watching Earth from space

George Tselioudis teaches applied physics at Columbia University and is a senior research scientist at NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS). He has also contributed to the UN's IPCC climate reports.

His course, **Observing Earth's Environment from Space**, treats the planet as one complex system and shows how satellites track the interactions among atmosphere, ocean, land and ice. Students learn the principles behind it, including black-body radiation, the motions of Earth and Sun, and satellite sensor technology, then analyze satellite data on climate change, resource management and natural disasters. In the research seminar, each team chooses one environmental system, such as a climate pattern or air pollution, and builds a group project around satellite observations of it.

The course requires a grounding in linear algebra, calculus and differential equations, so students with solid math and physics have an edge. It suits future climate scientists, aerospace engineers and environmental engineers, and anyone eager to work with satellite imagery or GIS tools.

Sample questions:

- What long-term climate trends show up in satellite records?
- How do aerosols affect cloud formation, and how does that relate to extreme weather?

Along the way, students learn to process satellite data and, like working researchers, test models against observations. Teams present their paper and poster at a conference-style poster session, good preparation for climate science, environmental engineering or satellite data analysis.

## Anastasia Romanou, Columbia: numerical models

Anastasia Romanou teaches applied mathematics at Columbia University and has conducted climate research with NASA and the US Department of Energy. Her course, **Numerical Models and Applications**, shows how numerical models describe systems of every kind, in physics, climate science and geophysics but also in economics, finance, the life sciences and the social sciences. Students learn numerical methods for differential equations, stability analysis and machine-learning-based models, and practice building computer models of real phenomena. Each team takes one modeling topic from literature review to implementation to analysis, ending with a paper and poster.

The prerequisites are first-year university linear algebra, calculus and differential equations. This is a course for students at ease with mathematical tools and keen on programming, whether their strength is math, computer science, physics or engineering. Because its examples range from climate models to economic ones, it also rewards broad interests, including in the scientific uses of big data and machine learning.

Sample questions:

- How do numerical climate models simulate the interaction between atmosphere and ocean?
- In a complex system, why can events that start from similar conditions lead to different outcomes?

Students design numerical experiments, analyze the results, and weigh their model's limits and uncertainties. That full research cycle is a solid base for meteorology, computational science, financial engineering and other fields built on quantitative modeling.

## Haifeng Xu, UChicago: algorithms and agentic AI

Haifeng Xu is a professor of computer science and data science at the University of Chicago whose research centers on algorithms and artificial intelligence. His course, **Algorithms & Agentic AI**, uses algorithms, data analysis and AI as tools for understanding the complex systems of modern society, from economic activity and digital platforms to the flow of information and human decision-making. Teams take on a real-world problem, write a paper and present a poster.

The course is recommended for students with a math foundation and basic programming skills, such as Python. It suits logical problem solvers curious about AI agents and reinforcement learning, particularly those who want to use technology to analyze social and economic systems, and it is a natural fit for future computer science and data science majors.

Topics students have researched in his course include:

- How can algorithms make energy or resource-allocation systems more efficient?
- How do market participants respond to incentives in a regulated economy?
- Can simulation predict the unintended consequences of an economic policy?
