Applying algorithms to real data sharpens critical thinking and creative problem solving, and the team format builds the collaboration that university research demands.

## More from the 2026 faculty

Part 2 of this series introduces the seven professors in the humanities and social sciences, whose courses range across language, law, design and the arts. You can find it on the [CRI blog](/blog), along with a full course profile for each professor above.

If one of these questions is the kind you would happily spend a summer chasing, the [Seoul and Global Research Programs page](/research/summer-camp) explains how the in-person summer programs work and which faculty tracks are open.
author: CRI Editorial

title: US pre-med roadmap, part 3: ten leading colleges and recent admissions trends
excerpt: How Harvard, Johns Hopkins, Penn, Duke and six other universities support pre-med students, what it takes to get in, and why medical school is harder still for international applicants.
content:
In the United States, medical school usually begins after a bachelor's degree, so for most students the road to becoming a doctor runs through a strong undergraduate pre-med experience. Yet American colleges don't offer a "pre-med" major. Pre-med is a track that students in any major follow while they prepare to apply to medical school.

That preparation has four parts:

- **Required coursework** in biology, chemistry and physics, taken alongside the student's major
- **Grades and the MCAT** (Medical College Admission Test), both of which need to stay strong
- **Clinical experience** through hospital internships and volunteering
- **Research experience**, which the most selective medical schools treat as essential

Part 1 of CRI's pre-med roadmap explained how combined BS/MD programs work, why many are closed to international applicants, and why it often makes sense to prepare for the traditional route in parallel. Part 2 compared BS/MD programs with the four-year pre-med path; both are on the [CRI blog](/blog). This third part profiles ten colleges known for pre-med, what it takes to be admitted to them, and the trends shaping medical school admissions, especially for international students.

## Ten colleges known for pre-med

The ten universities below, listed in no particular order, are widely cited for the strength of their pre-med advising and medical school preparation.

### Harvard University

Harvard gives pre-med students a structured advising system. From sophomore year, dedicated advisers and tutors guide each student through everything from choosing prerequisite courses to writing medical school applications. The life sciences curriculum provides a solid grounding in the required sciences, and nearby world-class hospitals, including Massachusetts General Hospital, offer abundant research and clinical opportunities. Students who reach graduation without the prerequisites can complete them through the premedical post-baccalaureate program at Harvard Extension School.

### Johns Hopkins University

Tied to one of the world's leading medical schools and hospitals, Johns Hopkins is an ideal setting for medical research and clinical experience. Affiliations with major teaching hospitals let undergraduates take part in clinical work and research projects, and a dedicated pre-health advising program keeps students of any major on a structured path to medical school. For those who decide on medicine after college, Hopkins runs a post-baccalaureate pre-medical program in which participants complete the prerequisites through at least one year of full-time study.

### University of Pennsylvania

Penn is home to the Perelman School of Medicine, one of the country's top medical schools, and its pre-med students have wide access to research and clinical volunteering. Dedicated advisers support them from required coursework through MCAT preparation. The results stand out: **81%** of Penn's medical school applicants were accepted, nearly double the national rate, a sign of the university's intensive support and strong alumni network.

### Columbia University

Columbia offers the pre-med prerequisites through both Columbia College and its engineering school, and students complete them alongside their major. Registering as pre-med brings a dedicated adviser. Students with strong records can be selected for the Gerald E. Thomson Undergraduate Pre-Medical Program (GET-UPP), which adds mentoring and the chance to shadow physicians in the hospital. For graduates who still need the prerequisites, Columbia's School of General Studies runs the largest and oldest post-baccalaureate premedical program in the country.

### Stanford University

Stanford's pre-med advisers help students with course planning, long-term goals and the search for clinical and research opportunities. Through the Stanford Immersion in Medicine Series (SIMS), students from sophomore year onward are paired one-on-one with physicians at nearby hospitals and gain clinical experience alongside a mentor. The School of Medicine also offers lectures, conferences and summer programs for students preparing for medical school. There is no official pre-med major, but popular majors such as biology and chemistry come with world-class teaching and research.

### Duke University

Duke has a strong reputation in medicine at both levels, for its medical school and for its undergraduate pre-med preparation. The health professions advising office helps students plan so they complete every prerequisite and build relevant experience, then guides them step by step through the MCAT and the application. Because Duke University Hospital is on campus, sophomores, juniors and seniors in good academic standing can shadow physicians there. The environment is competitive, but pre-med students prepare for medical school by working together with their classmates.

### Northwestern University

Northwestern's Feinberg School of Medicine, on the university's Chicago campus, ranks among the top medical schools in the US, and undergraduates have access to well-developed research and early-admission programs. Pre-med students can be selected for summer research internships at the medical school, and through the Northwestern Undergraduate Premedical Scholars Program (NUPSP), a small number of outstanding students receive early acceptance to Feinberg. The health professions advising office arranges study groups, connects students with mentors and helps them find clinical experience. For career changers, Northwestern also offers a post-baccalaureate premedical certificate.

### University of Chicago

UChicago runs its own cohort-based pre-med program, a structured path of professional development through clinical volunteering fellowships, workshops and other activities that build the skills a medical career demands. Its pre-health advisers go further, helping students use a gap year after graduation to gain experience that strengthens their medical school applications. Throughout, students balance demanding coursework with clinical and research work.

### Boston University

BU draws on the deep medical resources of the city of Boston to offer several routes into medicine. Students in any major can follow the pre-med track, with pre-professional advising on goals, course planning and clinical and research opportunities. Those selected for the Modular Medical/Dental Integrated Curriculum (MMEDIC) can earn early admission to BU's medical school after their sophomore year. BU also offers a post-baccalaureate premedical certificate for students who didn't finish the prerequisites in college, though only applicants who have completed fewer than three of the required courses are eligible.

### University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

North Carolina's flagship public university supports students through its Health Professions Advising office, which partners with UNC's medical school and related departments, as well as outside health care organizations, so that pre-med students can build hands-on skills and experience. Strong students may be invited to join national pre-med honor societies such as Alpha Epsilon Delta. UNC admits a larger share of applicants than the private universities on this list, partly because it enrolls a high proportion of North Carolina residents, but its incoming students are exceptionally accomplished. Pre-med students draw on the university's broad network for clinical volunteering and research assistant positions.

## Admissions numbers at a glance

Getting into any of these colleges is highly competitive. The table below collects recent admit rates along with the grades and test scores of the Class of 2028, the students who entered in fall 2024.

| University | Recent admit rate | Grades, Class of 2028 | SAT, middle 50% | ACT, middle 50% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvard | About 4% | Average GPA 4.21 (weighted) | 1510–1580 | 34–36 |
| Johns Hopkins | Under 7% | Average GPA 3.93 | 1530–1560 | 34–36 |
| Penn | Under 5% | Average GPA 3.9 | 1510–1570 | 34–36 |
| Columbia | Under 5% | 94% in top 10% of class* | 1510–1560 | 34–36 |
| Stanford | Under 4% | Average GPA 3.94 | 1510–1570 | 34–35 |
| Duke | 4.8% (Class of 2029) | 92% in top 10% of class | 1500–1570 | 34–35 |
| Northwestern | About 7% | — | 1510–1560 | 34–35 |
| UChicago | Under 5% | Most at GPA 3.75 or above | 1510–1560 | 34–35 |
| Boston University | 12.8% (Class of 2029) | Average GPA 3.9 | 1430–1510 | 32–34 |
| UNC Chapel Hill | 16.5% (Class of 2029) | 97% at GPA 4.0 or above | 1400–1530 | 28–34 |

*Among admitted students whose high schools reported a class rank. Test ranges reflect students who submitted scores.

## Medical school admissions today

Students who want to practice medicine in the US face intense competition that begins in college. Growing interest in health care has pushed the number of medical school applicants steadily upward, and because class sizes are capped, schools turn away even very strong candidates. Fewer than half of all applicants win a place at any US medical school. More students are therefore taking a gap year to add research or hospital work to their record, or completing missing prerequisites in a post-baccalaureate program before applying again.

![A physician in a white coat with a stethoscope around the neck, arms folded](/editorial/224140370463-01.jpg "US medical schools look for top grades, a high MCAT score and real clinical experience.")

Medical schools expect excellence on both of the numbers that matter most. Recent entering classes have averaged a GPA of roughly 3.7 to 3.8 on a 4.0 scale and an MCAT score of about 512 out of 528. At the most selective schools, many admitted students have MCAT scores in the 520s and GPAs above 3.8, and substantial research experience and clinical service are treated as essential.

## What international students should know

For international students, the path is harder still. Only a minority of US medical schools, most of them private, accept applications from students who are neither US citizens nor permanent residents, and most public medical schools admit very few international students. International applicants are accepted at a far lower rate than citizens and permanent residents.

Even with a US bachelor's degree, then, an international student needs a deliberate strategy:

- **Target the right medical schools.** Aim for highly ranked private medical schools that actively admit international students.
- **Build experience throughout college.** Use the undergraduate years to accumulate lab internships, hospital volunteering and physician shadowing.
- **Choose the college with medical school in mind.** Look for a robust pre-med support system, close ties to medical schools and hospitals, and an environment where you can do your best work.

For international applicants, a US medical school is a realistic goal only with that kind of thorough preparation and strategy.

## Where research fits

Research experience is part of every strong pre-med record, and it can begin before college. Students who want to explore a question in the life sciences or medicine with a university faculty mentor can do so in CRI's [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1), an individually arranged project that typically runs two to four months and ends with a paper the student writes in English.
author: CRI Editorial

title: US pre-med roadmap, part 2: BS/MD programs vs. the traditional pre-med path
excerpt: How the four-year pre-med route compares with combined BS/MD programs on workload, time and cost, the MCAT, flexibility and admit rates, and which kind of student each path suits.
content:
A combined BS/MD program offers something no ordinary college acceptance can: a place in medical school, reserved before a student has taken a single college class. Getting one is the hard part. Brown University's Program in Liberal Medical Education (PLME) admitted just 3.6% of its applicants in 2019. Most future doctors in the US take the other road, the traditional pre-med track, and the two routes differ in far more than their admit rates.

Part 1 of this roadmap explained how BS/MD programs work. Part 2 looks at the traditional route and compares the two on five points: academic intensity, time and cost, the MCAT, flexibility, and competition.

## How the traditional pre-med track works

On the traditional track, students earn a four-year bachelor's degree and then apply to medical school. In college they complete the prerequisite courses medical schools require, keep their grades up, and build clinical and research experience. They take the MCAT (Medical College Admission Test) and apply to several schools at once through AMCAS, the common application used by most US MD programs. No seat is reserved in advance, so each student has to build a competitive application.

Four features define the route:

- **College first.** Students finish a four-year degree before starting medical school, the standard US timeline.
- **Any major.** As long as they complete the prerequisites, students can major in anything, including the humanities.
- **Time to build a record.** College leaves room for research and internships, and a gap year can strengthen an application further.
- **Better overall odds.** Regular medical school admission is far less restrictive than BS/MD selection: about 40% of US medical school applicants are accepted to at least one school each year.

In short, the traditional route offers more choices and more time, but the medical school admissions race stays ahead of students until the very end.

## The two paths at a glance

| | BS/MD program | Traditional pre-med |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Medical school seat | Reserved from the start of college | Earned by applying through AMCAS |
| Length | As short as 6–7 years in some programs | Usually 8 years (4 + 4), sometimes plus a gap year or more |
| Workload | Compressed; some programs run through the summer | Spread across four years of college |
| MCAT | Often waived, or a set minimum score | Required; top medical schools expect high scores |
| Flexibility | Hard to change majors, careers or medical schools | Any major; free to switch; can apply to any medical school |
| Admit rate | Often below 5% | About 40% of medical school applicants accepted |

## Academic intensity

A BS/MD program folds college and medical school into as little as six or seven years. Pre-medical coursework has to be finished in a short window, and some programs keep classes and hands-on training going through the summer, a year-round load that puts real academic pressure on students.

Pre-med students use the full four years, so the work is spread more evenly and summers are free for rest or new experiences. The prerequisites are still demanding, but students can move at a steadier pace and study subjects in more depth. On workload alone, BS/MD is the more intense track.

## Time and cost

That compression saves time. The traditional route usually takes eight years, four in college and four in medical school, and some students add a gap year or more before applying. BS/MD students can start their medical careers one to two years sooner.

Time saved is money saved. Every year cut from college is a year less of tuition and living expenses, and on a road as long and costly as the one to becoming a doctor, many applicants see that as a big part of BS/MD's appeal. Pre-med students pay for the full eight years or more, plus medical school application fees and travel to interviews.

![A doctor in blue scrubs with a stethoscope around the neck, arms crossed](/editorial/224139025369-02.jpg "Both routes lead to the same MD; they differ in timing, cost and flexibility.")

## The MCAT

Many BS/MD programs ease the MCAT requirement. Some waive the exam entirely, and others ask only for a set minimum score, which takes much of the stress out of it.

For pre-med students the MCAT is unavoidable, and top medical schools expect very high scores. The computer-based exam runs about six hours and 15 minutes, and preparing for it takes a great deal of time and effort, all while students keep their college grades up. Skipping the exam, or clearing it with a minimum score, is a genuine relief for BS/MD students.

## Flexibility

A BS/MD curriculum assumes from day one that the student is headed to medical school, which makes it very hard to explore other fields or change majors midway. A student who realizes in college that medicine isn't the right fit has no easy way to change course and may end up leaving the program or transferring.

BS/MD students are also expected to attend the medical school linked to their program, so they can't freely apply elsewhere, whether to a school they prefer or one in another region. Some programs let students "apply out" after college, but that means giving up the guaranteed seat. In practice, most stay on course for their program's own medical school.

Pre-med students have far more room to move. They can major in the sciences or the humanities, switch majors along the way, take a leave of absence or a gap year to rethink their plans, and apply to any medical school they choose. If BS/MD is a narrow, dedicated lane, the traditional route is an open field where students can explore, find what suits them, and decide whether and when to head for medical school.

## Competition and admit rates

BS/MD programs are by far the harder door to get through. Because they guarantee a path to medical school, competition is fierce: many admit fewer than 5% of applicants, rates that rival or undercut undergraduate admission at Ivy League colleges. Some well-known programs draw thousands of applications for about ten seats. Brown's 3.6% is not unusual, and Drexel University's BA/BS+MD program has said it selects about 2.5% of applicants. At odds like these, winning a BS/MD place in high school is already as hard as getting into medical school.

Pre-med students enter college through regular admission, which is usually easier than getting into the same university's BS/MD program. The competition is postponed, not avoided, though the overall medical school acceptance rate of about 40% is still far higher than BS/MD admit rates.

That figure needs context: the applicants who get in are the well-prepared ones, and less competitive candidates are turned away. At the most selective medical schools, acceptance rates are only around 10%, and many pre-med students apply to dozens of schools in hopes of a single acceptance. BS/MD is a narrow gate at the entrance. Pre-med is open to everyone but ends in a long, demanding race for medical school.

## Which path fits which student

**A BS/MD program fits students who:**

- are already certain in high school that they want to become doctors
- have exceptionally strong academic records
- want to avoid the uncertainty of medical school admissions
- are ready to focus their entire college experience on medicine

**The traditional pre-med track fits students who:**

- want to explore different fields of study first
- would rather decide about medical school during college
- want a more flexible college experience
- would value four years to grow and build their medical school application

In the end, two questions decide it: how sure are you about medicine, and what kind of college experience do you want? Both paths lead to an MD, and neither works without strong academics and careful preparation. Choose the one that fits your temperament and goals, then plan your college years around it.

Part 3 of this roadmap turns to strategy, profiling ten leading US colleges for pre-med that international-school students often apply to: how competitive each one is, how to approach the application, and recent admissions trends.

## Testing your interest early

Whichever route you choose, it pays to find out early whether you enjoy the questions science and medicine ask, and research is one of the most direct ways to do that. In CRI's [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter), students spend winter break working with a university professor to develop a research question and write their own paper in English, with TAs guiding them day to day.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Why international law falters in a crisis: William Burke-White's winter online class
excerpt: Four students in Penn professor William Burke-White's online class wrote two papers on why international law stumbled over COVID-19 vaccines, school closures, and US tariffs.
content:
International law clearly exists. So why does it look so powerless at the moments that matter most, in a pandemic or a trade conflict? That question anchored William Burke-White's class in CRI's 2025 Winter Online Research Program, and his four students answered it through two very different global crises.

Burke-White, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania, did not treat international law as a list of provisions and definitions to memorize. His class asked whether the law actually worked when a real crisis or conflict hit, and if it did not, why. The students split into two groups of two, and each group completed one paper. His lectures gave everyone the same grounding in how international law is built and where its limits lie. In TA sessions and in their own research, the two groups took that grounding in completely different directions.

## Group 1: the pandemic and the limits of international law

The first group asked why international law failed to guarantee equitable access to vaccines and education during the COVID-19 pandemic. Its central argument is easy to state: the intentions and declarations were there, but the power to enforce them was not. The students examined what international organizations such as the WHO and UNESCO did during the crisis, and why that role was bound to be structurally limited.

### Student A: vaccines and COVAX

Student A took on vaccine access, explaining in structural terms why international law falls short in a crisis even when the goal is to share vaccines fairly. The starting point was an idea from Burke-White's lectures: international law is less a system for controlling states by force than a structure for drawing them into cooperation. From there, A analyzed why the WHO and global health norms carried so little practical weight during the pandemic.

The case at the center was COVAX. It was built to distribute vaccines fairly, but it ran on voluntary participation rather than legal obligation, so it had no real way to restrain the countries that had already secured their doses. Wealthy countries could put themselves first without violating any international norm. The group's slides made the gap concrete: by June 2021, COVAX had distributed 89 million doses, less than 5 percent of its 2 billion-dose target. A's analysis is balanced, presenting the problem less as a "failure" of international law than as a limit built into it.

![A Zoom screen shows a student slide titled Case Study 2 about COVAX, with the World Health Organization logo on the left and participant video tiles on the right](/editorial/224137801093-05.jpg "Group 1 presents its COVAX case study to Burke-White over Zoom.")

### Student B: education when schools went online

Student B handled the right to education. When schools closed and classes moved online, why did students in developing countries lose so much more? B approached the question through international law and education policy, arguing that the education gap had turned from a question of achievement into a question of access: whether students could get connected at all. Using Kenya and the wider region of sub-Saharan Africa, B traced the problem step by step:

- shortages of electricity, internet access, and devices
- teachers and school systems that were not prepared for the switch
- a widening gap between public schools and private schools, which moved to digital tools far faster
- learning losses that dragged on and became entrenched

B then turned to the UNESCO Education 2030 Framework. An international standard was already in place, so why could it not be upheld during the pandemic? Working through the framework provision by provision, B reached a clear conclusion: the framework was there, but the means to enforce it were weak.

## Group 2: why the trade rules began to break down

The second group studied how US tariff policy and the collapse of the WTO's dispute settlement system have affected the international trading order. It centered on one question: if the rules exist, why can they not stop the most powerful countries? The students identified two key causes, US tariff policy and the paralysis of the WTO Appellate Body. Their research question read: "How is US trade policy, including undermining the dispute settlement system and imposing unilateral tariffs, changing international trade law, and what can be done about it?"

Their thesis argued that by paralyzing the Appellate Body, the United States had cleared the way for unilateral tariffs. Those tariffs are often defended under the exceptions in GATT Articles XX and XXI but frequently lack the evidence those exceptions require, which leaves them legally vulnerable and the disputes largely unresolved.

![A Zoom screen shows a slide titled Research Question + Thesis Statement, with bullet points on the US-China trade conflict and a highlighted thesis about the Appellate Body and unilateral tariff measures](/editorial/224137801093-06.jpg "Group 2's research question and thesis on US tariffs and the WTO Appellate Body.")

### Student C: US-China tariffs

Student C used the US-China trade dispute to show why trade rules so often go unenforced. Starting from two basic WTO principles, non-discrimination and keeping tariffs within the rates countries have committed to, C explained why unilateral US tariff increases collide with international trade law. China did take the United States to the WTO. But with the Appellate Body paralyzed, no ruling could become final, and the tariffs stayed in place. C's analysis lays out plainly how a country can break the rules and face little consequence, and it makes the difference between law that exists and law that works unusually easy to see.

### Student D: the Appellate Body and the security exception

Student D argued that in international trade, the system that enforces the rules matters more than the rules themselves. D showed how unstable trade became once the Appellate Body stopped functioning. While it operated, countries could not easily break the rules; now a violation can simply go unresolved. D also analyzed the *Russia – Traffic in Transit* case alongside the national-security exception, connecting it to the scholarly debate over how far such exceptions should be allowed to reach. The result treats international law as more than a rulebook: it is a matter of trust and predictability.

### The group's recommendations

Group 2 closed its presentation with three proposals for repair:

- **Amend the Dispute Settlement Understanding** to put clear limits on vetoes and require a legally grounded reason for them, while recognizing that any change needs consensus, which in practice means US approval.
- **Win back US trust**, for example by updating how developing-country status works.
- **Modernize WTO provisions** such as GATT Article XXI, the security exception, to make them clearer, prevent abuse, take in modern issues, and give countries a fresh chance to negotiate.

![A Zoom screen shows a slide titled Recommendations + Conclusion, listing amendments to the DSU, regaining US trust, and modern modifications to the WTO](/editorial/224137801093-07.jpg "Group 2's recommendations for repairing WTO dispute settlement.")

## What students take from the class

For families, the greatest value of Burke-White's class is that students actually used international law as a tool for analyzing real problems. They move past simple assumptions (that international law is always just, or that international organizations can solve every problem) and learn to explain for themselves why the law works in some situations and hits its limits in others. Both papers show that enforcement structures and power relations matter more than whether a rule exists, a far more mature way of understanding the subject.

That maturity carries into college applications. Work like this signals to admissions officers that a student does more than know about international issues: they can take one global problem apart, analyze its structure, and explain it through their own reasoning. In essays and interviews, these students can talk naturally about how they worked through a problem and why they reached their conclusions, instead of listing activities.

The 2025 winter class was less a course in international law than practice in reading the world through it, and a solid starting point for students who plan to study international relations, politics, or law. Burke-White taught it as part of the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter), where students research and write with university faculty over Zoom during the winter break.
author: CRI Editorial

title: What makes a good prediction? Inside UChicago professor Haifeng Xu's winter AI class
excerpt: Three students in Haifeng Xu's online winter class each led one thread of a single NBA forecasting paper: which data to trust, how to combine forecasts, and how to act on a probability.
content:
Two people forecast the same basketball game. One gives a team a 55% chance of winning; the other says 75%. Who made the better prediction? University of Chicago professor Haifeng Xu put that question to his students in CRI's 2025 Winter Online Research Program, and it became one of the moments they responded to most. It also set the direction for the paper they went on to write.

## An AI course that starts with uncertainty

Xu's course on agentic AI started somewhere different from the typical "AI class" or "coding class." It was built around two questions: What is a prediction? And when the outcome is uncertain, what do we base our decisions on? Instead of diving straight into AI, students began by working to understand probability, uncertainty, and the limits built into any prediction.

## 55% or 75%?

Most students instinctively asked which forecaster would turn out to be right. Xu pointed out that before the game is played, there is no result to check either forecast against, so "who was right" cannot be the test. What counted in his class was how well-grounded the reasoning behind each probability was.

The moment stuck with students. It taught them to see forecasting as the work of explaining your logic and evidence, rather than a game of guessing the right answer.

## One paper, three lines of research

In the TA sessions, that way of thinking turned into a real research project. Xu's class had three students, and together they set out to complete a single paper. This was not a simple division of labor: each student took ownership of one research thread within the study.

### Student A: what goes into a forecast

Student A handled the data every forecast starts from. Beyond NBA game results, A researched and organized factors that could shape a prediction, including injury reports released before tip-off, whether a team was playing at home or away, and its recent form. Along the way, A raised a question of their own: does feeding in more information always produce a better prediction? Comparing a range of cases, A found that some information can actually cloud a forecast. That line of questioning fed directly into the problem the paper sets out to address.

![A spreadsheet named Brier listing six NBA matchups, with probability columns labeled 3 searchers, 2 searchers and injury next to a results column; a blurred student appears on camera](/editorial/224137620182-04.jpg "The team compared win probabilities produced from different inputs against the actual results.")

### Student B: many forecasts, one number

Student B took on the job of merging several forecasts into a single probability. When analysts, fans, and AI models disagree about a game, how should their views be condensed into one number? B tried methods ranging from a simple average to schemes that weight each source differently, testing them repeatedly to see which gave the most stable results. The data showed B firsthand that blending opinions is not always the right answer.

### Student C: acting on a probability

Student C worked on what comes after the forecast: the decision. The starting question was practical. If you had to trust this probability and act on it, what should you do? Working from the premise that any forecast could be wrong, C studied decision strategies that spread risk instead of staking everything on a single call, and worked through them in simulations. In the paper, C explains that a crucial step always sits between prediction and decision: managing risk.

## A paper about judgment, not basketball

Basketball supplied the data, but the finished paper reaches well beyond picking winners. It links three steps into one line of work: using AI to forecast game outcomes as probabilities, assessing how reasonable those probabilities are, and working out how to reduce risk when some predictions will inevitably miss. The team scored its forecasts with the **Brier score**, a standard measure of how close probabilistic forecasts come to actual outcomes.

At its core, the paper asks how people should reason in an uncertain world.

## More than using AI

For parents, the value of this course has little to do with how advanced the technology is. How much code a student wrote matters far less than whether they have practiced thinking on the assumption that a prediction can be wrong, and whether they can explain their own judgment. Students come away having done more than "use AI." They have questioned it and evaluated it.

That experience changes how a student can talk about their work. In an essay or interview, they no longer need to list activities. They can explain in their own words how they worked through a problem and why they made the calls they did, which is precisely what colleges value most.

## A first taste of university research

Data science and AI were the tools, but the real lesson of Xu's class was an early rehearsal of how university researchers approach a problem: refusing to take numbers at face value, and asking about the process rather than only the result. That habit of mind was the most important thing the course left with its students.

Xu's class ran as part of CRI's [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter), where students work with university faculty over Zoom during the winter break. If arguing over 55% versus 75% sounds like your kind of problem, that page explains how the program works and which courses are currently offered.
