title: The story of penicillin: inside Caltech chemist Brian Stoltz's winter online class
excerpt: Caltech's Brian Stoltz built his winter online class around the shape of one molecule. Here is how five students divided a review paper on penicillin, from its discovery to how the body clears it.
content:
"Why does this molecule look the way it does?" In Caltech chemistry professor Brian Stoltz's class for CRI's 2025 Winter Online Research Program, that question came before any formula. Stoltz would put up a drawing of a single molecule and start asking questions about it. The molecule at the heart of the course was one almost everyone has heard of: penicillin.

Many families picture organic chemistry as a hard subject built on formulas and memorization. Stoltz's class ran differently. Instead of drilling problem sets, it followed the story of one real medicine: how it is made, and why it works. Students did not stop at learning concepts. They went deep on a single topic and wrote it up as a research paper.

## Starting from shape

Rather than filling the board with complex calculations, Stoltz built his explanations around a molecule's shape and its distinctive features. From that first question about shape, he kept pushing further:

- Doesn't this part look unstable?
- Why does this structure break apart so easily?
- What reactions could this shape lead to, and what happens then?

Penicillin gave those questions a concrete answer. The molecule, Stoltz explained, contains a structure that breaks apart especially easily. (Chemists know that fragile part as the four-membered beta-lactam ring.) That fragility is what lets penicillin attack bacteria. It is also what makes the drug so tricky to make. Once students saw that trade-off, penicillin stopped being just the name of a medicine and became something they could explain.

## Five students, one paper

If Stoltz's sessions sketched the big picture, the TA-led sessions were where students worked as researchers. Rather than all five skimming the same material, they divided one paper into parts:

- **Student A:** how penicillin was first discovered, and the trial and error it took to work out its structure
- **Student B:** how fungi in nature produce penicillin
- **Student C:** the methods developed to manufacture the drug at industrial scale
- **Student D:** how penicillin attacks bacteria, and why it is relatively safe for people
- **Student E:** how long the drug stays effective once it enters the body, and how the body clears it

That division raised the stakes. Each student had to be able to explain their own section better than anyone else in the group.

## Reading the research, then drawing it again

The paper was a review. Students read a range of published studies, organized what they found, and drew the connections between them. This was not simple summarizing or translating. They had to explain what they understood in their own words, and instead of pasting in figures from the papers they read, they redrew them. Along the way, students kept asking themselves two questions:

- Do I really understand this part?
- Could I explain it to someone else?

![Zoom screen showing a slide titled Structural Difference Between Penicillin G/V with two annotated molecular structures, a student presenting in a small video inset, and Brian Stoltz in a tile at top right](/editorial/224135082244-03.jpg "A student walks through the structural differences between penicillin G and penicillin V while Brian Stoltz (top right) follows along on Zoom.")

## Why the process matters

For families weighing a class like this, the finished paper matters less than the process behind it. Has the student wrestled seriously with a topic tied to the field they want to study? Have they traded questions and feedback with a professor? Above all, can they explain what role they took on and what they actually did?

That experience changes how a student can talk about their interests. In a college application or an interview, instead of saying "I like chemistry," they can describe teaching themselves how a single drug is made and how it works, and writing up what they learned.

Stoltz's class was never really about teaching difficult chemistry. It gave students an early taste of the way of thinking they will meet at university, and of how research actually unfolds: moving from memorizing to understanding, and from studying alone to building a piece of research together. That shift is why CRI built the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter).
author: CRI Editorial

title: US pre-med roadmap, part 1: how BS/MD programs work, and who they suit
excerpt: BS/MD programs pair college with a conditional seat in medical school. How the tracks work, what they demand after admission, and why eligibility comes first for international students.
content:
Imagine being admitted to medical school before you have even finished high school. That is how BS/MD programs are usually described, and it is no surprise they draw so much interest from international-school students and their parents. The structure is one of the most distinctive in US medical education, with real advantages. It also comes with firm preconditions, and for international students the first is the most basic of all: many programs accept only US citizens and permanent residents.

## How a BS/MD program works

A BS/MD program links an undergraduate degree (a BS or BA) and a medical degree (MD) into one continuous track. The usual route to a US medical school is long: high school, then college, pre-med coursework, the MCAT, and finally a separate round of medical school applications. BS/MD students skip that last round: they enter college straight out of high school already holding a conditional place at a partner medical school.

The full program usually runs seven or eight years. As long as students meet the program's benchmarks during college (a minimum GPA, required courses and, in some programs, an MCAT score), they move on to medical school without applying again.

| | Traditional pre-med route | BS/MD program |
|---|---|---|
| When medical school admission is decided | After college, through a separate application | At the end of high school, conditionally |
| Typical length | 4 years of college + 4 years of medical school | 7 or 8 years in total |
| MCAT | Required | Varies: some programs set lower thresholds, a few waive it |
| Room to change course | Open | Limited in most programs |

## Check eligibility before anything else

For students at international schools, eligibility is where the conversation has to start. Many US BS/MD programs accept only US citizens or permanent residents, and relatively few are open to international applicants. Plenty of schools say so outright on their official pages; Albany Medical College's combined-degree programs are one example.

The best-known exception is Brown University's Program in Liberal Medical Education (PLME), which does accept international students. It is also one of the most competitive programs in the country. So before weighing a program's structure or reputation, an international student has a more practical question to answer: am I allowed to apply at all?

## Why the model appeals

The biggest selling point is reduced uncertainty. Traditional medical school applicants are evaluated all over again on their college grades, MCAT score, recommendations, activities and interviews. A BS/MD student who meets the program's benchmarks does not have to go through that process a second time, which makes it easier to plan college with a clear goal in mind.

Some programs also ease the pressure of the MCAT. Not all of them waive the exam, but certain programs set a lower bar than regular medical school admissions, and a few do not require it at all. With less testing pressure, students can put more of their college years into research or advanced coursework.

Then there is time. A seven-year track saves a year compared with the standard four years of college plus four of medical school, which can also cut the overall cost of training. For students with a firm career goal who value long-term planning, that predictability can feel reassuring.

## What the model demands

This is where the picture changes. Selection is fierce from the start. Places are so limited that many programs do not publish an acceptance rate, and where rates are public they are often in the single digits. Brown's PLME, for example, receives thousands of applications each year and admits fewer than 100 students. These programs are looking for more than good grades: they want high school students who already show exceptional academic ability and readiness.

Admission is also conditional. A BS/MD offer is not a final medical school acceptance; it is a status students keep only by meeting the program's standards throughout college. Each program spells out its own requirements for GPA, grades in prerequisite courses, the MCAT where required, and academic conduct and ethics. Students who fall short can lose their place in medical school, so the track calls for steady discipline long after the admission letter arrives.

The programs themselves show how high the bar stays. Well-known examples include:

- Brown University's PLME
- The University of Illinois Chicago's Guaranteed Professional Program Admissions (GPPA) in Medicine
- The University of Pittsburgh's Guaranteed Admissions Program (GAP)
- Case Western Reserve University's Pre-Professional Scholars Program (PPSP)
- Albany Medical College's combined-degree programs

Many of these do not publish exact acceptance rates, but their conditions for staying in say a great deal. Pittsburgh's GAP officially requires **a cumulative GPA and a science GPA of at least 3.7 each, plus an MCAT score of at least 517**. Getting in is only the beginning; students have to keep performing at the very top to hold on to their place.

Flexibility is the third consideration. Most BS/MD programs restrict changes of major or academic direction, and switching to a different medical school or a different career partway through is not easy. For a high school student who is already sure about becoming a doctor, that commitment can be a strength. For one who wants room to explore, it can become a burden.

## Who BS/MD suits, and a steadier strategy

A BS/MD program is neither an advantage for every student nor something to avoid. The fairest way to see it is as a good fit for students who know very early that they want to be doctors and can sustain a long academic plan without wavering. Students who want to explore different possibilities in college, or who need more time to decide, may be better served by the traditional pre-med route.

In CRI's advising, the far more stable strategy is often to pursue both: apply to the handful of BS/MD programs open to international students, such as Brown's PLME, while preparing for the traditional pre-med route in parallel. Building a medical school application in college, through a strong GPA, research experience, clinical exposure and well-planned MCAT preparation, often leaves students with more options in the long run.

In the end, the program's name matters less than how well its structure fits the student's temperament and way of preparing. BS/MD is one route to a US medical school among several. Part 2 of this series compares it directly with the traditional pre-med path and looks at which kinds of students each one suits best.

Whichever route you choose, research experience will be part of the picture. CRI's [research programs](/research) pair high school students with university faculty to develop a question of their own and write it up as a paper in English, a practical way to find out early whether scientific and medical research holds your interest.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Nature's 10 for 2025: a baby, an AI founder and a scientist who said no
excerpt: A baby given a one-of-a-kind gene edit, the founder of DeepSeek and a fired CDC director made Nature's 10 for 2025. Here is who they are and what their choices say about science.
content:
Every December, the journal *Nature* names ten people who helped shape science over the past year. The honorees are usually researchers behind landmark papers or bold new theories. The 2025 edition, released on 8 December, looked different. It included the founder of an AI company, a geoscientist who descended 9,000 meters into the ocean, a public-health official who lost her job less than a month after taking it, and a baby only a few months old when his treatment began. Why did *Nature* choose them?

## A therapy built for one child

KJ Muldoon was born in the United States in 2024 and, soon after birth, was diagnosed with severe CPS1 deficiency, an extremely rare inherited disorder that leaves the body unable to break down the protein in food properly. Without treatment, his chances of survival were poor, and the only established remedy was a liver transplant. The problem was time. A baby has to grow before surgery is possible, and KJ faced a high risk of coma or death before he would be big enough for the operation.

His doctors at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and Penn Medicine, led by Rebecca Ahrens-Nicklas and Kiran Musunuru, tried something no one had done before: a gene-editing therapy designed around KJ's own mutation. Instead of a conventional CRISPR edit, which cuts DNA, they used **base editing**, a CRISPR-derived technique that changes a single DNA letter with precision. KJ received his first dose at about six months old, in February 2025, followed by further doses in March and April.

It is still too early to call him cured. But KJ can now eat more foods and move around on his own. His case is a sign that medicine is starting to shift from treatments designed for the average patient toward treatments built for one person.

## The founder who changed how AI is shared

In January 2025, the Chinese company DeepSeek released its R1 model and caught the world's attention. It could hold its own against the best AI systems of the day, was far cheaper to train and, most important, was open for anyone to use and build on. In September, R1 also became the first major AI model to go through peer review, with the paper published in *Nature* itself.

That is why its founder, **Liang Wenfeng**, made the list. He was recognized not for building the most complex model but for changing how AI is developed and shared. DeepSeek's rise also marked a shift in China's place in the global technology race, from catching up to helping set the direction.

Liang's story makes a point that runs through the whole list: in science today, what counts is less how clever you are than which choices you make.

## The scientist who would not sign off

One of the most thought-provoking names was **Susan Monarez**, a microbiologist and immunologist who was sworn in as director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) at the end of July 2025. Less than a month later, she was out.

By her account, she had been asked to approve new vaccine recommendations in advance, without weighing the evidence behind them, and to dismiss career scientists. She refused. The Trump administration said she was removed because she was not aligned with the president's agenda. Testifying before the US Senate in September, Monarez told senators she had been fired for defending scientific integrity.

*Nature* honored her for standing up for evidence-based public-health policy. She made her stand not in a laboratory but inside government, and what she protected was a principle, not a paper. It cost her the job. It also sent the scientific community an unmistakable message about what evidence is worth.

## Four more stories, one common thread

Four more honorees shared a similar outlook:

- **Mengran Du**, a geoscientist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Deep-sea Science and Engineering, who rode a crewed submersible about 9,000 meters down into a trench northeast of Japan and documented animal communities living deeper than any recorded before.
- **Sarah Tabrizi**, a University College London neurologist at the center of clinical work on Huntington's disease. The inherited brain disorder went decades without any treatment that could slow it, until a therapy finally did.
- **Achal Agrawal**, a data scientist in India who tracked retracted papers at Indian universities and made the pattern public. His work helped bring about a change in the country's national university rankings, which began docking points from institutions for retractions.
- **Precious Matsoso**, a South African public-health official who co-led the talks that produced the first global pandemic agreement, adopted by the World Health Organization's member states in May 2025.

They worked in very different fields. Yet each of them chose principle over results, and direction over speed.

Three more researchers completed the list. Physicist Tony Tyson's decades of work on digital imaging for astronomy helped make the new Vera Rubin Observatory possible. Luciano Moreira is the scientist behind a Brazilian facility that mass-produces mosquitoes carrying *Wolbachia* bacteria, which make the insects far less able to spread dengue. And systems biologist Yifat Merbl of the Weizmann Institute of Science showed that the proteasome, the cell's protein-recycling machinery, also generates peptides that fight infection.

## What the 2025 list is really about

There are no celebrity scientists here, and no one competing on publication counts. Instead there is a baby who cannot yet talk, a founder who chose efficiency and openness, a scientist who stood by the evidence at personal cost, and a researcher who went down into places no one had seen.

In 2025, science earned its standing not by getting the right answers but by refusing to dodge hard choices. It is the same idea CRI returns to with every student: why you chose your question matters more than what you achieved with it. These ten stories show clearly where the standards for judging science and research are heading.

For students ready to pursue a question of their own with that kind of commitment, the [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1) pairs each student with a faculty mentor who guides the work from first idea to finished manuscript.
author: CRI Editorial

title: New master's programs at NYU, Penn and beyond: why a brand-new program can be an opening
excerpt: From NYU's new school of math, computing and data science to Penn's energy master's and Cambridge's digital policy MPhil, a look at why new interdisciplinary programs open doors.
content:
Students preparing for graduate school abroad often ask the same question: "Top universities are fiercely competitive. Is there still a realistic path in?" Part of the answer lies in what those universities are building: over the past few years, Penn, NYU, Columbia and their peers have launched new interdisciplinary schools and programs and expanded master's tracks tied directly to careers. Here is a snapshot of several of them from the 2025–26 cycle, and why a brand-new program can be worth a closer look.

## Why new programs deserve attention

In their early years, new programs tend to share a few traits:

- **They are not yet widely known,** so applicants do not always flood in.
- **They are admitting a first cohort,** so admissions can be run with some flexibility.
- **A perfect major match is not always required.** Applicants whose undergraduate major differs can still find a way in if they make a convincing case for why they want to move into the field.

None of this makes admission easy. But it does mean new doors are opening, and that is worth knowing when you plan where to apply.

## NYU brings math, computing and data science under one roof

In November 2025, NYU announced a new school: the **Courant Institute School of Mathematics, Computing, and Data Science**. The key idea is consolidation. Before the announcement, NYU's resources in mathematics and computing were spread across separate departments, research centers and its engineering school. The new school pulls them together into a single hub built around computing and data.

Applicants for fall 2026 could not select the new school directly on the Common App. Even so, the direction is clear. A new school tends to produce new degrees and tracks, and as existing programs are reorganized around interdisciplinary work, the kind of applicant they attract changes too.

Students with a solid foundation in mathematics plus programming and data skills should keep an eye on the new master's tracks NYU is likely to introduce in data science, computational mathematics and computing. The point is not the university's name. The newer a program is, the more sharply it signals what the school wants to build, and applicants who read that direction accurately have the advantage.

## Penn Engineering launches a master's in Energy and Sustainability

Penn Engineering opened a new master's degree in Energy and Sustainability (MESE) for 2026. Energy transition, carbon neutrality and climate technology have become familiar talking points. Penn's decision signals that universities now see the field as a core pillar of future industry, not a passing trend.

MESE is organized around four areas:

1. Environment and climate solutions
2. Clean energy technology
3. Society and policy
4. Economics and innovation

What makes the program interesting is its emphasis. Master's degrees in similar fields have often leaned toward policy and management. MESE puts STEM-based technical skills at the center, so sustainability is approached through technology, engineering and research and development rather than discussed only in the abstract.

Students can also take courses at Wharton and in the School of Arts and Sciences, adding a business and finance perspective to their technical training. In short, the program is built for an industry that wants people who understand the technology and the business behind it.

For its first admissions cycle, Penn reviewed applications on a rolling basis and did not require the GRE. The program favors applicants with STEM and engineering backgrounds, such as environmental, chemical, mechanical or materials engineering.

## A wider shift across leading universities

These are not isolated experiments at a handful of schools. The same shift is happening across top universities at once, driven by a shared concern: traditional disciplinary boundaries are no longer enough to explain the problems society faces today. Many universities are responding by lowering the walls between majors and creating master's programs where students from different backgrounds learn side by side. Four examples show how this looks in practice.

### Columbia University: MS in Project Management

Columbia's master's in project management is less about going deep in a single discipline and more about the ability to design, manage and carry out complex projects. Applicants may come from engineering, the social sciences or the humanities. For those with practical or project experience, a mismatched undergraduate major is usually not a serious weakness. Rather than following a traditional academic track, the program builds skills that companies and organizations use right away, which is why it has drawn growing interest from students.

### University of Chicago Booth School of Business: Master in Management

Booth's Master in Management is one of the clearest examples of the trend, because it was designed from the start for students who did not major in business. It gives graduates in engineering, the natural sciences, the humanities and the social sciences a foundation in management and a route into business, finance, consulting and tech.

The program cares less about how much business knowledge an applicant already has. What matters more is how well they can carry the thinking and problem-solving skills built in their own field into a business setting.

### University of Cambridge: MPhil in Digital Policy

Cambridge's MPhil in Digital Policy, offered through the Bennett School of Public Policy, is an entirely new program with a first cohort starting in 2026. The reason it exists is straightforward: AI, platforms, data and algorithms are no longer purely technical issues. They have become questions of policy and society.

The program is neither a computer science degree nor a pure policy degree. It aims to train people who understand technology and can also think about public policy and institutional design. Students from public policy, international relations, technology, data, law and ethics are meant to study at the same table, which makes it a textbook interdisciplinary master's.

### USC: a growing list of STEM-designated master's tracks

In recent years USC has been rapidly adding STEM-designated master's programs in areas including:

- Data science
- Geospatial information
- Human security
- Environment, urban studies and sustainability

What these programs share is a core of data analysis, technology-based problem solving and close links to industry and the public sector. For international students, STEM designation directly affects career paths and plans to stay in the United States after graduation, so USC's expansion carries real strategic weight.

## What these programs are looking for

Taken together, these examples make the direction of top universities fairly clear. They care less about how many years an applicant has spent in one major and more about whether that person can connect several fields to define a problem and solve it. That is why new and expanded programs are often more open to students who are still giving shape to their interests than to applicants with a polished, finished profile.

That habit of connecting fields around a real question is one students can start building long before graduate school. CRI's [research programs](/research) pair students with university faculty to investigate a research question, often one that crosses fields, and write their own paper in English.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Early vs. regular rounds at 10 top US universities: Class of 2029 admit rates
excerpt: Class of 2029 acceptance rates at Princeton, MIT, Harvard, Duke, Northwestern and five other top schools, and how much applying early changed the odds.
content:
At Duke, roughly one in eight early decision applicants to the Class of 2029 was admitted. In the regular round, fewer than one in 25 got in. Versions of that gap show up across the most selective US universities, and when you are deciding where and when to apply, it tells you more than any single headline acceptance rate.

Here are the results for ten top-ranked universities from the admissions cycle that closed in spring 2025 and produced the Class of 2029. For each school you'll find how its early program works, how selective the regular round was, and what else shaped the year.

## The Class of 2029 at a glance

The figures come from university announcements and press coverage of each school's results. Where a school does not report its regular-round results separately, only the overall rate is shown.

| University | Early option | Overall admit rate | Early vs. regular round |
|---|---|---|---|
| Princeton | Single-choice early action | 4.4% | Not reported separately |
| MIT | Early action (unrestricted) | 4.6% | EA about 6%; regular about 2.5% |
| Harvard | Restrictive early action | 4.18% | Not reported separately |
| Stanford | Restrictive early action | Not announced (3.61% the year before) | Not reported separately |
| Yale | Single-choice early action | 4.59% | Not reported separately |
| University of Chicago | EA, ED I and ED II | Not published | Not reported separately |
| Johns Hopkins | ED I and ED II | 5.1% | RD about 4% |
| Duke | ED (one round) | 4.8% | ED about 13%; RD under 4% |
| Northwestern | ED (one round) | 7.0% | ED about 20%; RD 5.3% |
| Penn | ED (one round) | 4.9% | Not reported separately |

## Three kinds of early application

Early programs at these schools come in three types, and the rules shape the rest of your list.

- **Restrictive or single-choice early action** (Princeton, Harvard, Stanford, Yale). The offer is non-binding, so an admitted student can still compare options in the spring. In exchange, you may not apply early to other private universities. Princeton, for example, makes an exception for early programs at public universities.
- **Unrestricted early action** (MIT, and one of UChicago's options). Non-binding, with no limits on applying early elsewhere.
- **Early decision** (Duke, Northwestern and Penn, each with a single November round; Johns Hopkins and UChicago, with both ED I and ED II). ED is binding: if you are admitted, you commit to enroll. At Hopkins and UChicago the ED II deadline falls in early January, the same time as regular decision, so students must choose between the two by then.

## School by school

### Princeton

Princeton received 42,303 applications for the Class of 2029, the most in its history, and admitted about 4.4 percent, down slightly from 4.6 percent the year before. Roughly three in four admitted students chose to enroll, a yield of 75.2 percent. Princeton stopped announcing its admission figures on decision day several years ago; these numbers came out in a 2025 report to the faculty.

The university has been gradually enlarging its undergraduate class. About 14 percent of admitted students were international, and expanded aid for lower-income families has brought the share of Pell Grant-eligible students to around a quarter.

### MIT

MIT has no early decision round. It admitted 1,334 of 29,281 applicants (4.6 percent), and the round-by-round split is revealing. In early action, 721 of 12,052 applicants (about 6 percent) got in, and another 175 early applicants were admitted later in the regular round. Of the roughly 17,200 students who applied only in the regular round, about 2.5 percent were admitted. Students admitted in early action made up about 54 percent of the admitted class.

MIT is unusually transparent, posting applicant and admit counts for each round on its admissions site. It again requires the SAT or ACT, and interest has not cooled. The middle 50 percent of admitted students scored 780–800 in math and 740–780 in reading and writing.

### Harvard

For the Class of 2029, Harvard brought back its SAT/ACT requirement, and applications fell from more than 54,000 to 47,893. The acceptance rate rose from about 3.6 percent to 4.18 percent: 2,003 students were admitted and 1,675 enrolled, a yield of about 84 percent.

Harvard no longer releases detailed statistics when early decisions go out. The overall numbers became public only in fall 2025, when the university released the class's demographic data. The higher rate owes much to the smaller applicant pool, so it is worth watching whether the test requirement keeps application numbers down. Harvard's expanded aid also showed in the class: nearly half of admitted students came from families earning $200,000 or less, who qualify for free tuition.

### Stanford

Stanford does not announce its acceptance rate when decisions are released, so no Class of 2029 figure came out alongside the other schools' results. It publishes its data later through its Common Data Set, where the rate for the previous year's class was 3.61 percent. Stanford's yield is among the highest in the country, with more than 80 percent of admitted students enrolling.

### Yale

Yale's overall acceptance rate for the Class of 2029 was 4.59 percent, higher than the year before. As at Harvard, Yale brought back a testing requirement for this cycle, and its applicant pool shrank. Yale did not officially announce separate early and regular rates. Its aid policies are unchanged: admission is need-blind, aid covers each student's full demonstrated need, and about half of admitted students receive financial aid.

### University of Chicago

UChicago offers more ways in than any other school on this list: non-binding early action, binding ED I in November, binding ED II in January, and regular decision, which shares its early-January deadline with ED II.

UChicago does not publish its acceptance rate. It draws applicants in the tens of thousands each year, and its selectivity rivals the Ivy League's. Its two binding rounds are widely seen as the more favorable path, but the university releases no round-by-round figures. UChicago became one of the first highly selective universities to go test-optional, in 2018, and paired that with aggressive recruiting that grew its applicant pool and pushed its admit rate down. It is also known for unusually creative essay prompts and for favoring self-directed, intellectually driven students.

### Johns Hopkins

Hopkins offers two binding rounds: ED I, due in early November, and ED II, due in early January alongside regular decision. For the Class of 2029, applications rose 8.8 percent to nearly 50,000, and the overall acceptance rate fell sharply to about 5.1 percent.

The regular round was especially tight. After admitting 793 students through ED I and ED II, Hopkins admitted 1,732 of 41,549 regular applicants, about 4 percent. Early decision accounted for about 31 percent of all 2,525 admitted students. The pattern favors ED, provided you are ready to make a binding commitment.

### Duke

Duke has a single binding ED round, due November 1. For the Class of 2029, it received a record 58,698 applications, about 4,500 more than the year before, and its overall acceptance rate fell to a record-low 4.8 percent.

The split tells the story. Of 2,818 admitted students, 849 came from a pool of 6,714 early decision applicants, an admit rate of about 13 percent. The remaining 1,969 came from 51,984 regular applicants, a rate under 4 percent. Duke's announcement also pointed to more admitted students from North and South Carolina and progress in enrolling Pell Grant-eligible students. Duke secures a large share of its class in ED and fills the rest in the regular round, so if Duke is your clear first choice, applying early can work in your favor.

### Northwestern

Northwestern has one binding ED round, due November 1, and is known for admitting ED applicants at a comparatively generous rate. For the Class of 2029, applications topped 53,000 for the first time, and about 3,700 students were admitted. The overall rate, 7.0 percent, was down from 7.5 percent and the lowest in Northwestern's history.

According to the university, about 20 percent of ED applicants were admitted, compared with 5.3 percent in the regular round. About 1,200 ED admits filled more than half of the incoming class, leaving roughly 2,500 offers for some 47,000 regular applicants. Northwestern has long leaned on ED to secure committed students and a stable class. Beyond the numbers, it is known for strong programs in theater, music and journalism.

### Penn

Applications to Penn for the Class of 2029 rose more than 10 percent, from about 65,000 to more than 72,500, and about 3,550 students were admitted. The acceptance rate of 4.9 percent, down from 5.39 percent, was the lowest in Penn's history.

Early decision typically fills close to half of Penn's class, which makes the regular round considerably more selective than the headline rate suggests. Beginning in 2025, Penn also expanded its financial aid: more families earning $200,000 or less now receive full-tuition support, and a family's home equity no longer counts in aid calculations. The university has become more cautious about releasing admissions data, so detailed figures may not appear quickly in future cycles either.

## What the numbers mean for your application

- **Rates move every year.** They shift with class size and the size of the applicant pool. A rising rate, as at Harvard and Yale in this cycle, can simply mean fewer people applied.
- **Early rounds usually admit at higher rates.** At Duke and Northwestern, the ED rate was more than three times the regular rate. ED is a binding commitment, though, so save it for a school you would attend without hesitation.
- **The regular round is often the hardest stage.** Early admits made up about 30 percent of admitted students at Hopkins and Duke and more than half of Northwestern's incoming class, so regular applicants compete for what remains.
- **Check the official pages every cycle.** Dates and requirements change slightly from year to year. Confirm them directly with each school, for example [Princeton](https://admission.princeton.edu/apply/first-year-application-dates-deadlines), [MIT](https://mitadmissions.org/apply/firstyear/deadlines-requirements/), [Harvard](https://college.harvard.edu/admissions/apply), [Yale](https://admissions.yale.edu/application-deadlines), [UChicago](https://collegeadmissions.uchicago.edu/apply/application/), [Duke](https://admissions.duke.edu/apply/), [Northwestern](https://admissions.northwestern.edu/apply/application-deadlines.html) and [Penn](https://admissions.upenn.edu/how-to-apply/first-year-applicants/application-requirements).

Applying early means your transcript, essays and activities need to be ready by November of senior year. If you are a younger student planning ahead and want to complete a substantial research project on that timeline, take a look at CRI's [research programs](/research).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Early Decision II at top US universities: how to use your last early card
excerpt: A handful of top-30 US universities and several leading liberal arts colleges offer ED II. Here is how six of them differ, and what two successful early applicants had in common.
content:
Early admission results arrive in a rush every December. In the 2025–26 cycle, Boston College released its decisions first, on December 3, with Princeton (December 11), Columbia and Brown (December 16) and Yale (December 17) close behind.

A few seniors are already committed through ED I by then, but most are weighing two paths at once: Early Decision II and Regular Decision. ED II carries the same binding commitment as ED I and, at many schools, admits a larger share of applicants than Regular Decision, which makes it the last early card most students have left to play. The catch is that very few top universities offer it.

## Six top-30 universities with an ED II round

In the 2025–26 cycle, these six top-30 national universities in the U.S. News rankings were among the few offering an ED II round:

| School | U.S. News rank | ED II note |
|---|---|---|
| University of Chicago | 6 | Also offers EA, ED I and RD |
| Johns Hopkins University | 7 | 242 ED II admits; ED II admit rate about 10% |
| Rice University | 17 | Second ED II round; about 6% admitted in the first |
| Vanderbilt University | 17 | ED II admit rate about 10% |
| Washington University in St. Louis (WashU) | 20 | A common second binding choice after ED I |
| Emory University | 24 | A common second binding choice after ED I |

On paper they offer the same thing. In practice, each one calls for a slightly different calculation.

### University of Chicago

UChicago is unusual in offering Early Action, Early Decision I, Early Decision II and Regular Decision side by side. More rounds mean more room for strategy. For an applicant who already has UChicago near the top of the list, ED II is not a window to let slip past.

### Johns Hopkins University

Hopkins introduced ED II in 2020, a sign of how much weight it now places on early applicants. In its most recent completed cycle, it admitted 242 students through ED II, out of 793 early admits in all. Its ED II admit rate was roughly 10 percent, against an overall rate of about 6 percent. Even so, the competition feels steep: Hopkins draws large numbers of applicants from across Asia, and its biomedical and engineering programs are especially strong magnets.

### Rice University

Rice is the newest member of the group. The 2024–25 cycle was its first ED II round, and 2025–26 its second. The university has announced plans to grow its undergraduate enrollment, yet that first ED II round admitted only about 6 percent of applicants, and the pool keeps getting bigger. Rice's ED II is not an easy opening.

### Vanderbilt University

Vanderbilt's ED II admit rate has been reported at roughly 10 percent, so if Vanderbilt is your clear first choice, the round deserves serious thought. But Vanderbilt cares more about the fit between student and school than about grades. "My grades are strong" is not an argument. Your application has to give clear, reasoned answers to three questions:

- Why Vanderbilt, specifically?
- How does the university's educational philosophy line up with the direction you are heading?
- How do its resources connect to the career you want to build?

### WashU and Emory

Students who narrowly miss in ED I elsewhere often turn to these two as a dependable second binding choice. As a result, their ED II rounds draw a flood of applications, even though ED II is usually the quieter early round.

## Liberal arts colleges with ED II

The option is not limited to research universities. Several of the most selective liberal arts colleges also run an ED II round, including **Swarthmore, Bowdoin, Pomona and Wellesley**. Their ED II deadlines, like the universities', fall in early January.

## What two early admits had in common

Two recent cases show what a binding early application looks like when it works. In both, the numbers were only part of the picture; each student built the application around one well-defined fit.

### Vanderbilt's Peabody College: one story about education

A student at an international school in Shanghai, with a predicted IB score of 45 (the maximum), decided early that Vanderbilt's Peabody College, the university's school of education, would be the target. The strategy came down to a single question: how do you turn an interest in education into one coherent story? The pieces were:

- ideas about learning that grew out of teaching a younger sibling
- a conviction that education should be about support, not correction
- research on educational leadership with a University of Pennsylvania professor
- social-commentary essays driven by the questions that research raised, which went on to win an award in an international competition

The Why Major and Why School essays tied these experiences together naturally, and the result was an offer from Vanderbilt.

### Wellesley: a modest profile, a precise fit

The second student came from a regular high school outside the major cities and did not have a dazzling résumé. What she did have was a clear-eyed analysis of her own strengths and of which schools genuinely suited her. Her record included:

- an economics research project with a Princeton professor
- a leadership role on the project team
- an academic paper presenting the research results

She was the youngest member of the team and still in high school, yet she could show leadership, academic ability and a finished piece of work at the same time. That combination matched what Wellesley looks for, and she was admitted in ED II.

## Admissions is won by design, not by information

ED II is not just one more binding application to send after ED I falls through. It only pays off when four things line up: your intended major, the design of your activities, the structure of your essays and the timing of your recommendation letters.

That is why the students admitted in ED II are, far more often than not, the ones who built a sound structure from the start rather than the ones who got lucky.

## Taking stock before you commit

If you are a senior weighing ED II in December, you may recognize yourself here:

- You are waiting on ED I results and can't shake the anxiety.
- Regular Decision alone feels like it isn't enough.
- ED II is still open, but you are not sure you should use it.

If so, what you need now is an honest read of where you actually stand, not more information. ED II deadlines arrive in the first days of January, sooner than most students expect. Treat ED II not as the round you use because it is what's left, but as the decision that most deserves a careful recalculation in those last weeks of the year. Ask whether your grades, your intended major and your activities genuinely fit these schools.

For seniors, the ED II decision rests on a fit they have already built. For students with a year or two to go, both cases point to the same lesson: an academic interest developed through real research gives your essays something solid to build on. CRI's [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter) is one place to start, with students working online over winter break under a university professor and writing their own research paper in English.
author: CRI Editorial

title: UCLA and UC Berkeley admit rates by major, and why research experience matters
excerpt: UC's fall 2024 data puts UCLA nursing at 1% and UC Berkeley public health at 2%. See the admit rates by major, and how research on nanomaterials, fluid dynamics and wearables backed each student's choice of major.
content:
At UCLA, 5,790 students applied to study nursing and 55 were admitted: an admit rate of 1%. At UC Berkeley, public health admitted 62 of its 2,713 applicants. Numbers like these, now published by major for every University of California campus, show that the field you apply to can matter as much as the campus you choose.

The figures come from the UC Information Center, the university system's official data portal, which breaks down admissions by broad discipline across all nine undergraduate campuses. Depending on the campus and the field, admit rates differ by a factor of ten or more. So the useful question for UC applicants is no longer "Which campus is easiest?" but "Which major am I applying to, and what is my plan for getting in?" The data below covers applicants for the fall 2024 term.

## UC Berkeley: public health, computer science and business

UC Berkeley admitted 11% of its applicants overall. Its most selective field was public health, at 2%. Computer science and business came next at 4% each. At the other end of the range, arts and humanities admitted 23% of applicants, more than twice the campus rate.

| Broad discipline | Applicants | Admits | Admit rate | Admitted GPA (25th–75th percentile) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Public health | 2,713 | 62 | 2% | 4.14–4.30 |
| Computer science | 13,437 | 515 | 4% | 4.20–4.30 |
| Business | 8,069 | 327 | 4% | 4.20–4.30 |
| Architecture | 2,939 | 211 | 7% | 4.14–4.28 |
| Engineering | 21,831 | 1,698 | 8% | 4.21–4.30 |
| Social sciences | 18,816 | 1,683 | 9% | 4.16–4.29 |
| Other/interdisciplinary | 6,847 | 807 | 12% | 4.15–4.29 |
| Undeclared | 11,956 | 1,432 | 12% | 4.11–4.29 |
| Public administration | 260 | 33 | 13% | 4.11–4.26 |
| Physical sciences/math | 11,487 | 1,821 | 16% | 4.19–4.30 |
| Life sciences | 16,970 | 2,998 | 18% | 4.16–4.29 |
| Arts and humanities | 8,917 | 2,052 | 23% | 4.07–4.28 |
| **Campus overall** | 124,242 | 13,639 | 11% | 4.15–4.29 |

## UCLA: nursing, engineering and computer science

UCLA's overall admit rate was 9%, and nursing was its hardest major by a wide margin: 55 admits from 5,790 applicants. Engineering admitted 6% and computer science 4%, and in both fields the middle 50% of admitted students had GPAs starting at 4.25.

One detail deserves a closer look. Undeclared applicants were admitted at 7%, below the campus average, so treating "undeclared" as a back door into UCLA rarely works.

| Broad discipline | Applicants | Admits | Admit rate | Admitted GPA (25th–75th percentile) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Nursing | 5,790 | 55 | 1% | 4.25–4.30 |
| Computer science | 10,530 | 435 | 4% | 4.25–4.30 |
| Engineering | 22,301 | 1,329 | 6% | 4.25–4.32 |
| Education | 1,265 | 79 | 6% | 4.07–4.28 |
| Undeclared | 10,059 | 693 | 7% | 4.17–4.31 |
| Business | 13,634 | 1,110 | 8% | 4.20–4.30 |
| Arts and humanities | 15,133 | 1,244 | 8% | 4.04–4.29 |
| Social sciences | 23,884 | 2,234 | 9% | 4.17–4.30 |
| Other health science | 2,470 | 285 | 12% | 4.20–4.30 |
| Life sciences | 23,472 | 3,092 | 13% | 4.21–4.30 |
| Other/interdisciplinary | 4,591 | 597 | 13% | 4.21–4.30 |
| Public administration | 826 | 117 | 14% | 4.20–4.30 |
| Physical sciences/math | 12,316 | 1,844 | 15% | 4.22–4.32 |
| **Campus overall** | 146,272 | 13,114 | 9% | 4.20–4.30 |

## Four more campuses where the major changes the odds

The same pattern shows up at other popular campuses, though the gaps look different on each one.

| Admit rate | UC San Diego | UC Irvine | UC Davis | UC Santa Barbara |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Campus overall** | 27% | 29% | 42% | 33% |
| Computer science | 13% | 20% | 17% | 17% |
| Engineering | 17% | 28% | 38% | 21% |
| Business | 18% | 13% | 33% | 32% (435 applicants) |
| Life sciences | 36% | 34% | 51% | 40% |
| Physical sciences/math | 36% | 44% | 59% | 47% |
| Public health | 19% | 42% | — | — |
| Public administration | — | — | 67% (130 applicants) | — |

*A dash means the discipline is not listed for that campus.*

- **UC San Diego**'s numbers work in favor of strong students drawn to the basic sciences. Life sciences and physical sciences/math each admitted 36%, nearly three times the rate for computer science.
- **UC Irvine** is a textbook case of the major alone moving the odds: 13% in business and 20% in computer science, against 44% in physical sciences/math and 42% in public health.
- **UC Davis**, with a 42% overall rate, is the most attainable of these campuses for students whose interests fit, with 59% in physical sciences/math and 67% in public administration. Computer science, at 17%, is a different story.
- **UC Santa Barbara** admitted 33% overall, but only 17% in computer science and 21% in engineering, compared with 47% in physical sciences/math and 40% in life sciences.

## Why research keeps showing up in UC admits

Look at recent admits to UC Berkeley, UCLA and UC San Diego and a pattern is getting harder to miss. Grades alone are not what set them apart. What does is research experience tied directly to the intended major, a recommendation letter from a professor, and a tangible output such as a research paper. Three cases show how that plays out.

### UC Berkeley chemistry: a first paper on biomimetic nanomaterials

This student had been interested in chemistry and materials since high school. To show that fit more clearly, the student chose biomimetic nanomaterials as a research topic and worked with Professor Anish Tuteja of the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor. The project covered the full cycle, from reviewing the literature and structuring the study to interpreting the results and writing the paper. The outcome was a first research paper with the student's own name on it.

That research and the professor's recommendation letter became the core academic evidence in the student's application to chemistry at UC Berkeley, and the student was admitted.

### UCLA, Johns Hopkins and WashU: fluid dynamics for renewable energy

The second student was already at university, with energy systems and engineering as the target field, and worked with Professor Nasr Ghoniem of UCLA on applications of fluid dynamics in renewable energy systems. The project did not stop at summarizing theory. The student analyzed fluid flow inside actual energy systems and extended the work into a structural analysis of how efficiency changes.

![A student in a black T-shirt typing on a laptop at a café table](/editorial/224103498804-08.jpg "The second student, whose research applied fluid dynamics to renewable energy systems.")

The finished research and the accompanying recommendation letter supported applications to UCLA, Johns Hopkins University and Washington University in St. Louis. All three offered admission, and the student chose UCLA.

### UCSD, Stanford, Brown and Penn: wearables meet machine learning

The third student, also at university, was majoring in mechanical engineering but broadened that focus, setting out to combine wearable devices with machine learning. Working with Professor Nabil Alshurafa of Northwestern University, the student analyzed sensor data and applied pattern recognition and predictive models. The project brought mechanical engineering and AI together and ended as a complete research paper.

In later applications, that work was read as evidence of genuine interdisciplinary research, not just a record of completed coursework. The student received offers from several universities, including UC San Diego, Stanford, Brown and the University of Pennsylvania.

What these cases share is not simply hard work. It is activity that connects precisely to the intended major, and that is becoming a key factor in who gets in. For more students who built their applications around research, see the [Student Success](/success) page.

## Three questions to answer before you apply

Read closely, these admit rates are less a set of odds than a test of strategy. Before you apply, make sure you can answer three questions:

1. Which major am I applying to?
2. What have I done that connects directly to that major?
3. Do I have a substantial academic story that a recommender can write about in depth?

When all three line up, a UC admission stops being a matter of luck and becomes the result of a plan.

If you want research that matches the major you will list on your UC application, the [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1) pairs you with a faculty mentor for an individually arranged project in your field, typically over two to four months.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Early admissions 2025–26: what Common App's data said about the applicant pool
excerpt: Common App's November 1, 2025, snapshot showed record applications, 9% fewer international applicants and 11% more students reporting test scores. Here is what CRI expected it to mean for early decisions.
content:
Early-round decisions arrive in December, but the shape of the 2025–26 competition was visible weeks earlier. Common App's snapshot of applications submitted through November 1, 2025, pointed to three shifts: the applicant pool reached a new high, standardized testing made a clear comeback, and the international field was reshuffled. Here is what the data showed, and what CRI expected it to mean for early results.

## A bigger pool than ever

Common App's figures covered 916 member colleges, and every headline number was up on the year before:

- **Applications:** 4,716,352, up 10%
- **Applicants:** 962,284, up 5%
- **Applications per applicant:** 4.90, up from 4.68

Applications have climbed every season since 2021–22:

| Season | Applications as of Nov. 1 |
| --- | --- |
| 2021–22 | 2,823,310 |
| 2022–23 | 3,309,764 |
| 2023–24 | 3,867,636 |
| 2024–25 | 4,268,736 |
| 2025–26 | 4,716,352 (+10%) |

Applications grew twice as fast as applicants. Because each student was sending more applications, the competition felt tighter than the head count alone suggests.

## Fewer international applicants, but no easier for them

International applicants fell 9%, to 72,405. Applicants from Asia still formed the core of that group: China and India remained the two largest countries of citizenship by a wide margin, and South Korea was among the top ten.

| Country of citizenship | Applicants, 2025–26 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| China | 13,004 | −1% |
| India | 8,560 | −14% |
| Multiple citizenships | 4,246 | 0% |
| Nigeria | 3,090 | −11% |
| Ghana | 2,517 | −43% |
| Canada | 2,399 | −13% |
| Pakistan | 2,374 | −10% |
| South Korea | 2,077 | −3% |
| Vietnam | 1,894 | +3% |
| Uzbekistan | 1,577 | +1% |

*Source: Common App, first-year applicants as of November 1, 2025.*

A smaller international pool did not make the top colleges any easier to reach. Among international students aiming for the most selective schools, competition stayed as dense as ever.

## Test scores are back

The sharpest change was in testing. Applicants who reported a test score rose 11%, to 543,844, while those who did not slipped 1%, to 418,440. In a single year, the gap between the two groups nearly doubled.

| | 2024–25 | 2025–26 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reported a test score | 489,562 | 543,844 | +11% |
| No score reported | 423,525 | 418,440 | −1% |
| Gap | about 66,000 | about 125,000 | |

With MIT and Harvard among the selective colleges that have made scores a formal requirement again, the weight of testing is hard to miss.

## Where the growth went

Applications to public and private colleges grew at the same pace, each up 10%, to 2,951,645 and 1,755,190 applications respectively. The split by selectivity was more revealing:

| Admit rate | Applications, 2025–26 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 75% or higher | 1,743,966 | +10% |
| 50–74% | 1,287,585 | +13% |
| 25–49% | 924,562 | +12% |
| Under 25% (most selective) | 743,327 | +4% |

Where students applied shifted too. The number of students applying only to out-of-state colleges fell 3%, while those applying in state, or in state and out of state together, rose by 6 to 10%. Students were building their lists more realistically and more strategically.

## Four trends CRI expected in early results

Reading Common App's data alongside recent policy changes at top colleges, CRI expected the 2025–26 early decisions to move in four directions.

### 1. A higher bar for grades and activities

The international pool shrank, but the students competing for top colleges were stronger than before. High scores and a typical set of extracurriculars no longer set anyone apart, and CRI expected more students with excellent scores to be turned down. Students who could show in-depth research, sustained academic inquiry and experience with a topic that is genuinely their own, by contrast, stood to gain a powerful advantage.

### 2. Scores return, and holistic review gets stronger

Harvard, Yale and MIT once again ask for test scores. Yale calls its policy "test-flexible": from the 2024–25 cycle it requires scores from all applicants but accepts AP and IB exam results alongside the SAT and ACT. Even colleges that remain test-optional clearly tend to view applicants who submit scores more favorably.

That does not mean a strong score is enough on its own. As scores cluster at the top, admissions officers look harder at a student's academic potential, depth of thinking and capacity for research. Every college still practices holistic review, and the transcript, essays, recommendations and the real depth of a student's activities have to add up to one coherent story.

### 3. Steady at the top, fiercest in the middle

Applications to the most selective colleges grew just 4%, while the next two tiers rose 12% and 13%, the fastest of any group. With students weighing stability, value and their realistic odds together, CRI expected competition in that middle range to be the fiercest.

### 4. Wider access, led by public universities

The number of applicants from underrepresented minority, first-generation and low-income backgrounds grew by 10 to 12%. CRI expected these groups to make up a somewhat larger share of admitted students than the year before, especially at public systems such as the University of California.

## What sets an application apart

As decisions arrived that December, two forces were at work at once: the return of standardized testing and a stronger emphasis on holistic review. The more important point, in CRI's view, is that competitiveness is not about how many people apply. **It is about how different your story is from everyone else's in the same pool.**

Three things have become the most credible evidence an applicant can offer:

- Substantive research experience with leading faculty
- Recommendation letters grounded in real observation of a student's growth, not formality
- Long-term inquiry that connects to a single intended field of study

By early December, two students who had joined CRI's summer 2025 programs and applied early had already reported admissions to Harvard and Boston College.

CRI's focus is less on adding credentials than on deepening how a student thinks about a subject. To see what that looks like in practice, explore the [Seoul and Global Research Programs](/research/summer-camp), where students work with university faculty on a research question and write the manuscript in English.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Beyond IB and AP: four reasons international-school students choose CRI
excerpt: Summer participants explain what set CRI apart for them: the faculty, interest-based matching, close feedback from professors and TAs, and a network that lasts.
content:
Spend time in any international-school community and the same questions keep coming up. How do you prove to a college that your interest in a field is real? Will an IB or American curriculum leave you short on research experience? And where is the "real story" that essays and recommendation letters are supposed to tell going to come from?

CRI's answer is depth. Strong grades are the starting point for competitive applicants; what increasingly sets them apart is how far they have taken their curiosity. CRI's research programs are built to develop exactly that, and in interviews with CRI, summer participants described four things that made the experience different.

## 1. Professors most students never meet

The first reason students give is the faculty. CRI's professors come from universities such as Oxford, MIT, Caltech, Penn, and UChicago: scholars most high school students never encounter, even at college information sessions. Programs that let students spend their summer doing research alongside faculty like these are rare.

> "It's not often that a high school student gets to meet professors like these and learn from them directly."
> — A summer participant

Another participant recommended the program "for the all-star faculty alone." A third pointed to the chance at a recommendation letter and publication as a strength when applying to college.

And students do more than listen. They design a paper with their professor, have their research design reviewed, and produce the results themselves.

## 2. A faculty match built on your interests

Before a program begins, CRI matches each student to the faculty team that best fits their interests, academic level, and goals. The matching works for students who have already settled on a major and for those who haven't.

> "I was originally interested in education policy, but because I lean toward quantitative analysis, I was matched to the economics track. It actually turned out to fit my interest in political science better."
> — A summer participant

Being new to a field is no barrier. Another participant arrived knowing nothing about international law and, through the classes and help from the TAs, worked from the fundamentals all the way to case studies. A third said that even when a student's interests don't line up with the topics on offer, the depth of support is on another level.

For undecided students, the program becomes a chance to explore. For students with a clear direction, it takes that interest to university level.

## 3. Close feedback from professors and TAs

Even students who have never written a proper research paper see their work through to a final report. One reason CRI earns such strong reviews is its TA system. The TAs are graduate students who do far more than assist: working between the student and the professor, they are the mentors who keep each project on track.

> "From the abstract to the methodology and the analysis, the TAs gave me specific feedback every time, so the research actually kept moving."
> — A summer participant

Another student said sessions with experienced TAs did more than anything else to clarify their thinking and sharpen the paper. A third said working with such knowledgeable mentors clearly moved their research forward.

With guidance that close, students with no research background learn to handle each part of an academic paper, from structure and methodology to data analysis and writing, in a short, intensive program.

## 4. A network that outlasts the program

When the summer ends, students leave with an alumni network: peers who keep following one another's growth and college applications.

> "At alumni events, I got real insight from talking with professors and other students."
> — A summer participant

Another participant came away struck by how accomplished the program's alumni are and how well they work together. A third swapped social media handles with friends from the program, and they became genuinely close.

That community brings together students with similar academic interests and international-school students from the US, Korea, and across Asia, along with alumni, current faculty, and TAs. Its value reaches past admissions, into university and beyond.

## How the programs are structured

CRI runs research programs in both winter and summer, and they share the same structure. The difference is format: the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter) meets online, while the [summer programs](/research/summer-camp) meet in person.

- Regular sessions with faculty from leading universities
- Research and paper design led by the student
- Close feedback sessions with TAs
- A completed final paper or report
- Follow-up support for publication, conference posters, and competition entries

## Who the programs suit

CRI recommends its research programs for students who:

- Want to develop an interest in a field into a story their college application can stand on
- Hope to do research at university but haven't found the opportunity in high school
- Need an in-depth extracurricular that school activities alone don't provide
- Are working toward a recommendation letter from a professor
- Want academic depth beyond what IB, A-Level, or AP coursework offers

If any of these describes you, see how the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter) works, from the faculty sessions to the final paper each student completes.
author: CRI Editorial

title: In the driver's seat: how CRI's Seoul Research Program professors teach
excerpt: In a newly released faculty interview video, Seoul Research Program professors explain why they teach through questions and let students lead, and what 30-plus hours together makes possible.
content:
"Why do you think that?" "Could something else explain it?" "What's your evidence?" Students in CRI's Seoul Research Program (SRP) hear questions like these constantly. In a newly released faculty interview video, the professors who taught the 2025 program explain how they work with high school students, and why they teach this way.

Faculty who appear on camera include Brian Stoltz of Caltech, Ryan Fang of the University of Chicago, Nabil Alshurafa of Northwestern University and Kit Hickey of MIT. Each year CRI invites professors from research universities such as Harvard, MIT, UChicago, Oxford and Cambridge. Yet where a professor comes from matters less than what happens in the room: how they treat students, how they build a student's thinking, and how closely they stay involved. On those measures, the way CRI's faculty work is different by design.

## Teaching the "why," not just the "what"

Most students can follow an explanation. Far fewer can say, in their own words, why it holds. As the faculty put it in the interviews:

> "Students know the result, but they have never thought deeply about why."
> — Seoul Research Program faculty, 2025 interviews

So CRI's faculty don't simply lecture. They keep pressing with questions like the ones above, and those questions are more powerful than they look. They move students from memorizing to investigating, and they quickly build the kind of analytical thinking universities expect.

## A driving coach, not an answer key

Several professors reached for the same analogy: the student sits in the driver's seat, and the professor rides alongside, ready to brake. Ryan Fang described his role as teaching students how to drive. "So I'm like a driving coach," he said, the kind who hits the brake only "when necessary."

It's a simple approach, and a highly effective one. The student chooses the topic, forms a hypothesis, works out how to test it, interprets the data and states their own conclusion. The professor watches the whole process, steers the student back when the work heads in the wrong direction, and shows them how to build a sound argument.

What students take away is the ability to lead a research project on their own. That is the capability universities value most.

## Thirty hours of close attention

This is where CRI's faculty differ most, and it is the point families should look at most closely. In the Seoul Research Program, professors and students spend **at least 30 hours** working together. Over that time, a professor comes to know each student in depth, through concrete moments in the work:

- what they are curious about
- how they think and how they generate ideas
- where their reasoning is strong and where it slips
- how diligent they are, and the attitude they bring
- how quickly they grow, and how they change over the program

That depth of observation cannot come from a few mentoring sessions or an online lecture course. It is also what makes a recommendation letter from an SRP professor read differently:

- **It is specific.** The professor writes from scenes they witnessed firsthand.
- **It is credible.** Evidence-based evaluation is what admissions officers weigh most heavily.
- **It shows growth.** The professor watched the student change from one day to the next.

A letter like that is more than a kind endorsement; it is strong evidence in an application. Observation this close is why CRI students, year after year, come away with compelling material for their essays, recommendations and interviews.

## The real steps of research

SRP projects are not literature summaries. In the video, Nabil Alshurafa of Northwestern points out that proper research is something students often haven't learned yet, and describes students collecting data on their own bodies. Across the program, students work through the core activities of actual research:

- collecting data
- analyzing and interpreting it
- defining the problem
- restructuring the project in response to feedback
- writing the final paper

This is how university labs work, which is why even a short, intensive program can give students genuine university-level research experience. It is exactly the kind of experience admissions officers recognize as real research.

## What sets CRI's faculty apart

The difference starts with how deeply CRI's faculty come to understand each student. In short, it comes down to three things:

1. **Question-driven teaching** that changes how students think.
2. **A coaching structure** that lets students lead their own research.
3. **Deep, sustained interaction** between professor and student, which produces strong recommendation letters and a clear story of growth.

These are strengths a merely good program can't offer. CRI is built around its faculty, and they know how to help students grow into real researchers.

To see how this approach plays out in a specific course, with a specific professor, explore the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: No business major at Harvard? Undergraduate business at top US universities
excerpt: Only two Ivy League schools have an undergraduate business school. See which top universities do, what students major in elsewhere, and how to choose a path.
content:
Plenty of students and parents preparing for US college admissions share the same goal: major in business at an Ivy League school. It sounds natural, but Harvard, Yale, Princeton, and Columbia offer no undergraduate business degree at all. A plan built around a major that doesn't exist can steer a student toward choices that don't match where they actually want to go. The good news is that business-minded students have strong options whether or not their school offers the major.

## Only two Ivies have an undergraduate business school

Six of the eight Ivy League universities have no undergraduate business school. The two exceptions are the University of Pennsylvania, home of the Wharton School, and Cornell, where undergraduate business degrees come through two schools in the SC Johnson College of Business: the Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management and the Nolan School of Hotel Administration.

Outside the Ivy League, several top universities do run undergraduate business programs. MIT is one of them: its Sloan School of Management offers undergraduate majors in management, business analytics, and finance, known collectively as Course 15.

| University | Ivy League | Undergraduate business school |
|---|---|---|
| University of Pennsylvania | Yes | The Wharton School |
| Cornell University | Yes | Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management; Nolan School of Hotel Administration |
| MIT | No | Sloan School of Management (Course 15) |
| UC Berkeley | No | Haas School of Business |
| New York University | No | Stern School of Business |
| University of Michigan | No | Ross School of Business |
| Carnegie Mellon University | No | Tepper School of Business |
| University of Notre Dame | No | Mendoza College of Business |
| Harvard University | Yes | None |
| Yale University | Yes | None |
| Princeton University | Yes | None |
| Columbia University | Yes | None |
| Dartmouth College | Yes | None |
| Brown University | Yes | None |

At the schools without one, students prepare for business careers through majors such as economics, mathematics, and political science.

## What business-minded students major in instead

At Harvard, Yale, and Princeton, most students headed for business choose **economics**. At Harvard it is consistently one of the two most popular undergraduate concentrations, and it asks for both mathematical reasoning and the ability to apply ideas to real business problems.

The other common route is quantitative: mathematics, applied mathematics, statistics, or data science. These majors open doors to finance, consulting, and technology. The name on the diploma differs, but the career destination is often the same: business.

## Four undergraduate business schools up close

### Wharton (University of Pennsylvania)

Wharton is widely regarded as the top undergraduate business school in the country. In their second year, students choose a concentration and specialize in an area such as finance, marketing, operations management, or business analytics.

### Stern (New York University)

Stern's New York location gives students an edge in landing Wall Street internships and jobs. The school also offers a wide range of double-major and dual-degree options.

![Pale stone building with a curved glass rotunda over an entrance inscribed 'Leonard N. Stern School of Business', between brick buildings, with purple NYU flags along the street](/editorial/224083626049-04.jpg "NYU's Stern School of Business in Manhattan.")

### Haas (UC Berkeley)

Many Haas students spend their first two years in Berkeley's general undergraduate program and enter the business school as juniors. Its proximity to Silicon Valley makes it a strong choice for students drawn to startups and technology.

### Ross (University of Michigan)

Ross is part of a public university, yet its curriculum rivals those of top private schools. Its graduates post strong results in job placement, starting salaries, and graduate-school admission, and its close ties with Fortune 500 companies are a major draw.

## Why schools without a business major still send graduates into business

1. **Brand and alumni networks.** Harvard, Yale, and Princeton award no business degrees, yet their alumni networks run deep on Wall Street, in Silicon Valley, and across the consulting industry.
2. **A liberal arts education.** Studying broadly builds analysis, communication, and problem-solving, which are the skills that matter most in business.
3. **The graduate school route.** Students can build business expertise later through an MBA, and Ivy League graduates are admitted to top MBA programs at high rates.

## The major's name matters less than the path

A student interested in business shouldn't choose a college based only on whether it has a business major. The better question is how you want to understand the world, and what background and experiences you want to build along the way.

- **If you want a hands-on business curriculum from the start**, an undergraduate business school such as Wharton, Ross, or Stern is a natural fit.
- **If you would rather build broad thinking and academic depth first, then specialize through an MBA**, universities centered on a liberal arts undergraduate education, such as Harvard, Yale, and Princeton, are an excellent choice.

A major is a means, not the goal. What counts is growing into someone who can look at a problem clearly and work out how to solve it. In the end, choosing the path that fits your interests and goals is what gives you the strongest edge.

If you're weighing a business school against an economics or quantitative major and want to think through which colleges and activities fit that plan, [talk with CRI's admissions team](/contact).
