title: Why new international enrollment at US colleges fell 17% in fall 2025
excerpt: IIE's fall 2025 snapshot found 17% fewer new international students at US colleges, with visa problems the top cause. Here is what the data shows and how applicants can plan ahead.
content:
In fall 2025, US colleges welcomed noticeably fewer new students from abroad. According to the Institute of International Education's **Fall 2025 Snapshot on International Student Enrollment**, the number of new international students, those enrolling at their US college or university for the first time, fell 17% from the year before.

International students have long been among the applicants American colleges recruit most actively, and they shape both the global character of a campus and its finances. So the figure matters beyond the number itself. What drew the most attention was the explanation: colleges traced the drop less to a shortage of interested students than to obstacles outside the admissions process, above all visas and travel. Here are the key findings, and what they mean for students planning to study in the United States.

## The numbers

IIE, a nonprofit that tracks international education, surveyed more than 825 US colleges and universities for the snapshot. Asked how their new international enrollment compared with the previous fall, they reported:

| New international enrollment vs. fall 2024 | Share of institutions |
|---|---|
| Decreased | 57% |
| Increased | 29% |
| No change | 14% |

The total international student population in the US is still substantial, at roughly 1.2 million. But a sharp fall in first-time students is seen as an early sign that the landscape for studying in America is changing.

## Visa delays and denials came first

Visas were the biggest single factor. Among institutions that saw fewer new international students, **96% cited visa application problems**, including delays and denials.

Over the course of 2025, student visa applicants ran into late interview appointments, tougher screening, and periods when US embassies paused visa services. Together, these appear to have thrown many students' enrollment timelines off track. Put simply, administrative hurdles now carry more weight in study-abroad plans, however well prepared a student is academically.

## Travel restrictions came second

Of the institutions reporting declines, **68%** also pointed to travel restrictions. Entry rules that differ from country to country, travel advisories, and limited flight options appear to have delayed some students' plans to come to the US.

## India saw an especially steep drop

The decline was not spread evenly. The report singled out India, where the fall in new students was particularly pronounced. Because India is one of the largest sources of international students at American colleges, fewer Indian newcomers likely weighed heavily on the overall figure.

## What colleges now face

International students add to the academic and cultural diversity of US campuses, and they are central to many colleges' budgets. They contributed nearly **$55 billion** to the US economy in 2024, according to the US Department of Commerce, a figure IIE cited when it released Open Doors 2025 alongside the snapshot.

A drop in new international enrollment pushes colleges to revisit several things at once:

- their global strategy
- their financial planning
- how they recruit students from specific countries

## What to do if you plan to study in the US

The findings point to three practical priorities.

1. **Start the visa process early.** Visa delays were the top reason for the decline, so move quickly on every step: receiving your I-20 from your college, booking a visa appointment, and preparing for the interview.
2. **Check the entry rules that apply to you.** Travel restrictions are affecting who actually enrolls. Well before you travel, look up the rules for your country, current travel advisories, and whether the US embassy or consulate you will use is operating normally.
3. **Plan for the hurdles that come after admission.** This decline had little to do with how competitive students were and a great deal to do with visas, policy, and mobility. Managing those risks deserves as much attention in your preparation as the application itself.

## Preparation, not anxiety

The 17% drop shows how strongly policy and mobility now shape the path to a US degree. As colleges adjust their international strategies, applicants will likely have more factors to weigh, not fewer.

What this moment calls for is accurate information and early preparation rather than worry. Keep your visa timeline on track, confirm the entry rules for your country, and find out how much support each college on your list gives its international students. Those are the steps that matter most for getting to campus on time.

Planning early applies to the application, too. For students building a research record before they apply to US colleges, the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) brings professors from American and British universities to Seoul each summer to guide small groups through writing their own research paper in English.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Engineering, computer science or AI? How three STEM majors really differ
excerpt: What engineering, computer science and AI majors actually study, how each would work on a self-driving car, and a quick checklist for finding the one that fits you.
content:
"Our child is a science-and-math kid, so engineering, computer science, AI... isn't it all pretty much the same?" It is one of the questions parents ask most often when CRI meets with international-school families.

It's easy to see why. All three are STEM fields, all three need math, all three involve some coding, and all three seem to promise strong job prospects. But engineering, computer science and artificial intelligence rest on different academic foundations, teach different material, and lead to different work after graduation. That is why they confuse students and parents more than almost any other choice of major. Here is what actually separates them, what each curriculum covers, and which kind of student each one suits.

## The short version

Oversimplifying a little, the easiest way to tell them apart is this:

- **Engineering** designs the machines, electrical hardware and systems of the physical world.
- **Computer science** builds the software and systems of the digital world.
- **AI** designs the algorithms that make software "smarter."

The tools can overlap. The way each field looks at a problem does not.

## Engineering: designing the physical world

Engineering is the discipline of designing and building things that physically exist. Cars, airplanes, robots, semiconductors, sensors, buildings and energy systems all run on the laws of physics, so engineers need physics-based thinking as much as they need math.

What you work on depends on the branch:

- **Mechanical engineering:** cars, robots, drones
- **Electrical and electronic engineering:** circuits, semiconductors, sensors, communications
- **Aerospace engineering:** airplanes, rockets, satellites

Typical courses include mechanics, electromagnetics, circuit theory, thermodynamics, mechanics of materials, control engineering, signal processing and CAD design. Each teaches, in its own way, how to design a real system so that it operates safely.

Engineering suits students who like devices they can see and touch. Those who are comfortable with physics and curious about structures and mechanisms tend to be the most satisfied.

## Computer science: building the digital world

Computer science studies how to solve problems with the computer as a tool. Many people assume coding is the heart of it, but the real core is logical thinking and algorithm design. Students take data structures, algorithms, operating systems, databases, networking, security and distributed systems, and every one of those courses is about the structures and principles for solving problems efficiently.

![A programmer in glasses works at two monitors showing code and system diagrams in a blue-lit room](/editorial/224083384384-02.jpg "Computer science works with data, memory, processes and packets rather than forces and voltages.")

If engineering is grounded in physics, computer science is grounded in logic and algorithms. Instead of force, voltage and vibration, it deals in digital concepts: data, memory, processes, packets. It fits students who attack problems like puzzles and think in clear logical steps. Students who want to build apps, games or web services usually land here as well.

## AI: teaching machines to learn

AI began as a branch of computer science. But as industry demand has exploded over the past few years, universities have started splitting it off into its own major or department. AI programs study machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision and reinforcement learning, all of them methods for getting a model to learn on its own from data.

![Illustration of robotic hands on either side of a glowing brain labeled AI, surrounded by floating data charts](/editorial/224083384384-03.jpg "AI majors lean heavily on linear algebra, probability and statistics, calculus and optimization.")

What sets AI apart is that math matters far more than coding. Linear algebra (matrices), probability and statistics, calculus and optimization theory are all required. AI is, in other words, more analytical and more mathematical than computer science. Its central questions are how a machine finds patterns, how it makes predictions and how it gets better on its own.

AI suits students who aren't put off by math and who enjoy data, modeling and prediction systems.

## One project, three roles: the self-driving car

The differences are easiest to see when all three fields work on the same project.

| Field | What it handles on a self-driving car |
| --- | --- |
| Engineering | Designs the physical hardware (sensors, circuits, engine, steering, brakes) and makes sure the car operates safely |
| Computer science | Designs the systems that collect and process sensor data, the mapping and route-finding algorithms, and the vehicle's software architecture |
| AI | Designs the algorithms that recognize objects in video, detect pedestrians, identify lanes and judge situations, plus driving strategies based on reinforcement learning |

Put simply, engineering builds the car itself, computer science builds the software that runs it, and AI builds the brain that lets it make its own decisions.

## Which one fits? A quick checklist

A few signs can show which major suits a student best:

- **The engineering type** likes physics, is drawn to machines, devices and structures, and enjoys products you can hold in your hands.
- **The computer science type** enjoys coding problems, thinks logically and wants to make apps or games.
- **The AI type** can handle a lot of math (especially probability, statistics and linear algebra), likes analyzing data and is fascinated by how machines learn.

## Similar names, different ways of thinking

Each of these is a promising STEM field. Which one is right depends on how a student wants to understand the world and solve its problems:

- **Engineering** understands and designs the physical world through physics.
- **Computer science** designs the digital world through logic and algorithms.
- **AI** makes machines learn the rules from data.

Choosing a major is not a promise to do one thing for the rest of your life. It is a decision about the angle from which you want to solve problems. Once families understand how these three fields really differ, they can read a student's temperament and strengths more clearly, and the choice becomes far less stressful and far more strategic.

## Try it before you decide

Knowing the differences helps, but the surest test is to do the work. Engineering, computer science and AI look alike on paper and feel completely different up close; a major is something students confirm through experience, not something they settle by thinking it over. Winter break is short, but it is long enough to set a direction, and one experience like that can change how a student approaches college applications. In CRI's [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter), students spend the break on a research project guided by a university professor, which is one of the most direct ways to find out which of these fields really fits.
author: CRI Editorial

title: How admissions officers actually read your application: fit, narrative, and how you learn
excerpt: Why do applicants with similar profiles get different decisions? What selective US colleges look for in a file: fit, a coherent academic story, and evidence of how you learn.
content:
Why do two students with nearly identical grades and activities get different answers from the same college? It is the question families ask most often every admissions season. Selective US colleges receive thousands of applications from students with high GPAs and strong résumés, yet within that sea of similar profiles, some are admitted and some are not.

The difference usually lies somewhere other than the numbers. Admissions officers look past the sheer volume of grades and activities for something more basic: a student's academic potential, the way they investigate a question, and how well they fit the college. As officers at several institutions describe it, an application is not a list of credentials but a chance to design your own academic story.

## Fit comes first

Ask admissions officers what ultimately decides a file, and most will point to the same thing. It is not a score or a credential but fit: how well a student matches the academic environment the college offers.

Laura Stratton, who heads admission at Scripps College, has explained it this way: when the academic and social direction a student is pursuing lines up with what the college can provide, the admissions office can be confident about that student's years on campus and the growth that follows. Colleges, in other words, are not simply hunting for outstanding students. They want the students who will grow the most at their school.

Dan Budak, head of admissions at Vermont Law School, frames it in terms of future success. The school looks for applicants who are likely to thrive, and that likelihood shows up in their academic preparation, their experience, and how well they understand the program they are applying to. Fit, then, is not a vague impression. A reader can see it in the academic path a student has built.

A first read of a file is short, often a matter of minutes. As officers move through the transcript, recommendation letters, activity list, and essays, they are mostly asking one question: do this student's way of investigating, the direction of their curiosity, and the way they think connect with how this college teaches? When the answer is visible, the student stands out on their own.

Because every college has its own academic temperament, readers sometimes come away with a gut sense: this student would thrive at MIT, or that one is made for the way UChicago teaches. That reaction is not personal taste. It means the college's educational philosophy and the student's way of exploring resemble each other.

## Every campus has an intellectual personality

Colleges tend to reward different habits of mind. For example:

- **Princeton** prizes the persistence to dig into a problem and keep digging.
- **MIT** likes students who experiment, build things themselves, and solve problems hands-on.
- **Harvard** values breadth and balance, the ability to move between the humanities and the sciences.
- **UChicago** looks for minds that push a question further and explore it in depth.

Admissions is less a contest over who is most impressive than a judgment about which student will grow best at a particular college. Officers judge that fit by how a student has learned and explored more than by their credentials.

That is also why fit cannot be manufactured. It becomes clear when an application shows, without strain, which problem caught a student's interest, how they went about exploring it, and how the experience shaped their thinking and plans. At that point a reader becomes convinced: this student belongs here.

## Your application tells an academic story

If fit sets the direction, the application is how the reader actually feels it. Many students lead with volume, listing every activity and award. What admissions officers want to see is how those experiences shaped the way the student thinks and grows.

Budak makes a related point: what admissions officers notice most is how a student has shown passion for a particular field, and the applicants who stand out are the ones whose coursework and experiences, taken together, make that passion unmistakable.

Yale's official podcast, *Inside the Yale Admissions Office*, strikes a similar note. Applicants do not need to be national-team athletes or Broadway performers, the podcast tells listeners, and there is no need to strain to seem extraordinary. What admissions officers want to understand is how a student has become genuinely absorbed in a subject, wrestled with it, and explored it, along with the feelings and insights that came out of that process.

Compare two sentences. Anyone can write "I love engineering." The second version lands differently: "While analyzing sensor data, I spent days stuck on a pattern that made no sense, and when I finally worked out what that tiny variation meant, I felt a real thrill." Reading it, an admissions officer travels with the student through a small act of discovery.

Kelly Nolin, who heads admissions at a university in Montana, describes the strongest applicants as students who not only tell their story well but can explain how the experience changed them. Admissions is not a storytelling competition. It rewards how clearly you can show the evidence of your own inquiry. That makes one skill matter even more than deciding what to include: connecting your experiences into a single, coherent story.

## Depth over a long list

St. John's University illustrates the difference on its website with two hypothetical students. One joins ten clubs, shows up now and then, and never leads anything. The other joins one or two clubs, stays with them for years, takes on leadership roles, and helps launch something new. The second list is shorter. The story behind it is far stronger.

The same logic runs through the whole file:

- **Service.** Volunteering for a long time is not remarkable on its own. But if you defined a problem you ran into while volunteering, then gathered data or tried a new approach to solve it, that becomes valuable academic evidence of how you think and how you solve problems.
- **Recommendation letters.** Glowing adjectives matter less than whether the recommender observed you closely at a specific moment. The best letters describe concretely how a student investigates, how they think, and how they work through difficulty.
- **Academic interests.** Readers care less about which subject you like than about the questions you asked in it and how you followed them up.

An application, in the end, is a narrative rather than a list. At its center sits one question: what kind of learner am I?

## What decides it is how you learn

Preparing for admissions brings a familiar pressure: to add more experiences, to build a more distinctive profile than everyone else. Listen to admissions officers, though, and the deciding standard turns out to be simpler and more fundamental. How does this student learn?

When the answer comes through naturally across the whole application, that student becomes exactly who the college is looking for. That way of learning does not appear overnight. It grows out of asking questions, investigating them, and pushing them further on your own.

An academic narrative is not a showcase of dazzling achievements. It is the story of how you have handled problems that matter to you, and a student who has that story can leave a strong impression through the application alone. Admissions outcomes are hard to predict. Your way of exploring, though, is always yours to shape, and a well-developed pattern of learning is what sets a student apart most clearly at any college.

That idea sits at the heart of CRI's winter and summer research programs. Students do in-depth research alongside professors from universities around the world, growing into people who learn and investigate in their own way rather than simply collecting activities. The questions, discoveries, and wider thinking that come out of that work carry naturally into essays, résumés, and recommendation letters. If you want to start building your own academic story, take a look at the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter).

title: Top 10 bio majors for international-school students, from neuroscience to bioinformatics
excerpt: What ten popular biology-based majors actually teach, which students each one suits, where it leads, and research questions a high school student could take on in each.
content:
US college admissions data for international-school students tell a consistent story: year after year, the life sciences rank near the top of the majors they choose. That covers neuroscience, biomedical engineering and bioinformatics, along with biology-based fields such as molecular biology, biochemistry, genetics and pharmacology, which together draw an outsized share of students.

Korean students have always leaned toward medicine, science and engineering. Lately, though, they have gravitated more clearly toward majors that blend medicine with AI, data and engineering, and the universities where many Korean students enroll, including the University of California campuses, Johns Hopkins, Northwestern and NYU, are especially strong in them. As many students now put it, medical school or not, a bio major pays off.

## Why bio majors keep growing

The popularity rests on real shifts in industry, not fashion:

1. **Medicine has become a tech industry.** AI diagnostics, robotic surgery and genome-based personalized medicine have carried health care well beyond the hospital, into the meeting point of biology, engineering and AI.
2. **Biological data is exploding.** Human genome data, cancer genomics, protein structure prediction and medical big data have made bioinformatics, genomics and biostatistics some of the fastest-growing majors, and people fluent in both AI and biology are scarce.
3. **The industry is recession-resistant.** Health care, pharmaceuticals, diagnostics and public health stay essential in any economy. Since the pandemic, countries have treated biomedicine as a strategic industry, and investment has risen sharply.
4. **It leads almost anywhere.** Medical, dental, pharmacy or veterinary school; graduate study in the life sciences or engineering; pharmaceutical companies; AI health-tech startups; hospital research.

A bio major multiplies a student's options rather than narrowing them, which is why international-school students in Korea see it as a choice they can make with confidence.

## 1. Neuroscience

Neuroscience studies the brain and nervous system and the cognition and behavior they produce. It suits students who love psychology and biology equally, who wonder why people behave as they do, who are curious about where AI meets brain science, and who enjoy data analysis as much as lab work.

![Digital illustration of a glowing blue human brain overlaid with a network of connected points](/editorial/224082371952-02.jpg "Neuroscience goes deep on one organ: the brain and the nervous system it controls.")

- **Courses:** neurobiology, cognitive and behavioral neuroscience, neural circuits, brain imaging (fMRI, EEG), computational neuroscience with AI and machine learning
- **Compared with:** psychology (less biology), cognitive science (more AI, language and philosophy), biology (broader, with less depth on the brain)
- **Where it leads:** Of the foundational majors, the best fit with medical, dental or pharmacy school; paired with AI, it feeds neuro-AI and brain-computer interfaces. A research PhD is a popular next step, and hospitals, drug makers and health-tech firms are hiring more graduates. Roles: neuroscientist, medical researcher, AI cognition researcher, cognitive UX researcher and, through medical school, neurologist.
- **Research ideas:** how sleep deprivation affects working memory; a model that detects stress from EEG data; a literature review on how social media and gaming change the dopamine reward circuit; how neural circuits break down in Parkinson's disease

## 2. Biomedical engineering

Biomedical engineering (BME) solves medical problems with electrical, mechanical and AI technology. It fits students who want engineering and medicine at once, enjoy coding, electronics, physics and calculus, and like solving problems with a mix of mechanical design, sensors and software.

![Two people at a lab workbench examine a black robotic prosthetic hand, with a prosthetic arm and tools nearby](/editorial/224082371952-03.jpg "Biomedical engineers turn sensors, mechanics and software into devices such as prosthetics.")

- **Courses:** medical device design, biomechanics, bioinstrumentation, medical imaging (MRI, CT), signal processing (ECG, EMG, EEG), machine learning in healthcare
- **Compared with:** bioengineering (broader and more lab-based), neuroscience (biology first, less technology), computer science (no medicine or biosignals)
- **Where it leads:** One of the strongest US job markets of any bio major, spanning medical devices, wearables, AI diagnostics and surgical robotics, and its mix of hardware and software opens the door to engineering jobs. As a STEM field, it qualifies international graduates for up to three years of US work authorization under Optional Practical Training (OPT). Roles: medical device engineer, AI healthcare engineer, robotics engineer, imaging specialist, technical staff at hospitals and the FDA.
- **Research ideas:** predicting stress from a wearable heart-rate sensor; analyzing muscle fatigue with an Arduino-based EMG device; a fall-risk algorithm built on gait data; a deep-learning filter that removes noise from MRI scans

## 3. Bioinformatics

Bioinformatics uses AI and Python to analyze biological data, from genomes and proteins to disease records. It suits students drawn to the overlap of computer science and biology who would rather write algorithms than run bench experiments and think in mathematical and statistical terms.

![Hand-drawn diagram labeled Bioinformatics, with arrows linking data sources, managing big data, data analysis, problem solving, and health and drug discovery](/editorial/224082371952-04.jpg "Bioinformatics runs from raw biological data through analysis to new health tools and drugs.")

- **Courses:** genomic data analysis, protein structure prediction, machine learning for biology, computational evolution, statistical modeling in R and Python
- **Compared with:** biostatistics (more mathematical), genetics (lab-centered, less data), computer science (no biology)
- **Where it leads:** Central to AI drug discovery, genomics research and precision medicine, with hiring as strong as in computer science and steeply rising salaries. Roles: computational biologist, AI drug discovery scientist, genomic data scientist, biotech AI engineer.
- **Research ideas:** how gene variants affect cancer rates, using public data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA); a lightweight, AlphaFold-style deep-learning model that predicts protein structure from sequence; identifying cancer tissue from RNA-seq data; clustering genomic data to classify disease subtypes

## 4. Biochemistry

Biochemistry studies the chemical reactions, proteins and metabolic pathways inside cells at the molecular level. It suits students strong in both chemistry and biology who enjoy lab work and are drawn to drug development or research.

- **Courses:** enzymology, protein chemistry, metabolism, structural biology, mechanisms of drug action
- **Compared with:** molecular biology (more biological), chemistry (less about living systems)
- **Where it leads:** A very high share of graduates go on to medical school; others move into pharmaceutical and biotech R&D or graduate school, mostly in lab-based careers. Roles: clinical scientist, biochemist, pharmacologist, medical researcher, pharmaceutical R&D scientist.
- **Research ideas:** how pH affects enzyme activity; how different antioxidants suppress free radicals; how protein misfolding leads to disease

## 5. Molecular and cell biology

Molecular and cell biology (MCB) follows information from DNA to RNA to protein and studies cell structure, signaling and how cancer develops, mostly through experiments. It suits students aiming for research careers, particularly in disease and cancer.

![Illustration of rounded purple cells, each with a glowing blue nucleus](/editorial/224082371952-06.jpg "Molecular and cell biology looks inside the cell, from gene regulation to programmed cell death.")

- **Courses:** gene regulation, cell signaling, cancer biology, developmental biology, lab techniques such as PCR, Western blotting and cell culture
- **Compared with:** genetics (centered on genes), biochemistry (centered on chemical reactions)
- **Where it leads:** The standard foundation for life-science research and the most common route into PhDs in cancer biology, immunology and developmental biology; very popular with future medical and dental students, and expanding into data-driven research. Roles: cancer researcher, immunologist, medical scientist, biotech lab researcher.
- **Research ideas:** how signaling pathways differ across cancer cells; how immune cells are activated; the molecular mechanisms of apoptosis

## 6. Genetics and genomics

This major studies genes, genomes, inherited disease and CRISPR-based therapies. It suits students fascinated by gene editing and the genetics of disease who like both experiments and data.

- **Courses:** human genetics, genomic medicine, gene editing, epigenetics, DNA sequencing analysis
- **Compared with:** bioinformatics (analysis first), molecular biology (the whole cell)
- **Where it leads:** A core major for precision medicine, with demand climbing for genetic counseling, genomic data analysis and CRISPR research, and R&D opportunities expanding as the field merges with AI and big data. Roles: genomic scientist, CRISPR researcher, genetic counselor, genomic data analyst.
- **Research ideas:** how BRCA mutations affect breast cancer risk; the ethics of CRISPR-Cas9; predicting disease from a map of genetic variants

## 7. Biotechnology

Biotechnology applies life-science tools to industry, medicine and the environment, which makes it a hands-on, application-driven bio major. It suits students who picture themselves at a drug or biotech company, like lab work with a real-world payoff, or want to start a company of their own.

![Gloved hands steady a seedling in a small glass dish with tweezers as a syringe hovers above its leaves, beside small brown bottles on a lab bench](/editorial/224082371952-08.jpg "Biotechnology puts life-science tools to work in medicine, industry and the environment.")

- **Courses:** synthetic biology, bioprocess engineering, vaccine development, industrial microbiology
- **Compared with:** bioengineering (engineering first), molecular biology (basic lab science)
- **Where it leads:** Its industry focus translates readily into jobs, especially in fast-growing areas such as vaccines, cell therapies and synthetic biology, and extends naturally into startups and ventures. Roles: biotech engineer, vaccine developer, process engineer, bio-startup founder.
- **Research ideas:** how mRNA vaccines work and what advantages they offer; using microbes to regulate carbohydrate metabolism; case studies of CRISPR in agricultural biotech

## 8. Biostatistics

Biostatistics analyzes medical and biological data with statistical models and uses them to design clinical trials and public health policy. It suits students who love math, want to work with health data, and prefer statistical reasoning to programming.

- **Courses:** regression and survival analysis, clinical trial design, epidemiological modeling, probability theory
- **Compared with:** bioinformatics (programming first), public health (policy first), general statistics (less medical and biological data)
- **Where it leads:** Biostatisticians are fast becoming the data scientists of medicine and public health, in high demand for clinical trials and at drug companies and hospital research labs; the skills carry into AI healthcare and into much the same job market as data science. Roles: biostatistician, clinical data scientist, epidemiological analyst, public health researcher.
- **Research ideas:** the correlation between exercise time and obesity rates; modeling how well different vaccines prevent infection; regional air pollution and respiratory disease

## 9. Cognitive science

Cognitive science combines psychology, linguistics, philosophy, AI and neuroscience to study how people think. It suits students who like psychology, are curious about AI and the brain, and want to understand thought, language and decision-making.

- **Courses:** cognitive psychology, artificial intelligence, linguistics, decision theory, computational modeling
- **Compared with:** neuroscience (more biological), psychology (less analysis and modeling)
- **Where it leads:** UX, human-computer interaction (HCI) and human-AI interaction are booming, and cognitive science has far more industry applications than psychology, making it a strong route into tech companies. Roles: UX researcher, AI cognition scientist, human factors engineer, behavioral data scientist.
- **Research ideas:** comparing how deep-learning models and humans process language; how social media algorithms shape decisions; a model for measuring cognitive load

## 10. Pharmacology and pharmaceutical science

Pharmacology studies how drugs act in the body (pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics) and the full process of developing a new one. It suits students who enjoy chemistry and biology and hope to work in drug development at a pharmaceutical company or research institute.

- **Courses:** drug mechanisms, pharmacokinetics, toxicology, medicinal chemistry, clinical pharmacology
- **Compared with:** biochemistry (molecular fundamentals), biotechnology (industry and applications)
- **Where it leads:** Built for drug development, clinical research and toxicology, with a strong pipeline into pharmaceutical companies and growing demand from biotech ventures; also a solid base for medical or pharmacy school. Roles: clinical pharmacologist, toxicologist, drug discovery researcher, pharmaceutical scientist.
- **Research ideas:** how anticancer drugs work and why resistance develops; why overdoses of fever and pain relievers damage the liver; a review of how drug candidates are screened

## Narrowing it down

If ten options feel like too many, sort them by what you want from a major:

- **AI and data:** bioinformatics, biostatistics, cognitive science, biomedical engineering
- **Lab work:** biochemistry, molecular and cell biology, genetics, pharmacology, biotechnology, neuroscience
- **A strong fit with medical school:** neuroscience, biochemistry, molecular and cell biology, pharmacology

## Difficulty and career flexibility at a glance

| Major | Difficulty | Career flexibility | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Neuroscience | Moderate | Very high | Connects to both medicine and AI |
| Biomedical engineering | High | Very high | Strong engineering job prospects |
| Bioinformatics | High | Very high | Core of genomics and AI drug discovery |
| Biochemistry | Moderate | High | Foundation for medicine and research |
| Molecular and cell biology | Moderate | Moderate | Research-based major |
| Genetics | Moderate | High | Expanding in the CRISPR and genomics era |
| Biotechnology | Moderate | Very high | Strong hiring in pharma and industry |
| Biostatistics | High | Very high | Data science track |
| Cognitive science | Moderate | High | Popular for UX, HCI and AI |
| Pharmacology | Moderate | High | Central to drug development |

## The right major is the one that fits

Bio majors are popular for good reasons: a fast-growing industry, the widest range of paths across medicine, AI, engineering and data, and academic depth that universities respect. Still, the question that matters most is whether a field suits the student's way of thinking, interests and strengths.

Bio can be an excellent choice, but it is not right for every student. The best major grows naturally out of a student's temperament, academic style and hopes for the future. If you are weighing majors now, keep exploring several fields and pay attention to which ones spark your curiosity and play to your strengths.

Trying the work is one of the surest ways to tell. Each research idea above is the kind of question a high school student can take on with the right guidance, and CRI's [research programs](/research) pair students with university faculty to develop one into a paper of their own, written in English.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Meet the nine TA mentors behind CRI's 2025 faculty teams
excerpt: From a cryo-EM specialist to an AI startup CEO, meet the TAs who worked with seven CRI faculty teams in 2025 and see how each helps students design, run, and write up their research.
content:
One CRI teaching assistant has operated 200- to 300-kilovolt cryo-electron microscopes. Another has presented research to the UN Security Council. A third co-founded an AI startup and has run AI transformation projects for companies such as Hilton. At CRI, a student's research takes shape under a professor's guidance, but the professor is never the only mentor involved.

That other mentor is the TA. TAs take a professor's expertise and put it into terms a student can work with. They help plan how a project will unfold, then stay with students at every stage, from gathering sources to analysis and writing. Each is a young researcher with real depth in their own field, and for most students, the first research partner they work with day to day. Here are the nine TAs who worked with seven CRI faculty teams in 2025.

## Chemistry: Brian Stoltz's team (Caltech)

Stoltz's team works in organic chemistry and biochemistry. Its TA started a PhD at Caltech in fall 2025, arriving with a solid research record in structural biology and biochemistry. At Seoul National University, the TA specialized in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), handling 200–300 kV instruments with an operator's level of skill. Membrane protein purification, nanodisc assembly, FRET analysis, SAXS experiments: few high school students ever see these techniques, and this TA has carried out every step of them firsthand.

With students, the TA:

- Turns an experimental idea into a logically structured plan
- Explains *why* an experiment is needed, not just how to run it
- Sets a clear bar for a finished paper: reliable data and interpretation with real depth

Thanks to that support, even demanding topics in organic synthesis and structural biology become ones a student can follow.

![A young man in a gray sweater points to handwritten notes high on a whiteboard while a young woman beside him follows along](/editorial/224079964888-01.jpg "A whiteboard session with Brian Stoltz's chemistry team.")

## Wearable tech and AI: Nabil Alshurafa's team (Northwestern)

Alshurafa's students study smart devices that analyze body movement and health. Two TAs supported the team.

### An XR and human-computer interaction researcher

The first TA, from UC Berkeley's master's program in design engineering, has carried out a range of advanced projects that combine extended reality (XR), user interfaces, computer vision, and design research:

- An XR system that corrects exercise form for rehabilitation patients
- Vision-based drone navigation using a ZED camera
- Avatar interactions driven by gesture recognition
- User-experience experiments for VR interfaces

The common thread is solving problems where technology meets user experience. This TA is good at recasting a technical idea as user-centered research and at helping students frame their own questions in interface and HCI work. Project-based research, more than paper writing, is a particular strength, which makes this TA a natural partner for students taking on AI, HCI, or XR topics.

### A medical AI engineer and founder

The second TA did medical AI research at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) and co-founded an AI healthcare startup that took the overall prize at Hong Kong's Techathon+ and was selected for incubation by Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks (HKSTP) and Cyberport. The TA has hands-on experience building technology that industry actually uses:

- Large-scale retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems
- Analysis of unstructured medical data
- Deep-learning detection of anomalous signals
- Multi-agent AI architectures

That experience means a high school project can go as far as a model that really runs. The TA explains AI architectures in language students can follow, makes a clear case for why a complex model is needed, and works through the details until an idea is something students can build. Students who want to build their research around AI will find this TA an exceptionally dependable guide.

## Evolutionary psychology: Max Krasnow's team (Harvard)

The psychology TA is a master's student in psychology at NYU, researching motivation, emotion, and behavior. The TA's grounding in language, cognition, and developmental psychology goes back to undergraduate years at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign:

- Research on how children acquire language
- Analysis of parent–child interaction
- Experimental design and data coding
- Speech and behavior analysis in ELAN

At NYU, the TA runs carefully designed behavioral experiments on questions such as how mood affects engagement, so the advice students get when designing a psychology project is highly practical. This TA excels at breaking an idea into testable pieces, can help with data processing in R and SPSS, and makes a first behavioral or cognitive experiment manageable for students who have never run one. Students preparing a psychology paper could hardly ask for a better research partner.

![Professor Max Krasnow, wearing a name badge, stands with five others at an evening event in a room with tall windows](/editorial/224079964888-04.jpg "Max Krasnow with members of his evolutionary psychology team.")

## International law and policy: William Burke-White's team (Penn)

### A specialist in policy, security, and humanitarian research

Burke-White's first TA has written two books and numerous papers on international politics, human rights, and security, and has presented research to bodies such as the UN Security Council, the US State Department, South Korea's presidential office, and international NGOs. That background helps students hold an international policy paper to high standards of depth, source reliability, and logical rigor. Having studied computer science alongside public policy at UChicago, the TA can also connect policy research with machine learning and data analysis. In practice, the TA:

- Shows exactly how to write a paper the way a strong policy report is written
- Helps design studies that draw on both quantitative and qualitative data
- Gives feedback that compresses an argument and sharpens it

That combination makes this TA an outstanding mentor for students researching international politics, law, human rights, or governance.

### An international education researcher and former Fulbright ETA

The second TA studies international education and the mobility of East Asian international students at Seoul National University's Graduate School of International Studies, and ran education programs at a Korean elementary school as a Fulbright English Teaching Assistant (ETA). With firsthand experience of schooling in the US, Korea, and China, and a record of planning and running international education programs, this TA gives students well-grounded advice when they choose a topic in education or the social sciences. Expect patient help designing qualitative research, from interviews to coding, a firm hand with the logic of social-science writing, and plain explanations of complex ideas in education, international mobility, and policy. This TA is at their best with students pursuing international education, policy, or cultural studies.

## Film: James Savoca's team (USC)

Jael holds an MFA from Emerson College and specializes in screenwriting and directing. She has also worked in industry, producing broadcast programs at Shanghai Media Group in China. A short film she directed was selected for international festival programs, including Focus on China at the Venice International Film Festival, and she brings expertise in advertising and brand video as well. That range lets her guide students through the full arc of a film: story concept, script, visual composition, and the structure of the edit.

Jael is skilled at turning an abstract idea into narrative structure and at explaining visual language, shot composition, and a director's intent. She can supervise written research on the arts as well as creative, practice-based projects, which makes her a strong mentor for students working on scripts, video, or film.

## Philosophy of education: Liam Gearon's team (Oxford)

The education TA is a PhD student in education at Yonsei University, holds a master's in educational psychology from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, and has worked on many international education policy research projects. That work has meant handling social-science questions with precision:

- Comparative policy analysis
- Qualitative coding in NVivo
- Writing grounded in educational psychology
- Research on multiculturalism, migration, and educational inequality

Having coached many international students on how to structure essays and papers, the TA is especially good at making writing logically clear. Students can expect concepts and theories re-explained at their level, a clean introduction–theory–discussion structure, and experienced guidance on qualitative research design. For a paper in education, philosophy, or the social sciences, this TA is an ideal partner.

## Entrepreneurship and innovation: Kit Hickey's team (MIT Sloan)

VA7 is the co-founder and CEO of the AI startup Metana AI and has carried out AI transformation projects for large companies such as Hilton. The rest of VA7's background is unusually broad:

- Winning a hackathon at ETHDenver
- Building a Web3 knowledge-network project
- Hands-on work in data engineering, AI modeling, RAG, and RLHF
- A habit of reading social problems and markets from a policy perspective

With students, VA7 focuses on what it takes to make an idea viable as a business, gives structure to data-driven market analysis, product strategy, and UX flows, and is especially strong on business plans and pitch decks: a good match for research in entrepreneurship and data-driven innovation.

## Research partners, not assistants

CRI's TAs are not there simply to help with assignments. They bring deep research experience in their fields and practical skills built in real projects, institutions, and companies, and they draw on both to design each student's research together with the student. When a professor's expertise meets a TA's feel for the work on the ground, students can go further than high school research usually goes. The point is not hard study for its own sake but the pleasure of chasing a question you genuinely care about.

The TAs CRI selected for its 2025 Winter Online Research Program were held to the same standards as the mentors above. They were chosen for:

- Research experience at leading universities around the world
- A strong command of papers, experiments, and data analysis
- Communication that works for students
- The ability to keep research moving smoothly between professor and student

In the summer Seoul Research Program, the professor–TA partnership is built into the schedule, with 20 TA hours alongside 30 hours of teaching by faculty. To see how the summer cohorts are organized, explore the [Seoul and Global Research Programs](/research/summer-camp).

title: What the new federal admissions data rules mean for US college applicants
excerpt: A new federal survey asks US colleges to report admissions data by race and sex, including test scores and GPAs. What it changes, what it doesn't, and what it means for international applicants.
content:
US colleges are being asked to show the federal government not just whom they admit, but the numbers behind those decisions. In August 2025, a memorandum from President Trump directed the Department of Education to require detailed admissions data from colleges, including applicants' race and sex alongside their grades and test scores, and gave the department until early December to start collecting it. The administration presents the memorandum as a matter of fairness and transparency: a way to confirm that colleges are following the Supreme Court's 2023 ban on race-conscious admissions.

Although the reporting requirement has since been challenged in court and partly blocked, it signals where admissions is heading after affirmative action. For families, the real question is whether it changes what colleges look for in a student.

## What colleges are being asked to report

The memorandum calls for colleges to send the federal government detailed admissions data, including:

- applicants' race and sex
- standardized test scores (SAT, ACT) and high school GPAs
- admission rates and financial aid, including scholarships

The data is collected through the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), the national college database run by the department's National Center for Education Statistics. Its stated purpose is to reveal whether colleges are still giving weight to race anywhere in their selection process.

That makes it more than another statistical report. Since the Supreme Court's 2023 decision in *Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard*, colleges have had to strike a new balance between diverse classes and race-neutral selection, and the federal government now intends to track that balance directly. Many observers read the reporting requirement as a message to colleges: be ready to justify your choices. Publishing outcomes is no longer enough; a college may need to show the criteria and data behind them.

## Selective colleges feel it most

The reporting requirement does not land equally. As [Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB)](https://www.opb.org/article/2025/11/03/college-admissions-trump-administration-application-changes/) reported, most US colleges admit the majority of their applicants and already decide largely on high school grades, so having to report those numbers is unlikely to change how they admit students.

It is more complicated at colleges with extremely low admission rates, such as Harvard, Princeton and Stanford. These schools once weighed racial background carefully to build diverse classes, and since the 2023 ruling some elite colleges have seen the share of Black and Hispanic students fall. In response, selective colleges increasingly read an applicant's background through essays, recommendations and activities, not as race but as context.

Background in itself is no longer what gets evaluated. What still counts is how it shaped a student's academic work, leadership and motivation. The standards have changed less than the way files are read. As experts put it, colleges now look at the context of a student's effort instead of race, trying to understand the circumstances that made an achievement possible, not just the score.

## Academic achievement stays at the center

Through all of this, colleges still treat academic achievement as the core measure. Nate Mannetter, who leads enrollment at Gonzaga University, told OPB that it is the most heavily weighted criterion. In practice, that means the high school transcript: grades and the rigor of the courses behind them.

That is not simply a matter of high or low marks. Colleges look at how far students challenged themselves within the options their school offered, and whether they built a steady record over time. An A in an AP, IB or honors course means something different from an A in a standard class.

Test-optional policies had shrunk the role of the SAT and ACT at many colleges, but some analysts expect the reporting requirement to bring scores back into focus as part of each college's admissions data. If the balance tips partly back toward numbers a college can show, a consistent, credible academic record matters even more.

The competition has grown more complicated. What colleges are ultimately assessing has not: intellectual curiosity, deep engagement with a subject, and steady growth.

## Activities and recommendations still show context

Colleges still want the story behind the numbers. Without weighing race or background directly, admissions readers use essays, recommendations and activity records to see which experiences shaped a student and how those experiences connect to academic interests. Two things are likely to count for more:

- **Depth over breadth:** sustained commitment to one field rather than a long list of unrelated activities
- **Process over titles:** how a student solved problems and what they learned, rather than awards or positions alone

Recommendations work the same way. A letter carries weight when it goes beyond praise and describes, concretely, how the student developed. With race out of the evaluation, these documents are one more way for colleges to understand who a student is and what they have achieved.

## What it means for international applicants

The reporting requirement focuses on data about domestic applicants, but it has indirect implications for international students.

**Comparable academic data may carry more weight.** As colleges analyze their whole applicant pool in finer detail, international students gain from presenting objective measures clearly: GPA, test scores and English proficiency.

**Context still sets applicants apart.** With race no longer a factor, essays and activity records that show what a student took on and achieved inside a different education system remain a genuine point of distinction.

The change is less a new opening than a signal to make every part of the application clearer and more coherent.

## What has happened since

The memorandum moved quickly from policy to a reporting requirement, and then into court. It took shape as a new IPEDS survey, the **Admissions and Consumer Transparency Supplement (ACTS)**, which applies to four-year colleges that do not admit every applicant. ACTS asks for data on applicants, admitted students and enrolled students broken down by race and sex, including test scores, GPA and family income, for 2025–26 and the six years before it.

| When | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| June 2023 | Supreme Court rules race-conscious admissions unconstitutional |
| August 2025 | Presidential memorandum directs the Education Department to expand admissions reporting |
| December 2025 | The ACTS survey is approved and opens to colleges |
| March 2026 | First submission deadline; 17 states sue in federal court in Massachusetts |
| April 2026 | The court blocks enforcement for public colleges in those states, then for about 178 more institutions |

Judge F. Dennis Saylor found that the survey had likely been rolled out in an arbitrary and capricious way, while noting that the department does have general authority to collect admissions data. Most of the roughly 178 additional institutions belong to six higher education associations that joined the case, including the Association of American Universities. Other colleges still had to report, and hundreds had already submitted. The department has said it plans to make the data public, but with many of the most selective universities covered by the injunctions, the first national picture is likely to have gaps.

## More transparent, same fundamentals

Whatever the courts decide about ACTS, the push behind it goes beyond its stated goal of fairer admissions: it aims to redefine how colleges use data to judge students. One thing has not moved. Admissions still comes down to the consistency of a student's achievement and growth. Even as policies and criteria shift, what colleges ultimately want to know is what problem a student noticed in their own surroundings and how persistently they worked to solve it.

So treat this moment as a chance to present your record more clearly, not as a reason for alarm. Grades, coursework, activities, recommendations and essays are separate pieces, but together they answer a single question: why do I learn, and what have I tried to change? Students who can answer it honestly still stand out, and greater transparency tends to make real ability and depth of thinking easier to see.

One way to build that kind of record is a sustained research project in a field you care about, where the question, the method and the revisions are your own. In CRI's [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter), university faculty guide students over the winter break through a research project and a paper written in English.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Algorithms, game theory, and agentic AI with UChicago's Haifeng Xu
excerpt: How UChicago computer scientist Haifeng Xu teaches reinforcement learning, mechanism design, and multi-agent systems, then guides students to an agentic AI research paper in ten sessions.
content:
Most people picture artificial intelligence as a model that learns from data and predicts an answer. Haifeng Xu, a computer scientist at the University of Chicago, studies what comes next: AI agents that make their own decisions, sizing up a situation, cooperating with other agents, and sometimes competing with them, much as people and companies do. His CRI course, *Algorithms & Agentic AI*, teaches high school students the algorithms behind those agents over ten live online sessions, then asks them to put the ideas to work in a research paper.

## What makes AI "agentic"

Where a prediction model calculates the right answer, an agentic system takes on a harder question: in this situation, what is the most effective thing to do? It works in a loop, producing a result, reviewing it, gathering feedback, cleaning its data, learning through reinforcement, and updating its model before going around again.

That kind of intelligence already runs through recommendation feeds, self-driving cars, game AI, and digital marketplaces, and it is one of the most active research areas at Google, OpenAI, and Microsoft. Industry is shifting its focus from large language models alone, a crowded field where products struggle to stand apart, toward agents built for specific applications that create real business value.

Universities are moving the same way. Stanford HAI studies AI that acts in the world, including the ethics of people and agents working together, and MIT CSAIL uses multi-agent systems to simulate policy. Xu's own lab concentrates on agent-based reinforcement learning, game theory, and market algorithms. The field also reaches well beyond computer science, into economics, psychology, political science, and education.

## Who teaches it

Haifeng Xu is a professor in UChicago's Department of Computer Science, where he directs the SIGMA Lab (Strategic Intelligence for Machine Agents). His research sits where AI meets economics: algorithms that let AI make decisions, game theory for situations in which people or firms act strategically toward one another, and mathematical models for making the best choice when information is limited. He publishes regularly at NeurIPS and AAAI, two of the top conferences in AI, and has collaborated with research teams at Google, JP Morgan, and Adobe Research.

His honors include an NSF CAREER Award, a Google Research Scholar Award, a Facebook Research Award, and a 2019 award from ACM SIGecom, the ACM's special interest group on economics and computation. He has served as guest editor of a special issue of the journal *Games and Economic Behavior* and co-organized a fall 2022 program on data economics at IDEAL, the Institute for Data, Econometrics, Algorithms, and Learning.

![A page from Haifeng Xu's list of refereed conference papers, with entries at NeurIPS 2022, EC 2022, COLT 2022, ICML 2022, and SODA 2023](/editorial/224060248453-05.jpg "Part of Professor Xu's publication list, including three papers at NeurIPS 2022.")

## The ideas at the core of the course

Students work directly with the building blocks of modern AI:

- **Reinforcement learning:** how an AI learns from its own experience
- **Mechanism design:** setting the rules for environments where many AI agents cooperate or compete
- **Strategic communication:** how AI agents share information and persuade one another
- **Market algorithms:** the platform-optimization structures behind Amazon, Uber, and Google
- **Recommendation systems:** how TikTok and YouTube come to "understand" you

None of this stays in equations. Students design how an agent behaves, run experiments on data, and analyze how an AI arrives at a decision, all in service of a larger question for their papers: how AI imitates human choices, and when it might outperform them.

## Ten sessions, two phases

The course moves from first principles to a finished short research paper in ten sessions, one per class day. After a kickoff meeting, each day brings a two-hour session with Professor Xu followed by a two-hour mentor session, and a mid-program evaluation checks progress partway through.

### Lecture phase: sessions 1–5

| Session | Topic |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | What is agentic AI? What it means for an AI to make its own decisions |
| 2 | Neural networks: how a system learns to reason from data |
| 3–4 | Reinforcement learning: learning by trial and error |
| 5 | Multi-agent systems and mechanism design: the mathematics of cooperation and competition |

Along the way, students use Python to train small neural networks and build simple simulations, so they can watch a learning system at work. They also start turning their interests into a research question of their own, some version of "How could an AI make decisions the way a person does?"

### Research phase: sessions 6–10

The second half turns theory into research. Students analyze data, run simulations, and draft their papers around themes such as:

- Recommendation systems and the logic of platform algorithms
- Market algorithms, and how competing AI agents reach equilibrium
- Strategic communication: how AI agents persuade and cooperate with each other
- AI ethics and safety, or decision-making that accounts for fairness and transparency

Each session combines a mini-lecture of about 30 minutes with a hands-on workshop led by TAs. The paper takes shape one section at a time, from literature review to methods, results, and discussion. Session 10 is the Final Research Paper Showcase, where students present their papers and take feedback from Professor Xu and their classmates.

## A class that does research

Xu does not teach students how to find the right answer. He teaches them how to ask a question and then test it. In every session, students check a hypothesis against an experiment, interpret the data, and write up what they found. It is less a class about AI than a class that carries out AI research.

After each lecture, TAs (master's- and PhD-level researchers from leading universities) help students sharpen their research direction. Because the work runs on individual feedback and small workshops, every student's progress is followed closely, even in a short program. Papers follow the conventions of published AI research in APA or IEEE style, so students practice structure, argument, data analysis, and interpretation the way working researchers do.

![Haifeng Xu speaks on a video call beside a lecture slide about Richard Roll's 1984 journal article "Orange Juice and Weather"](/editorial/224155877662-02.jpg "Professor Xu teaching online, with a slide on how orange juice futures can be used to predict the weather.")

## What students leave with

The final product is a research paper, revised with Professor Xu's feedback and presented in the last session. Grading reflects where the weight of the course lies:

| Component | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| Class participation and discussion | 20% |
| Data and coding assignments | 30% |
| Final paper and presentation | 50% |

CRI's editing and publication team then supports each paper through submission, to venues ranging from high school research journals such as the *International Journal of High School Research* (IJHSR) and the *Journal of Emerging Investigators* (JEI) to undergraduate- and graduate-level journals. Students come away able to say they did not just learn AI but researched it, a clear sign of depth on a college application, especially for a STEM major. The course can also be a first step toward individual research over the summer or a presentation at an international conference.

## What students have built

When Professor Xu taught the course in the 2025 Winter Online Research Program, which ran from December 2025 into January 2026, his class of three students worked as a team on sports outcome prediction and algorithmic trading. They collected and cleaned real NBA game data, built and compared machine-learning models to forecast results, designed a betting strategy based on those forecasts, and ran simulations of its returns and risk to judge whether the strategy made economic sense. The team wrote the work up together as a single research paper.

Another student who wrote a paper with Professor Xu asked how recommendation algorithms steer human choices, and how much of the resulting judgment still reflects free will. The student analyzed the recommendation systems of TikTok, YouTube, and Netflix through the lens of agentic AI and designed a reinforcement-learning simulation to test for bias in decision-making models. The finished paper drew together AI ethics, platform design, and behavioral economics. Building on that work, the student was admitted to UC Berkeley for computer science.

A paper like that moves from theoretical background to a hypothesis, an experimental design, the interpretation of results, and their social implications. It shows three things a coding project rarely does: an understanding of how AI reasons, the practical skill to design simulation experiments with real data, and the willingness to pursue an open question instead of a textbook problem.

## Joining a winter course

Professor Xu's *Algorithms & Agentic AI* is part of CRI's Winter Online Research Program, which runs live online over winter break in small, faculty-led groups. To see which faculty and courses are open for the coming winter, explore the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter).
