title: Early Decision vs. Early Action: why the early round rewards depth, not speed
excerpt: How Early Decision and Early Action differ, why early applicants are admitted at higher rates, and how three CRI students used research to earn early admission to Cornell, Vanderbilt and Penn.
content:
Each fall, the first round of US college admissions opens with Early Decision (ED) and Early Action (EA), and at most selective colleges the deadline falls on or around November 1. As it approaches, students and parents ask the same question: does applying early actually help? For a student who is ready, it does, but being ready has little to do with filing paperwork ahead of time. It means having a clear direction and a consistent record of exploring it, which is what admissions officers look for beyond high scores.

## ED and EA in brief

Both options ask you to apply in the fall, and at many schools you hear back by mid-December. The difference is commitment. **Early Decision is binding**: you apply ED to one school and, if admitted, you commit to enroll. **Early Action is not binding**: an admitted student can still weigh other offers.

Here is what the early round involved at two schools, one using each model, as their calendars stood for the 2025–26 cycle. Dates shift a little from year to year, so check each admissions office's current timeline.

### MIT: Early Action

| Date | What's due |
| --- | --- |
| November 1 | All application components: general information, essays, activities, academics |
| November 1 | Two teacher recommendations, one from a math or science teacher and one from a humanities, social science or language teacher |
| November 1 | Secondary School Report, including the high school transcript |
| November test date | SAT or ACT scores; English proficiency exams strongly recommended for some non-native English speakers |
| Mid-February | February Updates & Notes Form, including midyear grades |

### Cornell: Early Decision (international first-year applicants)

| Date | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| August | Common App opens |
| October | CSS Profile opens; recommended last date to sit the SAT or ACT |
| November 1 | Common App and Cornell Writing Supplement due, along with a portfolio, video interview or design supplement for applicants to certain programs; financial aid materials due for international applicants |
| November 14 | Remaining supplemental materials due (portfolios and design supplements excluded) |
| Mid-December | Admission decisions and financial aid offers released |
| January 20 | Deadline to reply to an offer of admission |

## Why the early round matters

The early round comes down to three things: your odds, what your application says about you, and the story it tells.

### The admit-rate gap is wider than most families expect

At most leading US universities, early applicants are admitted at higher rates than regular applicants. MIT is a clear example. For students entering in fall 2025, MIT admitted about 6% of its Early Action applicants, compared with roughly 2.4% in the regular round, so early applicants got in at more than twice the rate. Similar gaps show up at Harvard, Yale, Cornell and Stanford.

Smaller applicant pools are only part of the explanation. A college sorting through thousands of applications has to find the students who genuinely want to be there. An early application, and a binding ED application above all, tells a college that it is the student's first choice, and colleges consider those applicants all the more seriously.

### A strong early application is evidence in itself

Submitting a polished application before November 1 shows more than punctuality. It demonstrates time management, self-direction and planning. Early applicants whose research, essays and activities are finished and well organized come across to admissions officers as students ready to grow the moment they arrive on campus.

Most CRI students complete a research paper in a summer program and draw on it in their Common App activities list and essays. A real piece of research, backed by a recommendation from the professor who supervised it, is far more convincing than a sentence saying you are interested in a field.

### Strategy is about narrative, not numbers

Beyond scores and awards, colleges want to know why a student fits their school. A list of activities doesn't answer that. A storyline does: one in which research, projects and leadership connect logically around a single intended field of study.

This is where research stops being one more activity and becomes the thread running through the entire application. Genuine inquiry into a field is what completes the picture of fit that colleges look for. The early round doesn't reward whoever prepared first. It rewards whoever prepared most deeply.

## Three early admits, three uses of research

What early admits have in common is that they can explain why they chose their major, not just what they did well. Research experience is what gives that explanation weight, and three CRI students show how it works in practice.

### J.: Physics at Cornell, with no SAT or ACT score

J. is a clear case of depth outweighing scores. With no SAT or ACT score to submit, J. was admitted to Cornell University through Early Decision to study physics.

At CRI, J. worked with Princeton professor Joshua Winn on the mechanics of planetary and black hole motion, using data analysis and coding to turn an interest in physics into actual research. Learning to code for the first time in order to analyze physics data was, by J.'s own account, what made J. certain of the path ahead and gave J. the goal of research-focused study in college. The application didn't just claim a love of physics. It showed a student who had already explored physics through research.

### L.: Education at Vanderbilt's Peabody College

L.'s story is about the match between a student and a school. Long interested in education, L. joined University of Pennsylvania professor Andrea Kane's research on educational leadership at CRI. The project changed how L. understood education: not simply as teaching, but as a system shaped by policy and leadership, and as a way of bringing change within the structures of society.

That insight became the backbone of L.'s essays and interview. It tied L.'s own experience directly to the philosophy of Vanderbilt's Peabody College, which sets out to develop education leaders who can turn ideas into action, and L. was admitted to Peabody through Early Decision.

### Q.: Statistics at Penn, after a disappointing ACT

Q. showed that research can prove real ability even when a test score falls short. Q.'s ACT score was lower than hoped, but at CRI, Q. joined Yale professor John Emerson's research in statistics and data science.

Analyzing social phenomena with real data gave Q.'s essays the credibility of a genuine problem-solver. Studying social problems through data felt hard at first, but the process revealed what Q. truly enjoys: understanding how a problem is structured. Q. was admitted to the University of Pennsylvania through Early Decision to study statistics, and the professor's recommendation letter added real weight to the application.

### The common thread

None of the three simply showed what they had studied. Each showed how they learned, and how they pushed that learning further on their own. That is the difference CRI's research programs aim to make.

## Depth is the real early advantage

What a student has built by the early deadline is the clearest signal of maturity and direction a college receives. Colleges favor early applicants who have turned their goals into concrete achievements, not just scores or awards. In the early round, then, completeness counts for more than speed, and the depth of the process for more than the result.

CRI students go through that process in full. In a ten-day intensive program, they design and write a paper with a professor from a leading university, producing academic work of their own rather than a line on a participation list. Along the way, they learn to:

- set a goal and reach it within a fixed timeframe
- analyze data
- build a logical written argument
- revise their work in response to a professor's feedback

That is the mindset of a researcher, exactly what colleges look for, and it makes one of the most persuasive stories an application can tell. As CRI sees it, the early round is where you prove you are deeply prepared, not merely early. That depth is what CRI sets out to build, helping students grow an interest into real inquiry and present it in terms a college can trust.

More than any score, an application needs a clear answer to one question: why this major? For many CRI students, that answer starts with research. The [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter) brings the same approach to winter break: students develop a research question with a university professor, write their own paper in English with close feedback from graduate-student TAs, and receive support through journal submission once the program ends.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Forged applications in Hong Kong and why verifiable research now counts for more
excerpt: HKU and CUHK rejected hundreds of applicants over forged credentials. Here is why research a professor can vouch for now carries weight, from an NYU Early Decision admit to master's offers in Hong Kong and Singapore.
content:
In October 2025, two of Hong Kong's most selective universities disclosed that they had turned away hundreds of applicants for the 2025/26 intake over forged credentials. The University of Hong Kong (HKU) and the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) found applications built on fake transcripts and on secondary schools that did not exist. A risky shortcut taken by some applicants has become a question of trust for admissions as a whole, and it is changing what universities want to see.

## What HKU and CUHK found

According to the Hong Kong newspaper The Standard, HKU received hundreds of applications from non-local students suspected of using fraudulent qualifications, and none of them led to an offer. The university declared zero tolerance for breaches of academic integrity and promised new identity checks. CUHK rejected several hundred applicants on similar grounds, up from roughly ten cases the year before, and the South China Morning Post reported that its admissions staff now use AI tools alongside manual checks to confirm that each application is genuine.

The problem was not new. In July 2024, HKU Business School said it had found more than 30 master's students who had enrolled with falsified documents, and that the total could eventually reach 80 to 100.

## From scores to evidence

CRI sees the scandal as a sign of a broader shift: admissions is moving its center of gravity from grades to evidence that can be trusted. Transcripts and certificates reduce a student to numbers. What increasingly matters is what the student actually learned, and how.

Leading universities in Hong Kong and Singapore started moving in this direction years ago, because a GPA or a test score cannot show everything a student is capable of. Most of their applications include a section for research, publications, or other academic work, where applicants describe the projects they took part in and what came of them. For example:

- **HKU** asks applicants to list any research papers or publications.
- **The National University of Singapore (NUS)** asks for academic achievements, including research projects and published work.
- **CUHK** has said publicly that research and publication records help an application.

In these systems a paper is not just supplementary material. It is part of the formal assessment, and between two applicants with similar grades, the one with verifiable research experience earns far more trust.

## Why a paper is such strong evidence

Universities are not simply looking for students who scored well. They want students who can think and inquire like scholars, and no exam measures that. So admissions readers treat research experience, papers, presentations, and poster sessions as direct evidence of academic potential. Because admissions in Hong Kong and Singapore is built around documents, verifiable academic work carries particular force there.

US universities weigh the same work differently. Through holistic review, they consider a student's growth and story as a whole, so a paper matters less as a finished product than as part of the story of how a student's curiosity developed.

| | Hong Kong and Singapore | United States |
|---|---|---|
| How applications are read | Document-centered review | Holistic review of the whole applicant |
| What a research paper does | Serves as formal evaluation material | Shows intellectual maturity and curiosity |
| What it adds up to | Objective, verifiable academic evidence | A process-centered intellectual narrative |

The two systems look different, but they rest on the same premise: universities now treat a genuine process of learning as the strongest basis for trust.

## What a CRI research program leaves behind

CRI's research programs are not classes in how to write a paper. Students carry out real research alongside a professor, with direct feedback from faculty at leading universities, close mentoring from master's and PhD teaching assistants at top universities, and small research groups. Guided by the professor, each student defines a topic, then works through the project with a TA one stage at a time, from analyzing data to writing it up.

Every stage leaves a record:

- A recommendation letter from the professor
- A research paper or academic poster, prepared for submission to journals and conferences in Korea and abroad
- An official research certificate and a grade report

Together, these records turn the experience from one more activity into academic work a university can trust.

![A student types in a Google Docs research paper draft on a laptop](/editorial/224055372412-04.jpg "Drafting a research paper during a CRI program")

## Three students, three applications

CRI students build their projects around their own interests with a professor, then make a confident case for that work in their applications. Here are three of them.

### A Lingnan University student: four master's offers

A student at Lingnan University in Hong Kong worked with Duke University historian James Chappel on the historical roots of human rights and how values evolve as societies develop. The student went on to win admission to master's programs at four universities: NUS, HKU, CUHK, and Hong Kong Baptist University (HKBU).

> "Admissions at Hong Kong and Singapore universities isn't just about scores. They weigh your academic background and your ability to think, taken together. Doing research directly with a Duke professor through CRI deepened my thinking about scholarship, and the paper I presented at an international conference, along with my professor's recommendation letter, became the most persuasive part of my application."
> — Lingnan University student, mentored by James Chappel

### J.: an average SAT and an Early Decision offer from NYU

J., a student at a school in Beijing, did research in social and cognitive psychology with Vivian Zayas, a psychology professor at Cornell University. J. listed the research paper as the first item in the activities section and was admitted to New York University through Early Decision.

> "My SAT score was average, but the psychology research I did with CRI was the most important evidence of who I am. Finishing the paper myself let me define what I actually wanted to know, and that experience became the heart of my NYU essay. The CRI project turned my curiosity into real experience."
> — J., mentored by Vivian Zayas

### A ZUEL student: an interview that turned to the research

A student at Zhongnan University of Economics and Law (ZUEL) in China studied policy analysis through economic reasoning with Thomas Noe, an economist at the University of Oxford. When the program ended, Professor Noe wrote the student a recommendation letter. The student was later admitted to master's programs related to economics and law at both HKU and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST).

> "After the CRI program ended, I received a recommendation letter from Professor Noe. In my HKU interview, the interviewer asked about that research in detail. As I explained my topic and how I had carried out the work, I could feel the interviewer taking my experience very seriously. I was able to prove that it was real research."
> — ZUEL student, mentored by Thomas Noe

What these three students share is simple: substantive research with a professor gave admissions readers evidence they could trust. The paper and the recommendation letter were not trophies. They were a record of how each student learned and inquired.

## Trust starts with real experience

The forgery cases at HKU and CUHK are a reminder of what admissions is really about. Universities care less about how hard a student worked than about what that work actually produced. Scores and certificates show a result. Research with a professor shows that the process behind the result was genuine.

CRI's research programs are designed around that idea: students choose their own topics, stretch their thinking through a professor's feedback, and can leave with a paper and a recommendation letter that document the work. Beyond the application itself, that record is the clearest evidence of who a student really is. Admissions, in the end, is a search for what is real, and what is real is made where learning happens. To see how students at different stages take on faculty-guided research, [explore CRI's research programs](/research).
author: CRI Editorial

title: The Korea Code Fair: how a student software competition opens a route to ISEF
excerpt: How the Korea Code Fair's software competition works, from document review to live demos, and how silver-and-above winners can compete for a place on Korea's ISEF team.
content:
A pair of smart glasses that tells a visually impaired wearer what their finger is pointing at. A walking aid for the same users that guides them along their route in real time. A device that gives instant feedback so the person performing CPR gets each compression right. Each of these projects won at the Korea Code Fair's software competition, and each went on to earn a Grand Award at the International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF) in the United States.

For many high school students, coding has moved well beyond a hobby; building software trains problem solving and logical thinking. Fewer realize that Korea has official routes to ISEF, and the Korea Code Fair's software competition is one of them.

## What the Korea Code Fair is

The Korea Code Fair (KCF) is a national software competition for young people, hosted by the Ministry of Science and ICT and run by the National Information Society Agency (NIA). It is open to elementary, middle and high school students, or young people of equivalent age, and thousands take part every year.

The fair is not built simply to find the best coders. Its purpose is educational. Students take a problem from daily life, the environment or society and solve it with software, or build software that can contribute to progress in science and technology, developing creativity and teamwork along the way. The seventh edition, in 2025, ran under the theme "A future with AI: coding creative innovation."

## Three ways to take part

The Code Fair has three components:

1. **Software competition.** Students plan and build their own software and submit the finished work. The topic comes from a real-life problem or social issue, and the solution has to be their own.
2. **Hackathon.** Teams build software on an assigned theme within a fixed time limit. It tests hands-on skill and the ability to work as a team.
3. **Online software study room.** Online lessons in algorithms, programming and other software fundamentals.

The software competition is the most competitive of the three, and it is the one connected directly to ISEF.

## How the competition connects to ISEF

Under the official 2025 rules, **teams that win a silver award or higher** in the software competition earn the chance to take part in the selection for Korea's ISEF delegation. The delegation is chosen by interview from among the winners who meet ISEF's own eligibility requirement: students from the third year of middle school through the third year of high school (the equivalent of Grades 9 to 12) at the time of ISEF. The rules add two further points:

- The pool of candidates may change depending on the KCF award results and the organizing agency's circumstances.
- Participants are, as a rule, responsible for their own ISEF costs, including airfare and accommodation.

Students selected this way travel with Korea's delegation to the ISEF finals in the United States and compete against students from around the world.

## Three years of Grand Awards at ISEF

Students who reached ISEF through the Code Fair have won Grand Awards three years running:

| Year | Project | ISEF result |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | Finger-tracking smart glasses for visually impaired users | Fourth Award, Robotics and Intelligent Machines |
| 2023 | Autonomous walking-assistance device for visually impaired people | Fourth Award, Embedded Systems |
| 2024 | Real-time CPR feedback system | Second Award, Embedded Systems |

For anyone planning an entry, it is worth looking at how these teams earned their awards.

### 2022: Finger-tracking smart glasses

Built by a second-year high school student, the glasses track the position of the wearer's hand and use voice guidance to describe the direction or object the finger is pointing at. The design pairs image recognition with a voice guidance system, with particular attention to the user interface and real-time response. It was recognized for its technical feasibility and user-centered design.

### 2023: A walking aid for visually impaired people

This navigation aid helps visually impaired people walk safely, detecting what lies ahead and giving real-time route guidance through a smartphone app. Its strengths were an integrated hardware and software design and a problem of real social value.

### 2024: A real-time CPR feedback system

This device measures chest compressions as they happen and gives immediate feedback so the person performing CPR keeps the right rate and depth. It earned praise for its practical potential in emergency care, the precision of its engineering and its user-experience design.

What the three share goes beyond technical skill. Each was designed from the user's point of view, took a careful approach to a real social problem, and was engineered to work in practice, not just on paper.

## How the software competition is judged

The competition runs in three stages, with separate divisions for elementary, middle and high school students.

| Stage | What teams submit or present | Teams selected |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Document review | Application form, project summary, project description or development plan, confirmation from a supervising teacher | 210 (70 per division) |
| 2. Preliminary round: technical review (online) | Demo video (two minutes or less recommended), core source code, optional notes on the development process | 90 (30 per division) |
| 3. Finals: presentation and awards (in person) | Presentation of up to 10 minutes with a live demo, followed by questions from the judges | 10 award winners per division |

The technical review checks whether the software has actually been built, how complete its features are, and how closely it matches the plan submitted in the first round. The finals weigh technical completeness together with the social value of the idea, the logic of the presentation and how well the team handles questions.

Ten teams in each division take home awards: one Grand Prize, three gold, three silver and three bronze. Applications typically open in May–June, with the technical round and the finals later in the year. Check the official Korea Code Fair website for the current schedule and requirements.

## What the competition rewards

The software competition is more than a contest of coding skill. It evaluates the whole process: defining a problem, solving it with software the students build themselves, then explaining and defending that work in front of judges. Along with coding, it builds a student's skills in planning, presenting and working as a team. And because it is an official route to ISEF, a strong project can carry a student from a national stage to an international one.

Companion guides on the [CRI blog](/blog) cover Regeneron ISEF itself and KSEF, the Korea Science and Engineering Fair, another domestic path to ISEF.

Every project above began with a clearly defined problem and a plan to solve it. Students who want to practice that step, framing a research question and developing it with a professor's guidance, can look at the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter), which runs over the winter break, months before the Code Fair's application window typically opens.
author: CRI Editorial

title: After SRP, the research continues: the five tracks of the 2025 SRP Extension
excerpt: The SRP Extension lets Seoul Research Program students keep working with their professor. Here is what its five 2025 tracks involved, from real-data economics to a short film.
content:
In the SRP Extension, economics students test their summer models against real-world data, film students push a screenplay toward a short they can actually shoot, and future founders turn an idea into a pitch deck. It is where a paper finished in Seoul becomes the start of something longer.

The 2025 Seoul Research Program (SRP) ran from July 28 to August 7. When it ended, many students kept working with their professors through the Extension, a follow-on research and internship track that develops the topic each student explored over the summer. It is more than extra class time. Each track is designed by its professor, whether that means advanced research, paper refinement, an industry internship or a creative project, and each one ends in finished work. The relationship with the professor that began during SRP also becomes closer and more sustained.

## Summer program and Extension, side by side

| | Seoul Research Program | SRP Extension |
|---|---|---|
| Grades | 9–12 | 9–12 |
| Stage | The regular summer program: intensive, hands-on research | The advanced stage that follows the summer program |
| How it works | Students work in person with faculty from leading universities and write a paper with the professor | Students continue research with the professor and mentors, building on the topic from the summer program |
| What it produces | One completed research paper | An advanced research project, an industry internship or a startup |

## The five tracks in 2025

### Economics with Ryan Fang (University of Chicago)

Professor Fang's Extension takes the economics paper students completed over the summer and brings it into contact with real data. At SRP, students learned how to build a model. Now they find out how that model works in the world.

Students either test their model against real data or develop it into a more rigorous mathematical structure. A model of consumer behavior or a political campaign, for instance, might be checked against social media sentiment data or election statistics. Fang stresses the reasoning that connects theory to evidence and teaches students that research is a matter of proof, not assumption. TAs help with data cleaning, analysis and visualization in Stata, R and Python, bringing the paper up to the standard of an academic conference.

What comes out is an economics research paper at the undergraduate level, along with long-term mentoring from the professor that leads to an in-depth recommendation letter.

### Entrepreneurship with Kit Hickey (MIT)

Taught by a professor who has co-founded a company herself, this track takes the idea students sketched at SRP and turns it into a business model they could take to a real market. Students work through each stage of starting a company: market research, customer segmentation, revenue model design and building a pitch deck.

![Kit Hickey smiles beside a buffet counter while students wearing lanyards serve themselves in the background](/editorial/224074766455-02.jpg "Professor Kit Hickey at a dinner during SRP 2025.")

Professor Hickey draws on her own experience as a startup co-founder to make one point above all:

> "A business starts less with a good idea than with defining the problem precisely."
> — Kit Hickey, MIT

Mentor sessions cover competitor analysis, pricing strategy and telling the story the way an investor needs to hear it. Throughout, Hickey pushes students to look at their idea the way a founder would. The work adds up to a proposal strong enough to enter a startup competition or to pitch to real investors. Students finish with a completed pitch deck, an execution plan and a recommendation letter from a professor who is also a founder.

### Medical engineering with Nabil Alshurafa (Northwestern University)

This track, the **Industrial Internship at SenseWhy Inc.**, shows research moving into industry. Working with mentors at SenseWhy, a startup Professor Alshurafa co-founded, students study the market for wearable health sensors and weigh the product's technical constraints against what users need.

Weekly meetings with company staff cover data, design, regulation and market-entry strategy, so students see firsthand how research results become a real product. Over 10 weeks, each student completes a company report and a presentation. They leave with an internship certificate from SenseWhy, a recommendation letter from the professor and practical skill in market analysis.

### Film with James Savoca (USC)

The **Advanced Script Writing & Short Film Project** turns a written story into a work that lives on screen. It runs in two stages:

- **Advanced script writing.** Students revise the screenplay they completed at SRP, concentrating on story structure, each character's emotional arc and the flow of dialogue. Professor Savoca, who describes a good story as "a structure with an emotional rhythm," coaches students, scene by scene, on how to bring each one to life.
- **Short film project.** The script is then developed until it can actually be shot. Students learn shot composition, scene staging and visual storytelling, and experience how their story is realized on screen.

The track produces a complete script ready for short-film production, a piece students can use in a portfolio or submit to film festivals, and personalized feedback and a recommendation letter from the professor.

### Chemistry with Brian Stoltz (Caltech)

In **Research Paper Refinement**, Professor Stoltz helps students rewrite their paper in the language of professional researchers. Students return to the paper they wrote over the summer and, with the professor, systematically tighten its logical structure, the way it presents data, the design of its figures and tables, and its citations. In TA sessions they learn the principles of good scientific writing and practice revising in the format journals require for submission.

Behind the track is a simple conviction: rewriting a paper retrains your scientific thinking. Students finish with a paper ready for journal submission, an in-depth recommendation letter from the professor and stronger skills in scientific communication.

## Why the longer contact matters

The Extension's real value is depth and continuity. If SRP is where inquiry begins, the Extension carries an idea through to completion. As the collaboration grows closer, the professor sees a student's thinking, growth and achievements firsthand. That becomes a strong advantage in US college admissions, in three ways:

- **Deeper recommendation letters.** Long-term collaboration lets a professor describe a student's abilities in specific, concrete terms.
- **A stronger portfolio.** The work can be listed as "Extended Research / Internship under Professor [name]."
- **Research continuity.** It reads as sustained academic inquiry rather than a short-term activity.

In that sense, the Extension is the stage where a student's research identity, and the story it tells in an application, comes together.

Two students from this cohort have since shown where it can lead, and their stories are on the [Student Success](/success) page. D. co-authored a carbon-capture paper in Stoltz's SRP class that went on to journal publication, then used the Extension to write a new single-author paper on the same topic, which was also published. J. wrote an advertising paper with Hickey, applied what he learned to a sports app he launched in Korea, and continued in the Extension with the goal of entering the US market and setting up a company there.

## Who can apply

The SRP Extension is open only to SRP graduates, and only to those who have already completed a project with the participating professor. The way in is the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) itself.

## The next chapter

Through the Extension, a summer of research can become an internship, a market report or a film, and professor and student keep a research relationship going long after the program ends. For students who want that kind of sustained, individual work with a faculty mentor, the [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1) is built around it.

title: Regeneron ISEF: what 2025 finalists researched, and how Korean students compared
excerpt: How the world's largest high school science fair works, which fields and project types led among 2025 finalists, and what Korean students can do to compete more strongly.
content:
Every May, about 1,800 students from more than 75 countries gather in the United States to present their research to judges and to the public. This is the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF), the largest science competition in the world for high school students. What the 2025 finalists chose to study says a lot about what it takes to reach that stage, and about where Korean students are strong and where they have room to grow.

## How ISEF works

ISEF is run by Society for Science, a nonprofit organization, and is the most prestigious high school science competition in the United States. It began in 1950 and became an international event in 1958. Intel sponsored the fair from 1997 to 2019, which is why it was long known as Intel ISEF. Today [Regeneron](https://www.regeneron.com/about/our-company) is the title sponsor.

Most participants are high school students, and every finalist has already advanced through a qualifying fair in their own country or region. The fair itself lasts about a week, with projects competing across 22 scientific categories. Students present their findings to the judges and to the public, and reaching the fair as a finalist is a meaningful achievement in its own right.

## Which fields the 2025 finalists came from

At the 2025 fair in Columbus, Ohio, research in the life and health sciences was clearly the most popular choice. Engineering came next, and computer science trailed both.

| Field group | Share of 2025 finalists |
|---|---|
| Life sciences (Animal Sciences, Biomedical and Health Sciences, Microbiology, Biochemistry and related categories) | About half |
| Engineering and technology (Environmental Engineering, Energy: Sustainable Materials and Design, Robotics and Intelligent Machines, Embedded Systems) | The next-largest group; Environmental Engineering alone had more than 100 finalists, one of the biggest categories at the fair |
| Computer science | Noticeable, but smaller than life sciences or engineering; Systems Software, the category closest to pure computer science, was only about 4–5% |

## Three kinds of projects

Sort the 2025 topics by what they set out to do and three types emerge: developing innovative technology, solving social problems and theoretical research. The first two account for most of the field.

### Innovative technology

These projects put advanced technologies such as AI, new materials and robotics to work. One team presented a prosthetic limb controlled by EEG brain signals, designed to help amputees move. More broadly, cutting-edge engineering solutions stood out: medical assistive devices that combine AI with sensors, and a device that uses a new metal-organic framework (MOF) material to detect and break down harmful airborne substances in real time.

### Solving social problems

Research aimed at environmental and health problems formed another major group. One finalist designed an inexpensive, portable device that breaks down and removes formaldehyde, a carcinogen found in homes, to improve indoor air quality. Another developed a way to recycle waste plastic into 3D-printer filament, tackling both the waste itself and the sustainability of manufacturing materials. In medicine, a project synthesizing new antiviral compounds to treat viral diseases was highly rated. Across environment, energy, medicine and education, applied research on hard social problems stood out.

### Theoretical research

Projects built around mathematical models or algorithms were less common. One student built a theoretical model of how a ship's speed relates to the shape of swell waves, in order to predict the optimal sailing speed. Another simulated the effects of players' memory in the prisoner's dilemma, a classic game-theory problem, and drew insights that could inform how AI agents are designed to make decisions. Work like this showed real creativity and scientific curiosity, but the bulk of the 2025 field sat with applied technology and social problem-solving.

## Three trends to watch

The 2025 projects point to three strong currents in student research:

1. **AI everywhere.** Many projects used AI algorithms as a core tool, or made AI their subject. The brain-controlled prosthesis relied on an AI algorithm to interpret signals, and machine learning also turned up in environmental monitoring devices and in agriculture and ecology projects. Others, like the prisoner's dilemma study of how AI agents interact, set out to understand and improve AI itself.
2. **Sustainability and climate.** A large share of the environment and energy projects dealt with climate change, recycling resources or clean energy: recycled-plastic filament, cutting harmful chemicals, the effect of microgravity on plant growth. The pattern shows how much sustainability matters to the next generation of scientists.
3. **Digital health and biotechnology.** Finalists in medicine and the life sciences explored early diagnosis, drug development and regenerative medicine. Examples include a self-screening system for eye cancer that analyzes photos of the eye with AI, and research into the molecular mechanisms that help damaged nerve cells regenerate. Both show digital technology and the life sciences converging.

Materials science and space physics also appeared steadily, but these three stood out most strongly.

## How Korean finalists compared

Korean students at the 2025 fair followed a noticeably different pattern from the field as a whole.

| | 2025 field overall | Korean finalists |
|---|---|---|
| Where projects clustered | Life sciences (about half), then engineering | Computer science and applied engineering |
| Medicine and biology | The largest group | Almost no projects |
| Range of categories | All 22 categories | A tight cluster in computing and engineering |

**Concentrated fields.** Most Korean finalists competed in the Systems Software, Embedded Systems, Physics and Astronomy, Environmental Engineering and Materials Science categories. Instead of medicine or biology, many teams worked on software algorithms, robotics, new materials and technology for environmental problems. That contrasts with the global picture, where biomedical and pure science finalists are numerous. It is also striking because so many Korean students plan to apply to medical school; at ISEF, their strength showed up in applied engineering and IT.

**A build-first approach.** Korean projects emphasized putting technology to work. Many students built their own apps or devices and produced working prototypes, a real strength in turning a problem-solving idea into a concrete product or system. The trade-off was depth of experimentation: empirical testing with lab equipment or advanced research facilities was relatively limited.

**A narrow range.** Korean finalists' interests formed a fairly tight cluster in computing and engineering. Behavioral science, which draws on the humanities and social sciences, did not appear, and neither did earth science. By contrast, finalists from the United States and other countries tended to spread fairly evenly across all 22 categories.

In short, Korean students often competed on the strength of team projects and applied skill, specializing in particular areas of technology within a very broad international field.

## How Korean students can compete more strongly

For Korean students who want to stand out at ISEF and similar competitions, the 2025 results point to five priorities:

1. **Branch into the basic sciences.** Look beyond computing to fields such as biology and chemistry, and use connections with university labs to get the experimental facilities and mentoring those fields require.
2. **Combine disciplines.** Design problem-solving topics that pair AI with knowledge of the environment, materials or medicine.
3. **Go deeper than the application.** Do not stop at a working result. Add theoretical grounding and mathematical modeling so the research has real depth.
4. **Connect to global issues.** Make the link to social impact explicit, and show how the results could be applied in the real world.
5. **Practice presenting science in English.** Systematic training in communicating and presenting research in English can be the deciding factor that turns an excellent project into an award winner.

At CRI, students work with faculty from leading universities to turn research in a wide range of fields into finished papers. Lab work gives biology and chemistry projects experimental depth, and some students have also developed prototypes along the way. To see which format fits the project you have in mind, explore CRI's [research programs](/research).

title: Cornell's fall 2025 admissions: 8.38% overall, from 5% at Dyson to 22% at the Hotel School
excerpt: Cornell admitted 8.38% of 72,519 applicants for fall 2025. See how Early Decision and the choice of undergraduate college changed the odds, and what admitted students had in common.
content:
For the class that entered in fall 2025, 72,519 students applied to Cornell and 6,076 were admitted, an overall rate of 8.38%. That one number hides a much wider range. Depending on which undergraduate college a student applied to, the odds ran from 5.36% at the Dyson School to 22.27% at the Nolan School of Hotel Administration, and Early Decision applicants were admitted at nearly three times the Regular Decision rate. Here is what Cornell's figures show, and what CRI thinks they mean for applicants.

## A bigger class, the same competition

Cornell admitted 560 more students than the year before, yet its admit rate barely moved from 8.4% in 2024. Applications grew just as fast, reaching 72,519, a sign of how sought-after Cornell remains.

| | Fall 2024 | Fall 2025 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Applications | 65,612 | 72,519 |
| Acceptances | 5,516 | 6,076 |
| Admit rate | 8.4% | 8.38% |
| Entering students | 3,574 | 3,861 |

*Source: Cornell University Institutional Research & Planning, fall first-year data.*

A few other figures stand out:

- **Yield:** 63.5% of admitted students chose to enroll.
- **Waitlist:** 9,720 applicants were offered a place on the waitlist, and 6,598 accepted it.
- **International students:** 10.2% of the class.
- **Gender:** about 53% women and 47% men.

Standardized testing is also regaining weight at top universities after the test-optional pandemic years. Taken together, the numbers describe a university that balances diversity with academic excellence. The more important pattern, in CRI's view, sits underneath them: students who showed a clear fit with their chosen college and a defined academic direction were judged more favorably than students who simply had strong scores.

## Early Decision: nearly three times the admit rate

Early Decision applicants made up about 14% of Cornell's applicant pool but 31% of its admitted students. They were admitted at 18.78%, against 6.7% in Regular Decision: close to three times the rate.

| Round | Applicants | Admitted | Admit rate | Entering |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Early Decision | 10,057 | 1,889 | 18.78% | 1,834 |
| Regular Decision | 62,462 | 4,187 | 6.70% | 2,027 |
| Total | 72,519 | 6,076 | 8.38% | 3,861 |

Why does Cornell favor the early round? Students admitted ED are, for the most part, the ones who genuinely want to be at Cornell, and more than 97% of them enroll. For the university, ED is a way to secure students it knows will come.

But ED is more than an earlier deadline. Reading an ED application, Cornell is looking for answers to two questions:

- How well does this student understand their intended major and interests?
- Does the application make clear why it has to be Cornell?

That favors students who prepared ahead of time. Applicants who explored an interest steadily, built experience related to their major through research or projects, and told their own story logically in their essays often do well in the early round.

> "Early Decision isn't a race to submit first. It's a contest of prepared stories."
> — CRI

When research experience lets a student explain why they want to study a field, Cornell sees a candidate with greater potential.

## College by college, very different odds

Cornell works differently from the other Ivy League universities. It is one university made up of several undergraduate colleges and schools, and applicants choose the one they want to enter when they apply. That structure produces admit rates that vary enormously.

| College or school | Admit rate, fall 2025 |
| --- | --- |
| Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management | 5.36% |
| College of Engineering | 6.62% |
| College of Arts and Sciences | 7.91% |
| College of Human Ecology | 9.61% |
| Brooks School of Public Policy | 10.12% |
| College of Architecture, Art, and Planning | 10.44% |
| College of Agriculture and Life Sciences | 12.10% |
| School of Industrial and Labor Relations | 15.68% |
| Nolan School of Hotel Administration | 22.27% |

Dyson and Engineering admitted only 5 to 7% of applicants, while the Hotel School admitted more than one in five. Same university, very different competition. So the question that matters is which college fits you.

The gap reflects how heavily Cornell weighs fit with the college an applicant chooses. A Dyson applicant needs a clear interest in economics or business. An engineering applicant needs experience exploring questions in math and science. Applicants to Human Ecology or Public Policy should show an interest in social problems and in people.

Good scores alone do not settle it. The real test is **what experience you can point to that shows you genuinely belong in this college**, and how closely your own story and interests match its character.

> "Cornell admissions isn't a competition of grades. It's a competition of direction."
> — CRI

In CRI's programs, students explore a field they care about through real research and map out, in concrete terms, how that interest could lead into a major.

## What admitted students had in common

Look closely at students admitted to Cornell and one thread runs through them: each had genuinely explored their own interests. They showed not just that they did well in school, but why they love their field and how they have pursued it. Three traits stood out.

### 1. Deep academic interest

Cornell rates students who have dug deep into a subject above those who bring only high scores. A student who went beyond the classroom, running their own experiments, writing a paper or doing research with a professor, comes across as someone with real academic passion.

> "Schoolwork alone couldn't capture everything I was interested in. At CRI, I chose a topic with a real professor and wrote a paper, and that experience made the reason for my choice of major clear."
> — J., Seoul Global High School (admitted to Cornell's College of Arts and Sciences)

### 2. A clear link to the major

Because applicants choose a college from the start, Cornell reads closely for how their activities, research and essays connect to the intended major. An economics applicant whose research focused on consumer behavior tells a natural, persuasive story. An applicant to the life sciences whose activities are all about economics leaves the reader asking what this student really wants.

> "My CRI research on consumer decision-making and behavioral biases lined up exactly with my major. In my essays, I could build around that research and explain my interests in specific terms."
> — K., Korean foreign-language high school (admitted to Cornell's Dyson School)

### 3. Confidence in telling the story

Students who have actually done the work speak with far more confidence, whether in an essay or an interview. Instead of saying they are interested in something, they can say how they investigated it and what they found.

> "Finishing a paper and getting a recommendation letter from my professor let me tell my story with confidence in interviews. The professors valued that, too."
> — L., American international school (admitted to a PhD program in nutrition at Cornell, with a scholarship)

## A story, not a score

Thousands of students aim for the same goal. The ones who get in are not simply the highest scorers; they are the ones whose story is clear. Cornell wants to know why a student intends to study a field, and how genuine and specific that reason is.

The successful applicants connected their experience to their major. One took an interest in an environmental problem and analyzed real data on it; another observed how people behave and studied consumer psychology. Experiences like these came together into a story that says, in effect, "This is who I am."

> "It's not impressive credentials but a real story that gets students admitted."
> — CRI

CRI helps students develop a topic they love into real research, then carry that experience into their personal statement and their choice of major. That kind of connected story is the competitive edge Cornell looks for.

> "A strong application isn't written with elegant sentences. It's filled with experiences you create yourself."
> — CRI

For CRI students, writing a paper is more than an exercise: it is how they work out what truly interests them and which problems they want to pursue on their own, and that is exactly what universities like Cornell value.

Students ready to start building that kind of experience can begin with the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter), which brings students together online with university faculty over the winter break; each student writes their own research paper in English.

title: How to read journal rankings: JIF, JCI, CiteScore, SJR and SNIP
excerpt: Five metrics dominate journal rankings, and each measures something different. Learn how they are calculated, where to find them and how to use them to choose where to submit.
content:
Once a paper is written, a new question takes over: where should it be published? The journal you choose shapes who reads the work, how it is judged, how often it is cited and how much credibility it lends you as a researcher. To compare journals, researchers lean on five metrics in particular: the Journal Impact Factor (JIF), the Journal Citation Indicator (JCI), CiteScore, the SCImago Journal Rank (SJR) and Source Normalized Impact per Paper (SNIP).

None of them simply means "higher is better." Each has its own formula, time window and idea of what should count, and the right one depends on your field.

## What a journal metric measures

Almost every journal metric starts from citations: how often the papers a journal published during a set period were cited by other papers, expressed as an average. That number does not measure quality directly. What it reveals, indirectly, is how often a journal's work is cited in its field and how much other researchers trust it.

Metrics take one of two approaches:

- **Absolute indicators** rank journals by citation counts. More citations mean a higher score, which tends to favor journals in popular, heavily cited fields. JIF and CiteScore work this way.
- **Field-normalized indicators** correct for the fact that citation habits differ between disciplines. They compare each journal with a baseline average set at 1.0 (the field average for JCI and SNIP, the average across all journals for SJR), so journals in low-citation fields such as the humanities and social sciences get a fair comparison. JCI, SJR and SNIP work this way.

Why does that correction matter? A physics paper can collect many citations within a year or two of publication, while a history paper may take a decade to be widely cited. Rank journals on raw citations alone and the high-citation fields win every time. A field-normalized score instead tells you how far above or below its field's average a journal sits: a JCI of 1.5 means its papers are cited about 50% more than the field average.

## How to read a ranking

Treat a ranking as a clue to a journal's influence, not proof of its quality. A high score does not make every paper in the journal excellent, and a low one does not make a study less valuable. Part 6 of our paper-writing guide, on the [CRI blog](/blog), explains how to judge an individual paper on its own merits: its citation count, its design and its author's track record.

Rankings are often reported in quartiles, which place a journal within its subject category. Q1 is the top 25% of journals in the field, Q2 the next quarter, Q3 the band from 50% to 75%, and Q4 the bottom 25%.

![Pyramid diagram dividing journals into four tiers, Q1 at the top through Q4 at the bottom, with the percentage band for each](/editorial/224043492089-02.jpg "Journal quartiles: Q1 is the top 25% of journals in a field, Q4 the bottom 25%.")

## Clarivate's metrics: JIF and JCI

Clarivate, the company behind Web of Science, publishes JIF and JCI every year in its Journal Citation Reports (JCR). They are usually the first numbers to check when you plan where to submit.

### Journal Impact Factor (JIF)

JIF is the most widely used journal metric in the world. It averages the citations that a journal's papers from the previous two years receive in a given year. The 2024 JIF, for instance, counts citations made in 2024 to papers published in 2022 and 2023:

**JIF = citations in a given year to papers from the two previous years ÷ papers published in those two years**

Until recently, only journals in the Science Citation Index Expanded (SCIE) and the Social Sciences Citation Index (SSCI) received a JIF. Since 2023 it has also covered the Arts & Humanities Citation Index (AHCI) and the Emerging Sources Citation Index (ESCI), so humanities and arts journals now have one too.

JIF's strength is speed: it captures short-term citation performance quickly. Its weakness is that same two-year window, too short to reflect how citations build up in some fields. It is most informative where research moves fast, as in the life sciences and engineering. In the humanities and social sciences, read it alongside a complementary metric such as JCI.

### Journal Citation Indicator (JCI)

JCI draws on three years of citation data and normalizes it against the journal's field, where the average is 1.0. That makes it fair to low-citation disciplines and lets you compare relative influence across fields. Where JIF captures short-term citations, JCI also reflects longer-term influence and a journal's standing in its field.

The two numbers can tell different stories. A journal with a JIF of 2.5 and a JCI of 1.8 has considerably more influence than the average in its field. A journal with a high JIF but a JCI of 0.9 may sit below average in its own field. A few practical rules follow:

- JIF suits fast-cited fields driven by the latest research; JCI suits fields where long-term citation matters, such as the humanities, social sciences and arts.
- Before you submit, look the journal up in JCR and check both its subject category and its percentile rank within that category.
- A JCI of 1.0 or higher means the journal is at or above its field's average.
- When comparing several journals, weigh JIF and JCI together. JIF shows the volume of a journal's influence; JCI shows where it stands in its field.

## Scopus metrics: CiteScore, SJR and SNIP

Clarivate's metrics, built on Web of Science, are the traditional standard. Elsevier's Scopus covers a much broader range of journals, and the three metrics built on its data go beyond raw citation counts to capture the quality of citations and the character of each field. Our guide to Web of Science and Scopus, also on the [CRI blog](/blog), explains how each database selects and evaluates the journals it covers.

### CiteScore

CiteScore divides the citations a journal's papers receive over a four-year window by the number of papers it published in those same four years.

**CiteScore = citations over four years ÷ papers published in the same four years**

Because the window also includes citations made in a paper's year of publication, CiteScore takes a broader, longer view than JIF. Anyone can check it free on Scopus, and CiteScore Tracker shows how the number changes month by month. It moves more gradually than JIF and holds up reasonably well in the humanities and social sciences, which makes it useful in fields with long citation cycles or whenever you want to judge sustained influence.

### SJR (SCImago Journal Rank)

SJR weighs where citations come from, not just how many there are: a citation from a highly influential journal counts for more than one from a lesser journal. Scores are normalized so that the average across the world's journals is 1, and anything above 1 signals above-average influence.

SJR is free on the SCImago Journal & Country Rank website, searchable by journal title, subject area or country, with each journal's quartile (Q1 to Q4) shown alongside. Turn to it when the quality of a journal's citations matters more to you than their quantity.

### SNIP (Source Normalized Impact per Paper)

SNIP was designed to correct for differences in citation culture between fields. It sets each field's average citation rate at 1 and measures the journal against it:

**SNIP = the journal's citation rate ÷ the average citation rate in its field**

A SNIP of 1.3 means the journal is cited 30% more often than the field average. SNIP is free on the CWTS Journal Indicators website, which uses Scopus data and can be searched by title or ISSN. Like JCI, it picks up field-specific patterns that JIF or CiteScore alone would miss, and it is best for judging where a journal stands within your own research area rather than for comparing disciplines.

## The five metrics side by side

| Metric | Provider and where to find it | Citation window | Type | Best used for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| JIF | Clarivate, Journal Citation Reports | 2 years | Absolute | Short-term citation impact in fast-moving fields |
| JCI | Clarivate, Journal Citation Reports | 3 years | Field-normalized (1.0 = field average) | Standing within a field, including low-citation fields |
| CiteScore | Elsevier, Scopus (free) | 4 years | Absolute | A broad, steady view of citation volume |
| SJR | SCImago Journal & Country Rank (free) | 3 years | Normalized (1 = average across all journals), weighted by the citing journal's influence | The quality of citations, not just their number |
| SNIP | CWTS Journal Indicators (free) | 3 years | Field-normalized (1 = field average) | Relative influence within your own field |

In short, JIF and JCI show how much a journal is cited, while CiteScore, SJR and SNIP show how it is cited.

## One search, every metric: S2Journal

JCR and Scopus both help you judge whether a journal can be trusted, but each requires its own login and search, and the metrics have to be looked up one at a time. S2Journal, a Korean journal-information service, puts them in one place. It combines data on international and Korean journals from Clarivate's JCR, Scopus, Google Scholar and the Korea Citation Index (KCI), and it is used by individual researchers, university libraries and institutional evaluators alike.

- **Every metric in one search.** Enter a title or ISSN to see JIF, JCI, CiteScore, SJR, SNIP and KCI listing status at once, with the journal's subject category, country, publisher and open-access status.
- **Rankings within the field.** Percentile or quartile data show where a journal sits in its category.
- **Excel export.** Save results as a spreadsheet to compare candidates or bring a shortlist to a lab meeting.
- **Korean and international journals side by side.** Seeing KCI next to SCIE and Scopus helps researchers in Korea decide whether a topic suits a domestic or an international journal.

Say you are preparing a paper in environmental economics and look up *Ecological Economics*. One search brings up all five metrics alongside its SJR quartile (Q1), publisher (Elsevier), country of publication (the Netherlands) and the fact that it is not listed in KCI, so you can see at a glance that it ranks in the top quarter of its field.

## Fit matters more than a score

Publishing a paper is more than making results public. It decides which scholarly community will read the work and whether that community will trust it. Understanding journal rankings is not about memorizing scores; it is part of preparing to communicate your research well.

Each of these metrics shows, from a different angle, how widely a journal is cited and how much it is trusted. None of them can replace the value of the research itself. Metrics point the way, but the researcher still has to walk it. A good paper finds its home by matching its topic to the right journal, not by chasing the highest score.

CRI helps students learn not only how to write a paper well but how to publish it responsibly: choosing the right journal, understanding what its metrics mean, and sharing their results in a way others can trust. That is the first real step in becoming a researcher.

In the [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1), students spend several months writing an individual paper with a faculty mentor. Once the manuscript takes shape, picking a target journal becomes part of preparing it for submission, and CRI supports each student through that step.
author: CRI Editorial

title: After the first draft: editing, journal style and submission etiquette
excerpt: A finished draft is only the beginning. Learn how to handle feedback, match a journal's format and reference style, and deal with rejection and slow reviews the right way.
content:
When one of CRI's teaching assistants was a PhD student writing a first paper for a journal indexed in the Science Citation Index (SCI), the draft alone took a year. Editing it took another six months. Looking back, more than half of that time went into simply not knowing how to fix what was wrong.

Almost every first-time author falls for the same illusion: once the conclusion is written, the paper must be done. In fact, that is where the real work starts. A research paper is not a place to sort out your own thoughts; it is written to be understood by other people. Editing and proofreading are therefore about much more than grammar. They are the process of rewriting the paper in language a reader can follow.

## Editing and proofreading habits

What matters most in editing is not any single sentence but the overall impression. The goal is a reader who comes away thinking, "This is well organized." A few habits get you there.

### Draft fast, but make the draft complete

A first draft does not need to be perfect. What counts is speed and structure. Many students stall here, polishing one sentence after another, but energy is limited. The moment the draft is done, it goes to your coauthors or mentor, and if you are already worn out, you will have little left for the revisions that come back.

So finish the draft quickly, but clean up the logical flow and the basic formatting (font, margins, notation) before you send it. A draft that is complete in form gets far more useful feedback.

### Be selective with feedback

Comments from coauthors and mentors always arrive as a mix. If you cannot separate the changes you must make from the suggestions you can take or leave, revision drags on indefinitely.

You are the author, and you set the direction of the whole paper. Rather than folding in every comment, accept the ones that keep the paper consistent and persuasive. The aim is not a sentence that pleases everyone but one that carries a single, convincing line of argument.

### Aim for a typo-free document

The end goal of editing is a beautiful document: clean, orderly and free of typos. Eliminating typos matters even more than perfecting your grammar. A book full of typos loses a reader's trust, and an English research paper is no different.

If you are not confident in your English, make full use of professional editing services. Many universities and research institutes already partner with editing companies, and there is nothing embarrassing about using one; it is an essential step that fills the gaps in your own expertise. For detailed checklists on figures, results, sentences and references, see Part 7 of our Paper-Writing Guide on the [CRI blog](/blog).

### When the words stop coming

Sooner or later, concentration breaks. The analysis is finished, the data are organized, and still not a single line will come. Rather than forcing it, take a day or two off. Reading one good paper will do far more for you than aimless web browsing, and your brain keeps sorting patterns and lining up new sentences while you rest. Writing depends less on stamina than on a rhythm of focus.

If focusing alone is hard, set a time to write with a colleague. Each of you works on your own paper for two or three hours, then you check each other's progress. This simple ritual works better than you might expect, because much of what makes writing hard is the feeling that you are fighting it alone.

Editing and proofreading, in other words, are not about making a paper pretty. They are a design process meant to earn a reader's trust.

![Illustration of hands typing on a laptop, with a document on the screen whose last lines are marked in red](/editorial/224043341092-02.jpg "Expect several rounds of marked-up revisions between a finished draft and a manuscript ready to submit.")

## Matching the journal's style

Every journal has a style of its own. Open a few magazines and the typefaces, margins and photo layouts all differ; academic journals likewise have their own formats and conventions. Ignore them, and even an excellent paper can be screened out at the formatting stage and rejected without review. Matching a journal's style is not a box-ticking exercise. It is basic professional courtesy, and the first gate every submission has to pass.

### Format is your first impression

When a manuscript arrives, the editor looks at its format before its content. If the journal's required font, citation method, table titles and reference style have not been followed, that alone can mark you as a careless researcher.

Many journals now catch this at the editorial office and send the manuscript back with a request to revise it to the journal's style and resubmit. Reformatting at that point pushes publication back considerably. Getting the format right from the start is the fastest route.

### Reference styles differ in the details

Many researchers assume reference lists all look more or less alike. In fact, the conventions vary from journal to journal, down to small details:

| Detail | Some journals | Other journals |
|---|---|---|
| Author names | A period after the name | No period |
| Volume and issue | Both volume and issue number | Volume only; issue omitted |
| Page ranges | Written in full (100–108) | Shortened (100–8) |

Each difference is tiny, but they add up, and together they shape how polished and professional the whole paper looks. That is why you should use a reference manager such as EndNote or Zotero. You can fix references by hand, but it takes far longer and the chance of error is high.

## Rejection and submission etiquette

### A first rejection is normal

Most papers are not accepted by the first journal they go to. Out of ten papers submitted, roughly one gets through at its first journal. Others find a home at a second or third journal, and some only at the tenth.

So when a journal says no, reformat the paper to the next journal's style right away. It is tedious, but it is how papers get published.

### Never submit to two journals at once

Submission ethics matter most of all. Sending the same paper to two journals at the same time is regarded worldwide as a clear breach of research ethics. However long the review takes, do not submit anywhere else until the first journal has reached a decision.

If the wait becomes a real burden, write to the journal politely and ask where things stand. A short note is enough: "It has been six months since my submission and I have not yet received a response. Could you let me know the current status of the review?"

Some journals go months without starting the review at all, because they cannot find a suitable editor for the paper. In that case, politely request to withdraw your submission. Once it is withdrawn, the paper is free to go to another journal.

All of this tests a researcher's patience. But publication is earned only by those who keep to the ethics of the process. Publishing a paper is a promise made to the world, and respecting its form is part of how you keep that promise.

## Finishing is what earns trust

A paper is not finished when the draft is; it is a living document, completed through editing and proofreading. Polishing sentences, tightening the logic and fixing the format are more than steps toward publication. They reveal who you are as a researcher: editing shows care, proofreading shows humility, and following a journal's style shows responsibility.

Readers do not look only at the experiments and data. From the flow of the sentences, the choice of words and every single citation, they sense how honestly and carefully the author thought. That is why a beautiful document is the mark of a researcher people trust.

CRI's aim with students goes beyond teaching them how to write. It is to build the ability to see a paper all the way through, from editing and proofreading to applying a journal's style, because in research, the ones who last are those who keep refining until the work is done. In the [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1), students develop an individual paper with a faculty mentor, typically over two to four months, and CRI supports each manuscript through journal submission.
author: CRI Editorial

title: What makes a journal internationally recognized? Web of Science vs. Scopus
excerpt: SCIE, SSCI, Q1, CiteScore: a plain-English guide to how Web of Science and Scopus evaluate journals, and why it matters where a paper is published.
content:
"It was published in an SCIE journal." "It's indexed in Scopus, so you can trust it." Spend any time around researchers and you will hear lines like these, usually said as if everyone already knows what they mean. But what is SCIE, exactly, and why does it carry so much weight?

## What "internationally recognized" really means

An internationally recognized journal is not simply a famous one. The term refers to a quality standard that researchers worldwide share, a way of telling scientifically vetted work from the rest. Where a paper appears becomes shorthand for how far it can be trusted. That is why graduate admissions committees, faculty hiring panels and scholarship reviewers so often start with the same question: which journal published it?

Many organizations evaluate journals, but two are recognized worldwide: **Web of Science**, run by Clarivate, and **Scopus**, built by Elsevier. Both assess enormous numbers of journals and papers and express their influence and credibility as numbers. Together they have become the common language for judging whether research can be trusted, so if you want to do good research, knowing how they work is a sensible place to start.

## Citations: the currency of journal quality

The basic test of a good journal is simpler than it sounds: how often other researchers cite the papers it publishes. A frequently cited paper is one that other studies keep building on, so each citation works like a vote of confidence from the research community.

Several metrics turn citation data into a measure of a journal's standing. The best known is the **Impact Factor**, the average number of times a journal's recent papers are cited. An Impact Factor of 10 means that each of those papers was cited about 10 times on average, and a higher number generally signals greater influence. **CiteScore**, **SJR** and **SNIP** calculate influence from the same citation data in slightly different ways. Journals are also ranked into **quartiles** within their field, from Q1 to Q4. A Q1 journal sits in the top 25% of its discipline, where the field's most influential work tends to appear.

These numbers are more than statistics. They are a shared vocabulary for research quality, which is why professors, research institutes, university evaluators and scholarship committees treat a phrase like "SCIE Q1 journal" almost as a certificate. Claiming you did good research is one thing; showing that a strong journal published it is far more persuasive. Our guide *How to read journal rankings: JIF, JCI, CiteScore, SJR and SNIP explained*, on the [CRI blog](/blog), walks through how each of these numbers is calculated.

## Web of Science: Clarivate's curated standard

Web of Science, operated by the information analytics company Clarivate, is one of the most authoritative academic databases in the world. It selects journals and papers across the disciplines and classifies them by quality and citation performance. Its indexes are the names you will hear most often:

- **SCI (Science Citation Index).** Launched in the 1960s as the first science citation database, SCI originally covered only the top journals in foundational sciences such as physics, chemistry and the life sciences. The name still signals a core journal of the highest rank.
- **SCIE (Science Citation Index Expanded).** As research branched into engineering, medicine, biotechnology and other specialties, the index widened into SCIE, which now spans the natural sciences, engineering, medicine, the life sciences and environmental science. Universities and research institutes usually group the two as "SCI(E)" journals, the benchmark for an international-caliber paper.
- **SSCI (Social Sciences Citation Index).** Leading journals in economics, business, education, psychology, political science and sociology. These fields lean on statistical and behavioral research more than on lab experiments, so their citation patterns differ, but SSCI is still an important gauge of influence.
- **A&HCI (Arts & Humanities Citation Index).** Major journals in literature, history, the arts, philosophy and linguistics. Citation habits here differ sharply from those in the natural sciences, so the numbers are read differently, but the index remains central to judging a work's cultural and scholarly influence.
- **ESCI (Emerging Sources Citation Index).** Newer journals with growth potential that have not yet entered the flagship indexes. They are, in effect, candidates to move up to SCIE or SSCI.

The real strength of Web of Science is citation tracking: when each paper was cited, where and by whom. Search for "ChatGPT," for example, and you can see how many related papers have been published and cited worldwide, along with year-by-year trends and the citation network that connects them.

![Diagram of a citation network: paper icons connected by lines and grouped into clusters labeled Topic X, Topic Y and Topic Z](/editorial/224041959010-02.jpg "Every citation links one paper to another. Web of Science and Scopus track those links at scale.")

It also flags standout work. The **Highly Cited Paper** label marks papers in the top 1% by citations in their field, and **Hot Paper** marks recent papers that are drawing citations unusually fast. All of this makes Web of Science less a search engine than a map of how research moves around the world. For researchers, the names SCI, SCIE, SSCI and A&HCI are both a benchmark of international credibility and a point of pride.

## Scopus: Elsevier's wide-angle view

Scopus, run by the Dutch publisher Elsevier, takes a different approach. Where Web of Science is built around careful selection, Scopus is built for breadth. It indexes more than 27,000 active journals, plus conference proceedings, books and open-access papers, and covers nearly every field, from the natural sciences and engineering to medicine, economics, psychology and sociology.

What sets it apart is how much data it connects. Funding information, citation links and open-access status appear on a single screen, so researchers can move past "How often was this paper cited?" to "Who is working on this topic, and at which institutions?"

Scopus also has its own metrics. Instead of the Impact Factor, it reports three indicators side by side:

- **CiteScore:** average citations per paper over the most recent four years
- **SJR (SCImago Journal Rank):** gives extra weight to citations that come from highly ranked journals
- **SNIP (Source Normalized Impact per Paper):** corrects for different citation habits across fields, so journals in different disciplines can be compared fairly

Together they show not just how often work is cited but how influential the citing sources are. A "ChatGPT" search in Scopus returns more papers than the same search in Web of Science, and subject filters turn the results into graphs of which countries and institutions are most active. That breadth is why Scopus is seen as a measure of how far research spreads, and why most major university rankings, including QS, Times Higher Education (THE) and Korea's JoongAng Ilbo rankings, draw on its data.

## Web of Science vs. Scopus at a glance

The names are similar and the features overlap, but the philosophies differ. Web of Science prizes precise, carefully selected quality; Scopus prizes broad, rich coverage. One is a detailed map of rigorous research, the other a giant map of the entire world of scholarship.

| | Web of Science | Scopus |
|---|---|---|
| Operator | Clarivate | Elsevier |
| Main indexes | SCI, SCIE, SSCI, A&HCI, ESCI | A single Scopus index |
| Journals covered | About 15,000 (excluding ESCI) | 27,000+ active titles |
| Signature metrics | Impact Factor, quartile rank | CiteScore, SJR, SNIP |
