| Strength | Strict, quality-first selection | Broad coverage and connected data |
| Companion analytics tool | InCites | SciVal |
| Commonly used by | National Research Foundation of Korea, CWUR, Leiden Ranking | QS, THE, JoongAng Ilbo university rankings |

Which database matters most depends on who is doing the evaluating. In Korea, domestic university evaluations and government-funded research projects still tend to place more trust in Web of Science, while global rankers such as QS and THE mostly rely on Scopus, whose data is easier to access.

The two are complements rather than rivals: Web of Science shows a paper's depth, Scopus its reach. Neither is simply the more important one, and researchers who understand both can choose where to submit more strategically and see their own work in a wider context.

## Choosing where your work belongs

In the end, knowing the leading journals is less about where to send a manuscript than about how your research connects with the wider world. A strong study reaches its audience through the right journal, and researchers who can choose that journal well take their work further.

These questions become practical the moment you have a manuscript of your own. In CRI's [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1), students work individually with a faculty mentor on their own paper, and CRI supports each manuscript through journal submission, which is exactly when knowing SCIE from Scopus starts to pay off.
author: CRI Editorial

title: The 2025 Nobel Prizes defied the forecasts: lessons for young researchers
excerpt: Regulatory T cells, quantum circuits and metal–organic frameworks: how the 2025 Nobel Prizes upended the forecasts, and what that means for students learning to do research.
content:
The 2025 Nobel season opened with a surprise. The prize in physiology or medicine, the first to be announced, went to three pioneers of regulatory T cell research, a topic few forecasters had on their lists. The physics and chemistry prizes that followed also passed over flashy applications, honoring instead the patient, years-long study of the principles that made those applications possible.

The upset is more than a piece of trivia. It shows what science actually rewards: making a discovery and then proving it. For students learning to do research, that lesson matters more than any forecast.

| Prize | Laureates | Honored for |
|---|---|---|
| Physiology or Medicine | Mary E. Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell, Shimon Sakaguchi | Discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance |
| Physics | John Clarke, Michel H. Devoret, John M. Martinis | Macroscopic quantum tunneling and energy quantization in an electric circuit |
| Chemistry | Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson, Omar M. Yaghi | The development of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) |

## Medicine: a surprise, and a very Nobel choice

Brunkow, Ramsdell and Sakaguchi pioneered the study of **regulatory T cells (Tregs)**, now one of the central subjects in immunology. Their work revealed a delicate balance. The immune system has to fight invaders from outside the body, and at the same moment it has to be kept from attacking the body itself.

Regulatory T cells act as the immune system's security guards. They suppress misguided attacks on the body's own cells, which helps prevent autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. The same biology also offers leads for new treatment strategies in fields like cancer immunotherapy. In announcing the prize, the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet credited the three scientists with explaining how the immune system is kept from turning on the body's own tissues.

What made the choice striking was how rarely the topic had come up in predictions. Most forecasts clustered around newer buzzwords, especially CRISPR-based gene editing and protein phase separation. It was a surprise, but one earned on merit. It also showed that the Nobel standard has not moved: fundamental discovery counts for more than whatever is in fashion.

## Physics: quantum mechanics you can build

John Clarke (UC Berkeley), Michel H. Devoret (Yale) and John M. Martinis (UC Santa Barbara) observed and demonstrated quantum mechanical tunneling and energy quantization in an electric circuit. Their experiments took quantum behavior that had lived mostly in theory and brought it into a real laboratory device, at a scale large enough to be called macroscopic.

In effect, they turned quantum mechanics from equations into hardware. Today's superconducting quantum computers, quantum sensors and ultra-precise electronic measurement tools all rest on the foundation they laid.

## Chemistry: materials built around empty space

Susumu Kitagawa (Kyoto University), Richard Robson (University of Melbourne) and Omar M. Yaghi (UC Berkeley) were honored for **metal–organic frameworks**. A MOF forms when metal ions bond with organic molecules to build a lattice riddled with tiny pores.

Those invisible gaps have been put to work on some of the planet's hardest problems: capturing carbon dioxide, absorbing water, storing gases and speeding up chemical reactions as catalysts. Applications range from pulling water out of desert air to new materials that trap greenhouse gases. It is a vivid example of how one molecular structure can reshape what is possible.

## Why the forecasts missed again

Before the announcements, most experts expected this year's prizes to go to work on the cGAS–STING pathway, protein phase separation or noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT). The results went somewhere else entirely.

The reason is simple. The Nobel Prizes do not follow trends. The committees look first for fundamental advances in science, not for the topics dominating the current conversation. By that measure, this year's choices may have been the most Nobel-like outcome possible.

The predictions failed, but the science succeeded. Real discovery happens quietly, one steady step at a time.

## Why inquiry matters more than prediction

The 2025 prizes showed again that science is not a race to guess the right answer. It is a search for the right question. While everyone else named the fields that would win, the committees quietly sought out the people who had given real answers to long-standing questions.

That lesson applies to students, too. School trains us to predict: what will be on the exam, which problem has the correct answer, where a result will rank. Real scholarship doesn't work that way. It is built through inquiry and verification, and new discoveries often arrive precisely by overturning what people expected. That is why the Nobel Prizes keep surprising us.

### How CRI teaches inquiry

CRI's faculty don't simply hand students results. They have students ask, alongside them, why a result came out the way it did. Working directly with a professor, students go through the full cycle of a research project:

1. Choosing a topic
2. Forming a hypothesis
3. Designing an experiment
4. Analyzing the data
5. Writing the paper

> "If students find the work exciting, it isn't because I gave them the answers. It's because I helped them come up with their own questions."
> — Gioia Polidori, professor of human and evolutionary biology, University of Southern California

Along the way, students gain something that matters more than any single paper: the patience to sit with not knowing, and the ability to think their way forward on their own.

## The message worth keeping

The 2025 prizes defied expectations once more, but the surprise carries a truth that doesn't change. Genuine discovery comes to people who stay with one question for a long time.

AI can now draft papers, and speed can look like the only thing that counts. Yet what admissions officers trust has stayed the same: students who have done the inquiry themselves. CRI designs its programs around that process. Students choose their own topic, work through experiments with a professor and reach conclusions of their own.

Predictions can miss, as the 2025 Nobel Prizes showed, but real inquiry holds up. The [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter) puts that approach to work over winter break, with students developing their own question into a paper alongside a university professor.
author: CRI Editorial

title: How to ask a professor for a recommendation letter admissions officers trust
excerpt: Who to ask, when to ask, and what to send: a step-by-step guide to earning a strong recommendation letter from a professor, with a sample request email.
content:
Is it all right to ask my professor for a letter? What if the answer is no? What is the polite way to send my materials? Nearly every student wrestles with some version of these questions when application season arrives. The answer is simpler than it looks: a strong recommendation starts not with a clever request but with trust built by working together.

In an age when AI can write for you, what admissions officers trust is what a professor has seen firsthand. So which professor should you ask, when, and how, for that trust to come through on the page? Every year CRI watches dozens of students research alongside professors from leading universities and earn strong letters along the way. Drawing on that experience, this guide walks through how to ask with grace and come away with a recommendation that rings true.

## Why the letter carries so much weight

Every applicant knows the usual ingredients: strong grades, meaningful activities, a compelling essay. Yet one document holds an admissions officer's attention longer than the rest, and it is the recommendation letter.

Officers review thousands of applications with similar GPAs, similar activities, even similar personal statements. What separates them is what someone who actually worked with the student has to say. A letter is not a formality. It is third-party testimony from a professor or researcher who observed a student's attitude, reasoning, and potential for growth at close range. It is also the one part of the file AI cannot ghostwrite.

CRI faculty make the same point.

> "A good recommendation letter isn't empty praise. It's a record of how a student overcomes uncertainty and builds confidence."
> — Jason Sello, UCSF School of Pharmacy, formerly of Brown University

> "I write in specific terms about what the student actually did in the project, and about the depth and attitude they brought to that work."
> — Aidong Yang, University of Oxford

A strong letter, in other words, carries the student's journey. How persuasive it is depends on how long the professor was watching and what the two of them worked through together.

At CRI, professors stay with each student from choosing a research topic to finishing the paper and presenting it. That is why their letters go beyond general impressions to include:

- specific details from the actual research and the discussions around it
- the student's attitude, way of thinking, and approach to collaboration

This is what admissions officers mean by a "strong letter": a professor's observation and trust, and a student's real commitment, on the same page. A request alone can't produce that. It builds over time, through shared work and genuine exchange.

![Students work on laptops at classroom desks while an instructor in a green shirt leans in to talk with one of them](/editorial/224039848902-04.jpg "Students and an instructor working through a research session in a CRI class")

## Who to ask: the professor who knows your work

Good letters come from professors who know you well, not from the most famous name you can find. Admissions officers read for depth, not letterhead. The letter should leave them thinking, *this professor really did watch this student grow*.

The best candidates are professors who:

- supervised your research project directly
- worked with you regularly in class or during office hours
- saw how you handled yourself in discussions and presentations

Because CRI professors are involved in every stage of a student's research, the letters they write naturally include detail and concrete evidence.

> "In attitude and problem-solving ability, CRI students are no different from the students in my own lab."
> — Andrea Bernini, University of Oxford

![A professor in a white polo shirt talks with a student in a gray hoodie at an evening gathering, with other faculty standing nearby](/editorial/224039848902-05.jpg "A professor and a student in conversation at a CRI program gathering")

## When to ask: while the work is fresh

The best time to ask is while the professor still remembers you clearly. Ideally, that means right after:

- a course or project ends
- you finish a paper or report
- the professor has given you direct feedback

At that point your attitude and results are vivid in the professor's mind, and specific examples make their way into the letter without effort.

The calendar matters too. Ask **at least four to six weeks before the deadline** so the professor has enough time to write. Asking early shows both courtesy and a sense of responsibility.

At CRI, the final feedback meeting with the professor at the end of the program leads naturally into the letter. At that moment the professor understands the student's research better than ever, and is in the best position to write a genuine letter.

![Two students wearing lanyards stand with their professor in front of a projected slide titled "Amine-Based Carbon Capture: A Focus on CESAR solvent"](/editorial/224039848902-07.jpg "A research team with their professor beside the title slide of their carbon-capture presentation, August 2025")

## How to ask: make the letter easy to write

A polite request matters, but so does structure. Your goal is to make the letter easy to write: one clean email with everything the professor needs attached.

Put together a recommendation packet that helps the professor recall your work at a glance:

1. An updated CV
2. Your transcript
3. A draft of your personal statement
4. Your list of schools and their deadlines
5. A summary of the project and your role in it

These five items let a professor see quickly what you did and where your strengths lie. For CRI students, the whole research process is already documented, which makes the professor's job considerably easier. (For where the same research goes elsewhere in your application, from the Activities section to Publications, see "How research experience shows up on the Common App" on the [CRI blog](/blog).)

## A sample request email

Adapt the template below, replacing everything in brackets with your own details.

> **Subject:** Recommendation Letter Request – [Your Name] – CRI Research [Year]
>
> Dear Professor [Last Name],
>
> My name is [Your Name], and I took part in [project name, e.g., the CRI "Artificial Intelligence" Research Program], which you supervised during [dates].
>
> First, thank you sincerely for your careful guidance throughout the project. In particular, [one specific interaction, e.g., your advice while I was designing the study] taught me a great deal, and the experience deepened my interest in [research field].
>
> I am now preparing to apply to [undergraduate / master's / PhD] programs in [intended major] for [entry term and year] and am aiming for [two or three main schools]. I have always admired your research and accomplishments, and it would be a great honor to have your letter of recommendation in support of my applications.
>
> I believe [an achievement or role from the project, e.g., completing the final research report, or the positive feedback you gave on my work] can speak to my academic growth and my ability as a researcher.
>
> To make the letter as easy as possible to write, I have attached:
>
> - my updated CV
> - my transcript
> - a draft of my personal statement
> - a summary of the CRI project and my contributions
> - my list of schools and their deadlines
>
> I know how busy your schedule is, and I would be very grateful if you would consider my request. Please let me know if any other materials would help.
>
> Thank you again for your support and guidance during the project.
>
> Best regards,\
> [Your Name]\
> [Phone number / email address]

## Genuine experience shows through

Since Yale rescinded a first-year student's admission in September 2025 over false information on the application, colleges have put growing weight on experience that can be verified. When AI can write on anyone's behalf, what admissions officers trust is real experience a professor can vouch for.

Families can try a simple test: if an admissions officer checked every activity on your child's application, one by one, could you say with confidence that each was genuine? If that question gives you even a moment's pause, it is time to trade embellished credentials for experience that can be proven.

CRI is designed around that kind of experience. It is not simply a program for writing a paper but an academic journey taken under a professor's eye, one that ends in earned trust. If you would like to start building that relationship over the winter break, take a look at the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Yale revokes a first-year's admission: why fabricated credentials eventually collapse
excerpt: A Yale first-year lost their place over false application claims. What admissions officers now ask about your activities, and why verifiable, professor-guided research holds up.
content:
In September 2025, shortly after arriving on campus, a first-year student at Yale University was found to have put false information on their application. The admission was revoked immediately, and the student was removed from campus. It was a startling case, and its lesson reaches well beyond one student: fabricated credentials eventually fall apart.

## What Yale said next

A Yale spokesperson explained the stakes plainly: the university reviews thousands of applications, and the process depends on applicants telling the truth.

Yale did not stop there. As the *Yale Daily News* reported, the admissions office already vets applications and may step that up for the next cycle, with more fact-checking and more verification calls. Checking grades and awards is only the start. Officers may increasingly confirm:

- whether the student actually took part in the activity listed
- what position or role the student really held
- whether the activity can be verified at all

For parents following the news, the natural question is whether their own child's activities would hold up under that kind of scrutiny.

## Why an impressive list is no longer enough

The message from New Haven is clear. High scores plus a long list of impressive activities are no longer enough, on their own, to earn a college's trust. Admissions officers are asking sharper questions, and they come down to three:

1. **Authenticity:** Did you really do this?
2. **Responsibility:** What role did you play?
3. **Verifiability:** How can the result be checked?

Applicants from Asia often meet extra skepticism on exactly these points. The reactions tend to be familiar: the activities all look alike, the application seems too polished, and there is a lingering doubt about whether the student did the work. So however strong the grades and however many the awards, officers will keep asking detailed questions until they are satisfied the experience is genuine.

| If your application lists… | Expect to be asked… |
| --- | --- |
| Community service at school | What exactly was the project, and what was your role? |
| An internship | What material did you work with, and what did you actually contribute? |
| Research | Where can we see the paper or the project? |

Officers are not looking for eloquent descriptions. They want real experience that can be traced and checked, down to the details.

## Who watched the work: a chain of trust

As AI tools improve, the work students submit invites a new kind of doubt: did the student really produce this? Admissions officers also know they cannot personally check every activity on every application. So they look at who vouched for it.

Imagine a letter of recommendation from a professor who is widely known in the field. It is not generic praise but an account of having watched the student's research habits and growth firsthand. Admissions officers are people too, and they do not expect a scholar of that standing to lie. Who observed the process becomes the basis for trust.

CRI is built to create that trust. Students' research is guided by professors from leading universities and documented from start to finish, forming a verifiable academic chain of trust. It has four links:

- **Direct faculty guidance.** Professors from institutions such as Harvard, Oxford, Caltech and Penn give 30 or more hours of in-depth mentoring, working with students from framing a research question through analyzing the data.
- **A paper, not a report.** The result is an academic paper that can go through review, and it remains as evidence an admissions officer can look up at any time.
- **A letter based on observation.** The professor's recommendation reflects what they actually saw of the student's diligence and ability, rather than a string of flattering adjectives.
- **A record of the process.** Interim reports, a final presentation and the review of the paper leave an academic trail showing that the student grew into a researcher instead of simply attending.

![A professor speaks to a room of students seated at dinner tables beneath a 2025 Seoul Research Program banner](/editorial/224029879368-04.jpg "Caltech chemistry professor Brian Stoltz addresses students at a dinner during the 2025 Seoul Research Program.")

What students take away from CRI, then, is not a dressed-up credential but a record admissions officers can check. At a time when AI-generated writing and inflated activity lists are everywhere, experience that established scholars have watched and vouched for carries real weight.

## What that record has meant for students

Many CRI students have already used this experience to earn admission to selective universities and to present their work internationally:

- **Conference presentations:** students have presented at major international conferences, including those of IEEE EMBS, the Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society.
- **Admissions:** Stanford, Penn, Northwestern and UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business, among others.

Four cases show how the pieces fit together in an application.

- **A Stanford admit: a CRI paper and a research assistant role.** The student listed the CRI paper and a follow-up research assistant position as core activities on the Stanford application, and emphasized that work again in the admissions interview. In explaining the research topic, the student could draw on in-depth conversations with the professor, which made a strong impression.
- **A Penn admit: a professor's recommendation.** The student submitted a detailed, specific letter from a CRI professor. Because it vividly captured the student's attitude and curiosity as a researcher, it read as credible testimony rather than simple praise.
- **A Northwestern computer science admit: the CRI paper alone.** With no other high-profile activities, this student relied on the CRI paper to make a strong case for their academic interests. The message to admissions officers was that nothing had been manufactured: this student had genuinely done research in their field.
- **A UC Berkeley Haas admit: a business paper and group leadership.** The student wrote a business and economics paper at CRI and, as group leader, showed teamwork and leadership. Both the concrete role and the finished paper counted in the application.

None of these students simply "had a good experience." Each had work an admissions officer could actually check, backed by a leading professor's endorsement, and that combination is the evidence admissions offices trust most. Fuller accounts of individual projects are collected on our [Student Success](/success) page.

## Preparing for a more transparent process

The Yale case is a sign of where admissions is heading. Officers are looking less for students with a long list of credentials and more for students with genuine, verifiable experience, and the process will only become more competitive and more transparent.

For families, the takeaway is simple: fabricated experience can be exposed at any time, while genuine experience holds up anywhere. A transcript, a stack of awards and an activity list can look convincing at a glance and still come apart after a few pointed questions. What colleges trust, in the end, is real experience that a professor can vouch for.

So it is worth asking honestly: if an admissions officer examined your application with a magnifying glass, what could you show? If you can answer with confidence, you are already well prepared. If the question makes you uneasy, it is worth starting to build that record.

One place to begin is the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter), where students work online with university faculty over the winter break and develop a research question into a paper of their own, guided by a professor from the first idea to the final draft.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Stem cells, regeneration and genomics with Oxford biologist Aziz Aboobaker
excerpt: A planarian flatworm can regenerate its entire body. Meet Oxford biologist Aziz Aboobaker, who studies stem cells and regeneration, and see what his online winter research course asked of students.
content:
A lizard can regrow a lost tail. A planarian, a small flatworm, can rebuild its entire body. How animals regenerate, and what that reveals about the way our own cells repair themselves, is a question that runs through the work of Oxford biologist Aziz Aboobaker. For the 2025–26 winter break, CRI offered his course on stem cells, regeneration and genomics through the Winter Online Research Program.

Many of the biggest advances in biomedicine in recent years, including gene editing, stem cell therapies and personalized medicine, have come out of molecular biology. It is less a textbook subject than a science that is reshaping human health. For students weighing a future in medicine or biotechnology, working on the open questions researchers are chasing, rather than the settled facts of a curriculum, is a different kind of preparation.

## Researcher, editor and teacher

Aboobaker is a professor in the University of Oxford's Department of Biology and is widely respected across the life sciences. He is also a Fellow and Tutor in Biological Sciences at Lady Margaret Hall, one of the university's colleges, where he works directly with the next generation of scientists.

![Aziz Aboobaker, smiling, in a blue button-down shirt, standing outdoors in front of a lawn and trees](/editorial/223992633062-02.jpg "Aziz Aboobaker, Department of Biology, University of Oxford")

His standing in the field shows in the roles he holds beyond his own lab. He is an associate editor of *PLOS Genetics*, one of the journals that researchers in genetics and the life sciences trust most. Associate editors oversee the review of submitted studies, so he helps decide which work gets published and what standard it has to meet.

He has also served as a vice-president of the Genetics Society, helping to lead the UK's genetics research community. In the summer of 2023 he was a Whitman Fellow at the University of Chicago's Marine Biological Laboratory, studying the mechanisms that determine cell fate in *Parhyale hawaiensis*, a small marine crustacean.

## Four research themes

His research falls under four headings: stem cells, animal regeneration, molecular biology and functional genomics. They can sound abstract, but each connects directly to medical problems people face.

- **Stem cells.** Stem cell research lies at the heart of regenerative medicine, which aims to restore damaged tissues and organs. It could open new treatments for patients whose organs were injured in a car accident or whose nerves have been destroyed.
- **Animal regeneration.** Lizards regrow their tails, and planarian flatworms regenerate their whole bodies. Working out how they do it offers important clues to the mechanisms human cells use to recover from damage.
- **Molecular biology and genetics.** These are the foundation of personalized medicine: predicting which patients will respond well to a particular drug, or how genetic factors raise or lower someone's risk of developing a disease.
- **Functional genomics.** Instead of studying one gene at a time, functional genomics asks how whole networks of genes interact to produce the processes of life.

## Learning to think like a researcher

The winter course took these themes as its starting point, but the goal went beyond absorbing information. Students were there to learn to think like researchers: to ask scientific questions, form hypotheses and interpret data, and to build the habit of investigating on their own.

The course was structured so that Professor Aboobaker guided each student from choosing a research topic to completing a paper, through the full cycle of a study:

1. Framing a scientific question
2. Analysis
3. Organizing the results
4. Writing the paper

Although it was taught online, the course was designed for a small group, giving every student room for discussion and individual feedback. For students considering a life sciences major, that process builds academic confidence. For those preparing for medicine, it adds something coursework rarely provides: real research experience.

## Who the course was for

The course was open to students from Grade 9 through university. Its depth and difficulty meant that interest alone was not enough, so only students who passed an interview beforehand could join. As a result, participants worked alongside peers selected from around the world, each with genuine academic curiosity and a solid foundation.

It was designed for students who:

- are interested in molecular biology, genetics or the life sciences
- are seriously considering a career in medicine or biotechnology
- want to add a research paper, and the experience of submitting it to a journal, to their college application portfolio

The course held particular value for future doctors. Rather than studying textbook material, participants worked on stem cell, regeneration and genomics questions that scientists are actively debating, giving an interest in medicine a firsthand, research-based foundation.

## From a winter course to a summer project

What set the course apart was where it ended. Under Professor Aboobaker's guidance, each student was to write a research paper under their own name, with support through submission to a journal. A finished paper is concrete evidence of what a student can do, in college applications and in whatever comes next.

The course was also planned as the first stage of a longer collaboration. Professor Aboobaker was scheduled to visit Korea the following summer, and students who completed the winter course would have the chance to continue with him in an advanced summer program. Linking winter and summer this way lets a high school or university student build a sustained research relationship with a leading scientist, rather than taking a single class.

Professor Aboobaker's course was part of the 2025–26 winter lineup, and the faculty and topics change from year to year. To see which professors are leading the current cohort and how the online courses are structured, explore the [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Paper-writing guide, part 7: proofreading, the final design step
excerpt: Proofreading is more than fixing typos. Learn how to get useful feedback, restructure a draft and check figures, results, sentences, references and tone before you submit.
content:
The draft is finally done. The argument holds together, the figures are ready and the references are in order. So is the paper finished? Not yet. A first draft is not the end of writing; it is the start of the blueprint.

Proofreading, the last stage of writing a paper, is much more than hunting for typos. It is a design process: you check the structure and logic once more and refine the text until it reaches the reader clearly. This is where a well-written paper becomes an excellent one. The final part of CRI's seven-part paper-writing guide shows how, with checklists you can run on your own manuscript.

## Why proofreading matters

Most journals screen submissions before peer review and reject papers with formatting errors or illogical writing at that stage. Even strong research can stop being reviewed simply because the writing is a struggle to read.

Timing matters too. Review, revision and resubmission usually take one to six months, so the polish of your first submission shapes the whole timeline. Proofreading is not just fixing what's wrong. It is your final responsibility to make the paper something a first-time reader can trust.

## Show your draft to different readers

You write a paper alone, but you can't proofread it alone. Reread your own sentences enough times and you stop seeing both the typos and the leaps in logic.

Your advisor's review comes first, and one round is not enough. Revise, send it back, revise again: it takes at least two or three rounds before a paper becomes genuinely readable.

Just as important is a classmate or friend who doesn't know the topic. Because they aren't experts, they quickly spot jargon you never explained and places where the logic jumps. They ask the questions a real reader would ask, and their comments can be even more practical than a professor's. A paper isn't written only for the people evaluating it; a good one persuades a wider audience.

A few habits make feedback more useful:

- **For your advisor,** send one package: the draft, a short list of the key questions you want answered, the figure files and the references.
- **For peers,** ask for comments on two things: what they didn't understand and what seemed illogical.
- **Rotate your readers.** Instead of showing the same person every version, have different people review the draft at different stages.

![A printed essay covered in red-pen edits and margin notes, with a red pen lying across the page](/editorial/223984897221-09.jpg "A second reader catches what the writer has stopped seeing, down to a margin note asking for a source.")

## Don't be afraid to start over

Proofreading brings a familiar temptation: "If I just polish this one sentence, it'll be fine." But if a passage still reads awkwardly after several rounds of edits, rewriting it from scratch is often faster than patching it. A first draft records your thinking; it was not shaped for a reader.

Your own sentences always feel easy, because you already know the background behind them. A first-time reader doesn't, and what sounds natural in your head can look on the page like a series of gaps and jumps. At that point, re-examining the logical flow matters more than fixing individual sentences. Before polishing line by line, look at the skeleton of the whole piece:

- Does this paragraph have to be here?
- Where is the information the reader needs first?
- Would the logic be clearer if the conclusion came earlier?

Good structure keeps readers from getting lost. Here is a quick test: write the topic of each paragraph in a single line, then read only those lines. The logical flow of the whole paper appears at a glance, and if it feels off, tearing up the structure is a perfectly good strategy.

## Say deep things in plain words

Many students assume a paper is supposed to be hard to read. In fact, a good paper explains complex ideas simply. Your reader is not your advisor; picture a student at your own level, or someone new to the field.

Academic writing demands accuracy and depth, but it doesn't need to wrap them in difficult words and tangled sentences. When two options mean the same thing, choose the shorter one:

| Instead of | Write |
| --- | --- |
| utilize | use |
| demonstrate | show |
| in order to | to |

The longer the sentence, the faster the reader's attention fades. Simpler wording doesn't mean simpler content, though. Explaining a complex idea plainly is proof that you understand it. Three techniques help:

- Define each concept with an example.
- Link your reasoning with connectives such as *then*, *because* and *however*.
- Restate numbers and data in words.

Never assume readers will "obviously" know something; check every expression against their level. Convoluted prose can be a sign that the thinking behind it isn't sorted out yet. Write simply, precisely and with depth.

## Figure checklist

A figure is not decoration. It condenses the core of your argument and is key evidence for the reader, so no detail is too small. Before you submit, check the basics:

- [ ] **Scale bars, color bars and units are all there.** Without a scale bar, readers can't interpret an image or graph. If you use a colormap, include a color bar and legend. Always state units of measurement (cm, nm, sec and so on).
- [ ] **Every abbreviation is defined in the text or caption.** For example, if Fig. 2b shows an "ROI," explain that it means "region of interest," the area targeted in the image analysis.
- [ ] **The text calls out and explains each figure.** A figure is not a puzzle for readers to solve alone. Guide them: "The pattern observed in Fig. 1…" or "Fig. 2a shows condition X, and 2b shows condition Y…"
- [ ] **Labels are consistent.** Choose one style for subfigures, "Fig. 1a" or "(a)," and keep it. Notation that shifts between caption, text and figure confuses readers. Use "Fig." for one figure and "Figs." for more: "Figs. 2a and 2b show…"

A figure error spotted in review can leave the impression that the whole paper was put together carelessly. One small slip can undermine the credibility of everything else.

![A simple black-and-white bar chart showing frequency in percent for items 1 to 5](/editorial/223984897221-05.jpg "The y-axis states its unit, but only a caption or the text can tell readers what items 1 to 5 are.")

## Results and discussion checklist

Showing your results is not enough; you are also responsible for interpreting them. These sections are not a place to list data. They must explain, logically and persuasively, what you found, why it matters and what it could mean. When proofreading them, focus on three points:

- [ ] **Claims and possibilities are clearly separated.** Match your wording to whether a result is statistically significant or possibly a one-off. Definitive: "This result demonstrates…" Tentative: "This may suggest…" or "A possible explanation is…" Presenting an uncertain result as fact costs you credibility.
- [ ] **The order works for the reader.** Results should follow both the sequence of experiments and the logic of the argument, graphs should appear in the order the text discusses them, and nothing should be repeated.
- [ ] **Every technique gets a citation and a brief explanation.** This applies to any specialized statistical analysis, computational model or instrument, for example: "We performed two-way ANOVA (see Smith et al., 2021) to analyze the group differences."

Resist the thought "everyone knows this, so I can leave it out." Skipping what seems obvious to you can leave a reviewer struggling to follow.

## Sentence-level checklist

A paper isn't judged on its results alone. Small grammar errors, undefined abbreviations and unit mistakes, repeated often enough, drag down both credibility and clarity. Check these points:

- [ ] **Abbreviations are defined at first use.** Spell out the full term the first time: "Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM)." Abbreviate concepts that appear three or more times; an abbreviation you rarely use makes the text harder to follow.
- [ ] **Numbers and units are spaced correctly.** Put a space between a number and its unit: "10 mL," "25 °C" (not "25°C"). Percentages and angles are the usual exceptions and attach directly: "15% increase," "45° angle."
- [ ] **No sentence starts with a symbol or abbreviation.** Opening with "e.g.," "&" or a symbol reads as informal and awkward, so "& the results show…" is out. Start with an ordinary word.
- [ ] **Hyphens follow the adjective rule.** Hyphenate a compound that works as an adjective ("x-ray diffraction analysis") but not one that works as a noun ("The sample was exposed to x rays."). Writers slip on this often, so keep your usage consistent.
- [ ] **Informal expressions are gone.** A paper calls for objectivity, so replace casual wording:

| Informal | Use instead |
| --- | --- |
| kinda | somewhat / rather |
| ~10 | approximately 10 |
| ain't | is not / are not |

Set aside the idea that you can write the way you talk. A paper is an argument, and precise, formal language is what persuades.

## Reference list checklist

Automated tools aren't perfect, so the final check falls to you. The reference list backs up your writing and is evidence that it can be trusted. Yet many students slip at this last step, assuming EndNote will take care of it.

- [ ] **Citation numbers match, and nothing is listed twice.** A source cited as [13] in the text is often missing from the list, or [13] and [22] turn out to be the same paper. The numbering easily falls out of sync when you delete, move or add citations mid-draft. Tools like EndNote help a great deal, but in the end you have to check every line by eye.
- [ ] **No information is missing.** A journal may return a paper whose references lack the issue number, page range or year of publication; a DOI is recommended too. Conference papers, preprints and reports are formatted differently from journal articles, so check their fields separately.
- [ ] **You haven't trusted the software blindly.** If Google Scholar holds incorrect bibliographic data, EndNote imports it as is, producing authors in the wrong order or inconsistent capitalization in titles.

The rule: EndNote for the first pass, a human for the final review.

![Two entries from a numbered reference list in a research paper](/editorial/223984897221-08.jpg "Automated tools can pass along slips such as the lowercase 'inex' (for INEX) in the first entry, so read every line yourself.")

## Tone: point out limits, don't attack

A paper proves a claim; it is not a platform for criticizing anyone. One of the hardest parts of academic writing is how to critique: pointing out the limits of earlier studies, or pressing your own argument, can easily read as an emotional attack. Checking tone is part of proofreading.

Avoid sentences like these:

- "This study is meaningless."
- "The authors completely misunderstood the concept."
- "This method is seriously flawed."

To a reviewer, they sound unprofessional and emotional. Courtesy and objectivity are the baseline in academia, so ground your criticism in data and state it neutrally:

- "This study does not account for X, which may limit its applicability to Y."
- "An alternative explanation for this phenomenon could be Z."
- "The authors assume A, but recent studies suggest that B may also be relevant."

The point of criticism is not to cut others down but to show why your research is needed. Neutral vocabulary conveys expertise and respect at the same time, instead of leaving readers to guess at your tone:

| Aggressive | Neutral alternative |
| --- | --- |
| wrong | questionable, debatable |
| flawed | limited, constrained |
| fail to | did not address, did not consider |
| meaningless | inconclusive, lacking support |

Present your own claims with the same restraint. Rather than "Our findings clearly prove…", write "Our findings suggest…" or "These results may indicate…" When you do want to sound confident, back it up with numbers or statistical evidence.

## Keep a log of your recurring mistakes

The real purpose of proofreading is to get to know your own writing. Everyone repeats the same kinds of mistakes, and they don't vanish in a day or two, so the key is to recognize and manage your own patterns. These come up again and again:

- Missing prepositions ("explain to the reader")
- Article errors (a, an, the)
- Subject-verb agreement ("data is" should be "data are")
- Uncountable nouns made plural ("informations," "researches")
- Abbreviations such as DNA or AI never spelled out at first use
- Mixed-up tenses (past, present, present perfect)

Write each one down as it appears. With every paper you revise, your personal checklist gets sharper.

In a sense, your mistake patterns are your style. Everyone has language habits: some writers circle back over the same reasoning, some drift into abstraction, and some build sentences where the subject and verb end up far apart. Unless you notice these habits yourself, you will get the same comments every time. Start your own checklist with items like these:

- [ ] Preposition and article errors
- [ ] Abbreviations defined
- [ ] Sentence length: how many verbs are in one sentence?
- [ ] Hyphens, dashes and semicolons used consistently
- [ ] Figure and table numbers match the text
- [ ] Reference formatting errors

Let go of the idea of getting it perfect in one draft. What matters is training yourself to make fewer mistakes. Proofreading is less about correcting sentences than about looking honestly at how you write: logging your errors, finding the patterns and writing at least one line more clearly next time. That is the habit of a good researcher.

## The complete series

This is the last of seven parts in CRI's paper-writing guide:

1. Why write a research paper at all?
2. Decide what you'll say before you decide how to start
3. Figures are the face of your paper
4. Writing results and discussion that work
5. When and how to write the introduction and abstract
6. Finding, citing and managing your sources
7. Proofreading, the final design step (this part)

Every part is on the [CRI blog](/blog), along with a separate guide to editing a manuscript and matching a journal's style before submission.

If you'd like to take a paper of your own through rounds of revision like these, the [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1) pairs you with a faculty mentor for an individually arranged project. You write the manuscript yourself in English, and CRI supports it through journal submission.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Paper-writing guide, part 6: finding, citing and managing your sources
excerpt: Citations are part of research design, not a last-minute chore. Learn how to search the literature, judge what you find and let a reference manager handle the formatting.
content:
"Don't you just add the references at the end?" First-time authors ask this all the time. They write the whole draft, leave gaps marked [1] and [2], then rush to find papers that seem to fit. But citations are not a formality for filling out a reference list. They are part of the research design, work that begins before you write a word, and they carry much of a paper's credibility and persuasive force.

A good paper answers two questions at once: what new thing am I saying, and why have I earned the right to say it? The literature search is what earns you that right. This sixth part of CRI's seven-part paper-writing guide covers why citations matter, how to run a literature search, and which tools keep your references under control.

![A typed reference list in APA style with five entries, citing Newsweek, The Washington Post, The New York Times, a book and Science](/editorial/223976934361-01.jpg "A reference list in APA style: every entry follows the same pattern of author, date, title and source.")

## Three reasons citations matter

A literature search shapes every stage of a paper, from planning and design to carrying out the work and interpreting it. Beginners tend to ask, "Why do I have to cite this?" The better question is, "Will my argument still convince anyone if I don't?"

1. **To show that your idea is new.** Someone may already have answered your question. If so, cite that paper and explain how your work goes further. Skip this and a reviewer will ask the obvious question: how is this different from what's already out there?
2. **To borrow designs and analyses that have already been tested.** Few people invent a perfect experimental design from scratch, so the quickest route is to see what similar studies did. If you hypothesize that gene A affects a particular disease, earlier work shows how others measured that gene's expression and under what conditions they found significant differences. Your study becomes both more valid and more feasible.
3. **To give your discussion depth.** Sooner or later every paper needs a sentence like "Our results agree with X but differ from Y." Citations build those links, show where your findings sit and let you spell out what they imply.

A good paper is not a standalone text but an argument built on existing knowledge. Citations are its first building material, and the literature search is how you choose them.

## The search itself: question, keywords, search, organize

The most common complaint at the start is simple: "I don't know what to search for." Finding papers is often harder than reading them, so break the search into four steps.

### 1. Sharpen the question

Every search starts from what you want to know, so write down a specific research question rather than a broad interest. "Environmental pollution affects human health" is far too wide. "How does fine dust affect children's lung function?" is something you can actually search. The more specific the question, the more precise the results.

### 2. Pull out the keywords

Pick out the core concepts in your question and list the terms researchers use for each, synonyms included. If you think about your topic in another language, this is also the moment to translate it into English.

| Concept | Search terms |
|---|---|
| Fine dust | particulate matter, PM2.5 |
| Children | children, pediatric |
| Lung function | lung function, respiratory health |

Keep the terms broad at first and try them in different combinations.

### 3. Use the right search tools

| Platform | What it's good for |
|---|---|
| Google Scholar | The most accessible option for beginners. Start here. |
| PubMed | Life sciences and medicine, with generally reliable sources |
| Web of Science | Advanced features such as subject filters and citation counts |
| Semantic Scholar | Intuitive AI-based summaries, graphs and citation analysis |

Begin with Google Scholar, then widen the search in PubMed or Web of Science. Each result shows the title, authors, year and a "Cited by" count, a useful signal of a paper's influence. As a rough guide:

- **100+ citations:** a landmark paper, a reference point for theory or experiments in its field
- **50+ citations:** an influential paper most researchers in the area know
- **10+ citations:** credible work the field has taken seriously
- **0–5 citations:** a recent paper, or one whose influence hasn't spread yet, so read it with extra care

A low count doesn't make a paper worthless. Early in a project, though, starting with the most-cited work is safer and more efficient.

### 4. Organize as you go

A search can turn up dozens of papers, so decide how you'll organize them before you read. Skim titles and abstracts to build a shortlist, then save the papers you care about in a reference manager such as Zotero, Mendeley or EndNote, which stores each PDF alongside your notes, keywords and citation details.

What matters most is not how many papers you read but whether you record and summarize them. Papers you only read fade quickly. As you go, jot down the main point, the methods and any sentences you might cite.

## Follow the citation network

Citations trace the lineage of ideas and the flow of influence in a field. Every paper builds on earlier work and is later cited by others, so papers link to one another like a network.

Make a habit of asking who was influenced by the papers you cite. If paper A is cited by studies B and C, A is shaping the field. Follow that trail and you start to see the key concepts, the leading researchers and where the field is heading. Several tools make these links visible:

- **Web of Science** lays out a paper's citation network as a tree.
- **Semantic Scholar** has a Citations tab on each paper that shows the work that followed.
- **Connected Papers** takes a single paper and draws a graph of similar papers and how they cite one another.

Tracing these connections moves you from someone who has read a few papers to a researcher who understands how a field's knowledge fits together.

## Journal and researcher metrics, briefly

Beginners often ask how well regarded a paper's journal is. The usual yardstick is the **Impact Factor**, which measures how often a journal's recent papers are cited. A 2024 Impact Factor of 32 means that papers the journal published in 2022 and 2023 were cited an average of 32 times in 2024. *Nature Photonics*, at about 32, is very high; the *Journal of Consumer Research*, at roughly 4 to 6, ranks high for the social sciences.

Remember that it is an average. A few papers may be cited hundreds of times while others are barely cited, so a high Impact Factor doesn't mean every paper in the journal is excellent. For individual researchers, the common measure is the **h-index**: an h-index of 10 means 10 of their papers have each been cited at least 10 times. It reflects both productivity and influence, so it often figures in faculty hiring and funding decisions.

To judge a paper well, look beyond the journal: weigh the paper's own citation count, its content and design, and the author's track record. The [CRI blog](/blog) has a separate guide to journal metrics, from the Impact Factor to CiteScore, SJR and SNIP.

## Start with review papers

When you're new to a topic, it's hard to know which papers to read first or what really matters. The best starting point is a **review paper**, an article that surveys a topic's research and its key studies. Think of it as a map of the field. A good review:

- lays out the core theories and open questions
- shows which methods are most common and where the debates are
- spares you from reading a huge stack of papers one by one at the outset

Several journal families specialize in reviews:

| Review series | What it offers |
|---|---|
| Annual Review series | Flagship review journals by field, such as the *Annual Review of Neuroscience* |
| Trends series | Review-focused journals that quickly cover current issues, such as *Trends in Cognitive Sciences* |
| Nature Reviews series | Among the most influential review journals in the natural sciences |

Papers with "review," "meta-analysis" or "survey" in the title are usually reviews, and adding "review" to your Google Scholar or PubMed search will surface more of them. If you're moving into a new area, such as AI-assisted cancer diagnosis, read the reviews before you plan any experiments. They show which methods have been tried, where those methods fall short and where the research is going. A single paper shows you one path. A review shows you the whole forest.

## Never cite by hand

Few parts of a paper cause as many needless mistakes as the citations and reference list: typing (author, year) over and over, numbering, reordering, renumbering. Journals sometimes turn a manuscript away simply because the references are in the wrong format. So follow one rule: **citations are not done by hand.**

Almost every researcher now uses a reference manager. The three most common:

- **EndNote:** paid but powerful, and many schools and institutions provide a license
- **Mendeley:** free, with an intuitive interface and cloud storage
- **Zotero:** free, with strong browser integration

![Screenshot of an EndNote library listing references by year and title, with a Manage Tags dialog open](/editorial/223976934361-07.jpg "A reference manager keeps every source in one searchable library, with tags to sort papers by topic.")

Reference managers pair neatly with Google Scholar. Click the quotation-mark Cite icon on a search result, download the citation in a format your reference manager can import (such as a .ris file), and the reference is in your library within seconds. Installing EndNote also adds an EndNote tab to Microsoft Word, where Insert Citation drops a citation straight into your text. Beyond that, a reference manager takes over the tedious work:

1. **Style conversion.** Moving to another journal no longer means reformatting every reference. One click switches the style from Nature to APA to IEEE, which takes much of the pain out of resubmission.
2. **Numbering and order.** Add a citation mid-draft and the whole list reorders and renumbers itself, with no numbering errors, duplicates or omissions.
3. **Collaboration.** On a paper with several authors, a shared library lets everyone see each other's citations in real time and keeps the references consistent, which means fewer clashes and cleaner version control.
4. **One home for your sources.** PDFs, notes and topic folders all live in one place, so organizing your reading no longer takes separate time.

A reference manager automates the formatting so you can focus on the content. Once you've used one, writing a paper without it feels like doing math without a calculator. Doing citations by hand to save time usually costs you both time and quality.

## Plan your citations before you write

Many students only deal with citations once the draft is finished. That's like building a house without a blueprint and only then starting on the wiring.

A strong paper settles a few things before the writing begins: which literature it will build on, which claims in the field it will challenge and whose work it will cite to earn the reader's trust. The more solid that plan, the more logical the structure, the more persuasive the argument and the more trustworthy the finished paper.

**Do this now:**

1. If you don't have a reference manager yet, install one today.
2. Search for review papers on your topic and add three papers to your library.
3. Open Word, click Insert Citation and add a citation yourself.

Efficient writing starts with the right tools, and a paper's depth shows in its citations. Part 7, the last in this series, turns to proofreading.

In CRI's [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1), students put these habits to work on a paper of their own: they write the manuscript in English under a faculty mentor's guidance, and CRI supports the paper through journal submission.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Dinner with the professors: the hidden highlight of the 2025 Seoul Research Program
excerpt: At the 2025 Seoul Research Program dinner, students asked professors from other fields how they found their paths, then shared research ideas at an open mic.
content:
How did you end up in this field? That was the kind of question students brought to the professors at the 2025 Seoul Research Program (SRP) dinner. Some were seated beside faculty who didn't teach their class, and what they wanted to hear about was less the subject than the path each professor had taken to it.

## Why a dinner?

Few high school students have their major fully figured out, and that is normal. Plenty of adults are still working out what they love to do, and teenagers have seen far less of the world. So the SRP team asked itself how the program could give students a wider range of experiences.

Students were already working hard in class and digging deep into topics of their own. The dinner was a way to take that one step further. What if they could talk with a professor from a field outside their own course? What if they could hear what a peer in another class was wrestling with? For a student still undecided about a major, a conversation like that might offer a hint. For one who already has a direction, it might stretch their thinking.

That was the idea behind the SRP dinner party. It was never meant to be just a meal. CRI saw it as a small, low-key way to let students connect naturally with people they had been hoping to talk to.

## A slightly awkward start

Students from different SRP classes shared the room with faculty including Brian Stoltz (Caltech), Kit Hickey (MIT), Max Krasnow (Harvard), Nabil Alshurafa (Northwestern), William Burke-White (University of Pennsylvania), and Ryan Fang (University of Chicago).

At first, nobody quite knew how to begin. Between filling plates at the buffet and finding a seat, students traded glances, waiting to see who would speak first. Those sitting next to a professor from another course looked especially unsure of what to say.

Then, somewhere around the time plates were half empty, conversations started on their own. The questions went something like this:

- "How did you get started in this field?"
- "Where do your research ideas usually come from?"
- "Could your work connect to the topic of the class I'm taking?"

![A man stands in the middle of a crowded dining room, speaking to students and faculty seated at long tables, with a 2025 Seoul Research Program banner across the windows](/editorial/223956173133-11.jpg "William Burke-White (University of Pennsylvania) addresses the room at the SRP dinner")

## Questions a search engine can't answer

What students wanted most was not more information. They wanted the human story: the choices professors had made and the questions they had faced along the way. That, it seems, was what really helped, because it is not something you can look up.

As someone once put it, "I couldn't decide on a major because I didn't know what kind of people study that field." At the dinner, students got to hear those stories, the parts of an academic life that never appear in a paper, a class, or a curriculum. For some of them, those stories may have quietly shifted something.

![A professor in a white polo shirt speaks into a microphone beside tables of seated students](/editorial/223956173133-10.jpg "Nabil Alshurafa (Northwestern) speaks during the dinner")

## An open mic with no script

Midway through the evening, CRI opened the floor for an open mic. There were no assigned presentations and no competition. The only aim was to let students share, casually, whatever they were thinking about.

No one moved. It was an unfamiliar setting, and the hesitation was easy to read: What would I even say? What if it gets awkward? So nobody was pushed. The organizers left the microphone out and waited.

After a while, a few students stepped up, a little cautiously. Some described their paper topics. Others talked about a direction they were weighing, or simply a few keywords that had caught their interest lately. Nobody gave a polished talk, and there was no big emotional moment. Students just said out loud what was already on their minds.

That low-key quality was what made it work. When a speaker finished, listeners quietly came over to talk: "I've been thinking about something similar." "If you have time, could we talk about this some more?"

This isn't a story about students swapping social media or email contacts, or agreeing on the spot to co-write a paper. But for one evening, students could see that they were not the only ones puzzling over the same kinds of questions. CRI considers that enough.

![A student holding a microphone speaks at the far end of the room while a group of students and adults stand around listening](/editorial/223956173133-08.jpg "A student takes the microphone during the open mic")

## Can a dinner matter for college admissions?

A dinner is, literally, a meal. But a conversation from that evening can stay with a student for a long time. A question asked out of simple curiosity can prompt someone to change a paper topic, or open up an interest they had never considered.

One student said they hadn't known a particular field existed until a professor described it, and had started looking up material on it afterward. Another said it was the first time they realized other students were grappling with similar questions.

None of this shows up on a transcript or an activity list, and none of it is done to impress anyone. Yet in CRI's experience, colleges give real weight to change that grows out of informal connections like these.

What counts in admissions is not how much a student has done, but what ideas took shape along the way and how those ideas developed. Seen that way, an evening like this is more strategic than it looks. It may have been just a meal, but the connections and changes that come out of it can leave a deeper mark than a paper or an activity.

![A professor in a black shirt speaks into a microphone in front of floor-to-ceiling windows as students listen from their tables](/editorial/223956173133-12.jpg "Ryan Fang (University of Chicago) addresses the dinner")

## Depth, not more activities

Admissions have been moving in that direction, asking less about how much a student did and more about how they came to see things. That is why, rather than adding one more activity to students' schedules, CRI looks for time that deepens the work they are already doing. The dinner was one such time, and CRI wants to keep creating more of them.

Think of a conversation with a professor over dinner, a research idea from a friend in another class, or two students who had just met agreeing, "Let's talk more sometime." For one student, a connection like that might become the reason to change majors. For another, it might be the start of a new friendship.

These are small experiences, but important ones, and CRI believes they are what education is made of. SRP is designed so that the learning continues outside the classroom, too.

![Dozens of students and faculty stand together behind dinner tables beneath a 2025 Seoul Research Program banner](/editorial/223956173133-14.jpg "Students and faculty of the 2025 Seoul Research Program at the dinner")

The dinner is one part of a program built around small classes, close faculty guidance, and research papers written in English. To see the current courses and faculty, and how to apply, visit the [Seoul Research Program page](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: Eight professors by the Han River: how the 2025 Seoul Research Program began
excerpt: The night before SRP 2025 opened, eight visiting professors met by the Han River to talk about students. Here is who taught, who came to learn, and how the first classes went.
content:
The evening before the 2025 Seoul Research Program (SRP) began, a small group sat down to dinner on the banks of the Han River just as the sun started to set. From a distance it looked like any summer dinner in Seoul. The guest list said otherwise: eight professors from universities including MIT, Harvard, Oxford, the University of Pennsylvania and Northwestern, and the CRI team that had built the program with them.

## A dinner about people, not papers

Research could wait. The conversation that night was about the students. How do you get high schoolers to ask real questions, stop fearing failure, and leave having genuinely learned a lot?

![A group posing on a riverside dock at sunset beside a moored boat, with a waterfront building behind them](/editorial/223953636848-01.jpg "Faculty and members of the CRI team by the Han River, the evening before SRP 2025 began")

Word that the professors were coming to Korea had traveled fast. Universities, institutions and companies reached out as soon as they heard, asking for lectures, interviews and meetings. The professors graciously declined them all, explaining that this time they wanted to give their full attention to their students. They had come to Seoul for one reason: to teach students what real research looks like.

## The 2025 faculty

Each of the eight professors led a different research track:

- **Kit Hickey, MIT: business, entrepreneurship and venture capital.** An entrepreneurship leader at MIT Sloan and a Silicon Valley entrepreneur. The course ran from market segmentation and sizing a total addressable market (TAM) to quantifying a value proposition, business model design, product planning and supply-chain optimization.
- **Max Krasnow, Harvard: behavioral science, psychology, sociology and communication.** A Harvard psychologist and TEDx Cambridge speaker who studies evolutionary psychology and human behavior. Topics included natural and sexual selection, the domain-specific mind, adaptations for finding food, human mating psychology and kin selection.
- **Brian Stoltz, Caltech: medicine, biochemistry, pharmaceutical and materials science.** A leading chemist and a recipient of the Feynman Prize. The course built from organic structure, bonding and stereochemistry to functional groups, acidity, oxidation levels, reaction mechanisms, olefins and carbonyls.
- **Nabil Alshurafa, Northwestern: biotechnology, welfare and preventive healthcare.** A medical school professor, a pioneer in mobile health and wearables, and the leader of the HABits Lab. Students studied sensor-based health monitoring, behavioral interventions, nutrition and chronic-disease prevention, and the ethics and privacy of health data.
- **William Burke-White, Penn: international law, policy, international relations and environmental policy.** A law professor who served as a policy planner in the Obama administration and has advised the G8, the G20 and international organizations. The course covered the structure of international law, treaties, international institutions, investment protection, transnational threats and the regulation of the use of force.
- **James Savoca, USC: film, production, scriptwriting and cinematography.** A film producer for Amazon Prime, a Broadway director and an acting-workshop leader. Students studied cinematic storytelling, how to give a scene purpose and emotional weight, independent cinema, directorial technique in films such as *Parasite* and *Oldboy*, and scriptwriting.
- **Ryan Fang, University of Chicago: economics, behavioral economics and strategic interactions.** A specialist in game theory and behavioral economics. Topics included economic decision-making, strategic interaction and market dynamics, consumer biases, market structures from oligopoly to monopoly, and government intervention through welfare and subsidies.
- **Liam Francis Gearon, Oxford: pedagogy, education, policy and technology.** A UNESCO education expert whose work spans education, philosophy and religion. The course compared Asian and Western education systems and examined education's role in social mobility, educational inequality and the global spread of educational models.

## First morning: orientation

The next morning, students arrived at CRI's Seoul campus for day one. Some came in looking nervous and others visibly excited, but the room shared one mood. Everyone there had come ready to learn.

![A banner reading "2025 Seoul Research Program, July 2025: Driven by Research, Defined by Growth" hanging above a lobby](/editorial/223953636848-08.jpg "The welcome banner for the second annual Seoul Research Program, July 2025")

Orientation opened with a clear message: this was more than a paper-writing camp. Students could expect intensive one-on-one feedback from their professors, deep work on a demanding topic, and real growth as researchers along the way.

> "Our goal is not just a good result, but real growth."
> — CRI's CEO, speaking at orientation

Students nodded along, but the questions on their minds weren't hard to guess. *How different will this be from the way I've studied until now? What will the professors tell us? Can I really write a research paper?* With those questions still open, the first classes of SRP 2025 began.

## Forty-five students, many different paths

The 2025 cohort brought together 45 students from around the world and from a wide range of backgrounds. Some attended boarding schools in the United States, and some flew in from long-established schools in the United Kingdom. Others studied at Korea's specialized and autonomous high schools, including science, gifted and foreign-language schools, and many came from international schools in Korea.

Their nationalities, schools and daily routines differed, but they had two things in common: they wanted to learn, and they weren't afraid to ask questions. The 45 were selected from a much larger pool of applicants, but the point was less the acceptance rate than who the seats were for: students who arrived prepared. They earned their places not just by being smart, but by showing the courage to push their own ideas and the humility to listen to others.

They had taken very different routes to get there. Now they sat in front of the same questions, each ready to find an answer in their own way.

## When the classroom doors closed

The doors shut, and a professor's first words quietly filled each room. The tone was serious from the start. Questions came fast, and students' notebooks filled with their thinking. In one classroom a dataset was up on screen for analysis; in others, international politics, brain science, algorithms and environmental finance sparked lively debate.

![A classroom door with signs reading "Prof. Brian Stoltz" and "Classroom 203"](/editorial/223953636848-10.jpg "Caltech professor Brian Stoltz's classroom at SRP 2025")

SRP is closer to thinking together than to sitting and listening. Students organize their own ideas first, and the professor pushes them to dig deeper. Every professor teaches differently, but they share one habit: they treat students not as pupils but as researchers. That changes the questions, the feedback and the expectations. Students may hesitate or get stuck, and that is exactly where learning deepens and research begins.

Only one class in, there was already a slightly different look in the students' eyes. A quiet intensity hung over every classroom, and new questions, ones that weren't there that morning, were appearing in their notes. This was not a lecture series. It was the start of writing a research paper together.

## Why this summer is different

There is no shortage of summer programs that promise a paper, an admissions boost or competition prep. SRP starts somewhere else: whom you work with, how deep you go, and how much you change in the process. A strong final paper matters. The thinking that produces it, the experience of real feedback and the depth of the questions matter more.

The program is designed less as a place to absorb knowledge than as a chance to experience what being a researcher is like. That is why the professors see students as junior colleagues to work through problems with, not as people to be lectured. In that kind of relationship, a question stops being an assignment and becomes a tool for understanding the world.

SRP 2025 had only just taken its first step, and the CRI team was eager to see which classes, ideas and conversations the coming days would bring. To see current faculty and research tracks, explore the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp).
author: CRI Editorial

title: KSEF, Korea's national science fair: tracks, judging, and the road to ISEF
excerpt: How the Korea Science and Engineering Fair works, from its two tracks and 15-minute poster judging to required documents, and why only domestic-track winners can advance to ISEF.
content:
Nobody sits an exam at the Korea Science and Engineering Fair (KSEF). Students design their own research project, stand beside their poster, and defend it to a rotating panel of judges. For high school students the stakes run higher still: top finishers at the domestic fair can go on to represent Korea at Regeneron ISEF, the world's largest science fair for pre-college students, and at other international competitions. One rule matters most to ISEF hopefuls: KSEF runs two tracks, and only the domestic one leads there.

## What KSEF is

KSEF is Korea's official science project fair, organized by KSS, a Korean science and technology support body. Entrants pick a problem, investigate it through experiments, surveys, or data analysis, and summarize the results on a poster or slides that they present to judges.

Instead of testing memorized knowledge, the judges assess creativity, logical reasoning, and how rigorously the inquiry was carried out. Strong finishers in the high school division can qualify for international competitions.

## Two tracks: KSEF and KSEF International

KSEF runs two tracks to fit students' language and school backgrounds. The domestic fair, usually just called KSEF, is conducted in Korean. KSEF International serves students from English-speaking and international-school backgrounds, and everything, from the submitted materials to the on-site judging, happens in English.

| | KSEF (domestic) | KSEF International |
|---|---|---|
| Language | Korean (the paper may be in Korean or English) | English throughout, judged by English-speaking experts |
| Who can enter | Korean nationals, Grades 5–12 | Any nationality, Grades 5–12 |
| Entry | Individual or team of up to three | Individual or team of up to three, from any mix of schools or countries |
| Route to ISEF and other international fairs | Yes, for top finishers | No; the event itself runs as an international fair |

The same project can be entered in both tracks. Which one fits depends on your language strengths, where you live, and above all whether ISEF is the goal.

## Who can enter

**KSEF (domestic).** Any Korean national in Grades 5 through 12 may apply, including dual nationals who hold Korean citizenship; students without Korean citizenship cannot enter. The type of school does not matter. Students at regular, international, and alternative schools can all apply, as can students studying abroad, homeschoolers, candidates for Korea's high school equivalency exam, and students preparing for university entrance.

Entrants compete against their own age group:

- **Elementary division:** Grades 5–6
- **Middle school division:** Grades 7–9
- **High school division:** Grades 10–12

Students may enter alone or in teams of up to three. Teammates can come from different schools and grades, but a team's division is set by its highest grade, so a middle schooler paired with a high schooler competes in the high school division. The rules also place no limit on how many projects an individual or team may enter, and projects already entered in other domestic fairs, KSEF International included, are eligible.

**KSEF International.** Students of any nationality in Grades 5–12 can enter, whether they attend an overseas or international school, study abroad, learn at home, or are preparing for an equivalency exam. Teams of up to three may span schools and countries.

## How judging works

The fair has two rounds:

1. **Document review.** Judges evaluate each project remotely from its research summary, research plan, and supporting materials, weighing creativity, feasibility, and scientific soundness. They look at the whole submission, not the abstract alone, to decide who advances.
2. **Final judging.** Finalists present in person and take questions from the judges.

The domestic finals are held in Cheongju, North Chungcheong Province, where students set up their own posters and present on site. KSEF International finalists also present in person with a poster, giving both the talk and the Q&A in English. In both tracks, each judging session at the poster lasts 15 minutes: a seven-minute presentation followed by about eight minutes of Q&A.
