Several judges rotate through, each probing from a different angle, so no single evaluator decides the outcome.

That format rewards real understanding. You give the same talk several times, but every judge asks different questions, which shows how well you know your research and how quickly you think on your feet.

Domestic finalists receive a presentation slot and project ID after the document review, and slots are fixed by category and cannot be changed. At KSEF International, judging times vary by category, so students entered in both tracks should check early for clashes. Dates change every year; the official KSEF website (ksef.or.kr) carries the current schedule.

## What to submit

For the 22nd KSEF and the 6th KSEF International, the required materials were:

| KSEF (domestic) | KSEF International |
|---|---|
| Institutional recommendation letter | Not required |
| Personal-information consent form and pledge | Personal-information consent form and pledge |
| Research paper, up to 10 pages, in Korean or English | Research paper, up to 10 pages, in English |
| Research abstract, submitted online, in Korean | Research abstract, submitted online, in English |
| Not required | Personal or team photo |
| Not required | Self-introduction or country-introduction video, 30 seconds or less |
| Proof of registration payment | Proof of registration payment |

The details matter:

- **Paper.** Stay within 10 pages and cover the background, purpose, methods, results, and conclusion.
- **Abstract.** The domestic abstract must be in Korean (English is not accepted) and no longer than 800 characters. The International abstract must be in English and within 3,000 characters. Cover your motivation, methods, key results, conclusions, and next steps. Photos, charts, and graphs are not allowed.
- **Consent form and pledge.** Every participant completes one, and students under 14 need a parent's or guardian's signature.
- **Payment proof.** Submit the transfer receipt as a JPG or PNG file.
- **Poster.** Domestic posters measure 900 mm × 1,200 mm and are written in Korean. International entrants may use a three-panel board (left, center, and right) in English. Students install their own posters, though domestic entrants who send a PDF and a printing fee by the deadline can have the organizers print and install it.
- **International extras.** A high-resolution 3:4 passport-style photo taken within the past six months (JPG); for teams, a 16:9 group photo of every member (JPG); and a video of up to 30 seconds introducing yourself or your country (MP4 or similar, up to 100 MB).

## Not just a science fair

The name leads many families to assume KSEF is only for lab scientists. In fact it spans engineering, the social sciences, the humanities, and design, grouped into three areas: natural science (say, a particle physics experiment or a cell culture study), applied science (an autonomous-driving algorithm or a new biosensor), and convergence science, which covers interdisciplinary work such as AI-assisted mental health diagnosis, sustainable architectural design, or UX design that supports socially vulnerable groups.

For the 22nd KSEF and the 6th KSEF International, the categories were:

| Area | Category (code) | Subfields |
|---|---|---|
| Natural science | Physics (PHY) | Dynamics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, optics, particle physics, nuclear physics |
| | Chemistry (CHE) | Physical, organic, inorganic, and analytical chemistry; biochemistry |
| | Biology (BIO) | Molecular biology, animal sciences, plant science, genetics, ecology |
| | Earth science (EAR) | Astronomy, atmospheric science, oceanography, geology |
| Applied science | Engineering (ENG) | Mechanical, chemical, materials, and electrical engineering; energy |
| | Mathematics (MAT) | Discrete mathematics, algebra, geometry and topology, analysis, statistics |
| | Computer science (COM) | Algorithms, cognitive science, software, data analysis, robotics, artificial intelligence |
| | Applied biological science (APB) | Agriculture, food engineering, medicine, pharmacy |
| Convergence science | Social science (SOC) | Psychology, neuroscience, sociology, economics, anthropology |
| | Environmental science (ENV) | Pollution control, waste management, resource management, civil engineering, architecture, urban engineering |
| | Humanities and cultural arts (HUM) | Linguistics, historiography, philosophy, ethics, political science, arts |
| | Invention and design (INV) | Invention, service design, UI/UX |

In convergence science especially, projects that show social value or creative problem solving are rated highly. Students whose strengths lie in the humanities and social sciences can present a project that plays to those strengths.

## From KSEF to ISEF

Strong results at the domestic fair can earn a place representing Korea at Regeneron ISEF in the United States, the European Union Contest for Young Scientists (EUCYS), and other international fairs. KSEF doubles as Korea's national selection event: judges nominate some of the top-placing teams in each category for international competition, and the final national teams are then chosen through a follow-up camp or additional screening.

In 2025, the international fairs were:

| Competition | 2025 edition |
|---|---|
| Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF) | May, Ohio, USA |
| GENIUS Olympiad (GO) | June, New York, USA |
| International Greenwich Olympiad (IGO) | June, London, England |
| China Adolescents Science and Technology Innovation Contest (CASTIC) | August, China |
| European Union Contest for Young Scientists (EUCYS) | September, Latvia |
| MILSET Expo-Sciences International (ESI) | September, United Arab Emirates |
| Luxembourg International Science Expo (LISE) | November, Luxembourg |

These are demanding stages and a chance to engage directly with the global science community. ISEF, the largest, offers prizes and scholarships and can open doors in university admissions. Every one of these places goes to domestic KSEF winners only; an award at KSEF International does not lead to any of them.

One CRI student shows how the route can work. Building on a paper whose framework took shape in the Seoul Research Program, the student refined the project with a dedicated competition mentor, a PhD student in the UK, then won a gold medal at KSEF and qualified to represent Korea at ISEF.

## How to stand out

KSEF does not judge the finished product alone. Judges weigh the authenticity of the whole inquiry, the logic behind it, and the originality of the problem solving.

- **Start from a question.** Explain why you wanted to know the answer in the first place.
- **Solve a problem, don't just run an experiment.** Topics that tackle a real social problem have an edge.
- **Rehearse the Q&A.** Judges can ask hard questions, so practice fielding them with friends and teachers.
- **Keep visuals lean.** A clear presentation of the key data and message beats a complicated graph.

News of that gold medal reinforced the point for CRI's team. Hard work alone does not win a medal at KSEF; the research and the way it is explained have to be designed together. On the same topic, how you frame the question, which data you use to answer it, and how you structure what you show can change the result entirely.

## Preparing for KSEF

Because KSEF assesses the whole process of inquiry, a short burst of effort aimed only at producing results is a weak plan. What helps is doing every step yourself: choosing a topic, designing the experiment, analyzing the data, writing the paper, and preparing the presentation.

> "I had no idea that writing a paper from start to finish would feel so different. After practicing the presentation too, competitions stopped feeling so vague."
> — Participant, 2024 CRI summer program

If KSEF is on your horizon, a summer of hands-on research is a good place to begin. In CRI's [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp), students work with faculty from universities such as MIT, Caltech, and Harvard, choose their own topic, carry out the research, and finish with a complete paper.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Paper-writing guide, part 5: when and how to write the introduction and abstract
excerpt: Readers decide from your introduction and abstract whether the rest is worth reading. Learn the What-Why-How structure, the rules of a standalone abstract and why both come last.
content:
Open a research paper and the first two things you read are the abstract and the introduction. Those few paragraphs decide whether a reviewer stays interested and whether a reader moves on to the rest. Yet many researchers write them too late or too lightly, and students working on their first paper tend to stall on the same questions: What do I write first? Is the introduction just background?

![Cartoon of a student pointing at a long abstract, asking why it is so long, while one scientist says a passage belongs in the abstract, not the introduction, and another asks whether the two are the same](/editorial/223935715436-01.jpg "Abstract or introduction? Students often confuse the two, but each has its own job.")

This is Part 5 of CRI's seven-part paper-writing guide. After results and discussion in Part 4, it moves to the front of the paper: when to write the introduction and abstract, how to structure them and how to make them persuasive. Every example comes from one invented study about the ducks on the campus of KAIST (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology), so you can follow along even if you have never written a paper. The central lesson: even if you write them last, these sections are not an afterthought to squeeze in at the end; they need to be designed deliberately.

## What an introduction does

To you, the author, the results may look like the heart of the paper. To an editor, a reviewer or anyone meeting the paper for the first time, the introduction may be all that counts. It works like a trailer, answering three questions:

- Why does this topic matter?
- What is this paper trying to say?
- What has not been solved so far, and what does this paper solve?

If it cannot answer those clearly, readers will struggle to care about anything that follows.

An introduction is not a background section, a summary of earlier studies or a list of statistics. It raises a problem and argues for it, and it has exactly two jobs: convince the reader that the problem matters, and state clearly which question the paper sets out to answer. Do both, and readers decide the paper is worth their time. Reviewers, too, start reading with the right question in mind: why is this research meaningful?

## Structure it as What, Why and How, plus prior work

If you are unsure how to organize an introduction, build it around three questions and fold a review of prior work into the argument.

- **What does the paper address?** Not background, but the paper's central question, stated up front in a short, striking sentence. You want the reader to think, "Huh, that's interesting."
- **Why does it matter?** Answer "So why study this?" before anyone asks it, by stressing the question's academic significance, social impact or potential applications.
- **What is already known?** Show what earlier studies have established and what remains unknown. The point is how they differ from your work, not a catalog of them.
- **How did you do it?** Close with a brief summary of your method and main findings. The detail comes later, but this paragraph previews the whole paper and leads into the abstract, so hint at the conclusion without going too deep.

In practice, that makes three or four paragraphs:

| Paragraph | Its job | Duck-study example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What | The question the paper addresses | "We analyzed the pattern and causes of a daily behavior among ducks on the KAIST campus: crossing a road at set times." |
| Why | Why the topic matters | "Beyond the question of how ducks move, this topic can help us understand the ecology of birds in cities, and it bears directly on traffic safety on campus." |
| Prior work | How far earlier research has come | "Some studies have reported the periodicity of ducks swimming between ponds, but the correlation between the timing of their road crossings and external factors has not yet been studied." |
| How | How you answered the question | "Using GPS-based drone footage and algorithmic analysis, we found that the ducks' crossings are closely linked to the movements of nearby cats." |

## Five ways to make an introduction persuasive

A template alone won't win anyone over. What matters is how you write each part, always from the reader's side of the page.

**1. Keep the What short and strong.** Lead with your main topic and state it in one or two short, confident sentences, so the reader grasps at once what the paper sets out to do: *"Ducks on the KAIST campus cross the road every day, but the cause of this behavior is not yet known."*

**2. Treat the Why as persuasion.** Pair academic significance with social context, and leave a reviewer no room to wonder why the work needs doing: *"The ducks' road crossings are more than an ecological curiosity; they can be read as a textbook case of humans and animals sharing space."*

**3. Contrast prior work instead of listing it.** A roll call of who did what bores readers. Show where earlier research stops, then how your work fills the gap: *"The periodicity of ducks' swimming routes has been reported, but few studies have linked road crossings to external stimuli."*

**4. Don't overclaim.** "This is the world's first study!" sounds appealing, but it can put reviewers off, and it is especially risky for beginners whose literature search may have gaps. Take a step back and use measured language instead:

- *"To date, few experimental reports on this topic exist."*
- *"To our knowledge, this kind of pattern analysis has not been reported."*

**5. Spoon-feed your reader.** It's a point CRI makes often. Don't leave readers to work out for themselves why the study matters or why it is needed; tell them directly and simply. Reviewers are busy, and one may reject a paper on the introduction alone.

## How to write the abstract

The abstract is a reader's first contact with your paper and a self-contained summary of the whole. Many readers now scan search results and decide from the abstract alone whether to click through. So an abstract cannot be a mere summary; it has to be the opening that gets the paper read.

**It must stand alone.** An abstract has to make sense to someone who never reads the body, which brings three rules:

- Define abbreviations again, even if the body already defines them.
- Don't copy and paste text from the body.
- Don't cite references; the abstract must be understandable without them.

**Keep the structure lean.** Abstracts usually follow this sequence:

1. What did you study? (What)
2. How did you study it? (How)
3. What was the key result? (Result)
4. Optionally, why does the study matter? (Why)

Unlike the introduction, an abstract does not build the argument step by step; it carries only the essentials. For the duck study, it might read:

> We investigated the road-crossing behavior of campus ducks using GPS-equipped drones. We found that their movement patterns are strongly associated with the presence of nearby cats. This study provides insight into urban animal behavioral adaptations.

**Always rephrase.** The last paragraph of the introduction and the abstract cover similar ground, but they must never be worded alike. Change the rhythm, the vocabulary and the sentence structure. The abstract can be more concise and direct, with fewer transitions between sentences.

**Make it persuasive, too.** For many readers the abstract stands in for the entire paper. Rather than simply reporting that you did a study, it should convey why the work is interesting and why it matters, in sentences built to earn the click.

In short, the abstract is both a standalone piece of writing and the paper's advertising copy. Make it as concise and as persuasive as you can.

## Design them to be read, then write them last

The substance of a paper is its results and their interpretation, but what gets anyone to read that substance is the introduction and the abstract. The introduction should leave a reader thinking, "This looks interesting," or "This seems like an important problem." The abstract has to stand on its own and make the paper's core value obvious to someone skimming search results.

The order in which you write them matters as well. Many researchers start with the introduction and get stuck. In practice, the introduction is often written after everything else, and moving it to the end does not shrink its strategic role. In many cases it is only once the results and figures are in order that you can see how to make the case for your research. As the saying goes, when your figures are finished, you are finally ready to write the introduction.

Writing the introduction and abstract last can be the more efficient order, and it is the one this series follows: decide what you will say (Part 2), build the figures (Part 3), write the results and discussion (Part 4), then return to the front of the paper.

If you want to put this into practice on a paper of your own, the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) brings small groups of students together with visiting professors from US and UK universities to carry out real research and write it up in English. Part 6 of this guide turns to citations and reference management, and the full series is on the [CRI blog](/blog).

title: Bank of America Student Leaders: who can apply and what the paid internship involves
excerpt: A paid nonprofit internship plus a national leadership summit, open only to students who live and can work in the US. Here is how it works, what changed in 2026, and what successful applicants have in common.
content:
For two decades, about 300 American high school students a year spent their summer working full-time, for real wages, at nonprofits in their own communities. Then they flew to Washington, D.C., to meet leaders from government, business and the nonprofit world. That is Bank of America Student Leaders, and for students applying to US colleges it became one of the best-known examples of the leadership experience admissions officers notice.

Two things are worth knowing before you read further. The program is open only to students who live in the US and can work there legally, so students based in Korea cannot apply. And starting with its 2026 cycle, Bank of America rebuilt it for first-year college students instead of high schoolers.

## What the program is

Bank of America launched Student Leaders in 2004. In its high school format, the program chose roughly 300 juniors and seniors from across the country each year and gave them an eight-week paid summer internship, capped by a leadership summit in Washington, D.C. Interns worked at local nonprofits such as the YMCA, Boys & Girls Clubs and Habitat for Humanity. Over its first 20 years, the program supported more than 4,500 students, and Bank of America invested more than $42 million in it.

This is more than a corporate giving project. The program is built around three clear aims:

- **Financial independence.** A job with real wages is a first step toward standing on your own.
- **Community.** Working inside a local organization builds an understanding of the community and a habit of taking part in it.
- **A national view.** The summit widens students' perspective to the national level and deepens their understanding of social issues.

## Who can apply, and what changed in 2026

Under both the old and new rules, eligibility is tied to living and being able to work in the US. The main differences are summarized below.

| Rule | High school program (through 2025) | College program (from 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| Who | US high school juniors and seniors (Grades 11–12) | First-year college students: at least 18, high school diploma or equivalent within the past two years, and 12 to 18 college credit hours completed |
| Legal status | US citizen or permanent resident; F-1 visa holders not eligible | Legally authorized to work in the US without sponsorship |
| Where you live | A designated US city or county | An eligible program location |
| Internship | Eight weeks, full-time, over the summer (June to early August) | Six weeks, full-time (at least 35 hours a week), June to July |
| Summit (attendance required) | About a week in Washington, D.C., at the end of the summer | Three days in June, within the US |

The high school program also expected strong grades and a solid record of activities. In the college format, applicants submit a college transcript, an overview of their accomplishments and two recommendations, and anyone who was a Student Leader in high school cannot apply again.

The calendar has moved as well. The final high school cycle, for summer 2025, took applications from October to mid-January and announced decisions around April. For the first college cycle in 2026, applications ran from February to mid-March. Because details can change from year to year, check Bank of America's [official eligibility criteria](https://about.bankofamerica.com/en/making-an-impact/student-leader-eligibility-criteria) before planning around the program.

## Inside the internship

The internship is real work, not volunteering. Each Student Leader is placed with a nonprofit in the city or county where they actually live, and the organization is matched according to local needs and Bank of America's partnerships there. Beyond the YMCA and Boys & Girls Clubs, partners have included Feeding America, Junior Achievement and Special Olympics.

What interns do depends on the region and on the projects their organization is running:

- **New York and New Jersey:** planning programs for children and helping run a food bank
- **San Francisco:** designing financial-education workshops for young people
- **Los Angeles:** supporting immigrants and other community-service work
- **Boston:** creating content for donors and promotional videos for events

In 2024, for example, five Long Island students named Student Leaders spent their summer with two local nonprofits, EAC Network and Island Harvest.

## A week in Washington

In the high school format, once the eight weeks were over, every Student Leader in the country traveled to Washington, D.C., and spent a week there together. The program included:

- a visit to Congress
- panel discussions with leaders from government, nonprofits and business
- public speaking workshops
- a community service project
- visits to historic sites

Bank of America paid for flights, lodging and meals, and attending the summit was a condition of taking part. The college format keeps both rules but shortens the summit to three days.

## What it pays

| Item | Details |
|---|---|
| Cost to participate | None |
| Wage | $17 an hour or the local minimum wage, whichever is higher |
| Summit costs | Travel, lodging and meals covered by Bank of America |
| Financial education | Coaching through Better Money Habits, Bank of America's financial-education program |

Everyday living costs during the internship are the student's own responsibility. Even so, this is not an unpaid experience: participants earn a real wage and get training along the way.

## What participants take away

Former Student Leaders tend to point to the same things: real work experience, close friendships with other young leaders, and what they learned at the summit about policy and social issues. Many say the summer gave them strong material for college essays and interviews and helped them decide what to study and do next.

As they describe it, the work felt like making real change, not logging service hours; they still talk over career plans with friends they met at the summit; and the internship showed them they could accomplish more than they had expected. Many look back on it as a turning point.

## Who gets selected

In the high school years, thousands of students competed each year for roughly 300 places, which were allocated community by community. Two students with similar records could get different results depending on where they lived.

Successful applicants tend to share three traits:

- They have found a problem and worked to solve it themselves, rather than simply taking part in an activity.
- Their application shows, honestly and specifically, what they learned and how they changed.
- Their recommendations make a strong case for their potential as leaders.

## How to build a strong application

Student Leaders is not a line to add to a résumé. With so few places, what matters is showing your values and your potential as a leader in a way that rings true.

### Explain why, not just what

What you did matters less than why you did it and what you took from it. "I volunteered at a food bank" says little. Describing a problem you noticed in how the food bank ran, and what you did to help fix it, is far more persuasive. Show how the experience changed you, too. The strongest applications connect your motivation, what the work meant, how you grew, and why you want to attend the summit.

### Help your recommenders be specific

A recommendation is not just a letter of praise. It is a chance for someone to answer the question, "Could this student really lead?" The most useful letters describe, in concrete terms, how the teacher or mentor has seen you lead, work with others and solve problems. When you ask for one, hand over a short summary: "Here is what I have been doing, and these are the points I would be grateful if you could highlight." It makes a real difference to the finished letter.

### Go deep, not wide

The program weighs how deeply you led one activity more than how many activities you joined. A string of short volunteering stints is weaker than one project you ran yourself that changed something in your community. When you list your activities, explain the effect each one had on your community. Even a small change counts for a lot if you made it happen.

## Does it help with college admissions?

In its high school form, Student Leaders was regarded as one of the leadership experiences US admissions officers pay attention to. It was reputable, highly selective and centered on service to the community, which made it strong material across an application: the essay, the résumé and the interview. Top universities that prize community-mindedness and problem solving viewed it especially favorably, and many participants used the experience to settle on a major and a career path. In the college format, though, applicants have already finished high school, so the internship now comes after students apply to college, not before.

## The takeaway

If you live in the US, can work there legally and meet the current rules, Student Leaders can shape where you go next, so plan early and make sure your application shows real initiative and follow-through. For students in Korea, who can't apply, the lesson still holds: selective programs and colleges look for depth, initiative and an honest account of work you led yourself. A faculty-guided research project is one way to build that record, and the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) places students in small groups with visiting professors from US and UK universities, who guide them as they write their own paper.

title: Boys State and Girls State: how the civic leadership week works and who can apply
excerpt: Students run a mock state government for a week each summer. Here is how Boys State and Girls State work, what they cost, and why most students in Korea can't apply.
content:
Imagine running for governor while still in high school, or drafting a bill and steering it through a legislature made up of your peers. That is the premise of Boys State and Girls State, a one-week summer program in which American high school students build a mock state government from the ground up. It is a leadership tradition more than 80 years old, and it carries real weight with selective colleges that look for students who have led rather than simply joined.

Here is how it works, who can realistically take part, and how it compares with academic summer programs.

## What Boys State and Girls State are

Boys State and Girls State are civic education programs run by the American Legion, the US veterans' organization, and the American Legion Auxiliary. Each summer every state holds its own session (Hawaii holds only Girls State). Participants organize mock cities and a mock state government, then fill the roles that make them run: mayor, governor, state senator, reporter, attorney, judge. Everything happens in English, and the week is built around community and personal responsibility.

The program dates to 1935, when two American Legion members in Illinois organized the first Boys State in Springfield; Girls State followed in 1938. About 40,000 students now take part each year, and more than two million have attended since the program began.

The alumni list is long and varied. It includes a president (Bill Clinton), a vice president (Dick Cheney), the first person to walk on the moon (Neil Armstrong) and basketball great Michael Jordan, along with Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito, Apple CEO Tim Cook, news anchor Tom Brokaw, and a number of senators and governors, including Cory Booker and Chris Christie.

## Separate programs for boys and girls, mostly

Traditionally the two are separate. The American Legion runs Boys State and the Auxiliary runs Girls State; the content is similar, but the organizers differ. Some states hold them side by side: in Georgia, Nebraska, Oregon, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Maine, among others, Boys State and Girls State share a campus and a week while remaining distinct programs.

California now has two tracks:

- **California Boys & Girls State (American Legion).** The Legion's program, traditionally Boys State, has been co-ed since 2023, and about a third of its participants are female. Female delegates chosen here are not eligible for Boys Nation, the national-level program for boys.
- **ALA California Girls State (American Legion Auxiliary).** Still girls-only and run separately.

A girl may apply to only one of the two, not both.

## Who can apply

Rules vary by state, but applicants are generally:

- students who have completed 11th grade at a US high school
- officially nominated by their school
- US citizens or permanent residents, in most cases
- residents of the state, or students at a high school in that state

Because each program belongs to a single state, you cannot apply across state lines: a student who neither lives in Texas nor attends a Texas high school cannot apply to Texas Boys State or Girls State. Most states also limit eligibility to legal inhabitants of the United States, so **students at international schools in Korea generally cannot apply**.

The one realistic path is narrow. A Korean citizen enrolled at a US high school can apply if the school will nominate them. For international families, the program becomes an option only once a student is studying in the United States.

## How selection works

Nomination runs through schools, and in most states the calendar starts early:

1. **January–February: nomination.** A counselor, teacher, or the local Legion or Auxiliary chapter puts forward candidates from the junior class (next year's seniors), and the school sends its list to the local organization.
2. **February–March: interviews and review.** The local American Legion Post or Auxiliary Unit evaluates nominees on grades, leadership, activities and motivation. Some Girls State programs also ask for a personal essay or an oral presentation.
3. **March–May: results and registration.** Decisions usually arrive in March or April. Selected students then submit their registration paperwork (application form, medical consent, parental consent) online or by mail, typically by May.

Since each school can nominate only a few students, the time to talk with your counselor is before January.

## How competitive it is

Forty thousand participants a year makes the program sound big and open. In practice most high schools can nominate only one or two students, which means the competition begins inside your own school. Texas Boys State, for example, seats hundreds of delegates every year, but each high school can nominate only one, so the students preparing for those seats outnumber them several times over. Other states set similarly strict limits: Michigan allows one nominee per school, Ohio one or two.

## When and where it happens

Most sessions run between mid-June and early July, typically for seven days and six nights, Sunday to Saturday. Participants must arrive on campus by the day before the program begins, and most sessions are hosted by state universities. Here is how a few states scheduled 2025:

| State | Boys State (2025) | Girls State (2025) |
|---|---|---|
| California | California Boys & Girls State (co-ed), CSU Sacramento, June 21–28 | Co-ed program (CSU Sacramento, June 21–28), or the separate ALA California Girls State, June 14–19 |
| Texas | University of Texas at Austin, June 8–13 | Texas Lutheran University, June 15–21 |
| New York | SUNY Morrisville, June 28–July 3 | Same campus and dates |
| Florida | Florida State University, June 15–22 | Same campus and dates |
| Illinois | Eastern Illinois University, June 7–13 | Same campus and dates |

Dates and formats shift from state to state and year to year, so check your own state's program for details.

## What the week looks like

Students live in campus residence halls for the week. They form mock political parties, campaign and hold elections, introduce and pass bills, and run the legislature, the courts and other parts of state government. Some states add military-style morning formation, a student newsroom or organized debates. Along the way, students learn firsthand what independence and responsibility mean for citizens in a democracy. Girls State has traditionally put particular emphasis on women's leadership, along with community and teamwork.

> "I got to experience the democracy we learned about in school. We debated, wrote bills, and campaigned just like in a real election."
> — Girls State participant

> "Morning formation was like military drill, and activities ran from dawn until night. But when it was over, my self-esteem and sense of responsibility had clearly changed."
> — New York Boys State participant

Many alumni describe the week as a chance to take stock of themselves and discover who they are as leaders. One Boys State alumnus recalled arriving convinced the week would go badly and leaving having stepped out of his comfort zone by choice. What participants tend to remember most is working in teams with new friends and debating with people who see the world differently.

## Cost and scholarships

The program costs about $400 to $550 on average, but in most cases a local American Legion post covers the full amount. Students rarely pay anything beyond travel and pocket money, so for the student it is effectively free. Participants can also qualify for further scholarships, such as the Samsung American Legion Scholarship.

## Does it help with US college admissions?

Yes, clearly. In the United States, Boys State and Girls State have a reputation as leadership programs that selective colleges notice, and the experience often appears in the essays of applicants to universities such as Harvard, Stanford and Princeton. The US service academies, including the Naval Academy, the Air Force Academy and the Military Academy at West Point, regard it especially highly.

It is a different kind of experience from academically selective summers such as the humanities-focused Telluride Association Summer Seminar (TASS) or Yale Young Global Scholars (YYGS), which are valued for intellectual depth. Boys State and Girls State center on civic education and leadership, so the right choice depends on a student's temperament and goals.

## Worth it for the right student

Boys State and Girls State are more than a summer camp: students experience democracy by practicing it, working alongside peers and building leadership as they go. In admissions, what counts is not simply a "good activity" but an experience connected to your own interests, and for students drawn to civics and political leadership, this can be an exceptionally valuable summer.

For students in Korea who can't apply, or who want a summer built around academic inquiry rather than a civic simulation, CRI's [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) takes a different route: small groups work with visiting professors from US and UK universities to research and write their own paper in English.

title: Paper-writing guide, part 4: writing results and discussion that work
excerpt: Finish your figures first, then let the Results walk readers through every one. Learn how to build a Discussion that answers "So what?", pick the right tense and close with purpose.
content:
Every student who writes a paper reaches the same moment. The figures are drawn, the captions are written, and the question becomes: "Now what am I supposed to write?" The honest answer is that the real writing starts here, with a Results section that puts your figures into words and a Discussion that explains what they mean.

This is where many students stall. "Do I really have to describe all of this again in the text?" "What exactly goes in the Discussion?" This fourth part of CRI's seven-part paper-writing guide answers both: how to build the text around your figures, what each section is for and how to structure it, and the small details that separate a finished draft from a good one.

## Settle your figures before you write

Many students write a paper in the order it will be read: introduction, then methods, then results. The more efficient approach is to settle your figures first.

A paper, in the end, reports what you discovered and how you proved it, and your figures, which visualize the results, are the most direct and powerful evidence you have. That is why professors often tell students, "Once the figures are done, 80 percent of the paper is done." With the figures in place, you can see what data each one holds and what conclusions it supports. All that remains is to explain them. (Part 3 of this series covers how to design them.)

![A four-panel research figure labeled a to d, showing the same scores for five authors as a table, a color scale, a bar chart and a 3D surface plot](/editorial/223925907129-02.jpg "A multipanel figure. Every panel, from the table in (a) to the surface plot in (d), holds data the Results text has to walk readers through.")

Settling the figures first also gives the whole paper its logical structure. You start from your conclusion, choose the results that demonstrate it best and write the text to match. The two sections then split the work:

| | Results | Discussion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answers | What happened? | So what? Why does it matter? |
| Its job | Explain the data in your figures step by step, leaving nothing out | Logically interpret what those results mean |
| Covers | Numbers, trends, differences, experimental conditions, comparison with published data | Meaning, what the results add to earlier research, limitations, next steps |

## Results: put everything in the figures into words

The Results section is the core of the paper, and it runs on one principle: explain all the data in your figures, completely and logically.

**Describe every result, even the obvious ones.** Some numbers or graphs will seem too self-evident to mention. Mention them anyway. Whoever reads your paper is meeting your experiments for the first time, so never assume a figure speaks for itself:

- If a figure contains numbers, report them quantitatively in the text.
- If it contains a graph, spell out the trend or the size of the difference.
- Equations and experimental conditions belong in the text too, not only in the figure.

**Assume the reader knows nothing.** You have worked on these experiments for a long time, so the content feels obvious to you. Your reader may come from a completely different background, and "they'll know this much" is a dangerous assumption. Write as plainly as you can, move step by step so the explanation never jumps, and picture the questions a reader will ask so you can answer them first.

**Give each paragraph one message.** A Results section is a series of paragraphs, and each should carry a single experiment or a single idea. A typical sequence might run:

1. The purpose of the experiment and its key result
2. A summary of the method and the numbers it produced
3. The results of the control experiment
4. A comparison with published literature

Within each paragraph, lead with the point:

| Position | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| First sentence | States the summary or claim |
| Middle sentences | Give the explanation, evidence and numbers |
| Last sentence | Reinforces the point or bridges to the next paragraph |

**Explain it the way you would to your roommate.** The single best tip for this section is to imagine telling a friend about your results. You would say something like: "We ran an experiment. Here's how we did it. We got these values. They line up with earlier work, too. So here's what we can conclude." That sequence is the structure of a well-written Results section.

## Discussion: answer "So what?"

If the Results describe what happened, the Discussion explains why it matters and what it means. This is where you answer the question every reader eventually asks: "So why is this important?"

**Interpret, don't list.** A list of results does not make a paper. You need to explain, analytically and logically, what the results mean, why they are interesting and what they add to existing research. Sentences like these do that work:

- "The results shown in Figure 2 are consistent with existing theory X."
- "This result overcomes the limitation noted in previous literature [Ref]."
- "We show that the new analytical technique also applies meaningfully to Experiment B."

**Back every claim with evidence.** A Discussion is not a collection of impressions; it is a series of logical arguments. For each one, work in three steps: state the claim clearly in a single sentence, present the evidence behind it (experimental results, literature, numbers), then sum up what it means. Repeated claim by claim, this pattern is what gives the whole argument its force.

**One paragraph, one claim, one line of reasoning.** Paragraph structure matters here as much as in the Results. Keep each paragraph to a single claim and let the logic carry naturally into the next. A good paragraph moves through four beats: claim, evidence, interpretation, and then a conclusion or a limitation.

**Be confident without overstating.** You do need to explain why your results matter, but exaggeration and unsupported assertions cost you the reader's trust. Avoid phrases like "world first," and choose careful wording such as *suggest*, *indicate* and *may contribute to* over flat declarations. Don't retreat into a timid summary, either: say plainly in what context your finding is meaningful.

**End with a way forward.** The last paragraph of a Discussion usually sums up the study, acknowledges its limitations (sample size, analysis conditions, time and so on) and proposes follow-up research or the impact you expect. That sequence pulls the paper's message together and makes it persuasive; the final section below looks at each step in detail.

## Two ways to combine Results and Discussion

Once the figures are organized and the results interpreted, one task remains: deciding how to fit the two sections together. This is more than alternating result and interpretation. The arrangement is a strategic choice that shapes how the entire paper reads.

| | Interleaved | Separate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Order | Result A, Discussion A, Result B, Discussion B | All the results, then all the discussion |
| How it works | Each result is interpreted right after it is presented | Every experiment is presented first, and their meaning is analyzed together |
| Strengths and trade-offs | The most natural and common approach; it lowers the reader's cognitive load and keeps them engaged | With a strongly designed logical structure it can be even more persuasive, though readers can lose their bearings partway through |
| Best for | Results that stand largely on their own | Complex mechanisms, or papers where comparing experiments is central |

In an interleaved paper, you might describe a particular pattern in Figure 1 and explain right away why it matters, then confirm a new result in Figure 2 and move straight on to how it connects with earlier studies.

To choose between them, ask three questions:

- Are your results largely independent of one another? Interleaving usually works better.
- Are they steps toward proving a single, connected mechanism? Keeping the sections separate usually works better.
- Along which route does your argument reach its core claim more naturally? Let that flow make the final call.

## The details that decide quality

"I've written the results and the interpretation, but did I do it right?" It is one of the questions first-time authors ask most. In the Results and Discussion, quality often comes down to small details, and these are the ones students most often get wrong.

**Past tense or present?**

| What the sentence covers | Tense | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your own findings | Present | "These results suggest that…" |
| Details of specific experiments | Past | "We observed an increase in activity." |
| Previous literature | Past | "Smith et al. reported a similar trend." |
| Universal facts and formulas | Present | "ATP functions as an energy carrier." |

The logic is simple. Summaries and interpretations of your results are what the paper claims now, so they take the present tense. How you ran the experiments and what you observed happened in the past, so they take the past tense.

**Emphasize firmly, hedge politely.** A clear finding can be stressed, and stressed again, with phrases such as "consistently observed" or "robustly replicated." When the interpretation is uncertain or the sample is small, soften it: "may indicate," "potentially associated." The goal is language that earns trust without exaggerating.

**Match figures and text one to one.** Every piece of data in Figure 2 should be mentioned directly somewhere in the Results text, including the numbers, the conditions and the comparison groups. Use phrases such as "As shown in Figure 2…" to make the connection natural. The text is written around the figures, never the other way around.

## Three things your closing paragraph must do

After a long stretch of Results and Discussion, the final paragraph restates the paper's message and leaves a lasting impression. It can decide whether a reader remembers your paper as a good read or as a little vague. Make sure it does these three things.

**1. Summarize clearly what the study found.** In one or two sentences, restate the paper's core contribution in a confident, conclusive tone:

- "The main finding of this study is…"
- "We show that mechanism XX operates under condition YY."
- "These results differ from previous study ZZ in the following ways."

**2. Name the limitations instead of hiding them.** Acknowledging limits shows scholarly humility, and it naturally sets up why follow-up work is needed and where it should go:

- "Because this study was conducted only under condition A, caution is needed in generalizing the findings to situation B."
- "Variable C was not analyzed directly, which calls for further research."

**3. Propose the next question.** Point to where the work could go from here:

- "Future work could extend experiment X to a wider range of conditions."
- "Building on these results, applications to disease Y could be explored."
- "Longer-term effects and the underlying molecular mechanism remain to be investigated."

That last step is more than a sign-off. It tells the reader that the research is not an ending but a beginning.

A paper is, above all, writing meant to persuade, and the Results and Discussion are its heart: the place where you show what data you obtained and why it is meaningful and new. Put these strategies to work, and you will write something that fits the structure and purpose of a paper instead of reading like a lab report.

## The paper-writing guide series

1. Why write a research paper at all?
2. Decide what you'll say before you decide how to start
3. Figures are the face of your paper
4. Writing results and discussion that work (this part)
5. When and how to write the introduction and abstract
6. Finding, citing and managing your sources
7. Proofreading, the final design step

You can find every part on the [CRI blog](/blog). Next comes part 5, on the introduction and abstract.

Students in CRI's [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1) go through this process with a faculty mentor over several months: settling the figures, drafting the Results and Discussion in English and revising until the manuscript is ready for journal submission.

title: Paper-writing guide, part 3: figures are the face of your paper
excerpt: Editors and reviewers look at your figures before they read your text. Learn how to plan figures early, choose the right formats and tools, and design them for clarity.
content:
When you open a research paper, where do your eyes go first? Most readers skim the title and abstract, then jump straight to the figures, and editors and reviewers are no different. If the figures don't stand out, or look cluttered or clumsy, the paper can be rejected on the spot, before anyone properly reads the text.

That is why figures are the face of a paper. A single figure tells a reader how reliable the experiments are and how carefully the work was organized. This third part of CRI's seven-part paper-writing guide covers how researchers plan figures, which formats and tools they use, and the design principles that make a figure easy to understand.

## Why figures carry so much weight

In the natural sciences especially, the figures that visualize your results shape the first impression. A clean figure with an obvious main point says, "This study is well organized. It's worth reading." A messy one invites a reviewer to wonder how careful the experiments were, or to decide there is plenty of data but no clear message. One figure can color the verdict on the whole paper.

A figure is also more than a container for results. It is part of your argument, the place where you make your case visually. Good figures make a paper persuasive, and they are what get the text read.

## Plan your figures before you write

Figures are not supporting material you sketch at the last minute. They are closer to a blueprint for the whole paper.

When researchers start preparing a manuscript, the first thing they typically do is open PowerPoint and create a file called `Figure_v1`. Each figure gets its own slide. They drop in the key data and ask, "How should we show this?" Nothing has to be perfect yet; the point is to decide what role each figure will play in the overall story.

The slides then go to coauthors for feedback, and each revision is saved as a new version (`Figure_v2`, `Figure_v3`). This is where the real editorial calls get made: "We can drop this experiment," or "Let's shrink this into an inset."

The method works because the paper's structure forms around the figures. You learn which results are central and what needs emphasis, so by the time you start writing, the message of each section is already clear.

## Submission figures and publication figures are different

The format and resolution a journal expects at first submission are very different from what it asks for after acceptance.

**At initial submission**, keep it simple:

- Images embedded in your Word file are enough.
- High resolution isn't needed; figures just have to be easy to view in Word or PDF.
- Place each caption alongside its figure.
- JPEG, PNG, EMF or PDF files are all fine.

The goal is a tidy layout that lets editors and reviewers grasp the content quickly. There is no need to produce TIFF or AI files yet.

**After acceptance**, you resubmit your figures as high-resolution files that meet the journal's requirements. Journals commonly ask for these formats:

| Format | What it is used for |
| --- | --- |
| TIFF | The most common publication format, for photos and line art alike |
| AI / PDF | Vector-based, so text and lines never break up (typically made in Illustrator) |
| EPS / SVG | Line art and sketches; science journals sometimes require them |

Recommended resolution depends on the type of figure:

| Figure type | Resolution |
| --- | --- |
| Photo | 300 dpi |
| Mixed image | 600 dpi |
| Line art | 1,000 dpi |

Color mode matters too: **RGB** for online display, **CMYK** for print. In short, prepare each figure only to the standard its stage requires.

## Use vector formats wherever you can

File format is the single biggest technical factor in figure quality. The same data can make a very different impression depending on how it is saved.

| | Bitmap | Vector |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stored as | Pixels | Lines, shapes and text defined by mathematical coordinates |
| When resized | Blurs when enlarged; text smears when shrunk | Stays sharp at any size |
| Strengths | Quick and easy to produce | Line weight, font size and color stay editable; suited to publication |
| Common formats | JPG, PNG, BMP | PDF, AI, EMF, SVG |
| Best for | Photos and quick, temporary visuals | Graphs, schematics, data labels |
| Final submission | Not recommended | Recommended |

The figures that explain your core findings, such as Figures 1 to 3, should always be prepared as vectors.

## A practical workflow: MATLAB, PowerPoint, Photoshop

Many people assume figures must be drawn in professional software such as Adobe Illustrator. In practice, PowerPoint and Photoshop are enough for most high-quality figures, and PowerPoint is far more capable at planning and editing them than you might expect.

**1. Generate the graph.** Plot your raw data in MATLAB, GraphPad or a similar program. In MATLAB, copy the graph with **Copy as Vector**.

**2. Assemble in PowerPoint.** Paste the graph in, right-click and choose **Ungroup**, and every line, label and background becomes editable. Use **Align** and **Distribute** to tidy the layout, delete anything unnecessary, and add simple boxes or shapes to explain conditions or timelines between panels. This makes PowerPoint especially good for multipanel figures. Save the result as a PDF and it keeps its vector quality.

**3. Finish in Photoshop.** Copy the figure from PowerPoint or open the PDF, crop away excess margins, set the color mode (RGB or CMYK) and the dpi, and save as a TIFF, choosing to discard layers so the file meets journal requirements.

One caution: opening a vector file in Photoshop turns it into a bitmap. Keep your master figures as PDF or AI files, and convert to TIFF or other formats only when a journal asks for them. Throughout, remember that a paper figure has to be easy to read, not merely nice to look at. Crisp lines, legible fonts and a clear color scheme are what count.

## Design principles: the clearest figure is the strongest

A good figure is not the flashiest one. It is the one a viewer understands at once. Three principles get you most of the way there.

**Simplify.** Remove anything unrelated to the results, such as decorative backgrounds or unnecessary numbers. Too many overlapping lines or conditions weaken the message, and too many colors confuse it, so stick to three or four at most. Leave statistically insignificant conditions out of the figure; if they are needed, move them to the supplementary material.

**Clarify.** Always include scale bars and color bars. Give every label (axis names, units, conditions) the same font size and make it easy to see. Prefer plain wording to jargon: "Signal intensity (normalized)" can be clearer than "Relative fluorescence."

**Emphasize.** Give your key result the most space and put reference images or comparison samples in small insets. Set the condition you want to highlight apart with a darker color or thicker line; in a control-versus-treatment plot, draw the treatment line bolder and in a stronger color.

A few finishing details make a noticeable difference:

| Element | Tip |
| --- | --- |
| Font | Use one font and size throughout the paper; Arial and Helvetica are preferred |
| Alignment | Space all graph elements evenly and align them on a common axis |
| Layout | Keep every figure a consistent size, either square or landscape |
| Panel labels | Place lowercase labels, (a), (b), (c), consistently at the top left |

The aim is to make the reader understand, not simply to show them something.

## Build a collection of reference figures

One of the fastest ways to improve is to collect well-made figures and imitate them, the way writers copy out good sentences to sharpen their prose. When a figure in a strong paper catches your eye, capture it, save it to a PDF or a slide deck, and jot down what works: "the color combination stands out," "the inset placement is clean." As the collection grows, study:

- **Color:** background contrast, accent colors, how the colormap is built
- **Fonts and labels:** size, position, how units are written
- **Panel layout:** how panels a, b and c are arranged and separated
- **Emphasis:** how key conditions stand out through line weight or color
- **Information load:** how much a single figure tries to convey

Then practice. Borrow the structure of a figure you admire and apply it to your own data, or try several ways of visualizing the same result. Over time, you learn to build the story of a paper around its figures.

## Every figure shows how you work

Readers notice whether a figure is orderly before they weigh its data: a cluttered one suggests an overly complicated experimental design or a paper rushed out before the results were sorted, while a clean, precise one signals a study organized from the start and worth reading in full.

Good figures grow out of a few questions. How can I show this result most clearly? Can I make complex data persuasive at a glance? Will a reviewer understand it and move on? A figure is a researcher's language, and it says a great deal about how organized your work is, how logically you think and how seriously you take it.

If you want to put these habits to work on a paper of your own, the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) brings small groups of students together with visiting professors from US and UK universities to carry out real research and write it up in English. Part 4 of this series turns to writing the results and discussion.
