title: Paper-writing guide, part 2: decide what you'll say before you decide how to start
excerpt: Before you write a word, pin down the one sentence your paper argues. See how that core claim shapes your title, your figures and the order of your results.
content:
"I've finished all my experiments. So how do I actually start writing?" It's the most common worry among students writing their first paper. The data is all there, but the order and structure for laying it out are anything but clear. Plenty of students begin by writing up their experiments in the order they ran them, only to watch the logic fall apart halfway through and end up starting over.

Part 1 of CRI's seven-part paper-writing guide asked why researchers write papers at all. This second part is about structure, and its advice is simple: before you decide how to start, decide what you are going to say. Settle your conclusion first, and build everything else around it.

## A paper is a story, not a lab notebook

Scientific writing still needs a narrative. Think about explaining an idea to a friend. Some people lay it out clearly and make it interesting; others talk at length and leave you unsure what they meant. Papers work the same way. However important your research is, if it is hard to follow and dull to read, it won't hold anyone's attention.

A paper's job is to present your new finding so that others can grasp it easily and find it interesting. Structure is what makes that possible.

So you don't have to retrace the path you actually took: *we ran an experiment, it failed, and then something unexpected turned up.* Readers care less about the sequence of your lab work than about why you believe this result matters. Writing a paper starts with rebuilding its structure around the message you most want to deliver.

## Start with the conclusion

One secret of good paper writing is to pin down your conclusion before anything else. That doesn't mean the Conclusion section you write at the end. It means the core message of the whole paper: a one-sentence claim that answers the question, "So what did you discover that's new?"

Settle that sentence first and the paper hangs together far better. Research rarely goes as planned. Results can point somewhere you didn't expect, or a new insight can arrive midway. When that happens, don't cling to your original aims or the order you worked in. Rebuild the paper around the core claim.

Say experiment A failed but experiment B produced an interesting result. The paper doesn't need a long account of A's failure. Organize it around why B matters and which question it answered.

## Find your three keywords

Boiling a conclusion down to one sentence is harder than it sounds, especially when your experiments produced a range of results and you're not sure which should take center stage. A useful first step is to pick out the three most important keywords in the conclusion you want to argue.

One published optics paper summed up its conclusion like this:

> "We controlled optical near-fields by shaping the wavefront of incident light through random nanoparticle media."

Its three keywords are:

- **Controlled optical near-fields**
- **Wavefront shaping**
- **Random nanoparticles**

These three are the experiment's core concepts and the message that runs through the entire paper. Build the text around what each one means and how they connect, and the paper takes on a logical flow almost by itself. The same sentence also becomes the blueprint for the figures, the placement of the data and the interpretation. Everything in the paper is, in the end, material for making that one conclusion convincing.

## Let the title grow out of the conclusion

With the conclusion settled, turn to the title. Many people leave it for last, but in good papers the conclusion and the title fit together naturally.

The same three keywords can become your title. The trick is not to string them together as they are, but to turn them into a phrase that is interesting, catches the eye and gets straight to the point. The paper above was titled:

> "Subwavelength light focusing using random nanoparticles"

Here is how the keywords were reworked:

| In the core sentence | In the title |
| --- | --- |
| "optical near-fields" | Became "subwavelength light focusing" |
| "controlled" | Recast as the verb "using" |
| "random nanoparticles" | Kept as the key term, at the end of the title |

The meaning stays the same, but the phrasing is more intuitive and more likely to draw a reader in. A little reordering and rewording of your conclusion's keywords can give you a title that reads smoothly and makes an impact.

## Design your paper in figures

Most readers look at a paper's figures before its text. However well you write, if the figures are cluttered or their order feels awkward, the heart of the paper won't come across.

That is why many researchers draw their figures before they write a paragraph. They print out their results, spread them across the desk and ask which order would be most convincing.

Far more people read the abstract and then skim the figures from Figure 1 onward than read a paper from start to finish. Each figure therefore has to deliver its own message, and together the figures have to lead naturally to the conclusion. A typical plan:

- **Figure 1:** the background concept, the problem and the core setup of the experiment
- **Figure 2:** the first experimental result, supporting part of the core conclusion
- **Figure 3:** further results that settle the remaining questions and strengthen the claim

Every figure converges on the same sentence: your core conclusion. Fix the role and position of each figure in advance, and the introduction, results and discussion fall into place when you write. The text comes afterward.

## Experiment order is not paper order

Experiments never go entirely to plan. The first attempt fails; unexpected results pop up along the way. But a paper isn't a diary of everything you tried. It reconstructs your results to deliver one conclusion as persuasively as possible, so the question to ask is:

> "In what order should I show these results so readers accept my conclusion most easily?"

Suppose you ran experiments A, B and C in that order. If that sequence would leave readers asking, "Wait, why did they do this?", the paper doesn't have to follow it. B, then A, then C might work better:

| Order in the paper | Experiment | Its job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | B | Shows the core message most directly |
| Second | A | Supplies the background needed to understand B |
| Last | C | Answers doubts about the core claim |

Real research involves chance discoveries, failures and repetition, but a paper is an argument, and its results belong in the most efficient order. Reordering this way lets readers answer "So what's new here?" as quickly and clearly as possible.

As you plan the structure, ask:

- What role does this experiment play in the paper as a whole?
- Which experiment contributes most directly to the core claim?
- Which experiment gives readers the information they need first?
- Which experiment answers the questions or objections that might come up along the way?

Then arrange every figure and section to follow the flow of your argument. A paper is persuasive writing: it has to show why your finding matters and how you proved it, in the way readers will find most convincing.

## A worked example: how one published paper was built

If this still feels abstract, the quickest way in is to look at how a real paper was put together. The example below is reconstructed from the structure of the same published optics paper.

![Illustration of a woman holding a tablet beside a large screen showing a document titled Research Paper Example](/editorial/223920652349-05.jpg "Read in order, a published paper's figures reveal how its argument was designed.")

Put in the words of its title, the sentence at the heart of the paper reads:

> "We achieved subwavelength light focusing using wavefront shaping through random nanoparticle media."

The figures that support it appear in a somewhat different order from the one in which the experiments were done.

**Figure 1 presents the key concept.** A schematic of the whole experiment shows which physical principle brings the light to a focus and previews the paper's storyline. From the outset, readers can tell what the paper sets out to show and through which experiments.

**Figure 2 presents the results.** Its core data show how light converges after passing through the random nanoparticle structure, pairing actual experimental images with an intensity graph. It proves the "focusing achieved" part of the core sentence, and showing that result early gives the argument a strong start.

**Figure 3 fills in the supporting evidence.** Verification experiments take on the questions the main result might raise, such as "Is this effect statistically reproducible, or just a fluke?" Control conditions, repeated measurements and noise comparisons address likely objections before readers can raise them, which makes the argument more convincing.

The figures and the flow were redesigned around the message the paper set out to argue, not the order of the experiments. Someone seeing it for the first time should be able to look at Figures 1 to 3 and think, "I see what this paper is saying." That is what good structure looks like.

## What to remember

Writing a paper means persuading readers of one message, so its structure should grow from your conclusion, not from the order of your experiments.

1. **A paper is a story.** It isn't finished until readers can understand it.
2. **Decide your conclusion first.** Design the structure around a single central sentence.
3. **Pull out your keywords.** They steer the flow of the text, the title and even the figures.
4. **Build the structure around figures.** Design the results visually first; the writing follows.
5. **Logical flow beats experimental order.** Rearrange your results in whatever order helps readers understand.

Papers get easier to write with experience, but practicing conclusion-first thinking from the start is a foundation every researcher needs. Right now, just making sense of your results may feel like plenty. This way of structuring a paper will still pay off whatever topic you take on next, because it teaches you to design a paper rather than merely write one.

## The paper-writing guide series

1. Why write a research paper at all?
2. Decide what you'll say before you decide how to start (this article)
3. Figures are the face of your paper
4. Writing results and discussion that work
5. When and how to write the introduction and abstract
6. Finding, citing and managing your sources
7. Proofreading, the final design step

Every part is on the [CRI blog](/blog). Part 3 picks up from here with how to plan and build your figures.

If you'd like to try conclusion-first design on a paper of your own, the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) brings small groups of students together with visiting professors from US and UK universities to carry out real research and write it up in English.
author: CRI Editorial

title: Paper-writing guide, part 1: why write a research paper at all?
excerpt: Before your first paper, learn why scientists publish, how journals replaced letters, how peer review works, what each section of a paper does and which article type suits you.
content:
Most students writing their first research paper hit the same wall. The results are in, one way or another, but turning them into a paper raises questions no one has answered yet. Where do I start? What belongs in it? What shape should it take?

This first part of CRI's seven-part paper-writing guide steps back to a more basic question: why papers exist at all. It traces how journals grew out of letters between scientists, how peer review and editors decide what gets published, and what each section of a paper is for. Writing a first paper is not just a matter of good prose. It also means deciding how to put what you found on the record for everyone else.

## Why write a paper?

A paper is more than something to hand in for a college application or an evaluation. The deeper reason to write one is to spread scientific knowledge. A new result does not travel on its own. However meaningful an experiment is, if it never appears in a paper, no one else can learn from it, and the research community never gets to share it.

A paper also matters for a researcher's career. Publishing strong results in a good journal shows that the work has been judged fairly by a community of experts. For graduate students, researchers and professors, papers are an official record of achievement and often decide which opportunities come next.

The most important reason, though, is that science runs on sharing. One person discovers something, and others repeat the experiment, refine it, challenge it or extend it. Science is never the work of one person, and the paper is the tool that keeps that exchange going.

## From letters to journals

The research paper as we know it has not always existed. Before the 17th century, a scientist had two main ways to share findings:

- **Write a book.** After years on one subject, a scholar gathered it all into a single volume. Printing was slow and costly, so producing and circulating a book took enormous time and resources, and new knowledge reached the public only after a long delay.
- **Write a letter.** The alternative was to send findings to a trusted colleague. Isaac Newton, for one, wrote to friends about the books he was reading and the ideas they sparked.

Letters had obvious limits. Only a few people could take part, so knowledge stayed locked inside small circles. And because nothing was checked in public, plenty of wrong information circulated as well.

The scientific journal emerged to fix these problems. In the mid-to-late 1600s, formal publications for recording and sharing knowledge began to appear, led by England and France. In France, journals centered on religion and law came first. In England, the Royal Society of London launched *Philosophical Transactions* in 1665, the world's first scientific journal.

From then on, scientists shared their work through journals instead of letters, and with journals came the tradition of peer review, in which other experts examine and evaluate a study. Knowledge now spread in the open, where anyone could read it and anyone could check it.

## How scientific publishing grew

Those first journals were more than a new format. They laid the groundwork for making science public knowledge, and academic publishing has been the main way researchers communicate ever since.

### Nature, Science and the top tier

The best-known journals today are *Nature*, based in the UK, and *Science*, in the US. They carry some of the most influential papers in the world, and a single paper in either can change a researcher's career. Very few papers get in: review is demanding, and publication can take several months to more than a year. That selectivity is why these journals have become a symbol of trust, a home for thoroughly vetted results.

### Open access

Traditional journals mostly run on paid subscriptions, so reading a paper means buying it or having an institutional license, which critics say keeps knowledge locked inside certain institutions. The open access movement grew out of that concern, and its core idea is simple: science should belong to everyone.

The best-known open access journals are the PLOS (Public Library of Science) series. Authors pay a fee to publish, and in return anyone in the world can read and download the paper for free. More and more researchers now treat open access publishing as a natural choice.

### Measuring a journal's influence

With so many journals, it can be hard to tell which ones matter most. The standard yardstick is the **Impact Factor**: how often, on average, the papers a journal published over the previous two years have been cited. The higher the number, the more widely the journal is read and cited.

A high Impact Factor is no promise that every paper in the journal is excellent, and attention is increasingly shifting from the journal to the individual researcher or paper. Measures such as the **h-index** capture both how much an author has published and how often that work is cited.

## Peer review: how papers are judged

A published paper has been tested by other experts before it reaches the world, which makes it a product of shared scrutiny rather than one person's writing. The system behind that scrutiny is peer review, and a typical paper passes through six steps:

1. **Writing.** The researcher writes up the experimental results or theoretical analysis.
2. **Choosing a journal.** The author picks a journal that fits the topic and the level of the work, and submits to that journal only. Sending the same paper to several journals at once breaches research ethics.
3. **The editor's first screening.** The editor checks the basics: Is the format right? Does the topic fit the journal? Quite a few papers are rejected here.
4. **Assigning reviewers.** Two or three experts in the field are chosen to read and evaluate the paper, usually anonymously.
5. **The decision.** The editor weighs the reviewers' opinions and chooses an outcome:
   - **Accept:** published without changes
   - **Minor or major revision:** revised, then reviewed again
   - **Reject:** not published
6. **Revision and resubmission.** If changes are requested, the author revises the paper in response to the reviewers' feedback and resubmits it. Most papers go through one or two rounds of revision before the final decision.

Published results become a foundation for the whole scientific community, so something has to stop careless or unverified claims from spreading. That is peer review's job. Reviewers ask:

- Does the logic have any flaws?
- Does the experimental design hold up?
- How does the work connect to earlier research?
- Is anything overstated or misinterpreted?

Review is usually blind, so that reviewers can judge the work on its merits without personal feelings or conflicts of interest getting in the way. Some journals use other models. In double-blind review, authors and reviewers are hidden from each other; in open review, both sides are named.

All of this means that getting a single paper into print takes far more collaboration and verification than the writing alone.

## Who are the editors?

Once you submit, the first person to read and judge your paper is the journal's editor. Editors do far more than administration: they decide which reviewers see which papers, and whether a paper is published at all. They come in two main kinds.

**Academic editors** are professors and active researchers who edit alongside their own work. Their expertise runs deep and they know the latest trends. But editing is not their main job, so they may be short of time for it, and critics note that their choice of reviewers can lean toward their own networks and interests.

**Professional editors** work full time at journals such as *Nature*, *Cell* and *Science*. Most hold a PhD in a related field, and their job is to evaluate and edit papers rather than to do research. The model has three advantages:

- they focus only on editing, so decisions come faster and more consistently
- they maintain well-organized networks of reviewers
- they are relatively free of conflicts of interest with authors and reviewers

In practice, many journals mix the two: academic editors handle papers in particular fields while a full-time staff runs the core of the journal.

Because the editor is your paper's first gate, build the paper with the editor's view in mind: a clear cover letter, sentences that sum up your work, and a topic stated plainly from the start.

## The parts of a paper, from title to references

A paper is not just a record of what you did. It follows a format shared by scientists around the world, a kind of official language of research. Each part has a set purpose, and once you understand the structure, papers become much easier to read and to write.

| Section | What it does |
|---|---|
| Title | Sums up the topic briefly and clearly. Searches and citations start here, so it should carry the key terms. |
| Authors and affiliations | Lists the people who did the research and their institutions. The first author is the one who led the research and writing; the last author is often the head of the lab, the principal investigator (PI). |
| Abstract | Summarizes the whole paper, usually in 150 to 250 words. Most journals make it free to read, so the key points must come through. |
| Introduction | Explains why the study was done, briefly covers background and earlier research, and states the aim. |
| Materials and methods | Describes exactly how the experiments or analyses were carried out, in enough detail for another researcher to repeat them. |
| Results and discussion | Presents the findings with graphs and tables and interprets them, comparing them with earlier studies and with what was expected. Some journals split this into two sections. |
| Conclusion | Briefly sums up the results, their significance, limitations and future directions, and restates the message you want readers to remember. |
| Acknowledgments | Thanks funders, people who helped with the work and contributors who are not authors. |
| Conflict of interest | Discloses any financial or personal interests that could affect the results, a key safeguard for credibility. |
| References | Lists every source cited, in the style the journal requires, such as APA, MLA or Nature style. |

![Diagram of an open journal with labels pointing to each part of a research paper, from the title, authors and abstract to the results, discussion and references](/editorial/223920478444-08.jpg "The main parts of a published research paper, labeled")

None of these sections is a formality. Together they form a blueprint that lets research be shared openly and followed by others, and on a first paper, simply sorting your thinking into this structure can make the flow of your writing much clearer.

## Types of papers: not every paper reports new data

Students new to research often ask, "Aren't all papers basically the same?" In fact, papers take several forms depending on their purpose, and for a high school or college student, choosing the one that fits the research is an important first decision.

### Review articles

A review article summarizes and organizes existing research instead of reporting new experimental results. It:

- maps out the research done on a topic so far
- analyzes each study's contributions and limitations, and the trends across them, to show where the field stands at a glance
- creates something meaningful from a broad literature search, without running experiments yourself
- makes good practice for a beginning researcher

Reviews come in several forms, including literature reviews, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and none of them is easy. A review demands strong synthesis, a sharp sense of what matters and a logical structure, and every source has to be checked for reliability.

### Original research articles

An original research article presents your own findings based on new data. It is what most people picture when they hear "research paper": you design the experiment, collect the data, analyze it and draw a new insight from the results. This category splits further by length and structure:

- **Article:** a long, detailed paper that covers the background, methods and interpretation of results in full. Some journals expect 5,000 words or more.
- **Letter:** a short, focused write-up of a high-impact finding, used when there is not much data but the result is worth sharing quickly. Letters are reviewed and published fast, and high-profile journals such as *Nature* and *Science* have long used short formats like this to present just the core of highly demanding research.

![Diagram titled Types of Research Articles, branching into boxes for original, review, short communications, book chapter, book review and conference materials](/editorial/223920478444-10.jpg "Original research and review articles are two of several forms of research writing")

Which should you choose? For a first paper, a review that analyzes the existing literature can be good practice. If you have experimental results, the next step is to analyze the data and shape it into a structured original research article. The right format helps you present your research more effectively and plan a submission strategy that suits the journal.

## A paper is where knowledge begins

Writing a paper means more than writing well. It teaches you how to give knowledge a structure, and it carries the responsibility of sharing your results with the world. A paper is the last stage of a research project, but it is also the door that lets that research become someone else's starting point.

It can look daunting at first, with an unfamiliar format and a publishing system that seems complicated. But once you understand what a paper is for, how it flows and what each part does, the feeling of being lost fades, and paper writing becomes something you can learn.

## The complete series

This is the first of seven parts in CRI's paper-writing guide:

1. Why write a research paper at all? (this part)
2. Decide what you'll say before you decide how to start
3. Figures are the face of your paper
4. Writing results and discussion that work
5. When and how to write the introduction and abstract
6. Finding, citing and managing your sources
7. Proofreading, the final design step

Every part is on the [CRI blog](/blog).

If you would like to try this with research of your own, the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) brings small groups of students together with visiting professors from US and UK universities to carry out a real research project and write it up as a paper in English.

title: How middle and high school students publish in the Journal of Emerging Investigators
excerpt: Who can submit to JEI, which kinds of hypothesis-driven studies it accepts, how its peer review works, and the avoidable mistakes that get manuscripts returned before review.
content:
Every year, after the science fairs around Boston wrapped up, Sarah Fankhauser watched the same thing happen: research that students had spent months preparing ended up in the trash. Fankhauser, then a graduate student at Harvard, began asking why that work couldn't be preserved and shared, and why middle and high school students had no real scientific journal of their own. Her answer was the Journal of Emerging Investigators (JEI), now the name that comes up most often when students talk about publishing research.

## A real journal, built for students

Fankhauser and fellow graduate students at Harvard Medical School founded JEI in 2011, starting from a simple conviction: publishing is how a scientist completes a piece of research. The journal's first paper appeared in 2012, and it has published hundreds since.

JEI works the way a professional journal does. Students write their papers in English, and working scientists, from PhD students to senior researchers, review them and send back detailed feedback. Along the way, a student does what scientists do: forms a hypothesis, carries out the study, and writes it up. Papers are published online and are open access, free for anyone to read. Authors pay a modest submission fee, and there is no separate publication charge.

| | JEI at a glance |
|---|---|
| Founded | 2011, by Harvard graduate students |
| Authors | Middle and high school students worldwide |
| Subjects | Hypothesis-driven research in biology, chemistry, physics, psychology, environmental science and more |
| Access | Online and open access |
| Review | Peer review by PhD students and more senior scientists |
| Record | Every article receives a DOI, so it can be cited in applications and portfolios |

## Who can submit

JEI is not reserved for students at specialized science high schools or international schools. A student at a regular high school who can think scientifically and design a sound study can take it on. That doesn't mean it takes just any paper. JEI judges each manuscript strictly on its structure and logic as a scientific paper, so preparation matters.

| Requirement | Details |
|---|---|
| Grade | US grades 6–12 (in Korea, roughly the first year of middle school through the final year of high school) |
| Nationality | No restriction; students in Korea can submit |
| Language | The paper must be written in English |
| Mentor | One adult mentor, such as a science teacher or university researcher, is required |

The mentor supervises the paper, and the journal confirms the mentor's role by email during review.

## What counts as JEI research

The core requirement for the research itself is that it must be **hypothesis-driven**. A paper needs a clear arc: a scientific question and hypothesis, a study designed to test it, data, analysis, and a conclusion that follows logically from the evidence. That does not have to mean a lab experiment. Experiments are the classic route, but observational studies, analyses of existing data, and mathematical or simulation models all qualify, as long as they test a question rather than simply describe a topic.

| Type of study | Example |
|---|---|
| Experimental | How the wavelength of light affects plant growth |
| Observational | Correlating fine-dust (PM2.5) levels with respiratory disease across cities |
| Data analysis | Tracking climate-change trends with UN statistics |
| Mathematical or simulation | Building a model of infectious-disease spread; modeling wave motion |

What JEI will not publish:

- Literature summaries and reviews
- Reflective or opinion essays, such as an essay of personal reflections on fine-dust pollution
- Invention showcases and technology reviews
- Survey results that are simply compiled, with no question being tested

Recent papers show how wide the range can be. JEI's newest articles in mid-2025 included a study of how the dyes cochineal and Allura Red AC affect the growth of *E. coli* and *Bacillus coagulans*, predictive modeling of cardiovascular disease from exercise-based electrocardiography, reinforcement learning in a 2-D space with varying gravitational fields, and an analysis of what drives coffee ratings. Before settling on a topic, browse the archive of published papers on JEI's website and look for studies similar to the one you have in mind.

## From submission to publication

Manuscripts go in through JEI's online platform:

1. Create an account on the JEI website.
2. Name the mentor and enter the co-authors' details.
3. Upload the manuscript in JEI's required format.
4. Pay the submission fee.
5. The paper then moves through preliminary screening and peer review, usually with one or two rounds of requested revisions, before it is accepted.

Plan for the long haul. The process takes six to ten months on average, and lengthy revisions can push it past a year.

## Start from the template

JEI requires a strict manuscript template, and a paper in the wrong format can be sent back before it ever reaches reviewers. Write in the template from the first draft rather than reformatting at the end. Its core sections are:

- Title
- Summary (JEI's term for the abstract)
- Introduction
- Results
- Discussion
- Materials and methods
- References

## Mistakes that stop a paper before review

A handful of avoidable errors can get a manuscript returned without a review at all:

- Figures or tables missing captions or units
- Citation errors
- A missing mentor email address
- Too many grammatical errors

All four are easy to prevent with careful preparation from the start.

## The process is the point

In college admissions, the finished paper is only part of the story. What carries weight is what a student goes through to produce it:

- The full arc from hypothesis and study design to data analysis, writing, revising in response to reviewers, and publication
- Firsthand evidence of critical thinking, scientific communication, and intellectual maturity
- A concrete story to tell convincingly in essays and interviews

Universities such as MIT and Stanford use their application essays to learn what a student has explored in depth, and a JEI paper gives a student a direct, specific way to show exactly that.

## Preparing a JEI paper from Korea

JEI is based in the US, but it is well within reach for students in Korea. The number of Korean students publishing in JEI has grown noticeably in recent years, and students at regular high schools, not only Korea's specialized science and foreign-language high schools, are now taking it on as well.

Plan early for the mentor requirement, because JEI will not consider a paper without one. Whether a teacher or a scientist, the mentor guides the research, is entered in the submission system alongside the manuscript, and serves as a key point of contact during peer review. Students in Korea usually find one in three ways:

- **A teacher at school**, such as the teacher of a lab science class or a gifted-education program
- **An outside research program**, such as a university-linked program during school vacations or a research camp
- **An organization that specializes in research education**, such as CRI, which matches students with mentors experienced in supervising papers

## More than a credential

Many students whose research once ended at a science fair are turning it into a formal paper through JEI and gaining real confidence in the process. In Korea, too, the question is shifting from whether a student has a paper to how it was produced, who reviewed it, and where it appeared. By that standard, JEI is a trustworthy peer-reviewed journal, a potentially strong academic signal in admissions, and a realistic goal for students in Korea.

What most students need next is a clear direction and a mentor to work beside them. In CRI's [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp), students work in small groups with visiting professors from US and UK universities, write their own manuscripts in English, and are supported all the way through journal submission.
